Activation falls mostly on sentence boundaries and transitions between plot beats (periods, commas, "The", "As", "Ultimately", character names) and on words marking story progression or the climax and ending ("climax of the movie", "at the end", "finally free").

Words that open or form part of the title of an academic publication venue, especially "Proceedings (of the)", "Proc.", "Transactions of the", "Bulletin of the" and journal or conference names. These appear in citations and bibliographic metadata. The strongest activations are on "Proceedings" and "Proc." and on the following "of the". There is weaker activation on other venue words such as Publications, Report, Review, Rev and Ann, and on phrases like "presented at".

Abstract, uncountable nouns naming a quality, property, dimension or concept (mass, speed, trust, humidity, size, breadth/depth, efficiency, flavor), usually bare with no article and acting as a general category. They often appear in coordinated pairs ('X and Y', 'function for form-factor') or as the subject of a generic statement ('Trust is…', 'space is…'). The adjacent 'and', comma or 'is' is also marked.

A diffuse, weakly-firing feature on ordinary mid-sentence tokens, mostly function words and verb-phrase pieces that continue a clause. It favors infinitive or modal-style predicates such as "able to act", "allows them to", "enough to", "must", "could" and "would", plus their objects or complements. It fires most strongly on an incongruous inserted phrase ("drive on" in spam text).

A diffuse, weak feature that fires on tokens naming quantities or values, mostly in math and code: variables and arguments in formulas (z^2, n, the index in a_{n+2}, L(x)), numeric literals, and struct fields or parameters (date->year, data.Length). It also fires faintly on measurable nouns in prose (density, tablets, tones) and on scattered word fragments.

The word "optional" and its variants (Optional, optionally, 可选), which mark something as not required. It fires strongly in documentation, code and parameter lists, and on parenthetical "(Optional)" labels. Related words for non-mandatory choice, such as "voluntary", "elective" and "facultative", activate it weakly.

Code block openers: tokens that end a function/loop/conditional header and begin its body, e.g. a colon plus newline in Python, an opening brace plus newline in C-like languages, or a closing parenthesis, along with the indentation and first statement (often print) that follow. Activation is strongest right at the start of a new indented block. Activations on ordinary prose tokens are weak and sporadic.

Tokens inside fixed multi-word expressions (idioms, collocations, set phrases) where the next word is highly predictable from the phrase, e.g. "each [other]", "taken [place]", "in other [words]", "at the same [time]", "remains to be [seen]", "needless to [say]", "choose [from]".

A weak, diffuse feature that fires on tokens inside formulaic multiword expressions and predictable collocations, such as idioms, set phrases and discourse fillers ("of course", "in turn", "took place", "so far", "pretty much", "for what it's worth", "in pretty bad shape", "as if there is one"). It also fires on conversational clause starters like "I know what", "that's just", "this is" and "they're", mostly in informal or narrative prose. It responds most strongly where the phrase continuation is highly predictable.

Words naming a recommended or desirable quality, behavior or manner, usually as the object or complement of advice, guidelines or prescriptive statements (e.g. treat with respect, be kind, write clean/maintainable code, stay active, remain vigilant, be properly cited). Often appears in imperative or "should/must" contexts describing good practice or virtuous conduct.

Nouns naming bodies of prior precedent, evidence or reference material, i.e. things cited or consulted as authority. These include case law and legal cases, literature, research, references, sources, publications and precedents. Activation is strongest for legal "case law" and "cases".

The word "side" as a token, along with its variants (sides, sided, siding, sideways, sidetrack, sideburns) and compounds such as side effects, side dish, side by side, side to side, and side-channel. It also fires on look-alikes and translations like "Sid", "aside", Norwegian "siden" and French "côté". Activation is strongest for literal physical or positional senses (surfaces of objects, lateral position) and for set compounds.

A diffuse, low-intensity feature spread across generic web prose, mostly technology, software and service-marketing or tutorial text about tools, providers, platforms and solutions. It fires weakly on scattered function words, punctuation and filler phrases rather than on any specific content word. Examples include "you need to", "the right tools for the right task", "possible" and "even".

Words and phrases expressing spatial location, proximity, or distance relative to a reference point (e.g., "away", "nearby", "down the block", "next to", "across from", "opposite side", "10 meters away"). Activation peaks on the final word of such proximity or distance expressions, especially "away" and "block".

A weak, diffuse feature of web blog/article prose (entertainment, sports, movies, opinion pieces), firing mostly at structural and discourse points: sentence ends and paragraph breaks, bylines, author names, photo credits, tags and timestamps, and transitional or reader-addressing phrases like "let's take a look back at", "Here's" and "Let us know".

Tokens in scientific or technical prose about chemical or physical transformations, such as reactions, compounds forming, materials changing state, minerals and their composition. Activation is strongest on words that describe a process or its products (e.g. "reaction", "formed", "fumes", "-shift", "to" in "turn to"/"to a liquid"), and on connecting words inside these process descriptions.

Mostly weak, diffuse activations on the predicate words right after a subject, e.g. passive verbs like named, termed, inserted and issued, and tokens like this, that and only. The strongest activations fall on meta-discursive phrases where the writer comments on their own statement or sets up a justification or explanation. Examples are 'Why am I pointing this out?', 'what makes me think', 'my theory is that', 'I'm just saying' and 'How is that useful?'. These are often followed by 'because' or an explanation.

Tokens forming bird names (swallows, hawks, woodpeckers, pigeons, owls, doves, loons, Taillow), usually word-piece fragments inside the name, plus broader wildlife and nature terms such as "Wildlife" in organization names, wetlands and ecology.

over.name: Fires within low-quality SEO-style web prose, especially article-spinner or machine-paraphrased text. The strongest activations land on awkward synonym substitutions and unnatural phrasing, such as 'in consequence', 'along with your moniker', 'our very own sounds' and 'aptitudes'. Weaker activations hit stock discourse connectors and filler words like 'However', 'Nevertheless', 'Moreover', 'Additionally', 'In fact', 'you' and 'very'.

A weak, diffuse feature with no clear semantic theme. It fires mostly on function words and connectors in the middle of formulaic phrases, such as "and" joining paired terms ("clean and efficient", "maintenance and repair"), "the", "of", "by" and "at". It also fires on predictable word-piece continuations ("-F|actor", "BYJ|US", "Tel|ugu") and on filler such as table-of-contents dot leaders and code indentation. These are tokens where the continuation is highly predictable.

A diffuse, mostly weak feature with no single clear trigger. It fires most strongly on connective and function words inside formal expository sentences, such as prepositions, "was", "and", commas and colons (e.g. "Until the 19th century, geometry was the foundation of mathematics"). It also often fires on tokens within phrases or titles that repeat text seen earlier in the context, such as duplicated headlines, captions and repeated report lines.

Closing delimiters of code or template blocks, often merged with the newlines after them. The strongest case by far is PHP's closing tag "?>", especially when it ends a script. Weaker activations come from other closers such as Jinja/Django "%}", Handlebars "}}", code-fence backticks, triple quotes and XML declaration endings. There are scattered faint activations on ordinary prose words.

Sub-word fragments inside odd, opaque or unpredictable strings, such as random IDs, URL hashes, ticker symbols, model numbers, variable names, acronyms, and transliterated or misspelled words. It fires on pieces of letter strings that are not ordinary English words.

Fires on structural or formatting tokens in highly patterned, repetitive text such as code, HTML tables, LaTeX, lists, dates and data listings. Typical hits are indentation and whitespace before list bullets or numbers, newline runs, closing tags (tr, tbody), repeated identifiers and class names, brackets, and parts of dates (month, year digits, commas). These tokens tend to repeat or continue a pattern already set up earlier in the context.

Content words (mostly nouns and adjectives) that are semantically out of place or unpredictable for their context. It fires most strongly in incoherent, machine-spun or SEO-spam word salad, such as garbled academic or casino/pharma filler text. It also fires weakly on blanks in fill-in-the-blank exercises and on odd word fragments in noisy text.

Fires on the first token after an abrupt, incoherent break in the text, where one sentence or topic is cut off mid-flow and unrelated content begins. This is typical of spliced, scraped, or spam-generated text, such as "Amazon.com|Before you can sell…", "in|While recuperating…" or "pickup|Popular Mechanics". The activating token is often capitalized, starts a new clause, and follows no punctuation.

The "usr" token in Unix paths, especially in shebang lines (#!/usr/bin/python, #!/usr/bin/env) at the very start of scripts. It fires most strongly when the shebang opens the file and much more weakly for mid-text or non-shebang paths like /usr/share.

A diffuse, low-specificity feature that fires on scattered tokens (function words, digits, operators, identifier suffixes, separators) in technical, mathematical, scientific, code and structured web text. It is strongest mid-exposition, just before a specific variable, value or quantity is introduced, as in "the number…", "is calculated as" or "v01 for this… close to v1".

The token right after a command, function name or operator where an argument begins, in code and shell commands. These are usually space-prefixed symbols that open the argument: $ for variables, quotes, brackets, (&, <, /, a URL scheme, or line-continuation backslashes and backticks. The strongest cases are shell or Perl arguments such as `$1` and string concatenation like `"+str(`.

Tokens that open a curly-brace placeholder or interpolation, strongest for "${" in shell, Makefile and template variable substitution (e.g. " ${", "=${", "(${"). It fires more weakly on "{" in C#/Python f-strings and format strings, and on "${" starting LaTeX inline math.

Leading indentation whitespace (spaces/tabs) at the start of a code line, especially the first line of a newly indented block after a colon, brace, or control statement; weaker activation on line-break/delimiter tokens that separate statements or sections in code and math text.

Line-ending and indentation tokens at structural boundaries in code and markup. The strongest cases are the newline and indentation after the last line of a doc comment (e.g. after "@var array" or "@return"), just before the closing "*/". Weaker cases are the ">⏎" that closes a table cell or header ("" / "") before the next cell in HTML tables. The feature also fires weakly on stray prose tokens at clause ends.

The "bin" directory component in file paths, firing hardest on "/bin" and "/env" in shebang lines like "#!/usr/bin/env python" at the start of scripts. It is weaker on other bin paths (GOPATH/bin, cgi-bin, /sbin) and faint on nearby script-header tokens like "coding" and "import".

A diffuse, low-specificity pattern. It fires mostly on punctuation, operators and short connector tokens (commas, colons, parentheses, '&', '+', '/', arrows, '%>', '$(') that separate elements in structured or noisy text such as code, LaTeX, chemical formulas, file names, mojibake, spam and transliterations. It occasionally also fires on a function word or word fragment in ordinary prose where the next token is hard to predict.

Tokens that end or complete a phrase which is a repeat of an earlier one in the context. Typical cases are repeated lines, list items, boilerplate and refrains (e.g. "Invalid Input", "Show more", "Monthly Budget", "lived a method", repeated numbers or units). The feature is predicting the final word of a copy. Activation is strongest in highly repetitive text and grows with the number of repetitions.

A diffuse, weakly firing feature with no single clear trigger, scattered across arbitrary tokens (word pieces, punctuation, nouns) in noisy web text. It is somewhat stronger on keyword-stuffed or SEO/spam-like passages, such as repeated search phrases, tag lists and scraped titles (e.g., "Visual keyboard windows", "corticosteroid-induced", "environmental pollution"), especially on the repeated terms and the commas between them.

A weak, diffuse feature firing on structural and symbolic tokens rather than words. The most common triggers are the final digit of four-digit years (often in citations like "(Author, 201X)" or bibliographic dates), closing parentheses and brackets, and assorted symbols such as &, $, #, |$, and censor marks like *@. The strongest activations are on unusual symbol sequences, such as OCR-garbled "()" and censored profanity.

Tokens inside verbatim repeated text. The feature fires on words or phrases that recur several times in close succession (repeated lines, chants, list items, code lines, table cells, boilerplate such as "Invalid Input" or "Show more"), usually from the second or third repetition onward, as the model predicts a copy of earlier text. Activation is strongest in long, highly regular loops of identical multi-token lines.

Weak, diffuse activation on tokens inside repetitive, list-like or unstructured text that isn't ordinary prose: number and symbol sequences, code and URL fragments, keyword-stuffed tags, garbled spaced-out letters, line breaks in lists or verse, and math notation. It is strongest on repeated or sequential patterns such as "b b b 1 2 3", strings of underscores and dots, and runs of numbers.

Sentence and paragraph boundaries, mostly periods or closing punctuation fused with newlines (".⏎⏎", ").", "?⏎⏎") at the end of a sentence, along with the first token after a line break. It mainly appears in incoherent, spun or SEO-spam text where a topic shift follows. Activation is strongest on a period plus double newline closing a paragraph.

Misspelled, garbled or corrupted word fragments, typically subword tokens inside a word that come from typos, OCR errors, phonetic or joke spellings, or spun/nonsense text (e.g. 'te-ii', 'volt-ge', 'p-prn', 'combin-atioti'). The token is the point where the spelling departs from the real word.

Fires very strongly on the "/env" token of the shebang line "#!/usr/bin/env" at the beginning of Python scripts. Elsewhere activation is negligible, with weak scattered hits on structural tokens such as <tbody>, list bullets, newlines and colons.

Garbled or corrupted spots in noisy text such as OCR errors, spun or scraped spam, redaction blocks, censored swearing, stray symbols and digits inside words, and misplaced punctuation or spacing. It fires on the anomalous token that breaks the expected word or sentence, especially digits or symbols standing in for letters (s6ances, a9tion, ma&us, i8go) and censorship or redaction marks.

Fragment subword tokens in the middle of hard-to-predict text: foreign or transliterated words (Irish, Arabic, Hindi, Greek, Russian, Korean, Japanese), rare names, acronyms, reversed strings, ID numbers, symbols, and garbled or dialectal spellings. Activations are weak and are highest on non-English transliterated phrases.

Fires weakly and broadly on tokens inside structured or templated text such as HTML table markup (especially '>⏎' after closing td/tr tags), code, markdown links, LaTeX, tables of contents with dot leaders, data listings, and headings. The activating tokens are mostly delimiters, separators or repeated elements whose position is predictable from the surrounding repetitive formatting, rather than tokens carrying particular meaning.

Syntax tokens inside code or formula snippets, mostly operators, delimiters and short keywords in terse or unusual languages such as Mathematica, PARI/MAGMA, BASIC-like and Forth-like code. Typical examples are pure-function and application markers (&, ]&, @@, //), statement terminators and control words (End, exit, endif, DUP) and bracket or slash combinations. The strongest activations fall on symbols that mark function application or the end of an expression. Scattered prose and non-Latin tokens activate only weakly.

Word fragments in noisy or corrupted text, such as truncated, misspelled, hyphen-broken, or OCR-garbled words, and words split oddly across line breaks (e.g. 'n'+'ose', 'f'+'amiliar', 'devel-'/'op'). The feature fires on the subword piece where the normal word boundary is disrupted, often at the start of a line or a lost first letter.

Fires on garbled or invisible text, mainly empty/zero-width tokens, mojibake (�) fragments and stray combining diacritics inside corrupted, mis-encoded or binary-like text. It is strongest on runs of empty tokens in Cyrillic-looking binary garbage and only weak elsewhere.

A weak, diffuse feature that fires at clause and sentence boundaries: mostly sentence-final punctuation (periods, commas, paragraph breaks, also Chinese 。), the noun or word that closes a phrase just before it, and the first words of the following sentence (e.g. 'I', 'However', 'Please'). It is strongest in informal, run-on first-person prose.

A weak, diffuse feature that fires on tokens in hard-to-predict, high-entropy text rather than on a particular word. Typical contexts are random alphanumeric strings, hashes, IDs, URLs, IP addresses and numeric lists or codes. It also fires on rare non-Latin scripts, garbled LaTeX, and incoherent spam or machine-generated prose.

Fires on unpredictable tokens in noisy, incoherent or low-quality text, such as spun/SEO spam word salad, OCR garbage, DNA sequences, symbol/ASCII art, username lists, number lists, URL fragments and archaic or foreign scripts. It is strongest in long runs of nonsensical text. In otherwise normal sentences it fires weakly on a single oddly placed function word or noun.

Tokens that repeat an immediately preceding token or short pattern. The feature fires on the second and later copies in runs of identical words, symbols, numbers, or cells, such as "H H H H", "+ + +", "Unlimited Unlimited", "agree agree", "7 7 7" and "NA NA". Activation tends to grow the longer the repetition goes on.

A diffuse, low-intensity feature with no clear semantic focus. It fires sporadically on single mid-sentence tokens such as proper-name fragments, word-piece continuations, function words, punctuation and list separators. These tend to appear in formal, technical or noisy (OCR/spam-like) text. Slightly stronger activations occur within noun phrases naming specific entities, such as 'the 1996 American Book Award', 'Mahavir Chakra' and 'graphite'.

Diffuse, weak activations on tokens in noisy, low-coherence or structured text: garbled/encoded strings, ASCII art, ID and part numbers, URL encodings, tables, list bullets, and run-together or spam text. It fires mostly on repeated or fragment tokens (numbers, single letters, symbols, bullets) where the next token is hard to predict. No clear semantic meaning.

Tokens in garbled, noisy or atypical text: OCR errors, broken or misspelled word fragments, random character strings, odd capitalization or spacing, and spam-like or formatting junk. The strongest activations fall on dense OCR gibberish (stray letters, numbers and punctuation from scanned documents); weaker ones on single malformed subword pieces.

Fires weakly on function words, punctuation, or odd words sitting where the sentence breaks down. These are places where a token is grammatically unexpected or misplaced: dropped or extra words, disfluent speech-transcript phrasing, and garbled spun, spam or machine-translated text. It also fires mildly on commas at clause junctions.

A weak, diffuse feature that fires on content words, mostly abstract nouns and descriptive or evaluative adjectives (e.g., diversity, legacy, insight, portrayal, sustainable, noble). These usually complete a noun phrase or clause, often just before punctuation or a preposition. They appear mainly in elevated, academic or figurative prose, with no single topic tying the examples together.

A diffuse, low-intensity feature that fires on tokens that are surprising or out of place in context, especially in disfluent, ungrammatical, garbled or spun/machine-generated text. Typical cases are wrong word choices or broken syntax ("protected to therapeutic massage", "in order the design to work", "to initial aerosol formation"), odd fragments of names or URLs, and unexpected list items. It reflects local unpredictability rather than any specific meaning.

A diffuse, low-specificity feature that fires mostly on unpredictable tokens in noisy or garbled text: OCR junk, mojibake, random alphanumeric codes and serial numbers, unit letters stuck to numbers, odd single characters or scripts, and gene or sequence strings. It also fires weakly on ordinary punctuation and line breaks in plain prose, which suggests it tracks high-surprise or out-of-distribution tokens rather than any one meaning.

A weak, diffuse feature with no clear single-token pattern. It fires mostly on generic, low-information filler in noisy web text such as SEO spam, scrambled or nonsensical sentences, code and number snippets, and templated boilerplate. It is strongest on corporate-buzzword placeholder text (e.g., 'Organically grow the holistic world view…') and on generic website promo copy ('If you are ready, you can play some other games').

Fragments inside unpredictable, high-entropy character strings: random alphanumeric IDs, hashes, URL and filename codes, passwords, MAC addresses, mojibake or garbled text, and invented or foreign names split into odd subword pieces. Activation is strongest deep inside random codes and garbled Chinese. It is weak on occasional ordinary words.

The shell command "echo", strongest when it starts a command line in bash, batch, or other scripts. It responds more weakly to other output commands such as print, printf, println and Write-Host, and to echo-related words like echoed, echoing and noecho.

Tokens inside repetitive or patterned sequences, where the next token is predictable from earlier repetition: repeated phrases ("Loading...", "Final Four", "Sacred Valley"), number runs, list separators, whitespace or newline padding, HTML table tags, and repeated characters or symbols. Activations are generally weak and scattered, strongest on spaces and numbers in counting sequences.

Tokens inside repetitive or patterned sequences: repeated numbers, symbols, separators and code lines (e.g., 30, 31, 30…; -*-*; ~~88~~88; repeated '; ' lines; 16x16x16). The token itself repeats an earlier element in the same run, and activation is strongest in highly regular, predictable repetition. Weak, scattered activation on ordinary words elsewhere.

Punctuation, whitespace, newlines and separator tokens (commas, spaces, dashes, tags, line breaks) that act as delimiters between items, mostly in noisy, garbled, redacted, foreign-script or list-like text. Activation is strongest for commas separating repeated or masked items, such as runs of █ blocks or REDACTED.

A diffuse feature with no clear semantic content. It fires mostly on structural and formatting tokens, such as newlines, spaces, brackets, slashes, backslashes and punctuation. These usually sit inside markup, LaTeX, code, tables or garbled multilingual and symbol-heavy text, often at boundaries between segments. It also fires occasionally on ordinary function words like "of" or "in" in prose.

A diffuse, weakly firing feature with no clear single concept. It activates sporadically on many token types: numbers and items in comma-separated lists, math operators and LaTeX symbols, punctuation, and citation brackets. It fires most strongly on hard-to-predict or surprising content, such as citation markers like "[6", nonsensical word salad, and incongruous lists of unrelated nouns.

under.name: Tokens in the middle of long sequences of meaningless, non-word letter codes. Activation is strongest for DNA/RNA nucleotide strings (A/C/G/T/U) and amino-acid peptide sequences. Weaker activation appears on other repetitive, low-meaning filler, especially the dot leaders in tables of contents, and on similar letter strings such as H/T coin-flip lists or codon tables.

The ".LENGTH" token in Android Toast/Snackbar duration constants (Toast.LENGTH_SHORT/LONG, Snackbar.LENGTH_SHORT) in Java code; weakly also similar static constant prefixes like JOptionPane.PLAIN_MESSAGE.

The method name in UI popup/notification calls, overwhelmingly Android's "Toast.makeText" (strongest), and more weakly similar calls such as "JOptionPane.showMessageDialog" and "Snackbar.make". These show a short user-facing message. Other activations, such as "text" in LaTeX \textsuperscript, are faint and scattered.

The LaTeX citation command name "cite" (including variants like \citep, \citealt, \newcite, \textcite) right after the backslash, which marks references to literature in academic text. Activation is highest for repeated citations in a list. There are weak activations on other LaTeX reference commands like \secref and on scattered unrelated tokens.

Structural boilerplate in source code (mostly C#/Java), firing on indentation whitespace, comment closers (*/, ///), XML doc tags (summary, param) and the tokens right around them. It peaks at the transition from a doc comment to the next member declaration (annotations, access modifiers, method signatures and braces, e.g. Dispose()). It also fires weakly on formulaic structure in templated documents such as safety data sheet section breaks and spacing in nutrition labels.

Separators (spaces, commas, semicolons, parentheses, letter prefixes) placed just before the codes in lists of classification codes, such as MSC, PACS, JEL, ACM descriptors, patent classes, OEIS cross-references and 'Part of the ... Commons' disciplines. Activation is strongest on the space right before a numeric code, especially later items in a list.

A weak, diffuse feature that fires on structural tokens beginning a new element in formatted or list-like text. Most often this is the "</" of the closing </tbody> tag that follows </tr> at the end of an HTML table. It also fires on " =" in equations (the strongest case), on the first fragment of usernames in comma-separated name lists, and on indentation whitespace or bullet markers that start a new line.

The last digit of a year inside citation keys (author name + year + title word, e.g. \cite{liu2017smart}, @article{Howell2016...}), firing on the digit that completes the year right before the title word. It is strongest in LaTeX \cite{} keys. A weak secondary response shows up on boilerplate web phrases like "Related questions" and "save at Amazon".

Tokens immediately preceding a person's (or organization's) name in bibliographic or patent contexts: the final year digit before an inventor surname in patent citation lists, the colon after 'Inventor(s)', 'awarded/issued to', semicolons, commas or 'and' between author-year citations, and table-cell tags right before a name. In essence, the feature predicts that a proper name comes next.

Pieces of math notation used as prefixes or modifiers in named mathematical objects, chiefly the "C*-" / "C^k" / "σ-" / "K-theory" type: the letter, the superscript (^, *, ast, ∞), and the trailing "$-" hyphen that joins the symbol to a noun such as algebra or diffeomorphism. Activation is strongest on the "*$-" / "ast$-" in "C*-algebra". Weak scattered hits fall on other symbol fragments, numbers in compounds ("1-form", "NG9-1-1") and punctuation.

Separator punctuation inside structured classification or identifier codes, firing on the delimiter just before the final segment. It peaks on the '.Letter' token in PACS codes (e.g. 36.40.Gk), and is weaker on hyphens in CAS registry numbers and Japanese addresses, slashes in patent Int. Cl. codes (e.g. 48/00), and brackets in ACM subject codes.

Tokens just after the start of a statistical interval or spread in numeric data, strongest right after "95% CI" (and its colon, comma or "of"), then at the space, leading digit and especially the decimal point of the lower bound. It also fires more weakly on the separators before ranges ("range", "from", IQR, parentheses) and on the decimal points after "±" in error values.

Descriptions of particle or nuclear decay processes, firing most strongly on the parent particle and arrow in LaTeX decay notation (e.g. B_c \to, B^+ \to) and also on words like decays, beta-decay and decay products. Weak, diffuse activation appears across other physics and math text.

The leading segment (first digits or letter prefix) of formal classification or reference codes in academic, patent and grant metadata. Examples include MSC/AMS subject classes like 65M22, PACS numbers like 78.67.De, JEL codes like C100, patent Int. Cl. codes like G06F, EC numbers, and contract or grant numbers. Activation is strongest for the leading digits of math subject classification codes.

The final segment of alphanumeric classification codes, mainly in academic and patent front matter (PACS, MSC/AMS, JEL, Int. Cl., OCIS). It marks the trailing digits or letters after the code's prefix, such as the 'b' in 85.60.Jb or the '10' in 47H10. Activation is strongest on PACS letter suffixes and MSC digit endings. It is weak on stray text tokens.

A diffuse feature firing on mid-clause tokens (function words like 'and', 'of', 'to', 'him', verbs, and punctuation) where the sentence continues an action. It is strongest in classical Chinese biographical text and fires broadly on historical or biographical narrative about officials, emperors and generals, and on translated Chinese web-novel prose. It shows weak, scattered activation elsewhere, including scientific text, code and citations.

Tokens that mark the start of unit-test code. The strongest is the ".junit" token in Java imports such as "import org.junit...", especially its first occurrence in a file. It also fires more weakly on "(test" in Rust's #[cfg(test)] attribute before a tests module. Scattered faint activations on ordinary prose and HTML tokens appear to be noise.

The separator between the two bounds of a numeric range, strongest within confidence intervals (e.g. "95% CI 0.54–1.01"). It fires on the dash/en-dash, " to " or comma between the lower and upper values, and secondarily on the decimal point of the upper bound. It is weaker for general ranges ("range 8–60", "from 30 to 100") and fires only faintly on unrelated punctuation.

Mainly fires on "kinase" and the final "K" of "PI3K" in phosphatidylinositol 3-kinase signaling pathway text. It peaks on the "K" in PI3K/Akt. It responds more weakly to other enzyme-name endings such as "-ase", "-ases", PTEN's "EN" and PP2A's "A".

The word "the" right after a formulaic past-participle-plus-preposition phrase in front-matter or boilerplate text, such as "licensed/distributed under the" in license and copyright notices or "submitted to the" on thesis title pages. It is strongest in code-header license lines like "Licensed under the Apache License".

Chess move notation: fires most strongly on square coordinates and captures (e.g. 'e6', 'dxc4', 'xf2', 'g5', 'O-O-O') in game records. It also fires weakly on moves and actions in other play-by-play accounts (card games, poker, board/war games, sports, fights).

Headers for metadata and classification fields in scholarly paper front matter, usually right after the abstract. These include "Index Terms", "PACS numbers:", "JEL Classification:", "Key words:", "OCIS codes:", "MSC:" and "AMS subject classifications". The feature fires on the label word and its following colon or separator, and on punctuation between the classification codes. It peaks on "PACS numbers:". It also fires weakly on the "I." before INTRODUCTION and on similar labeled code fields such as HS Code, CAS Number and CPT Codes.

Fires on the noun that names the authority or governing document in legal, licensing and copyright boilerplate. It peaks on "License" in the Apache phrase "in compliance with the License". It is also strong on "author", "publisher" and "terms" in phrases like "without the consent of the author" and "consult the publisher's version". It fires weakly on other words in similar permission or usage text.

Numeric indices inside Lie/symmetry group names, especially gauge groups like U(1), SU(2), SU(3), O(3) (the number and its closing parenthesis/subscript), with strongest activation on U(1) and Standard Model gauge groups; weaker activation on related physics concepts such as electromagnetism, conserved quantum numbers (baryon/lepton number, R-parity) and other group subscripts.

The word "Gaza" (mainly as the Palestinian territory/Gaza Strip, especially in Israeli–Palestinian conflict contexts). Activation is weaker for unrelated uses or partial matches (a comic character named Gaza, "GAZA", "Gazel"), and other tokens fire only weakly.

The final digit of a publication year in an academic citation (e.g. the "6" completing "201" in "Smith et al. 2016"), occasionally with the closing punctuation. The feature also fires weakly on other closing citation markers, such as reference numbers and closing brackets.

Strategic moves and tactical play in competitive games, most strongly chess (forcing positions, threats, pawn sacrifices, breaking a defense). Weaker activations come from poker hand analysis, card drafting, sports and wargame scenarios. Isolated low activations on generic tokens in unrelated text are noise.

Names or abbreviations of regulatory codes and official legal publications in citations, especially "CFR" (Code of Federal Regulations) after a title number, plus "Federal Register"/"FR", "C.F.R.", NYCRR, Minn. R., Gov. Code and §. Other tokens activate only weakly and sporadically.

Physical or mathematical property terms in scientific (mostly physics and materials) text, usually the word or word-piece that completes a technical term naming a property, state or structure, e.g. "Fermi surface", "Goldstone bosons", "edge states", "sp2", "lossless", "light/massive", "curvature", "modulus". Activation is strongest on well-known condensed-matter terms like Fermi surface and Goldstone.

Strongest on supersymmetry labels in physics notation, such as the "𝒩=4" or "𝒩=(2,2)" count ("N", "=", the number) and the word "supersymmetric"/"super". Weaker activation falls on "=" in quantum-number assignments (S=1/2, I=…, n=…), along with assorted math and LaTeX tokens and scattered formatting whitespace.

Crystallographic orientation notation, chiefly Miller indices such as (001), (100), (110), (111), [001] and {01-12} written after material names or in surface/plane descriptions. Related crystal-geometry terms (axis, face, plane, cleavage, crystallographic, surfaces, grain boundaries, poles) activate weakly. Stray tokens like sentence ends and newlines show near-zero activation.

The word "conformal" (and related forms like conformable, quasiconformal), with the strongest activation on its final "al" piece. It fires most in math/physics settings (conformal field theory, conformal maps and transformations) and also in conformal radiotherapy and coatings. Weak activations occur on related scale and symmetry terms (scale, scaling, invariance, modular, Weyl) and on stray tokens such as bullet points.

Fires mainly in technical and mathematical prose on the words that open or qualify a noun phrase naming a class of objects. Typical spots are restricting adjectives and determiners such as 'a finite reflexive' (digraph), 'a closed, orientable' (manifold), 'such' (logics), 'infinite' (trees), 'binary' (codes) and 'single' (lossy lines). It also fires on the connectors leading into them ('of', 'with', 'for two', 'and/or' between contrasted properties). The strongest signal is on property-specifying modifiers inside definitions or statements of hypotheses.

Word-piece tokens inside anatomical terms for joint and tissue linings, by far most strongly the "ov" (and "ial") in "synovial", "synovium" and "synovitis". Weaker hits fall on similar anatomical fragments such as "articular", "periosteum", "pleura", "intima" and "joint capsule". Scattered faint activations on function words and punctuation appear to be noise.

In-text citation markers in academic or technical prose: the opening bracket or parenthesis of a reference, plus the reference numbers, author names, "et al." and especially the final digits of years in author-year citations. Activation is strongest at the start of the citation and on reference numbers or year endings.

The middle number segment of dotted classification codes, most strongly the second two-digit field of PACS physics codes (e.g. the "75" in 89.75.Hc). Activation is weaker on similar segments in OCIS, MSC, ACM, EC and industry codes, IP addresses and arXiv IDs.

Gravitational lensing, firing most strongly on "lens" (and "ensing" in microlensing) in astrophysics text. Weaker activations appear on related light-distortion and astrophysical terms such as bend/bent, mirage, mirrors, redshift, shear, Shapiro delay, curvature, polarization and clusters.

Academic/scientific prose, especially introduction and background sections that review prior work. Activations peak on literature-review framing such as "recent studies have", "researchers have found", "previous measurements", and "recent advances". They also fire on citation numbers and years and on discourse transitions at sentence starts ("For", "A", "On", "In").

Word-piece tokens within names of antioxidant enzymes, above all superoxide dismutase ('oxide', 'mut', 'ase', and 'OD' in SOD), along with catalase, glutathione peroxidase and GPx. Weaker activation appears on other enzyme name pieces such as 'activ' in plasminogen activator and 'synth' in nitric oxide synthase, and on the word 'enzyme'. The strongest signal is 'mut' in 'dismutase'. Unrelated text shows only faint activation.

Text on dark matter and hypothetical particles in physics (WIMPs, axions, gravitons, relic density, indirect detection, particle stability and mass). It peaks on phrases describing dark matter candidates and their properties, with weak, diffuse activation on other scientific or technical text.

A diffuse, low-specificity feature with weak activations spread across varied text. It is most consistent at structural boundaries where a new segment begins: paragraph breaks and newline/indentation runs (especially after forum headers like "Homepage" or before a reply), sentence-ending periods followed by newlines, list numbers and bullets, and commas separating list items. It also fires on scattered clause-initial or continuation words ("There", "These", "should", "like", "may then") and on some emotionally descriptive phrases.

Diffuse, weak activations spread across scientific/technical prose (physics, plasma, astrophysics abstracts and reports). The highlighted tokens are mostly function words and generic noun-phrase pieces such as "the", "of", "amount of", "effect", "nature" and "confinement", often inside descriptive phrases about physical quantities and processes. There is no single specific word; the common thread is academic scientific register.

Narrative prose in scriptural or archaic register, especially Bible verses. It fires most strongly on clauses that advance the story, typically 'And/Then + subject + past-tense verb' such as 'And it was so', 'he said', 'began to speak boldly' and 'approached and say to him'. Weaker activations appear on verbs and connectives in other storytelling text.

Fires on the term supersymmetry and its variants (supersymmetric, SUSY, MSSM, supergravity/SUGRA), with the strongest activation on the word-completing pieces after "super"/"sup" (e.g. "ymmetric", "metry"), mostly in particle-physics text. Weak activations also appear on unrelated tokens such as line breaks after "N Pages" headers or document metadata.

Mostly fires on Android boilerplate code, peaking inside the auto-generated onCreateOptionsMenu(Menu menu) method: the parameter, the opening brace and indentation, the "// Inflate the menu; this adds items to the action bar" comment, and getMenuInflater().inflate(R.menu..., menu). Related Android template lines ("Inflate the layout for this fragment", getSupportActionBar()., import android.view.Menu;) fire weakly. Elsewhere it gives very weak activation on predictable tokens in stock phrases ("on the other hand", "As a result", "However", "enables you to").

Scientific and taxonomic descriptive prose, mainly species and taxon descriptions in biology and paleontology (Latin genus and species names, family suffixes like -idae, author/year citations, statements of distribution, habitat and morphology). Activation lands on the function words, punctuation and name fragments inside these passages and is strongest in dense species-description text. Weak, scattered activation also appears on general academic and technical writing.

Nouns naming the document or work being described by its own text, mainly "invention" in patents (strongest after "object/advantage of the present"), the "ION" of "INVENTION" in patent section headers, and "paper", "research", "dissertation" or "investigation" in academic aims statements.

Single capital letters embedded inside alphanumeric classification or identifier codes, typically following a number. The strongest cases are the letter in Mathematics Subject Classification (MSC/AMS) codes such as 34A30 or 55P42. Weaker cases include the letter after the dot in PACS codes (03.67.Bg), JEL codes (C22), patent IPC classes (G06F), and letters in part, grant or gene identifiers.

Scientific journal names and their abbreviations in citations, especially the "J" in ApJ/EPJ bibcodes and "Journal" after "Astrophysical"/"Astronomical". Also fires on other journal abbreviation fragments (Sci, Natur, PhysRevLett, RMP, CQG, ApJS).

Technical/scientific text about classifying constituents into types, families or multiplets, firing most strongly on particle-physics content: quarks and fermions, their generations and flavors (up/charm/top), doublets, and left-handed doublet fields (Q_L, L_L) in LaTeX operators. It fires weakly on similar category terms in other fields (cell types, semiconductor family, ligand, units, bipolar cells).

over.name: A weak, diffuse feature that fires on awkward, non-native, machine-translated or SEO-spun English. It activates on tokens where the word choice or grammar is unnatural, such as redundant verbs, odd collocations and garbled phrasing. The strongest examples are spammy health copy and broken technical or product descriptions.

Fires within low-quality SEO-style web prose, especially article-spinner or machine-paraphrased text. The strongest activations land on awkward synonym substitutions and unnatural phrasing, such as 'in consequence', 'along with your moniker', 'our very own sounds' and 'aptitudes'. Weaker activations hit stock discourse connectors and filler words like 'However', 'Nevertheless', 'Moreover', 'Additionally', 'In fact', 'you' and 'very'.

A weak, diffuse feature with no clear semantic theme. It fires mostly on function words and connectors in the middle of formulaic phrases, such as "and" joining paired terms ("clean and efficient", "maintenance and repair"), "the", "of", "by" and "at". It also fires on predictable word-piece continuations ("-F|actor", "BYJ|US", "Tel|ugu") and on filler such as table-of-contents dot leaders and code indentation. These are tokens where the continuation is highly predictable.

A diffuse, mostly weak feature with no single clear trigger. It fires most strongly on connective and function words inside formal expository sentences, such as prepositions, "was", "and", commas and colons (e.g. "Until the 19th century, geometry was the foundation of mathematics"). It also often fires on tokens within phrases or titles that repeat text seen earlier in the context, such as duplicated headlines, captions and repeated report lines.

Closing delimiters of code or template blocks, often merged with the newlines after them. The strongest case by far is PHP's closing tag "?>", especially when it ends a script. Weaker activations come from other closers such as Jinja/Django "%}", Handlebars "}}", code-fence backticks, triple quotes and XML declaration endings. There are scattered faint activations on ordinary prose words.

Sub-word fragments inside odd, opaque or unpredictable strings, such as random IDs, URL hashes, ticker symbols, model numbers, variable names, acronyms, and transliterated or misspelled words. It fires on pieces of letter strings that are not ordinary English words.

Fires on structural or formatting tokens in highly patterned, repetitive text such as code, HTML tables, LaTeX, lists, dates and data listings. Typical hits are indentation and whitespace before list bullets or numbers, newline runs, closing tags (tr, tbody), repeated identifiers and class names, brackets, and parts of dates (month, year digits, commas). These tokens tend to repeat or continue a pattern already set up earlier in the context.

Content words (mostly nouns and adjectives) that are semantically out of place or unpredictable for their context. It fires most strongly in incoherent, machine-spun or SEO-spam word salad, such as garbled academic or casino/pharma filler text. It also fires weakly on blanks in fill-in-the-blank exercises and on odd word fragments in noisy text.

Fires on the first token after an abrupt, incoherent break in the text, where one sentence or topic is cut off mid-flow and unrelated content begins. This is typical of spliced, scraped, or spam-generated text, such as "Amazon.com|Before you can sell…", "in|While recuperating…" or "pickup|Popular Mechanics". The activating token is often capitalized, starts a new clause, and follows no punctuation.

The "usr" token in Unix paths, especially in shebang lines (#!/usr/bin/python, #!/usr/bin/env) at the very start of scripts. It fires most strongly when the shebang opens the file and much more weakly for mid-text or non-shebang paths like /usr/share.

A diffuse, low-specificity feature that fires on scattered tokens (function words, digits, operators, identifier suffixes, separators) in technical, mathematical, scientific, code and structured web text. It is strongest mid-exposition, just before a specific variable, value or quantity is introduced, as in "the number…", "is calculated as" or "v01 for this… close to v1".

The token right after a command, function name or operator where an argument begins, in code and shell commands. These are usually space-prefixed symbols that open the argument: $ for variables, quotes, brackets, (&, <, /, a URL scheme, or line-continuation backslashes and backticks. The strongest cases are shell or Perl arguments such as `$1` and string concatenation like `"+str(`.

Tokens that open a curly-brace placeholder or interpolation, strongest for "${" in shell, Makefile and template variable substitution (e.g. " ${", "=${", "(${"). It fires more weakly on "{" in C#/Python f-strings and format strings, and on "${" starting LaTeX inline math.

Leading indentation whitespace (spaces/tabs) at the start of a code line, especially the first line of a newly indented block after a colon, brace, or control statement; weaker activation on line-break/delimiter tokens that separate statements or sections in code and math text.

The "bin" directory component in file paths, firing hardest on "/bin" and "/env" in shebang lines like "#!/usr/bin/env python" at the start of scripts. It is weaker on other bin paths (GOPATH/bin, cgi-bin, /sbin) and faint on nearby script-header tokens like "coding" and "import".

A diffuse, low-specificity pattern. It fires mostly on punctuation, operators and short connector tokens (commas, colons, parentheses, '&', '+', '/', arrows, '%>', '$(') that separate elements in structured or noisy text such as code, LaTeX, chemical formulas, file names, mojibake, spam and transliterations. It occasionally also fires on a function word or word fragment in ordinary prose where the next token is hard to predict.

Tokens that end or complete a phrase which is a repeat of an earlier one in the context. Typical cases are repeated lines, list items, boilerplate and refrains (e.g. "Invalid Input", "Show more", "Monthly Budget", "lived a method", repeated numbers or units). The feature is predicting the final word of a copy. Activation is strongest in highly repetitive text and grows with the number of repetitions.

A diffuse, weakly firing feature with no single clear trigger, scattered across arbitrary tokens (word pieces, punctuation, nouns) in noisy web text. It is somewhat stronger on keyword-stuffed or SEO/spam-like passages, such as repeated search phrases, tag lists and scraped titles (e.g., "Visual keyboard windows", "corticosteroid-induced", "environmental pollution"), especially on the repeated terms and the commas between them.

A weak, diffuse feature firing on structural and symbolic tokens rather than words. The most common triggers are the final digit of four-digit years (often in citations like "(Author, 201X)" or bibliographic dates), closing parentheses and brackets, and assorted symbols such as &, $, #, |$, and censor marks like *@. The strongest activations are on unusual symbol sequences, such as OCR-garbled "()" and censored profanity.

Tokens inside verbatim repeated text. The feature fires on words or phrases that recur several times in close succession (repeated lines, chants, list items, code lines, table cells, boilerplate such as "Invalid Input" or "Show more"), usually from the second or third repetition onward, as the model predicts a copy of earlier text. Activation is strongest in long, highly regular loops of identical multi-token lines.

Weak, diffuse activation on tokens inside repetitive, list-like or unstructured text that isn't ordinary prose: number and symbol sequences, code and URL fragments, keyword-stuffed tags, garbled spaced-out letters, line breaks in lists or verse, and math notation. It is strongest on repeated or sequential patterns such as "b b b 1 2 3", strings of underscores and dots, and runs of numbers.

Sentence and paragraph boundaries, mostly periods or closing punctuation fused with newlines (".⏎⏎", ").", "?⏎⏎") at the end of a sentence, along with the first token after a line break. It mainly appears in incoherent, spun or SEO-spam text where a topic shift follows. Activation is strongest on a period plus double newline closing a paragraph.

Misspelled, garbled or corrupted word fragments, typically subword tokens inside a word that come from typos, OCR errors, phonetic or joke spellings, or spun/nonsense text (e.g. 'te-ii', 'volt-ge', 'p-prn', 'combin-atioti'). The token is the point where the spelling departs from the real word.

Fires very strongly on the "/env" token of the shebang line "#!/usr/bin/env" at the beginning of Python scripts. Elsewhere activation is negligible, with weak scattered hits on structural tokens such as <tbody>, list bullets, newlines and colons.

Garbled or corrupted spots in noisy text such as OCR errors, spun or scraped spam, redaction blocks, censored swearing, stray symbols and digits inside words, and misplaced punctuation or spacing. It fires on the anomalous token that breaks the expected word or sentence, especially digits or symbols standing in for letters (s6ances, a9tion, ma&us, i8go) and censorship or redaction marks.

Fragment subword tokens in the middle of hard-to-predict text: foreign or transliterated words (Irish, Arabic, Hindi, Greek, Russian, Korean, Japanese), rare names, acronyms, reversed strings, ID numbers, symbols, and garbled or dialectal spellings. Activations are weak and are highest on non-English transliterated phrases.

Fires weakly and broadly on tokens inside structured or templated text such as HTML table markup (especially '>⏎' after closing td/tr tags), code, markdown links, LaTeX, tables of contents with dot leaders, data listings, and headings. The activating tokens are mostly delimiters, separators or repeated elements whose position is predictable from the surrounding repetitive formatting, rather than tokens carrying particular meaning.

Syntax tokens inside code or formula snippets, mostly operators, delimiters and short keywords in terse or unusual languages such as Mathematica, PARI/MAGMA, BASIC-like and Forth-like code. Typical examples are pure-function and application markers (&, ]&, @@, //), statement terminators and control words (End, exit, endif, DUP) and bracket or slash combinations. The strongest activations fall on symbols that mark function application or the end of an expression. Scattered prose and non-Latin tokens activate only weakly.

Word fragments in noisy or corrupted text, such as truncated, misspelled, hyphen-broken, or OCR-garbled words, and words split oddly across line breaks (e.g. 'n'+'ose', 'f'+'amiliar', 'devel-'/'op'). The feature fires on the subword piece where the normal word boundary is disrupted, often at the start of a line or a lost first letter.

Fires on garbled or invisible text, mainly empty/zero-width tokens, mojibake (�) fragments and stray combining diacritics inside corrupted, mis-encoded or binary-like text. It is strongest on runs of empty tokens in Cyrillic-looking binary garbage and only weak elsewhere.

A weak, diffuse feature that fires at clause and sentence boundaries: mostly sentence-final punctuation (periods, commas, paragraph breaks, also Chinese 。), the noun or word that closes a phrase just before it, and the first words of the following sentence (e.g. 'I', 'However', 'Please'). It is strongest in informal, run-on first-person prose.

A weak, diffuse feature that fires on tokens in hard-to-predict, high-entropy text rather than on a particular word. Typical contexts are random alphanumeric strings, hashes, IDs, URLs, IP addresses and numeric lists or codes. It also fires on rare non-Latin scripts, garbled LaTeX, and incoherent spam or machine-generated prose.

Fires on unpredictable tokens in noisy, incoherent or low-quality text, such as spun/SEO spam word salad, OCR garbage, DNA sequences, symbol/ASCII art, username lists, number lists, URL fragments and archaic or foreign scripts. It is strongest in long runs of nonsensical text. In otherwise normal sentences it fires weakly on a single oddly placed function word or noun.

Tokens that repeat an immediately preceding token or short pattern. The feature fires on the second and later copies in runs of identical words, symbols, numbers, or cells, such as "H H H H", "+ + +", "Unlimited Unlimited", "agree agree", "7 7 7" and "NA NA". Activation tends to grow the longer the repetition goes on.

A diffuse, low-intensity feature with no clear semantic focus. It fires sporadically on single mid-sentence tokens such as proper-name fragments, word-piece continuations, function words, punctuation and list separators. These tend to appear in formal, technical or noisy (OCR/spam-like) text. Slightly stronger activations occur within noun phrases naming specific entities, such as 'the 1996 American Book Award', 'Mahavir Chakra' and 'graphite'.

Diffuse, weak activations on tokens in noisy, low-coherence or structured text: garbled/encoded strings, ASCII art, ID and part numbers, URL encodings, tables, list bullets, and run-together or spam text. It fires mostly on repeated or fragment tokens (numbers, single letters, symbols, bullets) where the next token is hard to predict. No clear semantic meaning.

Tokens in garbled, noisy or atypical text: OCR errors, broken or misspelled word fragments, random character strings, odd capitalization or spacing, and spam-like or formatting junk. The strongest activations fall on dense OCR gibberish (stray letters, numbers and punctuation from scanned documents); weaker ones on single malformed subword pieces.

Fires weakly on function words, punctuation, or odd words sitting where the sentence breaks down. These are places where a token is grammatically unexpected or misplaced: dropped or extra words, disfluent speech-transcript phrasing, and garbled spun, spam or machine-translated text. It also fires mildly on commas at clause junctions.

A weak, diffuse feature that fires on content words, mostly abstract nouns and descriptive or evaluative adjectives (e.g., diversity, legacy, insight, portrayal, sustainable, noble). These usually complete a noun phrase or clause, often just before punctuation or a preposition. They appear mainly in elevated, academic or figurative prose, with no single topic tying the examples together.

A diffuse, low-intensity feature that fires on tokens that are surprising or out of place in context, especially in disfluent, ungrammatical, garbled or spun/machine-generated text. Typical cases are wrong word choices or broken syntax ("protected to therapeutic massage", "in order the design to work", "to initial aerosol formation"), odd fragments of names or URLs, and unexpected list items. It reflects local unpredictability rather than any specific meaning.

A diffuse, low-specificity feature that fires mostly on unpredictable tokens in noisy or garbled text: OCR junk, mojibake, random alphanumeric codes and serial numbers, unit letters stuck to numbers, odd single characters or scripts, and gene or sequence strings. It also fires weakly on ordinary punctuation and line breaks in plain prose, which suggests it tracks high-surprise or out-of-distribution tokens rather than any one meaning.

A weak, diffuse feature with no clear single-token pattern. It fires mostly on generic, low-information filler in noisy web text such as SEO spam, scrambled or nonsensical sentences, code and number snippets, and templated boilerplate. It is strongest on corporate-buzzword placeholder text (e.g., 'Organically grow the holistic world view…') and on generic website promo copy ('If you are ready, you can play some other games').

Fragments inside unpredictable, high-entropy character strings: random alphanumeric IDs, hashes, URL and filename codes, passwords, MAC addresses, mojibake or garbled text, and invented or foreign names split into odd subword pieces. Activation is strongest deep inside random codes and garbled Chinese. It is weak on occasional ordinary words.

The shell command "echo", strongest when it starts a command line in bash, batch, or other scripts. It responds more weakly to other output commands such as print, printf, println and Write-Host, and to echo-related words like echoed, echoing and noecho.

Tokens inside repetitive or patterned sequences, where the next token is predictable from earlier repetition: repeated phrases ("Loading...", "Final Four", "Sacred Valley"), number runs, list separators, whitespace or newline padding, HTML table tags, and repeated characters or symbols. Activations are generally weak and scattered, strongest on spaces and numbers in counting sequences.

Tokens inside repetitive or patterned sequences: repeated numbers, symbols, separators and code lines (e.g., 30, 31, 30…; -*-*; ~~88~~88; repeated '; ' lines; 16x16x16). The token itself repeats an earlier element in the same run, and activation is strongest in highly regular, predictable repetition. Weak, scattered activation on ordinary words elsewhere.

Punctuation, whitespace, newlines and separator tokens (commas, spaces, dashes, tags, line breaks) that act as delimiters between items, mostly in noisy, garbled, redacted, foreign-script or list-like text. Activation is strongest for commas separating repeated or masked items, such as runs of █ blocks or REDACTED.

A diffuse feature with no clear semantic content. It fires mostly on structural and formatting tokens, such as newlines, spaces, brackets, slashes, backslashes and punctuation. These usually sit inside markup, LaTeX, code, tables or garbled multilingual and symbol-heavy text, often at boundaries between segments. It also fires occasionally on ordinary function words like "of" or "in" in prose.

A diffuse, weakly firing feature with no clear single concept. It activates sporadically on many token types: numbers and items in comma-separated lists, math operators and LaTeX symbols, punctuation, and citation brackets. It fires most strongly on hard-to-predict or surprising content, such as citation markers like "[6", nonsensical word salad, and incongruous lists of unrelated nouns.

under.name: In-text citation markers in academic or technical prose: the opening bracket or parenthesis of a reference, plus the reference numbers, author names, "et al." and especially the final digits of years in author-year citations. Activation is strongest at the start of the citation and on reference numbers or year endings.

Academic/scientific prose, especially introduction and background sections that review prior work. Activations peak on literature-review framing such as "recent studies have", "researchers have found", "previous measurements", and "recent advances". They also fire on citation numbers and years and on discourse transitions at sentence starts ("For", "A", "On", "In").

Narrative prose in scriptural or archaic register, especially Bible verses. It fires most strongly on clauses that advance the story, typically 'And/Then + subject + past-tense verb' such as 'And it was so', 'he said', 'began to speak boldly' and 'approached and say to him'. Weaker activations appear on verbs and connectives in other storytelling text.

Scientific and academic research prose, especially framing language that motivates or summarizes a study: statements of knowledge gaps ("little is known", "not well understood", "we still lack an understanding of", "we do not currently know"), research aims ("to better constrain", "to provide a basis for assessing"), and findings or implications ("the findings provide", "this helps us better understand"). Activations peak on these phrases and on sentence boundaries (periods, newlines) where such framing begins.

The first word of a new sentence or paragraph, usually the article "The"/"A"/"An", at sentence starts in formal academic or scientific prose (often right after a citation or period) that introduce a new topic noun phrase.

Language of public opinion measurement: polls, surveys, approval ratings and popularity, and the phrasing used to report their results (e.g. "polls showed", "72 percent disapprove", "is above 50%"). Activation is strongest on poll/approval/rating terms and the reported percentages. It weakly extends to related rankings, market share, odds and consensus.

Technical and engineering descriptions of physical apparatus, instruments and their specifications. It fires weakly and sparsely on words naming components, dimensions, units and physical properties (sensor, telescope, chamber, diameter, temperature, kg, KB), and most strongly on spans describing a device's construction or makeup (e.g., 'operates two 17 m diameter Imaging...', 'composed of particle identification suites including...').

The end of author-affiliation addresses in academic papers. It fires mainly on the country name that closes an address (Italy, USA, France, UK, etc.) and on the newline, comma, semicolon or 'and' right after it, where the next affiliation or section begins. It fires more weakly on other line-ending punctuation in scholarly text, such as the end of a reference or caption.

Narratives of combat, warfare and violent or dramatic action, such as battles, attacks, shootings, captures, escapes, kills and military operations. Activation is strongest within descriptions of the action itself and at the sentence breaks between steps of the battle account. Weaker hits appear on related physical-action narration, like finding, seizing or rescuing someone, and sporadically elsewhere.

Weak, diffuse activations on function words, punctuation and clause boundaries in expository or scientific prose. The feature fires most strongly where the text introduces, names or defines a novel kind of thing, as in phrases like "known as … a new type of … that is so new and special", "a new type of organism" and "such a 'liquid glass' … has not yet been explored".

A diffuse, low-intensity feature tied to formal scientific, biomedical and academic writing (paper introductions, reviews, citation-heavy prose). It fires on scattered content words, mostly technical nouns such as drugs, material, mice, oxide, nanotechnology and collagen. It also fires on citation numbers or brackets and on sentence boundaries inside expository statements. No single token type dominates; the common thread is the explanatory, research-literature register.

A diffuse, low-intensity feature in scientific and technical prose. It fires on the key terms of technical noun phrases and method descriptions, such as model parameters, processes and components. It is strongest where items are paired, coordinated or contrasted, as in "X and Y", "both … as well as", "horizontal/vertical" and "possibility/impossibility".

Author surnames in academic citations, firing mainly on the final subword pieces of the name and on the "et al." that follows it. These typically appear in parenthetical or inline references such as "(Smith et al., 2010)" and "Smith and Jones (1994)". It fires weakly on other proper names.

Opening tokens of in-text citations and reference markers in academic or encyclopedic writing, such as " [", ".[", " (", "\cite{", superscript markup and reference numbers, usually placed right after a claim or an author name like "et al.". The strongest activations are on " [" following author names or statements.

The word "Introduction"/"INTRODUCTION" as a section heading in academic papers, reports and tables of contents (e.g., after "1.", "I.", or in \section{}), often right after the abstract or keywords. Weaker activation on other front-matter headings like "Summary"/"Executive Summary".

A weak, diffuse feature with no single token focus. It fires sporadically on ordinary words and punctuation, most often in informal, TV Tropes–style commentary on fiction and pop culture: monsters, villains, myths, TV shows, games and cartoons. The strongest spans are narrative or evaluative remarks such as "the fascinating twist that…", "just plain weird aspects of" and "famously -".

Section headings and front-matter labels that open a document's main content after title or author info, such as Abstract, Contents/Table of Contents, Acknowledgements, Introduction, Chapter, Summary and Keywords. Activation is strongest on "Contents" and "Abstract".

A diffuse, low-intensity feature that fires mainly in scientific and technical writing about searching for, detecting, surveying or cataloguing populations of objects (pulsars, radio sources, planets, craters, dust grains, fires, database entries). The strongest activations fall on words tied to discovery and survey work, such as 'sources', 'density', 'survey', 'pulsars', 'discovered' and 'we have studied'. Weaker hits are scattered over nearby function words and punctuation.

Introduction of a generic or variable entity in definitional/technical contexts: the noun or symbol being posited as the subject of a definition, statement, or argument (e.g., "Consider a linear operator L", "a category $C$", "an object $x$", "a function", "If z_0 is a point"), including math variables in LaTeX and function parameters in code. Strongest in formal math definitions and hypotheses.

Author surnames (mostly their continuation subword tokens) and the tokens that follow them, such as "et", commas, spaces and years, inside academic citations. These appear as parenthetical (Author et al., Year) references, LaTeX \cite keys and bracketed reference codes. Author names in paper bylines and affiliations also activate.

Scientific and technical prose, mostly physics, astrophysics, chemistry and earth science, describing physical processes and mechanisms. Activation lands on the nouns and verbs that name physical entities and what they do: particles, photons, electrons, emissions, growth, transport, collisions, migration, form, accumulate. It is strongest inside causal clauses such as "photons are needed for ionizing", "scattering of seed photons off the electrons" or "would have been trapped there by".

The last token of a citation reference in academic text. This is most often the final digit of a publication year in author-year citations (e.g., 'et al., 201|6;'), and also the closing numbers in bracketed reference lists and the ends of BibTeX cite keys. It typically comes right before the punctuation that closes or separates citations.

Tokens in passages where the writer announces or frames the main contribution or topic of a text, as in abstract-like openers ("this paper proposes a method", "in this paper, the authors present", "this study investigates", "we here describe a case of", "To tackle this problem", "today announced"). The strongest activations fall on these framing verbs and nouns and on the sentence boundaries just before them. Weak, scattered activations also occur on transition words and the content that follows the framing.

Tokens inside formal mathematical/technical statements, strongest in definitional or hypothesis clauses that impose conditions on objects (e.g. "be a holomorphic function… Suppose |f(z)| ≤ 1", "satisfies f(t)≥0", "satisfy y(0)=y(h)=0", "assumed to be countable and connected"). Activation falls on connective words and inline LaTeX delimiters/symbols in these constraint-setting phrases. Weak scattered activations appear elsewhere on technical text, year digits, and code.

Mainly the "al" in "et al." within academic author-year citations (strongest inside parenthetical references); weak activations on other predictable continuation tokens in structured/formatted text such as LaTeX backslashes, HTML table tags, section numbers in tables of contents, and abbreviation periods.

Language that cites earlier research or past work, as in the related-work sections of academic writing. It fires most on perfect and passive verbs and nouns like "has been studied", "have been proposed/developed", "was shown in", "literature", "studies", "previous", "recently" and "many authors", which signal that a topic has already been investigated.

Notation-introducing phrases, mainly in mathematical and technical writing, that define or name a symbol or term. The strongest are "denote (by)", "we define", "let", "will be abbreviated by", "we will call", "the notation" and "we say", especially right before a LaTeX symbol. Weaker activations land on related convention-setting text such as nomenclature lists, symbol tables, code comments and syntax explanations.

Encyclopedic or travel-guide passages about the history of buildings and landmarks (churches, chapels, temples, cathedrals, palaces, statues, terminals). It fires on the building nouns and the historical narration around them, such as construction, dates, past locations, renovation or replacement, and later use, for example "was built in 1851 at the", "replaced a previous version", "redesigned", "(now the".

Variables and relation symbols in mathematical statements that define the domain or range of a parameter (e.g., "x \in [0,1]", "d \geq 2", "\epsilon > 0", "for every r > 0"). The strongest activations fall on the constrained variable name and the following \in/\geq/> symbol, especially in LaTeX. Weaker activations appear on prose about ranges and bounds ("less than", "take on a negative value", "will be between").

Sentence openings and connective phrases in the results and conclusion parts of scientific abstracts. Activation is highest on sentence boundaries and on the subject-plus-reporting-verb frames that follow them, such as "The results ... confirm", "our analysis reveals that", "We observed" and "values are".

In scientific and technical prose, this fires weakly to moderately on words just before or between mentions of observation and measurement methods, especially imaging types and electromagnetic bands (radio, infrared, thermal, VHE emission, nm ranges, RF/IF, radiography vs sonography, fMRI). The activating tokens are often connectives and modifiers such as 'and', 'or', 'of', 'at', 'both', 'multiple', 'conventional' and 'functional'. The strongest case is 'observed at radio wavelengths at very late times'.

The word "Introduction" (often as INT+RODUCTION in capitals) used as a section heading, usually in academic papers right after the abstract or keywords, often numbered ("1.", "I.", \section{}). It fires most strongly when numbered and weaker in tables of contents. Other document section headings such as Abstract, Summary or Update activate it weakly.

Biblical and archaic scriptural prose (KJV-style narrative and verse), firing most on connective and function words like 'and', 'with', 'of', 'that', commas, colons and semicolons that chain the clauses together. Weaker, scattered activations land on clause boundaries and sentence-ending punctuation in ordinary text.

Function words and connectives (of, the, in, to, and, can be, as) inside expository scientific prose, especially descriptions of physical emission and signals (light, radio waves, spectra, luminescence, synchrotron emission, echoes). It fires most strongly in astrophysics passages explaining how emission is produced or modeled.

Punctuation and abbreviation tokens inside academic citation and reference formatting, chiefly the "al" in "et al." in author-year citations, plus commas between citation numbers or author/year pairs, the period in "Fig." or section numbers, and line breaks after author/affiliation lines in scientific papers.

Scientific (especially spectroscopy/astrophysics) terms for measurable spectral features or tracers; strongest on "emission lines", "lines", "peaks", "bands", and ion/element notations like [OIII], O+, i.e., spectral lines and signals of chemical species.

Numbers (and number words or numerals) that label document sections, chapters, parts, list items or headings, especially after words like "Section", "Chapter" or "Part" or at the start of a heading line. Activation is strongest for in-text cross-references to sections in paper outlines ("Section 3 introduces...").

Boilerplate and metadata in academic repository or web pages: newline breaks (often double) after URLs, IDs, dates and citation fields, separating sections such as "Submitted on", rights, permissions and citation info. The strongest activation is "contact" in the repository phrase "For more information, please contact ...", along with the email's ".edu".

Separators between consecutive entries in academic citation lists, chiefly the semicolon after a year in author–year in-text citations (e.g. "Smith et al., 2005; Jones, 2007"), where activation is strongest. Weaker activation falls on commas, "and" or "&" between cited works or authors, and occasionally on words leading into a cited author name.

In academic citations, the space, opening parenthesis, or bracket right after an author name (e.g. "et al.," or "Smith and Jones") together with the first digits of the publication year that follows ("200", "199", "201"). In short, the point where an author name gives way to the citation year. Activation is highest in lists of several references.

Final tokens of person names in author lists (mostly academic paper bylines), usually the closing surname fragment or initials, often just before a comma, affiliation marker, superscript, or line break.

A diffuse, weak feature of scientific and technical expository prose (abstracts, papers, explanations in physics, materials science, biology, and math). It fires on scattered tokens within explanatory sentences: function words (the, of, that, is, with), clause-ending punctuation, and key technical nouns or phrases such as range, distance, phase transition and temperature dependence. It peaks on phrases describing physical quantities, conditions, or findings.

Technical and scientific descriptions of physical experimental setups and methods, such as samples, apparatus, materials, dimensions, placement or mounting of objects, and measurement procedures. Activation spreads across whole clauses describing how something is prepared, positioned or configured (e.g. 'placing 10 μL on copper grids', 'glued to a 10mm-thick board', 'suspended in water'). Function words and prepositions in these descriptions fire along with the nouns, and spatial-relation words like 'near', 'under', 'through' and 'at' also activate weakly in other contexts.

Tokens inside institutional affiliation and address strings, typically from academic paper author headers. The strongest activations fall on the commas, connectors ("of", "and") and words like "University", "Department" and "Centre" that join nested units (lab, department, university, city). Weaker activation appears on similar organization-name text in prose.

Sentence-ending punctuation (periods, often merged with paragraph breaks or closing parentheses) in formal academic, scientific, or legal expository prose, marking a boundary just before a new sentence or section. Discourse connectives that open the following sentence (e.g. "That is", "however", "but") and the first token after the break sometimes activate weakly.

Language describing transitions, contrasts or changes between two states, phases, categories or forms (e.g. "from liquid to plasma", "transition from first form to the second", "wet-to-dry", "chaotic or non-chaotic", "transformed into"), mostly in scientific or technical text. It fires most strongly on the connecting words (from, to, into, between, and/or, non-) and on the names of the contrasted states.

Opening bracket or parenthesis (mostly " [", also " (" and superscript "(^") that begins a numbered citation reference in academic/scientific text, typically right after a claim or author name. Weaker activation on periods or commas that directly precede superscript citation numbers or separate citation numbers.

Line breaks (and trailing markers like *, }, superscript-number syntax) right after the author-name list in academic paper headers, marking the transition to the affiliation block (Department, University, \textsuperscript{1}, "Affiliations:") or to the abstract. Weaker activations occur on similar header and metadata breaks.

Discourse transition points where a new clause or section begins, most strongly the contrastive connective "However/however" (sentence-initial or parenthetical between commas). Weaker hits fall on other boundary tokens that open new content: sentence-starting "There" or "Let", the comma after "said" before a quote, numbering periods, list-item spaces, and structural markup such as "thead" or "\begin".
