over.name: Phrases in technical or instructional text that spell out what an operation or task does and what it acts on, such as its object, target, range or parameters. Activation is strongest in code comments, docstrings and log messages describing a function's action (e.g. 'summarize points based off of HexID', 'for tickers, in date range… pull into a dataframe', 'adds an event binding to label one'). Weaker activation appears on similar descriptive object or argument phrases in programming questions, math problems and how-to steps.

Words tied to programming, software code and computing. It fires most strongly on "code", "programming", "coding" and code-block markers or language tags (```golang, ```swift, "Code Implementation"). Weaker activation falls on source-code keywords and package names (package, namespace, System.Text, .github), on software/tech terms, and on generic technical or work-related nouns.

Later items in enumerated lists or series (comma/and/or-separated, or run-on menus and tags): the final items, the separators and conjunctions leading up to them, and the closing element of the enumeration. Activation rises toward the end of the list.

Function, method, class and library identifiers in code, especially the name being called or imported (often right after a dot or ::, before an opening parenthesis), e.g. .get, .write_all, sprintf, WriteLine, Mutex, info. Weaker activation on similar call-like tokens such as LaTeX commands (eqnarray, limsup), shell commands (curl) and URL domain parts (.com, .org).

Punctuation, whitespace or newline tokens (colons, commas, line breaks, spaces, opening quotes/brackets) that come right after an unfinished phrase, often a preposition or introducing word like "is", "by", "that" or "because". They mark a break just before the expected continuation, such as a list, formula, quote, URL or name.

Comparison and relational operators, strongest for symbolic inequality operators (>, <, >=, <=) in code conditionals and math, weaker for LaTeX forms (\leq, \geq, >), word equivalents (above, below, exceeds, between, within, at least), and breadcrumb '>' separators.

A weak, diffuse feature that mostly fires on subword continuation tokens completing rare or unfamiliar names, acronyms and identifiers, such as the later pieces of personal names, product or company names, chemical labels and code variables. The piece is typically the second or later chunk of a word split into fragments. It occasionally fires on ordinary words or numbers in a noun phrase, with low activation.

Section/chapter numbering and identifier tokens in structured references: digits and separators in chapter/section numbers, LaTeX \label{sec:intro}/{s1} keys, figure filenames, DOIs, URL path IDs, and index codes. Peaks on the number or key that names a section or item (e.g. the "1" in \label{s1}).

A weak, diffuse pattern centered on short symbolic tokens in structured or technical text. Most often these are single-letter variables, indices, subscripts, exponents or numbers inside LaTeX formulas, equations and code arguments (e.g. e^{-t}, n m, uf.join(5, 6)). It also fires on formatting fragments such as table tags and on highly predictable completions in boilerplate text (New Zealand, skip to navigation).

Weak, diffuse activations on parts of technical names and terms, mostly in computing and software contexts: tool, OS and language names (Azure CLI/PowerShell, SSH, Solaris, R, edgeR), code identifiers and modules (csv.writer, /bin, ENV, .bat), and the second or later subword of multi-token proper nouns or brand names (Star Trek, Cartoon, Bashner). The strongest firing is on software tools and shell or CLI names.

A diffuse feature that fires mostly in structured or technical text on short, slot-filling tokens. These include newly introduced single-letter variable names in code and math (g, h, z, q, x, D), page numbers after dotted leaders in tables of contents, and the '>' newline after '<thead' in HTML tables. It also fires weakly on scattered function words in prose (as, between, via, the).

Tokens that repeat an identifier or word that appeared just before, most strongly a variable reused on the right side of its own reassignment (e.g. k = k^2, j = j + 1, line = line.strip(), m_hp = m_hpMax). Weaker activations fall on other near-copies of recent tokens, such as repeated names, terms, numbers or registers.

Delimiter and boundary tokens that close one item or row and begin the next in a structured, repeating sequence: line breaks after affiliation addresses, table/list row separators ("|⏎|", " \\⏎", "), ("), code line endings and indentation, and sentence- or stanza-ending punctuation. Activation is strongest on the row breaks of tables and aligned numeric columns.

Whitespace and line-break tokens, chiefly newlines that come after spaces or tabs (blank or trailing-whitespace lines). It is strongest on indented empty lines inside code and LaTeX blocks, and weaker on ordinary paragraph breaks after punctuation. Scattered word-fragment tokens get only faint activation.

A diffuse feature that fires on tokens inside structured, repetitive, non-prose text such as code, HTML/XML tables and tags, LaTeX math, file paths, and spec lists. It is strongest on HTML table markup (td/tr tags, closing brackets and newlines between cells) and on parts of identifiers in code. It seems to respond to tokens whose form is predictable from a repeating template or syntax pattern.

A diffuse, weakly firing feature on structural boundary tokens in formatted or scraped text: paragraph breaks (often right after a sentence-final period), list and enumeration spacing, separators such as hyphens and slashes, LaTeX \begin, and HTML tag ends. It fires most where the content shifts abruptly to a new, often unrelated segment, such as spliced spam sentences or a change of section.

Induction/copying: fires on a word or subword that repeats one appearing earlier in the same text (names, acronyms, terms, numbers, code strings), usually at the start of the repeated phrase, where it can be predicted by copying the earlier occurrence.

Tokens that introduce the divisor in a division or modulo operation. Most often this is "by" after divide/divided/divisible, but it also covers equivalents such as "with", "por", "of" (in "multiple of"), and "_by". Symbolic forms fire too: ÷, /, /=, %, mod, the }{ between numerator and denominator in \frac, and the comma before the divisor argument in function calls. Weaker activations appear on other arithmetic operators like "multiply by", minus and "equal to".

A diffuse feature with weak activation on many ordinary mid-sequence tokens, such as function words, list items, dates and phone-number digits. It fires most strongly inside arithmetic or mathematical expressions, peaking on operators like ÷ and minus, parentheses and numeric operands (e.g., "÷ 2 - ( 8 - 6 )", "+(-3)", "C/360").

The digit "3" as a standalone number token in numeric, mathematical, code, or tabular contexts (coefficients, decimals, operands, list items). It fires most strongly when 3 is a coefficient or term in an algebraic expression. It rarely fires on the word "three".

Opening delimiters that begin a value right after a key or assignment, e.g. an opening quote following '=' or ':' in code, config and JSON/YAML (sometimes '{' or '['), and opening <td>/<th> tags that start an HTML table cell.

Opening punctuation or markup tokens (quotes, brackets, asterisks, #, parentheses, HTML tags) placed right before the first word of a title, heading, quotation, or other delimited span. These usually appear at the start of a line or after a colon or label.

Placeholder or toy values in code, math, and examples. These are typically the first in a sequence: single-letter variable names (a, x, A), sample literals (1, 'a', "hello", 'bob'), and first elements of arrays or tuples. They appear in demo code, function parameters, and abstract statements ('state A', 'if A ⊢ B').

The final token of a function, method, command or operator name right before its arguments are applied, usually the last subword of an identifier right before an opening parenthesis (e.g. make_feed_request(, url_for(, add(). This also covers math functions and operators acting on operands (f(x), ReLU(x), \div, ->, *().

Closing delimiter tokens that end a nested or paired span, most strongly doubled closing braces "}}" in LaTeX subscripts, \text{}, \frac, \sqrt and template expressions. It fires more weakly on other closers: markdown bold "**", closing quotes, generic-type ">>" or ">", ")}", "})" and HTML closing tags.

Function words that come right before a name, label, description or quotation is applied to something, most strongly "as"/"as a" after verbs of naming or describing (referred to as, known as, describing it as, called). Also covers similar connectors such as "called", "a" after calls/calling, and the colons, commas and opening quotes that introduce quoted characterizations.

Short value-like content tokens in math, code and structured data, such as numbers, single-letter variables, string literals and dictionary keys. They often sit right after =, (, quotes or currency symbols. Many repeat or are determined by earlier context (e.g. a repeated bid amount, a variable or answer value), though there is a weak scattering of ordinary words too.

The strong activations are on the bodies of anonymous C/C++-style union and struct declarations: the opening brace, the indentation, member types and names (e.g. "float all[", "long long", "double d"), and the closing ";" or "};". Weak activations elsewhere fall on structural and list markers such as numbering, bullets, braces, newlines and indentation, plus occasional connective words.

Separators that come right after a URI scheme or resource prefix, mostly "://" (http, https, ftp, s3, postgresql, res, gs). Also fires on related prefix delimiters: ":" in jdbc:/dbi:/jar:/steam:, "mailto:", and "\\" or "//" at the start of a path. Activation is strongest for less common schemes such as postgresql, res, ftp and s3, and weaker for ordinary http/https.

Placeholder or redacted content standing in for missing, unknown or user-supplied information, such as "YOUR_API_KEY", "<username>", "N/A", "No Data", "TBD", "xxxx", "##", blanks, ellipses, masked digits or censored words.

Binary operators and connectives (+, −, →, ×, or) that come right after a closed parenthesis or bracketed group in math or code, joining it to the next expression. The feature also fires weakly and constantly on "content" in the web boilerplate "Skip to main content".

A diffuse, low-level context feature for technical computing text, especially networking, internet, web-browser and security topics (TCP, sockets, SSL, Tor, VPN, packets, scripts) and source code. It fires weakly on scattered tokens rather than on any single word type: function words, verbs, punctuation, and code indentation or closing braces. It is somewhat stronger on phrases about whether connections or functions work or fail (e.g., "seems to work ok", "loose some packets", "even when i allow").

The element name inside a closing markup tag: HTML/XML (, , ), BBCode ([/size], [/i]) and LaTeX \end{table}/\end{figure}. It fires on the word right after the closing slash or \end{, marking the end of a block. Weak, scattered activations also occur on other end-of-segment tokens such as code fences, closing brackets and line breaks.

Output/print statements in code across many languages (print, println, printf, cout <<, Console.WriteLine, echo, System.out.println, warn), firing on the print function name and its accompanying syntax such as the opening paren/quote, format specifiers (%d, {0}, \n), stream operators/endl and the closing paren/semicolon. Weakly fires on a few output-like prose words.

The token that comes right after a noun for a table or other structured display (table, chart, figure, diagram, template, box, list, tree, field, Table class), most often in tabular contexts. Usually this is a function word or punctuation continuing the phrase (to, for, in, are, be, comma, colon), or the markup that follows a table opening tag: '>' plus newline after <table, or ']' and '\' after \begin{table}. LaTeX table environments activate most strongly.

Fires very strongly on "imgur" in image-hosting URLs (especially ".imgur" in i.imgur.com), and somewhat on similar site-name pieces of URLs such as "reddit" in reddit.com. All other activations are faint: the leading space or bullet at the start of list items, numbered-list digits, and paragraph breaks.

First element of a coordinate pair or tuple, plus the comma after it, mostly in code and math (e.g. Point(50f, 50f), [0, 1], (3, 4)), with the x-coordinate activating most strongly. Weaker activation appears on other index or coordinate tokens inside arrays and point lists.

Mostly in math formulas and code, the token that completes a binary operation, i.e. the right-hand operand directly after an operator such as /, *, ^, + or %. This is typically a denominator, divisor, multiplier or exponent (numbers, variables, slash-variables like /n or /M). Activation is strongest when that operand ends a parenthesized or bracketed sub-expression, just before the closing ) or }. There are a few weak, scattered activations on ordinary prose words.

Words for rounding numbers (round, rounds, rounded, rounding, round off/up/down to), used for numeric approximation in math, programming and data reporting. Related terms like 'nearest', 'approximation' and the Russian 'округление' fire weakly.

A token that starts a new word glued directly onto the word before it with no space, as in compound identifiers, usernames, emails, URLs, code variable names, acronym chains and chemical names (e.g. noInitialize, newlab, acsmeetings, condgrad). Activation is moderate and fires on the second or later word part. Rare weak hits occur on ordinary function words.

The token "width", most strongly as an attribute or property name in HTML/CSS/code (width="…", width: …px), and more weakly in prose about dimensions. Rare weak hits on lookalikes such as "with" and "setw".

Punctuation, mostly an opening parenthesis (sometimes a bracket, dash or space), that comes right after a title, name or heading, especially near the start of a document, and opens a parenthetical or subtitle-like addition such as an acronym, year, credit, version or clarification.

Words naming collections or container data structures, i.e. a group of multiple elements. These include programming types like list, array, vector, tuple, set, map, Vec, HashSet, Container and seq, and general or mathematical terms like collection, set, sequence, series, mixture and samples. Activation is strongest on list, set, collection and Vec.

Tokens containing the letter sequence "ip"/"pip", especially the standalone word-start "pip" (Python's pip install, pipette, pipeline, Pippen, Piper). It fires most strongly on the Python package manager and on pipettes. Weaker activations appear for "pipe"/"piping" and for mid-word fragments like "ipp" (Kippur), "iper" (piperidine, Piper) and "IP".

Fires on the first token of a condition, right after a conditional or logical keyword (if, elif, else if, match, or, ||, &&). This is usually an opening parenthesis, a variable name, or 'the' or '$' in prose and math 'if' clauses. It marks the start of a boolean condition or clause.

A weak, diffuse feature that fires sparsely on scattered tokens, most often in text about reality, existence and the limits of knowledge: whether something is "really there" or "actually" happened, nobody really knowing, observation and measurement, causality, conditional independence, existence versus essence, Occam's razor, the universe/World. Many hits are on function words or name fragments with no clear shared meaning.

Tokens in the concluding step of a calculation or logical argument, where a result is derived or stated (e.g., "so the least amount is 301", "therefore ΔG < 0", "we get that P is also…", "= 1900", "Nm=3000 rpm"). The strongest activations fall on inference words (therefore, so, thus, hence, we get that, implies, means) and on the final value or statement that follows them, mostly in math, physics and code contexts.

Tokens that complete a highly predictable, formulaic unit, such as the final word of boilerplate phrases ("Best regards", "properly cited", "Getty Images", "In conclusion", "standard output"), measurement units after numbers (lb, MB), and closing code, LaTeX or HTML elements. These often fall right before a line break or punctuation that ends the segment.

The main verb or predicate, plus the words right after it, in titles, headings and questions, especially after "How to", "What is" or "Is it possible". It fires most strongly on action verbs that state the task or topic (filter, evaluate, replace, use, represent, administer).

An opening quotation mark or backtick (often with a leading space) that introduces a quoted name, term, title, UI label, command, or code identifier, usually right after a word like "the", "a", "click", or "called". Activation is highest when the quote encloses a technical or interface element such as a button, menu, tag, or keyword.

Programming code, especially string-searching and slicing logic that locates substrings (find/indexOf/substring) and computes offsets with lengths. It peaks on statement endings like ');⏎' and ')⏎', the assignments that follow them, and the index variables. Elsewhere in code and prose it fires only weakly on punctuation, line ends and loop or operator tokens.

Words derived from the root "calcul-" (calculate, calculation, calculated, calculator, calculus, calc), plus a few weaker hits on synonyms such as computation. They appear across math, science, code and everyday contexts, and fire most strongly on verb and noun forms meaning to compute something.

Coordinate pairs and tuples, mostly in code: commas, spaces and numbers separating x/y values in calls like Point(0, 0), moveTo(x, y) or arrays such as [[0, 0], ...]. Also fires on the 'y' variable in coordinate contexts and on space-separated number pairs or dimensions (e.g. 6 6, 1179 x 2556). Weak, scattered activation on unrelated prose tokens.

A diffuse, low-specificity feature that fires on the first token of a new name, term or code identifier, usually the first piece of a multi-token word. Examples include "Calc" in Calcitriol, "Cust" in CustCNV, "Process" in ProcessedLine and "tf". It also fires on separators and structural tokens such as "::", "{", "-", the dot in section numbers and commas in lists, mostly in technical, code or list-like text.

A diffuse feature with low, fairly uniform activations. It fires mostly on predictable tokens inside repetitive or templated text: unit-conversion pages, tables, lists, code, date sequences and repeated headings such as 'Fuel Cost from' or 'Angle Unit Converter'. The marked token typically continues a pattern already seen earlier in the context, which suggests copying or induction rather than any specific meaning.

Diffusely activates on tokens in contexts about challenges, puzzles, contests, and submissions, such as competitive-programming sites (HackerRank, 'Problem D', solved-problem tables), homework or math problems, game jams, competitions, rankings, and site boilerplate around them. The strongest hits are words like 'Problem', 'solution', 'find', 'submission', 'Runtime' and 'however'.

Names and terms tied to software frameworks, tools and web-dev tooling, especially PHP/web frameworks (strongest on "Laravel") and database-migration vocabulary (migrate, migrations, Migration, settings). Also fires weakly on completions of tech product and library names (Metasploit, Tailwind, Alamofire, OpenFOAM, PHP-FPM, Joomla) and framework identifiers in code (.Router, create_app, .Set, Application_Start).

A diffuse, weak feature that fires on tokens inside fixed names, titles and identifiers in structured or boilerplate web text, such as site or product names, section headers, menu items, URL path segments, DOI prefixes and code strings. It often lands on the first word of a heading or name, or on a line break right after one, where the following text is a predictable fixed label rather than free prose.

In source code, the whitespace indentation (or line-ending newline/semicolon) that starts the line right after a variable is initialized to an empty or zero value (x = 0, [] , {}, set(), ""). It fires most strongly when a loop (for/while) that uses that variable comes next, marking the transition from setup to loop body.

Numeric tokens in math contexts, especially perfect squares and powers (9, 25, 49, 81, 225, 441, 256, 125/625, 216) and computed results or answers (after '=' or 'result in'). The strongest activations fall on final digits of multi-digit numbers in number-pattern puzzles. Scattered weak activations on unrelated words are noise.

Functions and properties that measure or aggregate something, such as len, sum, size, .shape, .length, gcd and max, especially when called on a collection in code. In prose it picks up the matching measure phrases ("length of", "number of", "deviation of", "multiplicity of") and the "of" that links a quantity to what it describes. Activation is strongest for len/sum used as divisors and for size().

Special reserved identifiers and keywords in code that refer to the current context or module: mostly Python dunder names (__main__, __name__, __file__, __class__), Rust "use super::", os.getcwd/"current directory", ThisWorkbook, and the blog "<!--more-->" marker. Activation falls on the keyword itself, strongest for dunder names.

Line boundaries in code just before a new statement begins: closing tokens with a newline (")⏎", ");⏎", "))⏎") and leading indentation whitespace (or comment markers). Activation is strongest when the next line repeats a similar statement, especially consecutive print/assert/EXPECT/println calls.

Closing brackets, mostly ")" but also "]", "}", and LaTeX \right, that end a parenthesized or bracketed group. They fire most strongly when the group closes an arithmetic or code expression, such as (v * 100.0) or (1 + max * 2), before an operator or cast follows. Weaker activations occur on closing parentheses in prose, phone area codes, and citations.

Leading whitespace/indentation tokens at the start of a line, typically right after a newline and just before a bullet point (•), numbered list item or indented code/config line. Occasional weak hits on separators like commas, "and", "by" or quote-reply markers.

Tracks state that changes step by step, especially quantities being reduced over time. In code it fires on loop-state variables and their updates: while/if conditions, mutated variables (n /= i, x = x - 2, self.position +=) and the statements that follow them. In prose it fires on remaining or diminishing amounts, such as supply dwindling, the remaining error being smaller, days remaining, or 'this leaves eighteen'. Activations are mostly weak and diffuse.

Runs of whitespace (spaces or tabs) used for indentation or alignment, especially at the beginning of a line after a newline in formatted text, code, addresses, or documents. There is weaker activation on a few scattered tokens in boilerplate or structured text, such as "should" in "Correspondence should be addressed".

The right-hand side of an assignment in code, i.e. the value or expression being stored into a variable, strongest on the variable name just after "=" (e.g. "= b;", "= score;", "= tt;"). Weaker activation appears on function arguments, indices and other operands that supply a value.

Conditional range and comparison logic, mostly in code: comparison and modulo operators, logical &&/and, and the numeric thresholds in if-conditions. It also fires on prose range boundaries such as 'between 0 and 4' or 'from 18 until 59'. Activation is far strongest on leap-year divisibility checks (year % 4 / 100 / 400); elsewhere it is weak and diffuse.

A weak, diffuse feature. It fires on tokens that link a preceding subject or left-hand side to what comes next. The clearest cases are equals signs in code assignments and math equations, along with nearby variable names and numbers. In prose, it fires on verbs, auxiliaries and prepositions that directly follow a noun phrase (e.g. 'had', 'has', 'is moving', 'between', 'from the'). Activation is generally low, and slightly higher in code and math contexts.

The token "usr" (or "/usr"), almost always as the Unix/Linux system directory in file paths such as /usr/bin, /usr/local and /usr/share. It fires most strongly in path contexts and only weakly on "usr" as a letter sequence inside words or names (e.g., "Susruta", "Nusrat"). Rare weak hits on commas, spaces and other stray tokens are noise.

Words built on the root 'condition' (conditional, conditioned, conditionally, unconditional, Condiciones), firing hardest on 'conditional' in probability and logic contexts. It responds more weakly to related words for dependence or qualification, such as contingent, contingency, categorical, qualified and cautiously.

Units of measurement that follow a number, covering length, time, angle, pixel and screen, percent and dosage units (inch, cm, px, ms, °, pixels, DPI, mg, yrs, %). The strongest cases are display and size units such as px, pixels and inch.

Structural delimiters in structured or code-like text, chiefly the HTML "<thead" tag that opens a table, plus assignment operators (" =") after variable names in code and other separators such as table-cell tags, colons after keys or labels, and whitespace or newlines before list items. Activations are weak overall.

Relational connective tokens linking two sides of an expression, especially in math/LaTeX. Activation is strongest on “to” / “\to” denoting convergence or mapping (e.g. “converges weakly … to”, “u_n \to u_0”). It is moderate on “=”, “\equiv”, “\cdot” and the start of a right-hand side. Weak, diffuse firing appears on ordinary verbs or prepositions that link a subject to its object or complement (“depends on”, “has a”, “as”, “with”).

Tokens that sit mid-sequence inside repetitive, structured content such as numeric tables, grids, lists, arrays, code literals, filenames and enumerations. Numbers are the most common case, e.g. table cells, grid values, complex-number components and digits in IDs. Some non-numeric list items also fire, such as list entries, table field names and repeated characters.

Separator and formatting tokens (line breaks, comment markers like #, //, *, pipes, bullets, indentation) in document headers and metadata blocks, usually right after or before items such as titles, dates, authors and filenames. Comment-prefix tokens inside file header comments are the strongest cases.

The first value or number token right after an assignment/equals sign, operator or opening bracket, usually in math or code (e.g. "x = 1", "n = 77", "[2, 3"). It fires most on the first numeral or digit of the value being set. There are weaker, sporadic activations on other tokens.

Tokens that repeat or mirror an earlier token within a parallel, list-like or symmetric structure (e.g., the second item in a pair like "t1[1] == t2[1]", "eddie smith and joan smith", "opposite face", repeated values in parallel lines or code). The activation falls on the copied element that completes the parallel pattern.

under.name: Author bylines and affiliation blocks, especially at the start of academic papers. It fires on author names, the commas and 'and' between them, superscript affiliation numbers/markers (strongest), institution/department names, and nearby emails, dates and headers. It fires weakly on similar credit or attribution text elsewhere (bylines, 'Author', contact info).

Names of organizations and institutions, mostly government agencies, departments, and official bodies (e.g., USDA, NASA, Centers for Disease Control, Bureau of Land Management, police, ministry, commissioner), including acronym pieces and the final words of multi-word agency names. Activation is strongest on the head or last word of the agency name.

Words tied to the submission, filing, pending or publication status of documents. It is strongest on patent filings ("application", "Ser. No.", "divisional of", "filed") and also covers manuscripts or papers "submitted", "received", "preliminary", "ongoing", "pending" and "Manuscript". It also fires weakly on other metadata nouns such as paper, dissertation, publication, doi and arXiv.

Fires most strongly across spans of biblical or scriptural verse and archaic religious prose, such as quoted passages from Daniel, Luke, Psalms and Corinthians (e.g. 'thy', 'the flesh', 'Rahab and Babylon'), building up through the quoted phrase. There are weak, scattered activations on ordinary content words (verbs, nouns, adjectives) in other texts.

Tokens inside bibliographic citations and references, such as years, page numbers, volume numbers, DOI segments, journal names with their punctuation, dates, and legal case names (e.g. 'v.'). Activation is weak and spread across these elements, peaking on page ranges and DOI or date parts.

Weak, diffuse activation that is strongest on technical/scientific text, especially methods and results passages of papers. It fires on nouns naming the measured quantity, method or subject (volume, imaging, data, parameters, size), on passive reporting verbs (was measured, were analysed, assessed), and on sentence boundaries that introduce them ('. The', '. Inf').

Names of actors and performers, especially the final token of a surname, in casting or role contexts (e.g., "played by X", "starring", cast lists, "X would be playing"). Other personal names and name fragments activate weakly.

The word "method(s)"/"methodology" and other research-paper section headings (Materials and Methods, Experimental Procedures, Introduction, Results, Related Work, References), strongest on "Methods" headers in scientific abstracts and papers.

A weak, diffuse feature that mostly fires in technical, scientific or technology writing, especially about engineered materials, devices and methods such as nanostructures, polymers, porous carriers, sensors, assays and therapies. It lands on the content nouns of these passages (materials, devices, approaches) and on the connective words that follow them when describing function or purpose ("that", "to overcome", "to reduce", "and", "itself").

Words about crowds and mass public gatherings, especially protests and demonstrations: rallies, protesters gathering, petitions, protest votes, days of action, parades, celebrations, applause and cheering crowds, plus collective nouns such as multitude, groups and armada. The strongest responses are on explicit protest or demonstration terms, with weak scattered firing on surrounding context words.

Separators and numbers in academic citation references marking the transition from volume/issue to page numbers: the colon, space, or parenthesis after a volume/issue number, the first page number, and the dash in page ranges (e.g. "243:646–648", "82, 65-82").

Nouns, usually the final token of a proper name, for geographic places and political entities (countries, states, cities, regions) and, less strongly, organizations or groups tied to them. Typical contexts are locative ones like "in X", "from X", "around the world" and "abroad". Country names that stand for a national government or actor activate most strongly.

Function words and phrase content within adverbial or prepositional phrases that set the temporal or circumstantial backdrop for the main event (e.g. 'at a time when…', 'as the national debate shifts from…', 'on the eve of an election', 'during', 'after', 'following a', 'due to the', 'delayed by a fire drill'). Activation is strongest on extended 'when/as…' context clauses describing ongoing situations.

Names of bibliographic and literature-search databases, especially the completing subword tokens of names like EMBASE, MEDLINE, CINAHL, PsycINFO and Scopus, plus the word "database(s)" and similar index names, mostly in systematic-review search descriptions. The strongest activation is on "ASE" in EMBASE. Weak activations also appear on stray list or formatting tokens.

Scientific and technical process descriptions, mainly physical or chemical, that involve supplying, moving or treating substances. It responds most to phrases about introducing gases, reagents or particles into a system, such as feeding a hydrocarbon gas or admitting gases. It also responds to related process vocabulary like temperature, transport, solutions, baths, material removed from surfaces and dissolving agents.

HTTP request type tokens in web code, strongest on "HttpServletRequest" (in javax.servlet.http imports or as a servlet method parameter), with weaker activation on related request/context/session types (Request, HttpContext, HttpSession) and other framework parameter types such as JoinPoint, Model and CancellationToken. Non-code text is near zero.

Terms for health and well-being outcome measures, peaking on "quality of life" (especially "life") and its abbreviation QoL. It also fires on related outcome constructs and instruments (disability, health perceptions, EQ-5D, QALY, VAS), on parts of similar acronyms like QoS/QoE, and weakly on scattered other tokens.

Strongly fires on ".Collectors" in Java "import java.util.stream.Collectors;" lines. It responds weakly to related collection/utility tokens in code, such as Rust ".collect()" on iterators, ".ContextCompat" and "Itertools" imports, and to the "202" year prefix in dates.

Postal address unit designators that come right before a number, most strongly "PO Box" and its variants (P.O. Box, BP, C.P., GPO Box, CP), plus the following space. Weaker activations occur on similar address labels such as Suite, Room, Apt, #, Street/Highway, and UMR.

Subword fragments inside personal names, mostly non-English given names (especially Chinese, Korean, Thai and other Asian names) in author lists and bylines. It fires most strongly on the middle or later pieces of multi-token or hyphenated given names (e.g. "-Ki", "-Ho", "ih", "h").

Words naming prisons and the penal/correctional system, especially as part of facility or agency names (Correctional, Corrections, correction officers, jail, prison, penitentiary, Shawshank, San Quentin, Department of Justice). The strongest are 'correction(al)' forms. Other institution-name heads (Hospital, Convalescent, College of Education) fire weakly.

The final digit of the DOI registrant prefix (e.g. the last digit in "10.1371", "10.1109", or the "/j" after "10.1016"), i.e. the point where the publisher prefix ends and the slash begins the suffix in DOI citations.

Language describing selection, qualification, or allocation rules: who or what gets chosen, ranked, or advances (top teams, largest party, most votes, minimum/maximum limits, fractions of a group, candidates picked). The strongest activations fall on ranking and qualifying phrases in electoral, competition, and admission procedures.

Words marking the endpoint of a process or movement, such as the final destination, recipient, or end-use stage where something ends up or gets used (e.g., 'before installation', 'prior to utilization', 'distribution to individual people', 'end users', 'to those who need them', 'returned to their homes'). The strongest activations fall on use and consumption stages like installation, utilization and feeding.

Academic degree and graduation contexts, especially the tokens describing when, where, or what degree was earned (e.g., "degree in", "graduated from … in", "for the degree of"). It fires most strongly on the final digit of a graduation or award year ("B.A. degree in 1928"), and weakly on similar completion or award dates and on thesis boilerplate.
The speaker in a dialogue attribution: a pronoun or name (often its last subword) right after a closing quotation mark or quoted speech, naming who said the line (e.g. '"...," he said').

The format-type word that ends a scientific journal's name, especially 'Letters' or its abbreviation 'Lett'. It fires most strongly in 'Phys. Rev. Lett.' and in 'PhysRevLett' inside DOIs. Weaker activations come from similar journal-name endings such as Communications/Comm, ONE, Express and Reports, and from 'Short Communication' article labels.

Words naming the method, technique or approach used to carry out a procedure, chiefly in medicine and surgery (minimally invasive, laparoscopy/arthroscopy, robotic, laser, open, orthotopic, epidural). It fires most strongly on 'invasive'/'vasive' and also responds weakly to technique modifiers in other technical fields (batch, no-till, gel-free, RF discharge).

Words naming an institution, organizational unit, program, service or facility (e.g. Extension, Institute, Department, Lab, Centre, office, programs, services), often the head noun or acronym tail of an organization's name, plus nearby text describing what the organization offers or does.

The preposition "on" (and equivalents like Dutch "op", "starting") introducing a temporal expression — a date or weekday — especially after event or publication verbs (took place, born, launched, posted, submitted). It fires more weakly on locative or platform uses of "on".

The last token of a person's name, most often the surname after a first name or title, strongest for well-known political leaders (President Obama/Trump/Biden, Roosevelt). When the surname is split into pieces, the final subword fires (e.g. Gorbache-v, Hickenlo-oper), usually where the name is the subject about to say or do something.

Fires most strongly on the ".bind" segment of Java import paths (org.springframework.web.bind, javax.xml.bind) and on ".HttpServlet" in javax.servlet.http, i.e. a package segment within repeated import statements. Weaker activations occur on the optional-plural marker "(s" in form-style labels (Genre(s), Subject(s), Programme(s)) and on separators in repetitive boilerplate lists (semicolons in OEIS link lists, list dashes).

Final tokens or subwords that complete a multi-token proper name, especially titles of games, films, albums, products or series. These are often sequel numbers or subtitles ("2", "VI", "Fallen Kingdom", "Jr"), and the model predicts them once the name's opening is recognized.

Words naming infrastructure, utilities, public services and institutions that serve a locality or community (government services, post/mail, courthouses, police, hospitals, railways, wastewater, outlets, area codes, banks and companies operating in a town), plus phrases describing what connects to or supplies a place (e.g., 'railway reached Putney', 'blood supply from the artery'). Activation is strongest in local-geography or civic-amenity contexts.

Tokens inside proper names of institutions, especially hospitals, medical centers, universities and research institutes. Activation falls on the name-continuing words or word pieces after the first word (e.g., 'Hospital', 'Medical Center', 'Health', 'Museum', or the rest of a split name) and is strongest for hospital and medical-center names.

Words referring to a written work or study being discussed, mainly papers, articles, reports, studies, books and reviews ("this paper", "the study in question", "the report notes", "this article is well written"). It also fires on nearby discourse boundaries, such as the punctuation, commas and line breaks after author names, citations or sentence ends that lead into a summary of what the work found or claims.

Academic and research administrative boilerplate covering funding acknowledgments, ethics and review approvals (ethics committees, IRBs, IACUC), regulatory and supervisory bodies, trial registrations, and author/affiliation metadata. Activation lands on the function words and nouns that link to the approving or funding body ("approved by the", "funded", "support from", "Council", "Ethics Board") and is strongest on ethics and oversight terms.

A diffuse, low-specificity feature firing on mid-sentence connective tokens, mostly prepositions, determiners (especially "the" after a preposition or verb) and verb/preposition complements, that open or continue a phrase leading to an upcoming noun object (e.g. "in the development of", "targeted by the", "find out the"). It has no clear semantic theme.

Personal names, especially first names (and the start of full names), of authors, reporters, photographers, or people being quoted. These often appear in bylines, credits, or contact lines after cues like "By", "Author:", "Photo:", or "said". Activation is strongest on the given name, weaker on surnames and on surrounding punctuation or initials.

Words describing investigation, discovery and evidence-gathering, such as searching, finding, examining, tracking down, suspecting, proving or identifying something. These show up mostly in police, crime, legal or detective contexts, e.g. interviewing, finding sufficient evidence, or information leading to identification. Activation is strongest on the action verbs and on 'evidence/information' phrases.

The subword token "raf" inside words, firing most strongly on the middle of "zebrafish" (zeb-raf-ish). It fires only weakly on "raf" in other words such as Musharraf, Ashraf, Trafalgar and dabrafenib, and weakly on other fragments of model-organism or fish names.

Words for blood cancers, mostly the 'leukemia/leukaemia' token or its suffix pieces (strongest), plus their abbreviations (AML, CML, CLL, DLBCL) and the '-oma'/'-coma' endings of lymphoma, myeloma, sarcoma, glioma and similar tumor names.

Multi-character tokens that begin a recurring technical or web identifier: ":b" in the boilerplate "tag:blogger.com" ID, ".TimeUnit" in Java "java.util.concurrent" imports, and ".azure" inside URLs/domains. These fire strongly. Ordinary prose words and punctuation, often the word just after a noun, fire only weakly.

Second part of compound honor or event names, chiefly "-Star" after "All" (e.g. All-Star Game). Activation is strongest for capitalized sports "All-Star" and weaker for lowercase "all-star" lineups and similar forms (All-American, All-Pro, All-State). It also fires weakly on other award or event name completions such as Hall of Fame, Pro Bowl and Ryder Cup.

Tokens inside academic citations and bibliographic metadata, such as journal names, volume/issue numbers, page ranges, years, author-name separators, DOIs, and table-of-contents page numbers. Activation is strongest on the spaces, punctuation and numbers that sit between citation fields, for example the space before a volume or year.

Comparison operators in code conditionals, especially " !=" in Go's "if err != nil" error-checking idiom (strongest). It also fires on " ==" checks against nil, 0 or status codes, and only weakly on structural tokens like "<thead>" newlines or switch cases.

Geographic place names, mostly cities and towns, along with the words that set them up in location contexts: prepositions like "in"/"at", "including", "comprises of", and the commas and list separators in addresses and lists of places. The first subword of a multi-token place name (e.g. Kh-arkiv, Delf-t, Kiel) often fires as the model anticipates the location.

The word "treatment" and its forms (treat, treating, treatments), plus related words like management, diagnosis, cure, therapeutic, medication and solution. These mostly appear in medical contexts as the action applied to a disease or condition, often in the phrase "the treatment of [disease]". Activation is highest for "treatment" right after "the" or "for" when a named disease or condition follows.

Technical/physiological measurement terms, strongest for pulmonary function test terminology (vital capacity, FVC, FEV₁, forced expiratory volume/flow, airflow, airways). Weaker activation on other scientific quantities, variables and abbreviations (torque, Vmax, kcat, conduction velocity, perfusion).

The word "neck", most strongly when it refers to the literal body part (human or animal anatomy) or the neck of an object such as a guitar or jar. Weaker activation for idiomatic or compound uses like "breakneck", "neck of the woods" or "neck-and-neck", for "necklace", and for nearby body words like "head".

Words in narratives about people relocating or traveling between places, such as migration, immigration, arrival, departure, refugees and settling somewhere. The strongest activations fall on movement verbs (came, moved, arrived, leave) and on the prepositions and time phrases attached to them (to, in, from, a year, ago).

The "async" keyword in code, especially as a method modifier in C# function declarations (after public/private/static/override, before Task), also in Python/Rust async defs and related coroutine markers; weak, scattered activations on unrelated tokens.

Content words and connecting function words (prepositions, articles, of/in/on) inside dense technical or scientific prose, especially abstract-style descriptions of mechanisms, measurements, and processes (e.g., adsorption kinetics, electrical conduction, gene regulation). Activation is diffuse and spreads over noun phrases and the prepositional links between them, not over one particular word.

Methods-section language in scientific papers and abstracts. It fires on the transition into describing study design, participants, materials and procedures, such as "Methods", "Patients were investigated by", "N = 121", "was assessed via", "were available", and "is obtained by". It also catches sentence boundaries and section headers (INTRODUCTION, METHODS, Materials and Methods) that lead into these descriptions. Activation is strongest at the start of methodological statements about subjects, data sources and procedures.

Names of GUI widget classes in code import statements, mostly the class token after android.widget (TextView strongest, then Button, EditText, Toast, ListView, ImageView) and javax.swing (JLabel, JPanel, JButton), plus similar UI components in other frameworks (kivy Label, gtk Label, JavaFX). Activation sometimes extends weakly to the following semicolon/newline.

Words that refer back to a prominent person, usually a leader, politician or other public figure such as a president, monarch, general or coach. They are mostly possessive pronouns and possessive 's (his, her, their, Trump's), subject pronouns and relative "who". Activation is strongest in political or governing contexts, such as a person's administration, government, campaign, reign or office.

Fires overwhelmingly on the ".LoggerFactory" token in Java imports of "org.slf4j.LoggerFactory", usually right after "import org.slf4j.Logger;". It responds much more weakly to other final class names in dotted Java import paths (.Logger, .RequestMethod, .ActionListener, .Paths) and very faintly to scattered predictable boilerplate tokens ("ABSTRACT", "Wikipedia β", "SET NAMES").

The ".id" token immediately following "R" in Android Java resource references (R.id.xxx), typically inside findViewById() calls. Other R resource types such as ".string" activate weakly. Scattered weak activations on unrelated prose tokens appear to be noise.

The "-Co" token right after a hyphen in compound terms, strongest for SARS-CoV(-2). It is moderate in acetyl-/acyl-CoA and weak in chemical cobalt (Cu-Co, Sm-Co, WC-Co) or place and name compounds. A similar hyphenated-fragment case ("-se" in ChIP-seq/RNA-seq) and other scattered tokens activate only faintly.

Middle subword pieces inside rare technical or scientific words, mostly Latin or Greek taxonomic names of organisms (genera, families such as -idae or -oid forms, e.g. ixodid, Phytoseiulus, Pheidole, Bacillariophyceae) and other specialised terms. Activation is strongest on fragments within the word rather than at its start. There are occasional weak hits on ordinary words.

Sentence-ending punctuation (period, often fused with a paragraph break, or a closing parenthesis or bracket) at the end of a paragraph or section. It fires most strongly in scientific and methods-style writing, where the next text starts a new section, heading or step, such as Results or a methods subheading.

Tokens describing an opposing or rival party, especially a sports opponent: its name, its record or condition (e.g. win-loss record, struggles, strengths), and the verbs that state that condition (are, has, had, was). Activation is strongest in sports previews and match reports. It fires weakly on subjects and predicates that characterize a third-party entity in other contexts.

Numeric digits of a secondary or uncertainty value, firing most strongly on the number after ± (standard deviation or error margin) and also on standard errors, confidence bounds and tolerances. It fires weakly on other numbers that follow a primary value, such as the second column of a table or a percentage change.

The capitalized token "Json" (mostly ".Json") in code, peaking in namespace/package imports such as Newtonsoft.Json, System.Text.Json and javax.json.Json. It fires more weakly on Json in class or identifier names (JsonUtil, JsonParser). Faint activations on unrelated function words and punctuation are noise.

Weak, diffuse activation on economic and resource-flow language: supply, demand, capacity, production and quantity. It peaks on words like "supply", "capacity" and "production", on shortages, and on phrases such as "exceed supply", "as much as possible" and "produces more than". It also fires lightly on surrounding context about acquiring, distributing or scaling up amounts of goods, energy or resources.

Words naming behaviors, emotions, drives and physiological or psychological functions of organisms (feeding, eating, aggression, mood, motivation, fear, appetite, learning, memory, libido, responses), mostly in scientific or biomedical writing. The strongest hits are terms for behavioral and motivational processes. Weaker hits include cited author names in psychology and biology papers.

Opening tokens of in-text citations and reference markers in academic or encyclopedic writing, such as " [", ".[", " (", "\cite{", superscript markup and reference numbers, usually placed right after a claim or an author name like "et al.". The strongest activations are on " [" following author names or statements.

Mentions of the fruit fly Drosophila, strongest on the "ros" subword of "Drosophila" (weaker on "ila"/"aster" of melanogaster), plus words like "fly"/"flies" (especially as model organisms) and occasionally other model organism name fragments; weak spurious activation on "<thead>" newline tokens in tables.

Nouns (and some verbs) naming the source or venue through which information is communicated, typically after 'in a', 'according to', 'based on': study, report, interview, presentation, survey, statement, meeting, data, post. Activation is strongest for research or press sources used to attribute a claim.

Tokens inside titles and headlines, mostly article or blog headings, product pages, breadcrumbs and section headers, and especially the first such heading near the start of a document or right after a paragraph break. The signal is spread weakly across the words of a headline, with peaks on colons, 'Is'/'Vs', 'Everything to know about'-style phrasing and subject names.

Fires on the "Yugoslav" tokens (" Yugosl", " Yugoslavia"), most strongly in country and adjective uses, and on the matching "-osl-" and "-isl-" pieces inside Slavic names ending in "-slav" (Yaroslav, Stanislav, Branislav, Jaroslav, Miloslav). Weak firing on unrelated tokens is noise.

Prefix tokens of member/field variable names in code, chiefly the Hungarian-style "m" (as in m_foo, mFoo) and the leading underscore (_foo), plus occasional "g" for globals. They usually come right after return, this->, an opening parenthesis/bracket, or at the start of an assignment line. Activation is strongest for "m" followed by an underscore.

Low-intensity activations in expository, encyclopedic or scientific prose that explains how something works, is structured or is made. They fall mostly on the verbs, prepositions and articles that link a subject to its mechanism or property, just before the key noun phrase (e.g. 'occurs via', 'regulated through', 'stored in', 'contains a', 'made of a', 'has an').

Nouns (and related verbs) naming a position, title or role held by a person, especially leadership or authority roles such as president, emperor, director, chairman, commander, prime minister, host. They typically follow words like "become", "named", "as" or "the next".

Language about filling official positions through appointment, nomination, selection or election. The strongest hits are words like "appointed by", "nominee(s)/nomination" and "selected". It also fires on the officeholders and offices involved, such as judges, justices, secretary, minister, director and administration, and on confirmation hearings. Unrelated tokens get only weak, scattered activations.

Separators in lists of people's names (commas, "and", newlines, list numbering, closing parentheses or affiliation markers) that come right before the next personal name, as in author lists, credits, rosters and committees. Activation is strongest in long runs of comma-separated full names.

middle.name: Romantic, sexual and marital relationships: words such as partner, spouse, wife, widow, boyfriend, marriage and civil partnership, plus phrases about falling in love, kissing, seduction or impregnation. The strongest activations are on these relationship and intimacy terms. Weak activations fire on loosely related fragments, like the 'Partners' in 'Partnerships', 'Romantic', 'KISS' in 'Kissimmee', 'Wed', 'Singles' and bedrooms.

The final word or token of a short noun phrase that ends a parenthetical, appositive, or list item, i.e. the token immediately before a closing parenthesis, comma, dash, or period, such as "(the loop)", "(3.6 m)", "Google Chrome," or "de facto standard,". It marks the completion of an inserted or clarifying phrase.

Opening parenthesis tokens (" (", "(", "[(", ">(", "(('") that start a parenthetical, such as an abbreviation, citation year, clarification, enumeration, count, or math/code argument. Activation is often highest when the parenthesis begins a line or opens a standalone aside.

Words expressing attempt, effort, ability or goal toward an action, most often the infinitive "to" after verbs like try, able/unable, managed, working, aim, along with "can", "if you can", and "as ... as possible". The common thread is striving or capacity to accomplish something.

Separators and coordinating conjunctions (commas, "and", "or", "&", "/or", "such as", "including") that join items in coordinated lists or pairs of nouns, especially enumerations of proper names, platforms, or technologies. Activation is strongest late in longer lists, at the final ", and" or "and".

Weak, diffuse feature that fires at positions where a number is about to follow, especially the standalone space token before a numeral. It is strongest in ranges, dates, years and numbered sequences ("to 90.0", "November 2019", "1997 to 1999", list indices). It also fires more weakly on separators and first digits within such numeric patterns, such as dashes, periods, "%", commas and "or".

Words that set up a comparison, resemblance or perceived impression, mainly perception and seeming verbs (sounds, looks, feels, seems, appears, comes across as) and comparison markers (like, as if, than, equivalent of, more X than Y). Activation is strongest on 'like' and the verb right after it, and covers the words that begin the description of what something resembles or seems to be.

A diffuse, weak feature, densest in code. It fires on highly predictable tokens: second halves of split words (Hou-this, l-umin-osity, Countergl-omp), and identifiers, variables and arguments copied from earlier context (user.password_hash, message, average, InstallMode). It also fires on boilerplate continuations such as 'top of page' and 'Date of Birth:'.

Tokens about language and acquired skills: names of languages (English, Spanish, Python, Go), the word "language" itself, including foreign forms like Czech "jazyky" and Greek "Γλώσσα", and words for speaking, translating, reading, writing or learning. Strongest on explicit language mentions such as "native language skills", "speak a common language" or "Spanish". Weak activations land on loosely related words like learn, play or guidelines.

Interrogative words (what, why, how, who) that open a question or a wh-clause, plus the words right after them (e.g., "What more could you", "What's wrong", "How to"). Activation is strongest on rhetorical or conversational questions and on free relative "what" clauses ("what really matters is"). It is weaker on headings such as "How to…" or "What is X?".

Words tied to schooling and education levels, such as school names, grade or year levels (high school, 10th grade, Class XII, elementary, varsity), degrees, majors and university names. Activation is strongest on terms for school stages like high school, grade and class, and weak on scattered unrelated word fragments.

Generic plural nouns (mostly groups of people like students, people, researchers, fans) used as the subject or agent of a clause, often right after a conjunction, comma, or sentence start, referring to a class of actors rather than specific individuals.

Numeric tokens inside numbers (years, prices, measurements, codes, counts), especially multi-digit chunks containing or ending in the digit 3 (e.g. 33, 133, 933, 193, 203, or a final '3' in years like 2013). The strongest activations are on tokens with repeated 3s. A few non-numeric subword fragments, such as parts of Japanese names, also activate weakly.

Capitalized word-start tokens within concatenated or CamelCase identifiers, chiefly code method and function names (Parse, Union, Find, Print, Message), plus Twitter handles, usernames, URLs and library names. Activation is strongest on the first capitalized piece of a code identifier. Weak, scattered activations also appear on title-cased words in ordinary prose.

Marks the recipient or addressee of an action, request, or communication: the person or entity being asked, told, contacted, helped, or sent something (e.g. 'ask your husband', 'told his father', 'contact us', 'asked me', 'mentioned this to Owen', 'sent ... to him'). Strongest on nouns and pronouns that follow verbs like ask, tell, contact, or discuss with. Weaker activations fall on destination nouns that receive something (website, Tribunal, network) and on requested things (help, advice, attention).

Definitional or characterizing statements about a topic, especially in an expository or medical register. Activation falls on the copula and the words that open the description, e.g. "X is a common problem that…", "the disease is distinguished by…", or a parenthetical gloss like "(a rare cancer)". It is often triggered right after the subject noun (a disease, condition, process or concept) when a description or classification of it is about to follow.

Phrases describing how a product or thing is built, composed, tested or certified: technical specs, materials and ingredients ("made from", "composed of", "free from"), technologies used, and quality claims ("upgraded hardware", "undergone thorough testing", "Premium Selected certificate", "scientifically proven"). Activation is strongest in promotional or technical product descriptions.

Weak, diffuse feature that fires on terms naming measurement or assessment methods, indices, scales and evaluation tools (e.g., drought severity index, assessment tool, numeric scale, quantify, Delphi method, JC-10 assay, OEE) in scientific and technical text. Activation is strongest inside the names of these methods, with only scattered weak hits elsewhere.

A diffuse, weakly firing feature with no single topic. It fires on a token that completes a highly predictable fixed phrase, collocation or word, given the immediately preceding context. Examples include 'Public Domain', 'in press', 'laid off', 'free shipping', 'promoted to partner', 'No. 1', 'IP67', 'arrow-up', 'click OK', 'Rated 6/10' and \in'fty'. Subword pieces finishing a word, such as 'bacteric-idal', 'Havild-ar' and 'mon-oph-yly', also count.

Words for streets and other named places, strongest on "street/Street/streets" and on the type word that ends a street name in an address (Avenue, Road, Close, strasse, Plaza). Weaker on other location words such as Hill, River, village, neighborhood and intersection.

A weak, diffuse feature that fires on words in phrases about deliberate intervention, meaning an agent actively manipulating, controlling or acting on something. The strongest cases are "manually control … position" and "medical intervention allows women to". Similar phrases include "cut the cord", "addition of", "overexpression of", "directly admonish", "take charge" and "government policies … supporting". Most other activations are low and scattered across unrelated technical or descriptive words.

Weak, diffuse activation on nouns and names (people, companies, organizations, groups, countries) that serve as the agent, subject or referent of a clause, typically an entity performing or receiving an action, often appearing just before a verb or a possessive 's. The strongest cases are named people and movements (e.g. a surname followed by 'claimed', 'Black Lives Matter').

Language about technological or scientific progress and advancement, such as words like "advancements", "progress", "new technologies", "cutting-edge", "high-tech", "improved" and "modern", plus phrases like "progress has been made in recent years". Activation is strongest on explicit progress/advancement nouns and their following "in [field] technology" phrases.

A weak, diffuse feature that fires mostly within narrative clauses about motion, travel or journeys. Typical contexts are going along a way, road or route, walking past, heading somewhere, reaching an altitude or destination, and objects popping out or being carried along. It also fires on related nouns such as roads, vehicles, paths and streams, and on the clause connectors or commas inside these event descriptions. The strongest hits are phrases like "on the way I said to" and "driving down a rural road at".

Language tied to to-do lists, checklists and task management: lists, items, tasks, things to do, prioritizing, getting work done, pending items, check marks and checkbox brackets. It fires most strongly on "to-do" and an empty checkbox "[ ]".

Concessive hedging: modal verbs (especially "may be"/"might") and "while/though" clauses that grant something as possibly true before a contrasting "but". Activation is strongest on the concession itself ("may be X,") and on the comma just before "but".

The subword token "yst" (including "myst"/"syst") inside a longer word, e.g. crystalline, polycystic, systolic, mystic/mystique, demystify, cholecystectomy. Activation is highest in medical and biochemical words (polycystic, cholecystectomy, homocysteine).

Marks the end point of a time span: the closing date, time, or year of a range, plus the words that introduce it (until, thru, to, into, end on, dashes between start and end). The strongest activations come right after range connectors, as in 'thru January 15' and 'into early January'. The pattern occasionally carries over to the end point of spatial ranges, as in 'mouth to anus'.

Weak, diffuse activation on phrases that describe what something can do or enables: its capabilities, advantages, uses, or functional properties. Typical cases are "can slow down... and sort on any field", "capable of reaching an enormous amount of users", "the ability to manage", "which let you control" and "starts up from rest". Activation is strongest on verbs and prepositions of capability or action and their objects, often in lists of benefits or features.

The word "future" and its variants (futures, futurist, futuristic, Tomorrow), including capitalized names. Activation is strongest on financial "futures" and "futurist", and weaker on everyday uses such as "sustainable future" or "future-proof".

The word "email" (also "e-mail", "Email", "inbox") and related contact or identifier terms such as phone, IP, ZIP and username. It fires most strongly on "email" in form or contact contexts like "your email address", sign-up prompts and registration fields.

Segments of file system paths and URLs, particularly server directory paths in PHP/CMS error messages (e.g., /wp-content/plugins/, /sites/all/modules/, /themes/), with the strongest activation on the directory components after the site root. Weak, scattered activations also appear on other code-like or technical identifiers.

Words and phrases describing conduct, behavior or the manner and course of action: how someone acts, lives or behaves. Examples include the actions people take or avoid, ways or approaches of doing something, staying within or transgressing bounds, and doing right or wrong. Typical cases are 'act and behave', 'walk in the', 'how they live', 'doing nothing wrong', 'in such a way that', 'strategies' and 'trying to be'.

The subword token "ube" (and variants like "UBE", "ubes", "ubectl", "kube") inside larger words, mostly names and proper nouns. It is strongest for Kubernetes terms (Kube, KubeCon, kubectl) and the province Hubei, and weaker in personal names (Rube, Dube, Steube) and words like lube. Occasional weak activations appear on bullet points and short function words.

Prepositions (mostly "of", "in", "to", "for", "on", "about") that come right after a noun, adjective or verb and introduce a prepositional phrase. Strongest when the phrase ties a head word to a following noun phrase ("members of", "efforts in", "to all"), and it often extends onto a following "the".

Language about change or development over time, especially present-perfect phrasing describing how things have shifted, grown, evolved or been transformed since some earlier point. Typical forms are "has changed since", "have grown", "evolved over the years", "huge changes have begun" and "in the meantime". The strongest activations come from explicit descriptions of change since a past reference point. Weaker activations land on scattered nouns and verbs nearby.

Words about explaining or accounting for something, giving a cause or reason for a phenomenon. "explain" is the strongest, especially after modals or hedges ("may explain", "partly explain", "would explain"). Related forms ("explanation", "explained"), "account for", "understand", "makes sense", "reason" and "why" activate more weakly.

Binary operators that combine sets or functions, mostly set intersection: the LaTeX \cap token (strongest), the ∩ symbol, and the words "intersection" and "union". Weaker activations go to related operators such as \cup/∪, \circ (function composition), ∧, Python & between sets, and .intersection. Isolated non-math tokens (e.g. "Pages", "the") activate only faintly.

Terms for biological or physical specimens collected for testing or analysis, chiefly "blood" and "samples" (blood tests, blood work, serum, saliva samples, specimen, biopsy, tissue, swab), plus verbs of collecting or sampling. Activation is strongest on phrases like "blood samples" and "saliva samples".

Tokens inside URLs, file paths and web addresses (domains like .com/.org/.uk, github.com, path segments such as /blob/master, /uploads/2018/05, relative ../ paths), especially image/link sources in markdown or HTML. Strongest on domain names and path components. Weaker hits fall on source or credit attributions (website, publisher or organization names, e.g. 'CBC', 'Facebook', 'Survey').

A diffuse, weak feature found in expository scientific, technical and health writing. It fires on scattered function words, punctuation, list separators and content words, most strongly within explanatory clauses that describe mechanisms, roles or effects (e.g., "nutrients may play a role", "vitamin E utilization", "filters and … technology remove").

Boilerplate, machine-generated technical strings, chiefly browser user-agent strings (AppleWebKit/537.36 (KHTML, like Gecko), rv:, Gecko, OS/version numbers). Activation peaks on the predictable version numbers and punctuation inside them. Weaker activation appears on other templated metadata, such as forum profile fields (Posts:, Schools:, Followers), website-stats lines, DOI fragments, software version numbers and NASA/JPL-Caltech credits.

Words right after temporal modifiers that place something earlier (or occasionally later) in time, such as "previous", "previously", "earlier", "past", "last", "at first", "traditional" or "future". The feature fires on the modified noun or verb (version, ones, thought, described, identified, week, emotions, approaches) and on the clause that follows, often past-tense verbs like "were" or "had" in sentences contrasting an earlier state with the present.

Words built on the root "susp-" (suspend, suspended, suspending, suspension(s), suspense, suspicion), firing most strongly on the initial "susp" token. It covers every sense: halting or banning (flights, sales, users, dividends), hanging or particles dispersed in a fluid, vehicle suspension, and narrative suspense. The suspend/suspension senses fire more strongly than "suspense". Weak activations appear on similar-looking fragments in other languages.

The first token of a word, name or compound that the tokenizer splits into several pieces, so the word is unfinished at that point. These are often single capital letters or short prefixes that begin acronyms, brand names, chemical or technical terms, usernames, or hyphenated compounds (e.g. E-skom, P-glycoprotein, she-wolf, Co-founder).

Code statement boundaries where an object, widget, or variable is being instantiated or assigned. The strongest activations fall on the closing parenthesis, semicolon and newline (");\n") that end constructor calls such as new X(...) or Widget::new(...). Weaker activations fall on the class names and variable names involved in these creation and assignment lines, especially for GUI components like labels, toolbars, shells and boxes.

A diffuse feature found in expository, advisory or policy-style prose about practices and processes, such as healthcare, management, public engagement and wellbeing. It fires on words that name means or approaches for achieving an outcome: nouns like methods, measures, steps, ways, tool, factors, involvement, engagement and communication, and action verbs like help, create, streamline, enhance, implementing and focusing. It also fires on nearby function words like "to", "in" and commas within those purpose and benefit statements. Activations are strongest on terms for participation and engagement and on tools.

The word "property"/"properties" (also Chinese 属性), firing most strongly on its programming sense of an object attribute or field (code, XML, config, APIs). It fires more weakly on scientific or mathematical attributes and weakest on real-estate or proper-name uses.

The last word (or final subword piece) of a short heading, section title, or page/UI label, usually a generic noun like Information, Details, Reviews, search, content or features. It typically follows a newline and comes just before another line break or colon, as in web boilerplate and document headers.

Words in purpose/result constructions that describe a cause producing an effect, usually a beneficial or enabling one. They typically come right after causative verbs (make it, helps, gives, boost, ensure) or open infinitive or purpose phrases (to achieve, to attract, to improve, for interest), as in 'make it easy', 'makes the music more potent' and 'ensuring that'. Activation peaks on explicit improvement or goal phrases such as 'to attract students and maintain their interest', 'even better' and 'more of a push'.

Tokens spelling the letter sequence "map" (map, Map, MAP, mapping, maple, /map, imap), strongest for the acronym MAP (MAP kinase, mean arterial pressure, MAPT). Also fires on "protein" in "mitogen-activated protein" (the P of MAPK) and weakly on look-alike acronym pieces such as "AP" or ".p".

Tokens spelling "hang"/"hung" (and "-hung-" fragments like in power-hungry, hungrier, Hangzhou, Hangover), most strongly on the verb "hang" in all forms (hang out, hang up, hanging around, get the hang of) and capitalized name pieces containing "Hang".

Tokens immediately following the number three ("3", "three", "third", "3rd"). These are usually the unit or noun being counted (years, days, minutes, stars, features), or the continuation of a number or expression (",558", "%", "/4", "b", "-year", "hundred"). Weaker activations occur after other numbers or in numeric and date contexts.

The final digit(s) of a phone number (also weaker on endings of ISBN/ISSN or other long ID codes), plus sometimes the punctuation or space right after it. Activation is strongest on the last digit of a hyphenated contact phone number.

Prepositions, chiefly "of" and occasionally "for" or "from", that link a head noun such as version, episode, launch, title or members to the specific entity it belongs to or describes ("version of iOS 8", "episode of the program"). Activation is strongest when the head noun names a part, instance or edition of a named work, product or organization.

The "/**" token that opens Javadoc/doc-block comments in code, firing most strongly when it begins a documentation comment right before a class member, field, constructor or method. It is weaker for "/**" used as a path wildcard (e.g. "/css/**") or in URLs, and there is only faint, scattered activation on unrelated punctuation or formatting tokens.

Modifier words, mostly nouns used attributively or relational adjectives, that name a domain, field or aspect (safety, security, health, design, ethical, technical, measurement, logistic). They typically come right before a head noun such as concerns, issues, challenges, standards, applications or standpoint, or after 'due to' or 'a matter of', and specify the dimension in which a problem or quality applies.

Fires in mathematical/formal text on the listed generators, variables or elements that define a structure: entries inside group presentations (\langle x_1, x_2, … \rangle), set braces {a, b, c}, polynomial-ring variables (F_q[t]) and function arguments (x). It also fires on the words introducing such generating data ("generated by", "span", alphabets, predicates). The strongest activations are on presentation generators, the separating commas and ring indeterminates.

Fires on the subword "amin", most strongly as the word-initial piece " lamin" (laminate, laminated, laminar, laminations) in technical or materials contexts. It fires more weakly on "amin" inside other words, such as chemical names (acetaminophen, amino-, deaminase), foraminifera, and names like Jamin.

Personal names, chiefly the first names or first name/surname fragments of people (especially female names like Lisa, Emily, -isa), often in bylines, author lists, or credits; also occasionally proper-noun or taxonomic name fragments (Pis-, Mayo).

Fires at the boundary right after a named term, variable, label, heading or function signature, on the token that introduces its definition, value or body (e.g. " =", ":", " {" + newline, "is equal", " if", a closing quote-period, or a line break after a header). It marks the transition from the thing being defined to its content, in both code and prose.

Denominators in fractions and divisions, meaning the tokens right after a slash, "over", or inside the second brace of \frac{}{} in math, code and formulas (e.g. "1/N", "/n", "\frac{1}{r^n}"). Single variables, powers and constants in that position fire most strongly. There are occasional weak hits on 'per'-type units after a slash.

Separators and items in enumerations of alternative values, chiefly "or", commas, "and", and slashes in phrases like "X or Y", "A, B, or C", or "either 1 or 8". It is strongest in chemical or math definitions that list allowed substituents or values, such as "represent hydrogen or methyl" or "K = ℂ or K = ℝ". It also fires weakly on the listed options themselves.

The distinguishing token that follows a repeated prefix or stem in parallel or list-like structures, i.e., the varying part of a repeated name or label (escalaX→escala Y, Temperature F→Temperature C, petal_length→petal_width, VG-BART→VG-T5, snake→snake2/3, Tank→Tank(Clone)). It is common in code identifiers, specs, file lists and enumerations.

A weak, diffuse feature that fires mostly at the start of a new clause, on the subject or relativizer that comes just before its verb. It is strongest on person nouns and relative pronouns introducing a clause, especially with past perfect 'had': 'officer who had served', 'the person had committed', 'the other party had reached', 'those that my…'. It also fires weakly on clause-initial pronouns (I, you, he, she) and on sentence boundaries or periods where a new clause begins.

Comma (occasionally the noun right before it, or a following "then") that closes a fronted introductory phrase or subordinate clause (time, cause, condition, context, e.g. "After deployment," "Since August 1998,"), marking where the main clause begins.

The noun (or first word of the noun phrase) right after a possessive determiner, especially "our", "your", "my" and "their". Activation is strongest for "our" plus a work or group noun, as in "our proposal", "our study", "our method" or "our company".

The subword token "del"/"Del" (and close variants like "dele", "delic", "deline", "el") at the start of a word that it only partially spells, as in delve, deliver, delirious, deleterious, delicacy, delineate, or names like Delphine, Delly and Delin. Activation is strongest for a capitalized " Del" beginning a proper name or sentence-initial "Delve"/"Delivered".

Diffuse feature with no single strong token type. It fires on the word that opens the main content of a statement, item or heading. This is usually the key verb or noun right after a subject, list number, section number or question word: findings, objectives, accusations, titles and questions (e.g., 'found', 'determine', 'Testing', 'What', 'blamed', 'association', 'benefits'). The strongest activations are on clauses stating a claim or issue under judgment or investigation, such as 'whether the government was legally', 'judge was wrong' and 'differed significantly'.

Structural boundaries where one unit ends and the next begins, mostly in code: closing parentheses/brackets followed by newlines, opening braces, indentation, and the first keyword of a new line or block (e.g. after function signatures). It also fires on prose and document structure such as sentence-ending periods, list numbers, headings and blank lines.

A diffuse feature that fires weakly on mostly function words and phrase fragments in passages about practices, procedures, routines and methods. It peaks where established practices or habits are described or evaluated, e.g. 'routine', 'steps', 'measures', 'has been in place', 'shown to be a bad practice' and 'tend not to brush their teeth'.

Weak, diffuse activation on commentary clauses that follow a mention of a name, word, term or title, i.e. text discussing naming, word choice or a term's origin (e.g. a name being adopted, changed, dubbed, that 'stuck', or 'is simply a fun word'). It also fires on casual, chatty asides in the author's voice, such as 'so I'll just', 'we're fresh out' or 'I have no idea why'.
