The token that ends a return expression in code, usually the semicolon (or closing paren/newline) right after the returned value in short getter-style functions such as `return name;` and `{ return x; }`. Activation is strongest for simple getters returning a field and weaker for method-call returns and Rust/Python implicit returns. There are faint stray hits on line endings in non-code text.

The letter "p"/"P" used as the p-value symbol in statistical reporting (e.g. "p < 0.05", "P = .003"), often in parentheses after results. The following "=" or "<" activates more weakly. Related statistical-significance terms ("significance", "p-value") and other statistic symbols (r, r², Ki) fire weakly, as does the "p" in "pH".

The verb "found" (occasionally "find", "located", "encountered"), chiefly as a passive participle meaning something exists or is present somewhere ("found in the petals", "can be found in", "ports found in a standard router"). It is strongest when the participle directly follows a noun and leads into an "in" location phrase.

A generic head noun that comes right after a proper name, brand, acronym or other specific modifier, saying what kind of thing that name refers to (e.g. "Stinger project", "TeraShake simulation", "Data Access specification", "Bodele depression").

Fires at the boundary right after a clause or phrase that is already grammatically complete, on the token that opens an add-on: a parenthetical, clarification, qualification or elaboration. Typical triggers are opening parentheses (strongest), dashes, colons, and connectives such as "including", "albeit", "except", "rather", "like", "but", "either" and "sometimes". It also fires weakly on sentence-ending punctuation at that same point. A secondary pattern is definitional phrasing (e.g., '“Elimination of contaminants” is defined as').

Words in website boilerplate, navigation menus, metadata labels, and page headers (e.g., 'Sign Up', 'Item ID', 'Article INFO', 'Related Links', 'Now Reading', 'Home'), typically the second word of a short UI/label phrase rather than running prose.

Words expressing difference, distinctness, or sameness/comparison between things ("different", "differ", "unique", "same", "identical", "disparate", "distinction", "homogeneous"), plus tokens completing such comparisons ("from", "between", or the noun that follows). Strongest on "different" after an intensifier like "very" or "completely".

over.name: Weak, diffuse activation on tokens inside repetitive, list-like or unstructured text that isn't ordinary prose: number and symbol sequences, code and URL fragments, keyword-stuffed tags, garbled spaced-out letters, line breaks in lists or verse, and math notation. It is strongest on repeated or sequential patterns such as "b b b 1 2 3", strings of underscores and dots, and runs of numbers.

Comment delimiters in code, mainly the '#' and '//' tokens (also '/*', '/**', ';', '\\', '*') that start a line or inline comment. Activation is strongest when the marker opens a comment line at the start of a code block after prose. Weaker activations occur on similar separator symbols in non-code text.

A weak, diffuse feature that fires on content words, mostly abstract nouns and descriptive or evaluative adjectives (e.g., diversity, legacy, insight, portrayal, sustainable, noble). These usually complete a noun phrase or clause, often just before punctuation or a preposition. They appear mainly in elevated, academic or figurative prose, with no single topic tying the examples together.

The program or executable name at the start of a shell command line (e.g. python, php, ruby, gcc, curl, cat, npm), especially interpreters invoked to run a script file. Activation is strongest for interpreter names like python/php/ruby, weaker for flags and subcommands that follow.

Function, method, or command names that execute or invoke something, mostly in code. The strongest cases are calls like os.system, runString, run, and search, which execute commands, code, or strings. Weaker hits include shell commands, macros (try!, html!, assert_eq!), asm blocks, and words like "execute" or "Type" in instructions. Activation usually falls on the method or call token just before its arguments.

Formatting and structural tokens in tables, code, and other structured text: row-ending pipes plus newlines, indentation and alignment whitespace, line breaks, and separators that mark cell, line, or column boundaries ahead of the next aligned item.

A diffuse feature active across technical, software, and documentation-style text, such as programming, editors, config files, rules, and syntax. It mostly fires weakly on function words, sentence-ending punctuation, and newlines. It peaks on terms about code editing and programming languages, such as "highlighting", "snippets", "language name", and "React".

Tokens inside verbatim repeated text. The feature fires on words or phrases that recur several times in close succession (repeated lines, chants, list items, code lines, table cells, boilerplate such as "Invalid Input" or "Show more"), usually from the second or third repetition onward, as the model predicts a copy of earlier text. Activation is strongest in long, highly regular loops of identical multi-token lines.

Syntax tokens inside code or formula snippets, mostly operators, delimiters and short keywords in terse or unusual languages such as Mathematica, PARI/MAGMA, BASIC-like and Forth-like code. Typical examples are pure-function and application markers (&, ]&, @@, //), statement terminators and control words (End, exit, endif, DUP) and bracket or slash combinations. The strongest activations fall on symbols that mark function application or the end of an expression. Scattered prose and non-Latin tokens activate only weakly.

Tokens of repeated characters within elongated or repetitive strings, such as stretched words and exclamations ("yeeeeah", "Aaaaah", "maaaaybe"), repeated punctuation, laughter, block glyphs, and placeholder runs like "xxxxxxxx" or "AAAAAAAA". Activation is mostly on the middle/later chunks of the run and grows as the repetition continues.

Zero digits (and similar placeholder values) repeated within structured sequences such as matrices, arrays, tuples, tables, and numeric lists, firing most on zeros that follow other zeros or repeated filler cells (e.g., "", "*", ".").

Tokens inside long runs of the same repeated token or short pattern, such as dashes, asterisks, quotes, stars or "true". Activation builds the longer the repetition continues, peaking in decorative separator lines. Ordinary prose words fire only weakly.

A weak, diffuse feature with no clear semantic theme. It fires mostly on function words and connectors in the middle of formulaic phrases, such as "and" joining paired terms ("clean and efficient", "maintenance and repair"), "the", "of", "by" and "at". It also fires on predictable word-piece continuations ("-F|actor", "BYJ|US", "Tel|ugu") and on filler such as table-of-contents dot leaders and code indentation. These are tokens where the continuation is highly predictable.

Backslash characters (\, \\, '\\') across contexts: LaTeX commands (\textsubscript, \begin, \cite), escape sequences (\n, \t), file paths, stray escaped text, and the word "slash" in "backslash"; occasionally other odd separator/escape-like tokens.

A diffuse, low-specificity feature that fires on scattered tokens (function words, digits, operators, identifier suffixes, separators) in technical, mathematical, scientific, code and structured web text. It is strongest mid-exposition, just before a specific variable, value or quantity is introduced, as in "the number…", "is calculated as" or "v01 for this… close to v1".

A weak, diffuse feature that fires on tokens in hard-to-predict, high-entropy text rather than on a particular word. Typical contexts are random alphanumeric strings, hashes, IDs, URLs, IP addresses and numeric lists or codes. It also fires on rare non-Latin scripts, garbled LaTeX, and incoherent spam or machine-generated prose.

Fires on structural or formatting tokens in highly patterned, repetitive text such as code, HTML tables, LaTeX, lists, dates and data listings. Typical hits are indentation and whitespace before list bullets or numbers, newline runs, closing tags (tr, tbody), repeated identifiers and class names, brackets, and parts of dates (month, year digits, commas). These tokens tend to repeat or continue a pattern already set up earlier in the context.

Boundary tokens at the end of a text segment, just before a new section, post, comment, or list item begins. These are mostly sentence-final punctuation fused with newlines, bare newlines, the leading space or number of a new numbered entry, and the colon inside timestamps. Activation is weak.

Tokens in garbled, noisy or atypical text: OCR errors, broken or misspelled word fragments, random character strings, odd capitalization or spacing, and spam-like or formatting junk. The strongest activations fall on dense OCR gibberish (stray letters, numbers and punctuation from scanned documents); weaker ones on single malformed subword pieces.

Mentions of the Python programming language ("python"/"Python", including shebang paths like /usr/bin/python, "python manage.py", python.org, .py, pip, sys.path). It fires more weakly on other programming language names (Ruby, Haskell, Basic) and on technical or path-like code tokens.

The word "Python" or "python" used as the name of the programming language, in prose, code fences, shebang lines, package names and language lists. It fires weakly on unrelated tokens such as the snake sense or docstring quotes.

Tokens that repeat an immediately preceding item in a run of identical elements, typically the third or later occurrence of a repeated number in lists, arrays, tables or sequences (e.g. "9, 9, 9", "10, 10, 10"). It also fires on repeated words, characters or HTML cells, and is strongest for repeated numbers in comma-separated lists.

Fires on unpredictable tokens in noisy, incoherent or low-quality text, such as spun/SEO spam word salad, OCR garbage, DNA sequences, symbol/ASCII art, username lists, number lists, URL fragments and archaic or foreign scripts. It is strongest in long runs of nonsensical text. In otherwise normal sentences it fires weakly on a single oddly placed function word or noun.

Separator tokens such as commas, spaces, ampersands, and HTML <td> tags inside long, repetitive sequences like number lists, table rows, and coin-flip strings. Activation is strongest in the middle of a long run of repeated delimiters. Weaker activations fall on function words (and, with, that, the) in formulaic, promotional-style prose.

Command-line program or tool names, typically the first word of a shell command a user is told to type or run, and most often a package manager or build tool followed by a subcommand like "install" (npm, go, composer, pod, pip, make, rails). Weaker activations fall on other command-like tokens: subcommands, flags, SQL keywords, menu commands and code identifiers.

Tokens that end or complete a phrase which is a repeat of an earlier one in the context. Typical cases are repeated lines, list items, boilerplate and refrains (e.g. "Invalid Input", "Show more", "Monthly Budget", "lived a method", repeated numbers or units). The feature is predicting the final word of a copy. Activation is strongest in highly repetitive text and grows with the number of repetitions.

Terms for web or app routing and addressing, such as routing, route, navigation, url/uri, path, location, link, address, permalink, pages and controllers. They mostly appear in software, web-development and config contexts. Activation is strongest on "routing"/"route"/"navigation"; there are weak spillovers to other routes (road Route 60, iptables nat, Spanish 'ruta').

A weak, diffuse feature with no clear single-token pattern. It fires mostly on generic, low-information filler in noisy web text such as SEO spam, scrambled or nonsensical sentences, code and number snippets, and templated boilerplate. It is strongest on corporate-buzzword placeholder text (e.g., 'Organically grow the holistic world view…') and on generic website promo copy ('If you are ready, you can play some other games').

Fires on the opening token of a document or structured block, such as the very first word or symbol of a text (namespace, using, #define, #ifndef, ![, <!--, titles), and especially the <thead token that starts the header right after a <table> tag.

Tokens inside long runs of the same repeated character or token (dot leaders, dashes, spaces, nbsp, -*, ;\, repeated letters or symbols). Activation is strongest deep in the run, and a few sequence positions stand out as peaks. There are weak, sporadic activations on ordinary tokens, mostly prepositions like "in".

Diffuse, weak activations on tokens in noisy, low-coherence or structured text: garbled/encoded strings, ASCII art, ID and part numbers, URL encodings, tables, list bullets, and run-together or spam text. It fires mostly on repeated or fragment tokens (numbers, single letters, symbols, bullets) where the next token is hard to predict. No clear semantic meaning.

Tokens inside repetitive, predictable runs of text, such as repeated words or phrases ("Image Image Image", "very, very", "Skip to"), repeated symbols or separator lines, and boilerplate markup like HTML table tags (, ⏎, ),
and blockquote ">⏎" lines. Activation increases the longer the same pattern keeps repeating.

Tokens in multiple-choice quiz/test text where the correct answer is about to be revealed: answer labels like "Answer:", "the correct option is", "Option" and "【答案】", the line break after the last listed choice, and the separators in answer keys (e.g. "3.", "B)", "6~10"), all of which come right before an answer letter or value.

The double-slash token "//" in any role: code comments, integer division, URL and path separators, XPath, and decorative separators in bylines or headers. Activation peaks where it joins a URL or template placeholder (e.g. "{{site.github}}//") or appears as a quoted string literal. Weak activations also land on unrelated tokens.

File extensions in filenames, strongest for executable scripts that are being run (.sh, .py, .rb, .pl, .m, .php). Words that refer to running code, such as "script", "program", "run" and "make", also activate weakly.

Separator tokens (commas, spaces, dots, newlines, <td> cells, 'x') placed between items in repetitive lists or sequences of numbers/values/words, firing most strongly when the same item is repeated many times (e.g. '50, 50, 50…').

A diffuse, low-specificity feature that fires mostly on unpredictable tokens in noisy or garbled text: OCR junk, mojibake, random alphanumeric codes and serial numbers, unit letters stuck to numbers, odd single characters or scripts, and gene or sequence strings. It also fires weakly on ordinary punctuation and line breaks in plain prose, which suggests it tracks high-surprise or out-of-distribution tokens rather than any one meaning.

Fires at the very start of a document on leading boilerplate or list formatting: indentation spaces, bullet points (•) and numbering like "1.", plus the first word that follows. These are usually navigation menus, breadcrumbs and list items. It responds weakly to other opening structural markers such as runs of newlines, section commands, separator lines and stray header or menu words like "Stations".

Fragments inside unpredictable, high-entropy character strings: random alphanumeric IDs, hashes, URL and filename codes, passwords, MAC addresses, mojibake or garbled text, and invented or foreign names split into odd subword pieces. Activation is strongest deep inside random codes and garbled Chinese. It is weak on occasional ordinary words.

Vertical bar / pipe characters ("|", and similar box-drawing verticals like ⎢ or ║) used as separators or borders in tables, ASCII diagrams, comment boxes, matrices, and website navigation/metadata strips. Activation is strongest inside ASCII-art diagrams and grids with many aligned bars, and weaker for single inline separators.

Numbers or values that serve as a target, bound or reference point in a comparison, rounding, range, limit or equation (e.g. "rounds to 300", "closer to zero", "less than 150", "0 to infinity", a coordinate or result value). Activation is strongest on numerals in math-style questions and weak on scattered non-numeric nouns and symbols.

A diffuse, weakly firing feature with no clear single concept. It activates sporadically on many token types: numbers and items in comma-separated lists, math operators and LaTeX symbols, punctuation, and citation brackets. It fires most strongly on hard-to-predict or surprising content, such as citation markers like "[6", nonsensical word salad, and incongruous lists of unrelated nouns.

Punctuation, whitespace, newlines and separator tokens (commas, spaces, dashes, tags, line breaks) that act as delimiters between items, mostly in noisy, garbled, redacted, foreign-script or list-like text. Activation is strongest for commas separating repeated or masked items, such as runs of █ blocks or REDACTED.

Delimiter and separator tokens, such as spaces, commas, pipes, ampersands, dashes, newlines, and quote-comma pairs, that sit between items in long repetitive sequences like number runs, page lists, table specs, and data arrays. Activation grows as the repeated pattern continues and becomes more predictable.

Tokens that repeat an immediately preceding token or short pattern. The feature fires on the second and later copies in runs of identical words, symbols, numbers, or cells, such as "H H H H", "+ + +", "Unlimited Unlimited", "agree agree", "7 7 7" and "NA NA". Activation tends to grow the longer the repetition goes on.

Fires weakly and broadly on tokens inside structured or templated text such as HTML table markup (especially '>⏎' after closing td/tr tags), code, markdown links, LaTeX, tables of contents with dot leaders, data listings, and headings. The activating tokens are mostly delimiters, separators or repeated elements whose position is predictable from the surrounding repetitive formatting, rather than tokens carrying particular meaning.

Tokens inside repetitive or patterned sequences: repeated numbers, symbols, separators and code lines (e.g., 30, 31, 30…; -*-*; ~~88~~88; repeated '; ' lines; 16x16x16). The token itself repeats an earlier element in the same run, and activation is strongest in highly regular, predictable repetition. Weak, scattered activation on ordinary words elsewhere.

A diffuse feature with no clear semantic content. It fires mostly on structural and formatting tokens, such as newlines, spaces, brackets, slashes, backslashes and punctuation. These usually sit inside markup, LaTeX, code, tables or garbled multilingual and symbol-heavy text, often at boundaries between segments. It also fires occasionally on ordinary function words like "of" or "in" in prose.

Tokens inside repetitive or patterned sequences, where the next token is predictable from earlier repetition: repeated phrases ("Loading...", "Final Four", "Sacred Valley"), number runs, list separators, whitespace or newline padding, HTML table tags, and repeated characters or symbols. Activations are generally weak and scattered, strongest on spaces and numbers in counting sequences.

The ".py" Python file extension token that completes a filename or path (scripts, modules, command-line invocations, code comments). It fires most strongly on clear file-reference contexts, weakly on bare "py" after a dot, and only marginally on a few unrelated tokens.

under.name: The middle number segment of dotted classification codes, most strongly the second two-digit field of PACS physics codes (e.g. the "75" in 89.75.Hc). Activation is weaker on similar segments in OCIS, MSC, ACM, EC and industry codes, IP addresses and arXiv IDs.

The ".support" package segment in code import paths, strongest in Java "import android.support..." (AppCompat, annotation, v4/v7 libraries) and weaker in other libraries (Spring, Selenium, Elasticsearch). Other package segments after a dot (.validation, .context, .Security) fire only faintly.

The token ".Context" in code qualified names, strongest in the Java import "android.content.Context" and weaker in other packages (org.mozilla.javascript, org.apache.catalina, echo.Context, C# namespaces). Scattered prose tokens show only negligible activation.

Scientific and taxonomic descriptive prose, mainly species and taxon descriptions in biology and paleontology (Latin genus and species names, family suffixes like -idae, author/year citations, statements of distribution, habitat and morphology). Activation lands on the function words, punctuation and name fragments inside these passages and is strongest in dense species-description text. Weak, scattered activation also appears on general academic and technical writing.

The path or namespace separator segment that follows a library or package name in code imports and qualified references (e.g. ".api", ".Framework", "::", ".core" after junit, NUnit, assertj, failure). It fires most strongly on testing-framework imports such as org.junit.jupiter.api, junit.framework and NUnit.Framework. It also fires weakly on "add" after paket.

Repeated package-name tokens in sequential Java import lists, chiefly " android" (and the "import" before it) in Android import blocks. Activation builds the deeper into the list it gets, peaking around android.widget/android.view imports; it also fires weakly on the next "import" line once the android imports end. Weak scattered activations appear at list or section transitions, such as an abstract's closing period before its keyword list.

Package‑name segments in code import paths, especially Java imports: strongest on Spring's ".stereotype" (preceding Service/Component/Controller/Repository), with weaker activation on other library namespaces such as lombok, butterknife, github.com/stretchr, ".RestController", and ".Spring". Rare, faint activations appear in unrelated prose.
The parameter name "savedInstanceState" following "Bundle" in Android Java lifecycle method signatures (onCreate, onCreateView, onCreateDialog). Other weak activations are incidental.

The ".annotation" package segment in Java import statements (e.g. org.springframework.beans.factory.annotation, javax.servlet.annotation, androidx.annotation), and occasionally similar namespace segments like PHP "\Annotation". Activation is strongest in Spring and javax imports. Unrelated tokens such as table-of-contents dot leaders fire only very weakly.

The Android method name "setContentView" (or its "ContentView" piece) in Java Activity code, typically called right after super.onCreate(savedInstanceState) to set the layout via R.layout. Other weak activations are scattered and uninformative.

The ".annotation" (or ".annotations") package segment in Java import statements. Activation is strongest in Android/androidx/javax imports of nullability annotations (NonNull, Nullable) and weakest in Spring imports (beans.factory, web.bind). Other tokens fire only sporadically and weakly.

The "import" keyword at the start of Java import statements, mainly in the later lines of an existing import block, where it follows earlier imports, often ones that share the same package prefix. One weak exception is "to" in English prose.

The access modifier "protected" at the start of a method declaration in object-oriented code (Java, C#, PHP), along with the words right after it ("void", "override", "function"). It is strongest right after an @Override annotation in Android code such as "protected void onCreate(Bundle savedInstanceState)". Other method modifiers like "public" or "private void" fire weakly, and the few prose examples are only trace activations.

Package-name tokens in Java import statements, strongest by far for ".junit" right after "org" (import org.junit...). It fires more weakly on other test frameworks (testng, plain junit) and on "lombok" after "import". Activations on ordinary prose are near zero.

Technical and scientific writing about observation, measurement and data collection, especially astronomy: instruments such as telescopes, cameras, filters, spectrographs and CCDs, observing sessions and patterns, survey cycles and phases, date ranges, and units or quantities. Activation is diffuse and weak, spread over nouns and phrases that describe observational setups or measurement procedures and parameters. It peaks on astronomy terms like observing patterns, observation cycles and instrument names.

The final dotted class-name token in Java/C# import statements, chiefly annotation types. It fires most strongly on ".Test" in JUnit/TestNG test imports (e.g. org.junit.Test) and more weakly on Spring stereotype annotations (.Service, .Component, .Controller, .Repository, .Configuration).

Final numeric digits inside bibliographic and identifier strings: DOIs, astronomy bibcodes (e.g., 2022MNRAS.511..829H), patent dates, call numbers. Activation is strongest on the page/article number just before a closing author-initial letter in bibcode-style citations, and weak on other trailing digits within such codes.

Affiliation markers placed right after author names in academic paper bylines: superscript numbers, letters, Roman numerals, or symbols (*, †, ⋆) that point to institutional affiliations. Activation is strongest for the first affiliation marker (especially "1"/"¹"/"a") and when the same marker repeats across several authors, and weaker for later or secondary indices.

The class-name token right after a package path in Java import statements, most often annotation names like .NonNull/.NotNull following "annotation", plus Lombok/Spring names such as .Component, .Data, .Param. It peaks on null-check annotations (.NonNull). Weak, scattered activations also appear on odd filler words like "typically" in spammy prose.

The first digit chunk of an article, page or grant ID number in citations, DOIs and funding notes, usually right after a volume number, period or dash. It fires most strongly on Physical Review / APS-style article numbers such as PhysRevB.94.245… or "Phys. Rev. Lett. 126, 045…", and fires weakly on page ranges and grant numbers.

Affiliation markers placed right after author names in academic paper bylines: superscript numbers, letters, or symbols (1, ¹, a, †, *), including LaTeX \textsuperscript arguments. The first affiliation marker ("1"/"¹"/"a") activates most strongly, while secondary markers (2, ‡) and separating commas activate weakly.

Separator punctuation inside citation identifiers such as DOIs, arXiv IDs, bibcodes and URLs, typically the dot, dash, slash, space or underscore between a volume or number and a following page or article number. It fires most strongly on the padding dots in ADS bibcodes (e.g. 'ApJ...499..810C'). Activation on ordinary words is weak.

Names of laboratory culture media, buffers, and solutions that cells or samples are grown, bathed, or dissolved in (DMEM, Eagle's medium, PBS, saline, Ringer's, Hanks', broth, agar, media, solvents). It fires most strongly on the final token of the name or on the head noun 'medium'. There is weak spillover to other substrate or base nouns such as soil, diet, and Snapdragon chipsets.

Java persistence/ORM identifiers in code, most strongly the ".jpa" package segment in Spring Data imports (org.springframework.data.jpa), plus EntityManager, Hibernate ".Session", Doctrine "\ORM", and similar framework names like FLAG_ACTIVITY. Activations on ordinary prose tokens are weak and scattered.

Android/Java "Context" objects in code: the Context type and its context variable (field declarations like "private Context context;", constructor parameters, calls passing context). It is weaker on context-like stand-ins such as passing "this" or getActivity(), Application, env, plugin, request, and imports of android.content.Context. Activation peaks on declared Context fields and variable names.

The format-type word that ends a scientific journal's name, especially 'Letters' or its abbreviation 'Lett'. It fires most strongly in 'Phys. Rev. Lett.' and in 'PhysRevLett' inside DOIs. Weaker activations come from similar journal-name endings such as Communications/Comm, ONE, Express and Reports, and from 'Short Communication' article labels.

The ".widget" token in Java import statements, chiefly "android.widget" (and android.support.v7.widget), the package that holds UI components such as Button, TextView and Toast. Similar UI-component packages in other frameworks (SWT ".widgets", JavaFX ".control", libGDX ".ui") activate only weakly.

Dependency-injection annotation names in code, chiefly Spring's "Autowired" (after or including "@") placed above class fields, constructors or setters. Related annotations that mark a member for injection or binding (Inject, InjectMocks, InjectView, SerializeField, FXML, PersistenceContext) activate more weakly. Prose tokens show only negligible activation.

The " org" package prefix in Java import statements (e.g., import org.springframework / org.junit), strongest when it follows a preceding org import line (repeated org imports, especially junit test imports). Weak scattered activations on unrelated prose tokens and paragraph breaks.

The ".onCreate" token in Android Java code's super.onCreate(...) call inside an overridden onCreate method. Other superclass lifecycle/override calls such as super.paint and super.onStart, plus bare onCreate method names, get only weak activation, and unrelated prose tokens are near zero.

Code annotations and attributes that bind or map method parameters and fields to external data, mainly Java/Spring ones like @PathVariable, @RequestParam, @JoinColumn, @Param and @ModelAttribute, plus C# [FromBody]. The closing quote-parenthesis after the annotation's name argument (e.g. ("id")) also fires. Weaker activity appears on request-parameter accessors such as .getParameter and .params.

The final class name in Java import statements that bring in annotation types (e.g. Spring's Service/Controller/RestController/RequestMapping, JPA's Entity, Lombok's Data/NoArgsConstructor, JUnit's RunWith, WebServlet), which are later used as @-annotations. It fires most strongly on '.RunWith'. Rare weak activations appear on word endings in ordinary prose.

The " com" token that begins a reverse-domain Java package name right after the "package" or "import" keyword (e.g. package com.example..., import com.google...). It fires more strongly after "import", especially when it follows a block of android/org/javax imports, than after "package". Weak, scattered activations on other word-initial tokens are noise.

Month names (full, abbreviated, or capitalized) in the second or later date of a publication or revision timeline, coming right after words like "Accepted", "Revised", "Updated", or "Published". These appear mostly in academic manuscript headers. The strongest activations come when the month directly follows the keyword. Weaker activations fall on the space before the day number in day-month formats.

Tokens that begin a metadata or key–value field line in structured or boilerplate text, typically right after a line break. It fires most strongly on "ms" in Microsoft-docs front-matter keys (ms.date, ms.topic, ms.author). Weaker activations come from other field labels and prefixes such as "Document Version", "Molecular Weight" and "Job Type", page boilerplate, and the "ms" unit.

The top-level domain prefix (mostly "org", also "com" and "io") that begins a package path right after "import" or "import static" in Java/Scala files. "org" activates most strongly, especially for third-party libraries like Spring, JUnit and Apache, while "com" is weaker, particularly for project-local packages.

The end of author-affiliation addresses in academic papers. It fires mainly on the country name that closes an address (Italy, USA, France, UK, etc.) and on the newline, comma, semicolon or 'and' right after it, where the next affiliation or section begins. It fires more weakly on other line-ending punctuation in scholarly text, such as the end of a reference or caption.

Code annotations/decorators (mostly Java/Spring, e.g. @Component, @Entity, @RestController, @Controller, @Service, @Data), strongest when the annotation sits directly above a class declaration; weaker for method/field annotations (@Test, @JsonProperty), C# attributes in brackets, and decorators in other languages.

Sentence-ending punctuation fused with a paragraph break ('.⏎⏎', '?⏎⏎', '".⏎⏎') at the end of a news article's main body, right before unrelated boilerplate such as 'Related news', 'Latest News', 'More news:', or another story's headline. A mid-paragraph period gets weaker activation, and other tokens barely register.

Pieces of institutional affiliation and postal address lines, especially Japanese ones such as university and department names, city and ward names (Sendai, Nagoya, Chofu-shi) and hyphenated postal codes. The strongest activations fall on postal-code digits and hyphens (e.g. 980-8579, 814-0180) and on street-number blocks like 1-7-1. Similar address and affiliation tokens from other countries, plus URL pieces, get weak activations.

The ".id" token immediately following "R" in Android Java resource references (R.id.xxx), typically inside findViewById() calls. Other R resource types such as ".string" activate weakly. Scattered weak activations on unrelated prose tokens appear to be noise.

Class and type names for programming objects, mainly UI menu items and views. Activation peaks on "(MenuItem" inside Android's onOptionsItemSelected(MenuItem item) signature and is strong on "android.view.MenuItem" imports and getItemId. It is weaker on related types such as AdapterView, ItemStack, JMenuItem, ToolStripMenuItem and (Message, which usually appear in import lines or method parameters.

Symbols and letter-based names of subatomic particles and physical states, chiefly mesons, bosons and leptons (D⁰, B⁺, K, J/ψ, η′, Z/W bosons, Υ). Activation peaks on the particle letter or Greek name and its charge or superscript, often in LaTeX. Weaker activation appears on other physics notation such as molecular term symbols (Σ, Π), subscripts and isotope labels, plus occasional stray tokens like '(' after usernames.

The first three digits of a year (e.g. "201", "202", "199") split off from the final digit, mostly in academic citations. Activation is strongest when the year is fused into a BibTeX-style citation key directly after an author name (e.g. "gowal2019scalable" inside \cite{}), and weaker in ordinary "Author et al., 2017" citations, dates and URLs.

Single capital letters embedded inside alphanumeric classification or identifier codes, typically following a number. The strongest cases are the letter in Mathematics Subject Classification (MSC/AMS) codes such as 34A30 or 55P42. Weaker cases include the letter after the dot in PACS codes (03.67.Bg), JEL codes (C22), patent IPC classes (G06F), and letters in part, grant or gene identifiers.

Line breaks that fall mid-sentence inside boilerplate text, mostly license and template comment headers in code (Apache/MPL license text, NetBeans "To change this template" notes, 42-school header lines ending in " */"). They fire most strongly in Apache license lines, e.g. after "licenses this file" and "Version 2.0". Weak activations also appear on spaces or tokens just before a continuation in other templated, repetitive text.

The method name "onCreate" in Android Java code, firing most strongly when it is declared as an overridden lifecycle method ("@Override protected void onCreate(Bundle savedInstanceState)") in Activity classes. Activation is somewhat weaker for public, Fragment, Dialog or ContentProvider variants and for prose mentions of the method. Weak activations on unrelated tokens in ordinary text are just noise.

The opening parenthesis fused with the first named parameter ("(name", "(value", "(feature") in code annotations, attributes and decorators such as Java @Column/@RequestMapping, C# [Display] and Rust #[cfg]. Activation is highest for @Column(name, which typically names a database column or table. Non-code tokens activate only weakly.

Headers for metadata and classification fields in scholarly paper front matter, usually right after the abstract. These include "Index Terms", "PACS numbers:", "JEL Classification:", "Key words:", "OCIS codes:", "MSC:" and "AMS subject classifications". The feature fires on the label word and its following colon or separator, and on punctuation between the classification codes. It peaks on "PACS numbers:". It also fires weakly on the "I." before INTRODUCTION and on similar labeled code fields such as HS Code, CAS Number and CPT Codes.

Person names in scholarly contexts, mainly author bylines and citations in scientific papers. It fires on first names, surname fragments, initials and the separators between authors (commas, semicolons, "and", "et al.", affiliation superscripts, years). It is strongest at the start of author lists that follow a paper title.

over.name: A diffuse, low-intensity feature that fires on tokens that are surprising or out of place in context, especially in disfluent, ungrammatical, garbled or spun/machine-generated text. Typical cases are wrong word choices or broken syntax ("protected to therapeutic massage", "in order the design to work", "to initial aerosol formation"), odd fragments of names or URLs, and unexpected list items. It reflects local unpredictability rather than any specific meaning.

Weak, diffuse activation on tokens inside repetitive, list-like or unstructured text that isn't ordinary prose: number and symbol sequences, code and URL fragments, keyword-stuffed tags, garbled spaced-out letters, line breaks in lists or verse, and math notation. It is strongest on repeated or sequential patterns such as "b b b 1 2 3", strings of underscores and dots, and runs of numbers.

Comment delimiters in code, mainly the '#' and '//' tokens (also '/*', '/**', ';', '\\', '*') that start a line or inline comment. Activation is strongest when the marker opens a comment line at the start of a code block after prose. Weaker activations occur on similar separator symbols in non-code text.

A weak, diffuse feature that fires on content words, mostly abstract nouns and descriptive or evaluative adjectives (e.g., diversity, legacy, insight, portrayal, sustainable, noble). These usually complete a noun phrase or clause, often just before punctuation or a preposition. They appear mainly in elevated, academic or figurative prose, with no single topic tying the examples together.

The program or executable name at the start of a shell command line (e.g. python, php, ruby, gcc, curl, cat, npm), especially interpreters invoked to run a script file. Activation is strongest for interpreter names like python/php/ruby, weaker for flags and subcommands that follow.

Function, method, or command names that execute or invoke something, mostly in code. The strongest cases are calls like os.system, runString, run, and search, which execute commands, code, or strings. Weaker hits include shell commands, macros (try!, html!, assert_eq!), asm blocks, and words like "execute" or "Type" in instructions. Activation usually falls on the method or call token just before its arguments.

Formatting and structural tokens in tables, code, and other structured text: row-ending pipes plus newlines, indentation and alignment whitespace, line breaks, and separators that mark cell, line, or column boundaries ahead of the next aligned item.

A diffuse feature active across technical, software, and documentation-style text, such as programming, editors, config files, rules, and syntax. It mostly fires weakly on function words, sentence-ending punctuation, and newlines. It peaks on terms about code editing and programming languages, such as "highlighting", "snippets", "language name", and "React".

Tokens inside verbatim repeated text. The feature fires on words or phrases that recur several times in close succession (repeated lines, chants, list items, code lines, table cells, boilerplate such as "Invalid Input" or "Show more"), usually from the second or third repetition onward, as the model predicts a copy of earlier text. Activation is strongest in long, highly regular loops of identical multi-token lines.

Syntax tokens inside code or formula snippets, mostly operators, delimiters and short keywords in terse or unusual languages such as Mathematica, PARI/MAGMA, BASIC-like and Forth-like code. Typical examples are pure-function and application markers (&, ]&, @@, //), statement terminators and control words (End, exit, endif, DUP) and bracket or slash combinations. The strongest activations fall on symbols that mark function application or the end of an expression. Scattered prose and non-Latin tokens activate only weakly.

Tokens of repeated characters within elongated or repetitive strings, such as stretched words and exclamations ("yeeeeah", "Aaaaah", "maaaaybe"), repeated punctuation, laughter, block glyphs, and placeholder runs like "xxxxxxxx" or "AAAAAAAA". Activation is mostly on the middle/later chunks of the run and grows as the repetition continues.

Zero digits (and similar placeholder values) repeated within structured sequences such as matrices, arrays, tuples, tables, and numeric lists, firing most on zeros that follow other zeros or repeated filler cells (e.g., "", "*", ".").

A weak, diffuse feature with no clear semantic theme. It fires mostly on function words and connectors in the middle of formulaic phrases, such as "and" joining paired terms ("clean and efficient", "maintenance and repair"), "the", "of", "by" and "at". It also fires on predictable word-piece continuations ("-F|actor", "BYJ|US", "Tel|ugu") and on filler such as table-of-contents dot leaders and code indentation. These are tokens where the continuation is highly predictable.

Backslash characters (\, \\, '\\') across contexts: LaTeX commands (\textsubscript, \begin, \cite), escape sequences (\n, \t), file paths, stray escaped text, and the word "slash" in "backslash"; occasionally other odd separator/escape-like tokens.

A diffuse, low-specificity feature that fires on scattered tokens (function words, digits, operators, identifier suffixes, separators) in technical, mathematical, scientific, code and structured web text. It is strongest mid-exposition, just before a specific variable, value or quantity is introduced, as in "the number…", "is calculated as" or "v01 for this… close to v1".

A weak, diffuse feature that fires on tokens in hard-to-predict, high-entropy text rather than on a particular word. Typical contexts are random alphanumeric strings, hashes, IDs, URLs, IP addresses and numeric lists or codes. It also fires on rare non-Latin scripts, garbled LaTeX, and incoherent spam or machine-generated prose.

Fires on structural or formatting tokens in highly patterned, repetitive text such as code, HTML tables, LaTeX, lists, dates and data listings. Typical hits are indentation and whitespace before list bullets or numbers, newline runs, closing tags (tr, tbody), repeated identifiers and class names, brackets, and parts of dates (month, year digits, commas). These tokens tend to repeat or continue a pattern already set up earlier in the context.

Boundary tokens at the end of a text segment, just before a new section, post, comment, or list item begins. These are mostly sentence-final punctuation fused with newlines, bare newlines, the leading space or number of a new numbered entry, and the colon inside timestamps. Activation is weak.

Tokens in garbled, noisy or atypical text: OCR errors, broken or misspelled word fragments, random character strings, odd capitalization or spacing, and spam-like or formatting junk. The strongest activations fall on dense OCR gibberish (stray letters, numbers and punctuation from scanned documents); weaker ones on single malformed subword pieces.

Mentions of the Python programming language ("python"/"Python", including shebang paths like /usr/bin/python, "python manage.py", python.org, .py, pip, sys.path). It fires more weakly on other programming language names (Ruby, Haskell, Basic) and on technical or path-like code tokens.

The word "Python" or "python" used as the name of the programming language, in prose, code fences, shebang lines, package names and language lists. It fires weakly on unrelated tokens such as the snake sense or docstring quotes.

Tokens that repeat an immediately preceding item in a run of identical elements, typically the third or later occurrence of a repeated number in lists, arrays, tables or sequences (e.g. "9, 9, 9", "10, 10, 10"). It also fires on repeated words, characters or HTML cells, and is strongest for repeated numbers in comma-separated lists.

Fires on unpredictable tokens in noisy, incoherent or low-quality text, such as spun/SEO spam word salad, OCR garbage, DNA sequences, symbol/ASCII art, username lists, number lists, URL fragments and archaic or foreign scripts. It is strongest in long runs of nonsensical text. In otherwise normal sentences it fires weakly on a single oddly placed function word or noun.

Separator tokens such as commas, spaces, ampersands, and HTML <td> tags inside long, repetitive sequences like number lists, table rows, and coin-flip strings. Activation is strongest in the middle of a long run of repeated delimiters. Weaker activations fall on function words (and, with, that, the) in formulaic, promotional-style prose.

Command-line program or tool names, typically the first word of a shell command a user is told to type or run, and most often a package manager or build tool followed by a subcommand like "install" (npm, go, composer, pod, pip, make, rails). Weaker activations fall on other command-like tokens: subcommands, flags, SQL keywords, menu commands and code identifiers.

Tokens that end or complete a phrase which is a repeat of an earlier one in the context. Typical cases are repeated lines, list items, boilerplate and refrains (e.g. "Invalid Input", "Show more", "Monthly Budget", "lived a method", repeated numbers or units). The feature is predicting the final word of a copy. Activation is strongest in highly repetitive text and grows with the number of repetitions.

Terms for web or app routing and addressing, such as routing, route, navigation, url/uri, path, location, link, address, permalink, pages and controllers. They mostly appear in software, web-development and config contexts. Activation is strongest on "routing"/"route"/"navigation"; there are weak spillovers to other routes (road Route 60, iptables nat, Spanish 'ruta').

A weak, diffuse feature with no clear single-token pattern. It fires mostly on generic, low-information filler in noisy web text such as SEO spam, scrambled or nonsensical sentences, code and number snippets, and templated boilerplate. It is strongest on corporate-buzzword placeholder text (e.g., 'Organically grow the holistic world view…') and on generic website promo copy ('If you are ready, you can play some other games').

Fires on the opening token of a document or structured block, such as the very first word or symbol of a text (namespace, using, #define, #ifndef, ![, <!--, titles), and especially the <thead token that starts the header right after a <table> tag.

Tokens inside long runs of the same repeated character or token (dot leaders, dashes, spaces, nbsp, -*, ;\, repeated letters or symbols). Activation is strongest deep in the run, and a few sequence positions stand out as peaks. There are weak, sporadic activations on ordinary tokens, mostly prepositions like "in".

Diffuse, weak activations on tokens in noisy, low-coherence or structured text: garbled/encoded strings, ASCII art, ID and part numbers, URL encodings, tables, list bullets, and run-together or spam text. It fires mostly on repeated or fragment tokens (numbers, single letters, symbols, bullets) where the next token is hard to predict. No clear semantic meaning.

Tokens inside repetitive, predictable runs of text, such as repeated words or phrases ("Image Image Image", "very, very", "Skip to"), repeated symbols or separator lines, and boilerplate markup like HTML table tags (, ⏎, ),
and blockquote ">⏎" lines. Activation increases the longer the same pattern keeps repeating.

Tokens in multiple-choice quiz/test text where the correct answer is about to be revealed: answer labels like "Answer:", "the correct option is", "Option" and "【答案】", the line break after the last listed choice, and the separators in answer keys (e.g. "3.", "B)", "6~10"), all of which come right before an answer letter or value.

The double-slash token "//" in any role: code comments, integer division, URL and path separators, XPath, and decorative separators in bylines or headers. Activation peaks where it joins a URL or template placeholder (e.g. "{{site.github}}//") or appears as a quoted string literal. Weak activations also land on unrelated tokens.

File extensions in filenames, strongest for executable scripts that are being run (.sh, .py, .rb, .pl, .m, .php). Words that refer to running code, such as "script", "program", "run" and "make", also activate weakly.

Separator tokens (commas, spaces, dots, newlines, <td> cells, 'x') placed between items in repetitive lists or sequences of numbers/values/words, firing most strongly when the same item is repeated many times (e.g. '50, 50, 50…').

A diffuse, low-specificity feature that fires mostly on unpredictable tokens in noisy or garbled text: OCR junk, mojibake, random alphanumeric codes and serial numbers, unit letters stuck to numbers, odd single characters or scripts, and gene or sequence strings. It also fires weakly on ordinary punctuation and line breaks in plain prose, which suggests it tracks high-surprise or out-of-distribution tokens rather than any one meaning.

Fires at the very start of a document on leading boilerplate or list formatting: indentation spaces, bullet points (•) and numbering like "1.", plus the first word that follows. These are usually navigation menus, breadcrumbs and list items. It responds weakly to other opening structural markers such as runs of newlines, section commands, separator lines and stray header or menu words like "Stations".

Fragments inside unpredictable, high-entropy character strings: random alphanumeric IDs, hashes, URL and filename codes, passwords, MAC addresses, mojibake or garbled text, and invented or foreign names split into odd subword pieces. Activation is strongest deep inside random codes and garbled Chinese. It is weak on occasional ordinary words.

Vertical bar / pipe characters ("|", and similar box-drawing verticals like ⎢ or ║) used as separators or borders in tables, ASCII diagrams, comment boxes, matrices, and website navigation/metadata strips. Activation is strongest inside ASCII-art diagrams and grids with many aligned bars, and weaker for single inline separators.

Numbers or values that serve as a target, bound or reference point in a comparison, rounding, range, limit or equation (e.g. "rounds to 300", "closer to zero", "less than 150", "0 to infinity", a coordinate or result value). Activation is strongest on numerals in math-style questions and weak on scattered non-numeric nouns and symbols.

A diffuse, weakly firing feature with no clear single concept. It activates sporadically on many token types: numbers and items in comma-separated lists, math operators and LaTeX symbols, punctuation, and citation brackets. It fires most strongly on hard-to-predict or surprising content, such as citation markers like "[6", nonsensical word salad, and incongruous lists of unrelated nouns.

Punctuation, whitespace, newlines and separator tokens (commas, spaces, dashes, tags, line breaks) that act as delimiters between items, mostly in noisy, garbled, redacted, foreign-script or list-like text. Activation is strongest for commas separating repeated or masked items, such as runs of █ blocks or REDACTED.

Delimiter and separator tokens, such as spaces, commas, pipes, ampersands, dashes, newlines, and quote-comma pairs, that sit between items in long repetitive sequences like number runs, page lists, table specs, and data arrays. Activation grows as the repeated pattern continues and becomes more predictable.

Tokens that repeat an immediately preceding token or short pattern. The feature fires on the second and later copies in runs of identical words, symbols, numbers, or cells, such as "H H H H", "+ + +", "Unlimited Unlimited", "agree agree", "7 7 7" and "NA NA". Activation tends to grow the longer the repetition goes on.

Fires weakly and broadly on tokens inside structured or templated text such as HTML table markup (especially '>⏎' after closing td/tr tags), code, markdown links, LaTeX, tables of contents with dot leaders, data listings, and headings. The activating tokens are mostly delimiters, separators or repeated elements whose position is predictable from the surrounding repetitive formatting, rather than tokens carrying particular meaning.

Tokens inside repetitive or patterned sequences: repeated numbers, symbols, separators and code lines (e.g., 30, 31, 30…; -*-*; ~~88~~88; repeated '; ' lines; 16x16x16). The token itself repeats an earlier element in the same run, and activation is strongest in highly regular, predictable repetition. Weak, scattered activation on ordinary words elsewhere.

A diffuse feature with no clear semantic content. It fires mostly on structural and formatting tokens, such as newlines, spaces, brackets, slashes, backslashes and punctuation. These usually sit inside markup, LaTeX, code, tables or garbled multilingual and symbol-heavy text, often at boundaries between segments. It also fires occasionally on ordinary function words like "of" or "in" in prose.

Tokens inside repetitive or patterned sequences, where the next token is predictable from earlier repetition: repeated phrases ("Loading...", "Final Four", "Sacred Valley"), number runs, list separators, whitespace or newline padding, HTML table tags, and repeated characters or symbols. Activations are generally weak and scattered, strongest on spaces and numbers in counting sequences.

The ".py" Python file extension token that completes a filename or path (scripts, modules, command-line invocations, code comments). It fires most strongly on clear file-reference contexts, weakly on bare "py" after a dot, and only marginally on a few unrelated tokens.

under.name: Diffuse, weak activation on journalistic/news-style narration, especially the words that report factual events and their context: past-tense reporting verbs (announced, released, disclosed, convicted, died, says), time expressions (in March, earlier this year, recently, yesterday) and the sentence boundaries or commas joining such factual statements. It tracks the flow of encyclopedic or news exposition rather than any single word.

Fires on function words and verbs inside stock, formulaic phrasing typical of news writing, especially sports journalism. Examples include "held on to the one-goal lead to seal", "has been hard hit by a", "rules out knee-jerk", "coming into this fixture with some happy memories of" and "continue to dominate". These are predictable collocations and connective words (prepositions, articles, auxiliaries) within clichéd narrative expressions, rather than any specific content word.

Content words and connecting function words (prepositions, articles, of/in/on) inside dense technical or scientific prose, especially abstract-style descriptions of mechanisms, measurements, and processes (e.g., adsorption kinetics, electrical conduction, gene regulation). Activation is diffuse and spreads over noun phrases and the prepositional links between them, not over one particular word.

Attribution context for named people (often researchers or experts) in news and science writing. It fires on the words just after or around a name that describe the person's role, title, or affiliation: appositive commas, “who…”, “lead author/co-author of”, “professor”, “said/says”, “and his colleagues”, “at/of [institution]”. Activation peaks on the comma right after a name and on role words like “author” or “who” that start a description of the person's part in a study.

Sentence openings and connective phrases in the results and conclusion parts of scientific abstracts. Activation is highest on sentence boundaries and on the subject-plus-reporting-verb frames that follow them, such as "The results ... confirm", "our analysis reveals that", "We observed" and "values are".

Weak, diffuse activation on tokens that narrate how an event unfolds over time. It is strongest in sports match reports and play-by-play: goals, scores, minute marks, wrestling moves and counts. It is weaker in event schedules and agendas (breaks, sessions, time slots), weather forecasts (tonight, tomorrow, Saturday) and other sequential narration (then, began, after which), including sentence boundaries between steps.

Analytical, report-style prose about trends and conditions, especially in economics, markets, energy, and policy. It fires on wording that describes change, drivers, outlooks, or the current state of things (e.g., weighed on, expected to boost, has slowed, remains, gradual, escalating, key trend). Activation is strongest in financial and market commentary such as currency forecasts and inflation.

Paragraph-break tokens: sentence-final punctuation (period, closing quote, question mark, parenthesis) fused with a double newline, which ends a paragraph and moves to a new one. These are mostly in news-style prose and often come right after a quote attribution like "he said" or a quoted statement. Activation is strongest when the break follows a quoted remark in reporting.

Fires in journalistic or expository prose, mainly where a sentence's subject (a named person, organization or report) is introduced and then described. Activation peaks on the clause structure that attaches information to that subject: relative pronouns and auxiliaries ('who is working on', 'which functions as'), appositive commas, attribution verbs ('said that', 'says') and time framings ('Six years ago'). Isolated weak hits on scattered word pieces elsewhere are mostly noise.

Fires weakly in scientific and technical prose, chiefly materials science and chemistry, at points where a specific material, compound, sample or system has just been named. Activation lands on the function words, commas, closing parentheses and final subword pieces that end or follow that noun phrase, just before its predicate or description ("has", "have", "was", "of", "for", "as a", "which"). Peaks occur on complex compound names and their trailing punctuation. There are scattered low-level hits elsewhere.

Phrases in news-style sports recaps describing athletes’ or teams’ performance and results. The strongest cases are box-score statistics and outcomes such as “led a balanced attack with a game-high 14 points,” “scored nine runs in the fifth inning” and “winless in two matches.” Much weaker activation appears on similar report-style quantity or condition words in weather and nutrition text, such as clouds, rains and carbs.

Language that expresses predictions, expectations or intentions about future outcomes. It is strongest on modal and forward-looking phrasing such as "will/'ll be", "expect that", "hoping to get", "sure to", "promises to be" and "primed to", especially in sports previews and forecasts. Activation peaks on the auxiliary or infinitive "to" that sets up the anticipated event.

Author surnames in academic citations, firing mainly on the final subword pieces of the name and on the "et al." that follows it. These typically appear in parenthetical or inline references such as "(Smith et al., 2010)" and "Smith and Jones (1994)". It fires weakly on other proper names.

Tokens in scientific and technical writing, mostly abstracts and methods sections, that describe a material, device or method being made, prepared or studied. The strongest hits are the words that name or connect the material and its preparation, such as synthesis, polymer, nanoparticles, deposited, coated with, obtained by, and "the synthesis of a". Weaker hits fall on connectives and component lists in materials and method descriptions.

Fires weakly and diffusely in formal technical and scientific prose, such as research abstracts, patents and product specs. It mostly lands on structural and connective tokens rather than content: sentence-ending periods and the sentence starts that follow them ('The', 'A'), clause commas, 'and', 'to' and 'that', and reporting or methods verbs ('was measured by', 'results show a', 'showed that', 'can be achieved'). Activation is strongest at sentence and clause transitions in academic-style writing.

Affiliation markers right after author names in paper bylines, mostly superscript numbers, letters, or symbols (¹ ² ³, †, ‡, \textsuperscript{a}) that tie an author to an institution. Weaker activation falls on other byline separators (commas, newlines after names), the word "Affiliations", and occasionally on citation or footnote numbers.

A diffuse feature of news-style journalistic prose. It fires weakly on scattered content words and phrases in factual reporting and fires most strongly on longer spans that give the substance of a reported statement, claim, ruling or official directive. Typical examples are text following 'said', or clauses like 'ensure the implementation of Corona SOPs…' and 'the 16 cows that died is worth over N5m'.

Fires weakly and diffusely on ordinary words inside direct quotations and reported speech, such as interview remarks ending in “,” he said. Activation tends to grow over longer spans of quoted spoken language, especially conversational or opinion-giving phrasing. Some activations appear outside quotes but are weak and scattered.

Words describing a person's (often an athlete's or performer's) participation, tenure, or career with a team, organization, league, or venue, such as joining, playing for, returning to, leaving, or future with. Activation peaks on the prepositions and nouns linking the person to the institution ("in Pittsburgh", "future in the Reds organization", "at Man Utd", "at the club since").

Scientific and academic research prose, especially framing language that motivates or summarizes a study: statements of knowledge gaps ("little is known", "not well understood", "we still lack an understanding of", "we do not currently know"), research aims ("to better constrain", "to provide a basis for assessing"), and findings or implications ("the findings provide", "this helps us better understand"). Activations peak on these phrases and on sentence boundaries (periods, newlines) where such framing begins.

In-text citation markers in academic or technical prose: the opening bracket or parenthesis of a reference, plus the reference numbers, author names, "et al." and especially the final digits of years in author-year citations. Activation is strongest at the start of the citation and on reference numbers or year endings.

Academic/scientific prose, especially introduction and background sections that review prior work. Activations peak on literature-review framing such as "recent studies have", "researchers have found", "previous measurements", and "recent advances". They also fire on citation numbers and years and on discourse transitions at sentence starts ("For", "A", "On", "In").

Tokens inside direct quotations of spoken remarks, typically an expert or source quoted in news/science journalism explaining something. Activation spans the running content of the quote (verbs, prepositions, nouns mid-sentence), strongest in the middle of explanatory clauses (e.g., 'what we want to do is use...', 'it may be that they are experiencing...'). It is weak or sporadic in non-quoted narrative text.

Personal names of researchers and authors, especially in academic author bylines, citations, and reference lists. It fires on name pieces such as initials, given names, and surname-ending subword tokens, and on the separators between names (commas, 'and', affiliation superscripts and markers). It is strongest near the end of a name or author list, just before affiliations or the year. It also fires weakly on academic role words like 'professor' or 'senior author'.

Narrative prose summarizing fictional characters' backstories and plots, as in wiki or fandom character biographies (e.g., 'X was a lab assistant to...', 'Blaze decided to travel there'). Activation is spread across the running text, mostly function words, character names, verbs and clause boundaries, and is strongest at the start of a new biography section or sentence about a character.

The first word(s) of a new sentence or paragraph, typically a preposition, conjunction, or transition that opens an introductory/adverbial phrase (In, On, At the, Before, Since, However, Other, In addition). It fires most strongly on "In" and "On" right after a paragraph break.

Academic citation markers, mainly the final digit of the year in author-year citations (e.g. "et al., 201[1]") and the numbers and opening brackets of numeric references like [18] or (10–12). It also fires weakly on 'et al.' and author names inside citations.

Technical or scientific nouns and verbs that name the process, quantity, or outcome being measured or changed. They typically come right after words for effect or change such as 'decreased', 'reduces', 'induce', 'increased', 'high', 'stable' or 'to', and the strongest cases are biomedical, e.g. 'PEPCK transcription' or 'induce TDCC activity'.

Affiliation markers in academic author lists: footnote symbols, numbers, letters or superscripts (and the separators/newlines/parentheses) that come right before an institution or department name, marking where one affiliation begins. Activation is highest on the index marker itself (1, ², †, *, a, closing brace of \textsuperscript), and weaker on following words like 'Department of' or punctuation.

Tokens that open a parenthetical or nonrestrictive modifier attached to a just-named noun (often a person or organization): relative pronouns like "who", "which" and "whose" after a comma or dash, plus the comma or dash itself and appositive starters such as "a" or "the". These signal that extra descriptive information about the entity is coming.

Literature-review style attribution of prior work to its authors. The feature fires on author names, citation markers (closing ] or ), \cite{...}, et al.) and the reporting verb that follows (proposed, reported, showed, studied, designed), as in "X et al. [5] proposed...". It is strongest on the closing citation bracket and "al" right before the verb. Weaker activations appear on commas or periods introducing a subject, and on agents or actions in similar non-academic descriptions.

Sentence-ending punctuation (periods, often merged with paragraph breaks or closing parentheses) in formal academic, scientific, or legal expository prose, marking a boundary just before a new sentence or section. Discourse connectives that open the following sentence (e.g. "That is", "however", "but") and the first token after the break sometimes activate weakly.

Technical and scientific descriptions of physical experimental setups and methods, such as samples, apparatus, materials, dimensions, placement or mounting of objects, and measurement procedures. Activation spreads across whole clauses describing how something is prepared, positioned or configured (e.g. 'placing 10 μL on copper grids', 'glued to a 10mm-thick board', 'suspended in water'). Function words and prepositions in these descriptions fire along with the nouns, and spatial-relation words like 'near', 'under', 'through' and 'at' also activate weakly in other contexts.

A diffuse feature of formal, academic or scientific prose, especially research abstracts. It fires weakly on structural and connective tokens: sentence-ending periods and commas, section or list numbers ("1. Introduction"), discourse transitions ("In addition", "In conclusion", "Despite the", "To"), and research-methodology words (study, evaluation of, tested for, quantify, results, characterized, studied).

A diffuse, weakly activating feature that mostly fires on clause and phrase boundaries: commas, periods, paragraph breaks and connectives such as "and", "in" or "with a" right after a completed clause, just before the narrative continues. The strongest hits come from event-reporting text like sports results or historical accounts (e.g. "heats, … Time, and"; "Rohit was on hand to"), where the boundary leads into the next action or outcome.

Fires in physics and spectroscopy text about quantum or particle states and energy levels. It is strongest on the noun "states" and its descriptors (narrow, excited, bound, quasi-bound), on resonances and levels, and on particle masses such as the Higgs mass M_h = 125.7 GeV. Weak activations spread diffusely across other scientific and technical text.

Physics measurement terminology, especially particle and nuclear physics: measured quantities and kinematic variables (transverse momentum p_T, azimuthal modulation, muon yields, angular distributions, coincidence detection of electrons and ions, emitted particles, spectra). Activation is strongest on these experimental-physics phrases and weak or scattered on other technical nouns.

Tokens within technical specification details, chiefly in scientific methods sections and product or catalog listings: reagent purities (e.g., 99%), catalog, model and part numbers, manufacturer or brand fields after colons, antibody and reagent descriptions, and instrument settings. Activation is weak and diffuse, with the strongest values on purity numbers, catalog codes and reagent names.

A diffuse, weak feature for structured informational, guide-like text such as travel itineraries, tour descriptions, event agendas and schedules, and step-by-step instructions. It fires most strongly inside day-by-day itinerary entries (e.g. "Day 1: New Delhi … Morning Visit: It will"). Weaker activations land on list or step markers ("1.", "First", "Then"), agenda or table cells ("Registration", "Panel Discussion"), and promotional travel or experience phrasing ("expedition visits", "options available for a journey").

Journalistic news-story prose, strongest on attribution and narrative-reporting phrases (e.g., ',” said X while attending…', 'he concluded, as reported by', 'shared:', 'Reportedly,') and clauses describing what a public figure did or is doing in celebrity, sports and news reports. Activation is weak and diffuse on other tokens.

News-report prose, especially wire-style coverage of violent or conflict events such as attacks, bombings, killings and security incidents. It fires most strongly on the narrative connective tissue of the reporting: casualty phrases like "At least 13 soldiers killed", "which killed two", "bombing by the Taliban targeting", attribution words like "reported", "according to" and "announced", and sentence or paragraph boundaries and transitions like "Earlier,", "But" and "Adding to this".

A diffuse, mostly structural pattern. It fires on tokens at segment boundaries or at the start of a new unit: paragraph breaks after a sentence (the strongest), bullets, table and line-break tags, and statement-initial code keywords inside a namespace or class block ('using', 'internal', 'private'). It also fires on sentence-opening connectives ('However', 'Furthermore', 'If', 'The company'). Isolated tokens such as 'assigned' or 'mathrm' also activate, with no clear semantic theme.

Text about people being hired, cast, attached, or brought onto projects (especially films, art and entertainment), with the feature firing on the predicate and function words around who joined, was chosen for a role, or collaborated (e.g. "attached … to", "was given", "who would be best for the role", "teamed up with"). There is weaker activation on scattered punctuation and connectives in similar narrative contexts.

Narrative news-report prose describing events, scenes and reactions in the past tense (who did what, where, and how people responded). The strongest activations fall on main-clause verbs, auxiliaries ("were", "was", "had"), collective subjects such as people, groups or communities, and scene-setting phrases about circumstances or aftermath. Sentence boundaries followed by paragraph breaks also activate.

Footnote and affiliation markers (superscript numbers, letters, asterisks, daggers, or LaTeX superscripts) that start a line after an author list in academic papers, introducing institutional affiliations or author notes. Weaker activation on similar note markers and on words like "Department" that begin an affiliation line.

A weak, diffuse feature that fires on mid-sentence function words and verb phrases (modals, auxiliaries, conjunctions such as "but" and "and", prepositions). It is strongest in narrative or argumentative clauses about decisions, deals, offers and their outcomes or alternatives, as in "could have added a fourth", "must be able to make an appealing offer" and "I'd replace that with". These clauses typically carry contrastive or hypothetical reasoning.

Discourse framing in academic or expository writing, especially introduction and literature-review language. It fires on section openings such as "Introduction" headers and the line breaks after them. It also fires on references to prior work ("et al.", "previous studies", "existing works", "this review", "the authors", "Researchers"). Further triggers are transitional or framing phrases like "However", "In recent times,", "We will show that" and "was presented in". Activation is strongest where a sentence pivots to situate or survey research.

The property or field name part of a setter method in code (the token(s) right after "set", e.g. setNeighbours, setId, setReduction), plus its parameter type and name. Weaker hits land on other method or field names and assignment parts of property setters.

The first token of a speaker's or subject's name (usually a surname, often split into subword pieces) appearing right after a quotation or clause boundary, typically in quote attributions like '" X said' or 'said X'. Activation is strongest on the opening subword of unusual surnames and weaker on titles or generic roles such as 'the official' or 'spokesman'.

Tokens inside institutional affiliation and address strings, typically from academic paper author headers. The strongest activations fall on the commas, connectors ("of", "and") and words like "University", "Department" and "Centre" that join nested units (lab, department, university, city). Weaker activation appears on similar organization-name text in prose.

over.name: Decimal points in numbers, firing most strongly on the period right after a leading zero ("0." before a fractional value such as 0.50, 0.375). Weaker activations appear on decimal points after other digits, the "0" itself, and assorted punctuation or separators (colons in times, stray commas or periods, sentence-ending breaks).

Binary operators and operands inside mathematical or code expressions (=, +, -, %, /, ==, <=, \times, \cap, \implies, closing braces, numbers). It fires at the point where an operation links two terms, including prose phrasing of arithmetic such as "by 2", "from 360" and "60 times".

The attribute name "class" inside HTML/JSX tags (e.g. <div class="...">) is by far the strongest trigger. It fires weakly on related styling and selection words such as style, id, setStyleSheet and getElementsByClassName, on "class" used as a code or programming concept, and on a few scattered unrelated tokens.

Word-initial fragments beginning with a vowel plus p/b (mostly "hyp"/"Hyp", with weaker "imp", "hip" and "yp"), firing on the first subword of words like hypotension, hypertrophic, hyperspectral, impressive and impacts. "hyp" fragments activate most strongly; whole words and unrelated tokens activate only weakly.

Weak, diffuse activation on structural boundary tokens in formatted or code-like text: line breaks, closing brackets/braces followed by newlines, indentation whitespace, list numbering periods, table row tags, and the first token starting a new line, field, or list item. It marks the point where one structural unit ends and the next begins.

A diffuse, weak feature with no clear semantic focus. It fires sparsely on scattered tokens: verbs, nouns and punctuation in prose, and identifiers or operators in code. It is somewhat more frequent in procedural or sequential text such as instructions, steps, "then do X", lists and code. The strongest activations fall on code annotations and formula operators.

Diffuse, low-level activation with no clear semantic theme. It fires mostly mid-way through arbitrary character strings such as numbers in phone numbers, IDs, URLs, prices and codes, subword fragments of names and foreign words, and occasionally on function words or paragraph breaks. The strongest hits are numeric chunks inside codes or prices (e.g. "SM 1417", "$187."). Overall it reads as a generic token-continuation feature for unpredictable sequences.

Weak, diffuse feature on structural and technical text. It fires most strongly on generic placeholders or templates that describe a format rather than real content, such as "[Author names]. [Article title]", "name of author, name of recipient", "(ACCOUNT_LENGTH + 1)", "foo: f("foo")" and "/path/to". It also fires weakly on punctuation and delimiters in structured text: colons introducing a spec ("Received:", "rulestring: B"), braces, equals signs, tags, and code or math syntax.

Operators and connective symbols that come right after a number (or variable) in math, LaTeX, or code. The strongest cases are multiplication signs (*, \cdot, ×) and the backslash starting a LaTeX command such as \pi or \times, especially in coefficient patterns like "2\pi" or "2 *". There is weaker activation on other separators that follow a numeric token.

Tokens that close a structured block: HTML/XML closing-tag openers ", , ), the brace after LaTeX \end, final closing braces of code classes/functions, and "End"/#endregion. Also weakly fires on boundary text after a section ends (e.g., "Leave a Reply", list labels).

Numbers or variables serving as the second operand right after an arithmetic or comparison operator (−, +, ×, ÷, /, ±, >, 'to'), mostly in math, code, or numeric comparisons. Activation is strongest after a minus sign in subtraction expressions.

Tokens (spaces, opening parentheses, punctuation, operators, newlines, short words) that immediately precede a number such as a year, measurement, count, price, or code. The feature seems to anticipate that a numeric token comes next.

Items that sit inside an enumeration or sequence: the nouns, numbers, arguments or names that come after the first entry in a comma/slash/plus-separated list. Activation is highest on middle or later items such as "Weight", "Family", "stores", "readings" and "2MP", and on the separators or line breaks next to them. The same applies to repeated code arguments and number series.

Fires weakly and diffusely on fragmented, disjointed or garbled web text: SEO keyword-stuffed spam, scraped boilerplate, metadata, URLs, product codes and incoherent run-on phrases. It is strongest on spammy strings of unrelated keywords (e.g. 'research posters phd researchers music recommender systems', 'essay on environmental awareness wikipedia pollution tuesday').
