Backslash characters (\\ tokens), especially in code strings, regex escapes, Windows file paths (C:\\), and LaTeX line breaks or comments. Activation is strongest in code and path contexts.

Tokens in the middle of long runs of repeated identical tokens or symbols, such as dash or asterisk separators, big blocks of whitespace, daggers, quote marks, dots, zeros, repeated table cells or matrix entries. Activation peaks deep inside decorative or filler repetition, especially symbol-based separators.

Separators and delimiters between items in long repetitive enumerations, such as commas or "and" in author and name lists, pipes in tables or menus, spaces in number sequences, newlines and tabs in lists or code, and brackets in citation runs. Activation tends to rise deeper into the sequence, and the next list item sometimes also activates.

Long runs of the same token repeated over and over, such as dashes, spaced dots, ";amp", ";\", repeated letters, or empty table cells. Activation rises the deeper it is into the repetitive run. Ordinary prose tokens get only weak activation.

Separator tokens (commas, spaces, ampersands, pipes, slashes) between items in repetitive lists, arrays, matrices, tables and other sequences of numbers or symbols, strongest in long uniform patterns like LaTeX matrix '&' cells.

Whitespace separator tokens, mostly tab characters and odd/extra spaces, that sit between fields or words rather than serving as normal word-leading spaces. Typical spots are tab-delimited columns, code indentation, headers and odd spacing in scraped web text. The strongest activations are tabs between fields in tabular data and code. There is weak firing on fragments in run-together boilerplate text (e.g., "PETITION", "Holidays").

Tokens in the last columns of grid-like, tabular, or repetitive structured text (matrices, ASCII art, tables, number grids, LaTeX arrays, repeated symbol rows), especially the last cells right before a line break or row terminator such as \\, |, or ]. It also fires weakly on the last item of repeated patterns in prose.

Highly predictable tokens inside repeated or templated text: words that copy an earlier pattern in the context, such as "Lorem ipsum", "TEXT TO BE EDITED", item_five, test3, ncis~, "Life! death!" or 제목/내용 table cells, and stock web boilerplate like "Your email address will not be published", "Tu dirección de correo" or "forgot password". Placeholder and dummy text activates most strongly.

Weak, diffuse activation on tokens inside repetitive, list-like or unstructured text that isn't ordinary prose: number and symbol sequences, code and URL fragments, keyword-stuffed tags, garbled spaced-out letters, line breaks in lists or verse, and math notation. It is strongest on repeated or sequential patterns such as "b b b 1 2 3", strings of underscores and dots, and runs of numbers.

Fires weakly on tokens that repeat or continue a pattern already in context, an induction-like copying signal. Typical cases are repeated words or strings (Image Image…, true true…, Why? Why? Why, abcabc, Omnomnom, eewwwwwww, JcakJcak), continuations of ordered sequences (alphabet letters, CDEFGABC, 12345678) and pieces of random or ID-like character strings.

Fires weakly and diffusely on tokens inside repetitive, formulaic, or low-information text. The strongest cases are HTML table cell tags (td/th and their closing brackets and newlines) and suffixes in spam-like gibberish prose (-ized, -ability, -atively). It also responds to repeated song-lyric phrases, dot leaders, LaTeX spacing runs, and lists of numbers or prices. In ordinary prose it picks up sentence-final periods and paragraph breaks where one section or topic ends and another begins.

A diffuse, low-specificity feature that fires on scattered tokens (function words, digits, operators, identifier suffixes, separators) in technical, mathematical, scientific, code and structured web text. It is strongest mid-exposition, just before a specific variable, value or quantity is introduced, as in "the number…", "is calculated as" or "v01 for this… close to v1".

A diffuse, low-specificity feature that fires mostly in structured, repetitive or technical text such as code, numeric tables, timestamps, dates, lists and file names. It favours separator and boundary tokens: commas between list items, plus signs between odds, colons in times, periods after list numbers, spaces and units in data rows, and closing braces. It also catches partial-word or number fragments inside such patterns. It rarely responds to semantic content in ordinary prose.

Tokens partway through long repetitive, highly predictable sequences, such as runs of dots, dashes, symbols or separators (table-of-contents leaders, ASCII rules), table cells (LaTeX &, HTML <td>), numeric lists and grids, and IP-address segments. The latent fires on later repeats in the pattern, where the next token can be predicted from what came before. It fires weakly on occasional ordinary words in spammy or garbled text.

Literal escaped line-break markup within text, chiefly the "\n" escape sequence (or the "n" after a backslash) inside code string literals, printf/print statements, and serialized text. It also fires more weakly on other break or separator markers, such as "<br" tags, "\t", "<td", and trailing double spaces before newlines.

A diffuse, weakly firing feature with no clear single concept. It activates sporadically on many token types: numbers and items in comma-separated lists, math operators and LaTeX symbols, punctuation, and citation brackets. It fires most strongly on hard-to-predict or surprising content, such as citation markers like "[6", nonsensical word salad, and incongruous lists of unrelated nouns.

Line breaks, closing brackets/tags and separators that end an item in a repeated, list-like or tabular structure, such as code lines, table cells, list entries or repeated phrases. Activation is strongest where the same pattern is about to repeat.

A weak, diffuse feature with no clear single-token pattern. It fires mostly on generic, low-information filler in noisy web text such as SEO spam, scrambled or nonsensical sentences, code and number snippets, and templated boilerplate. It is strongest on corporate-buzzword placeholder text (e.g., 'Organically grow the holistic world view…') and on generic website promo copy ('If you are ready, you can play some other games').

Separators inside long repetitive sequences, mostly the commas between numbers in number lists and arrays, plus spaces between numbers in columns or rows and repeated filler patterns like " -", "-*" and ";\". Activation is strongest midway through a long run of items, rather than at its start or end.

Separator tokens (spaces, newlines, double newlines, ">\n" in HTML tables, pipes, dashes) placed between items of a repetitive, predictable sequence, such as numbered pagination (1 2 3 4), number or year runs, alphabet indexes, figure labels, answer options, list entries, and table rows/cells. Activation is strongest deep inside long runs of structured, enumerated content.

Tokens inside runs of repeated characters or symbols, such as strings of the same letter or digit ("000", "111", "CCDD", "WWLLW"), elongated interjections ("yeeeah", "ooooh"), placeholder X's, repeated stars, daggers or block glyphs, and doubled backticks. The feature fires partway through the run, where a character or chunk repeats what came just before it.

Fragments inside unpredictable, high-entropy character strings: random alphanumeric IDs, hashes, URL and filename codes, passwords, MAC addresses, mojibake or garbled text, and invented or foreign names split into odd subword pieces. Activation is strongest deep inside random codes and garbled Chinese. It is weak on occasional ordinary words.

Tokens of repeated characters within elongated or repetitive strings, such as stretched words and exclamations ("yeeeeah", "Aaaaah", "maaaaybe"), repeated punctuation, laughter, block glyphs, and placeholder runs like "xxxxxxxx" or "AAAAAAAA". Activation is mostly on the middle/later chunks of the run and grows as the repetition continues.

Whitespace-only tokens (indentation spaces/tabs combined with newlines) forming blank or trailing-whitespace lines, especially between blocks of code (methods, statements) and occasionally in prose. Weak, sporadic activation on boilerplate tokens such as HTML closing tags and repeated page-template words.

Standalone punctuation or symbol tokens, often combined with newlines (e.g. "---", "…", ":", "/", ".", "{"), that act as separators or filler at section and document boundaries. They typically appear where one text segment ends and an unrelated one (a new heading, a scraped fragment, a code block) begins.

Tokens inside long runs of the same repeated character or token (dot leaders, dashes, spaces, nbsp, -*, ;\, repeated letters or symbols). Activation is strongest deep in the run, and a few sequence positions stand out as peaks. There are weak, sporadic activations on ordinary tokens, mostly prepositions like "in".

A weak, diffuse feature that fires on tokens in hard-to-predict, high-entropy text rather than on a particular word. Typical contexts are random alphanumeric strings, hashes, IDs, URLs, IP addresses and numeric lists or codes. It also fires on rare non-Latin scripts, garbled LaTeX, and incoherent spam or machine-generated prose.

Fires on structural or formatting tokens in highly patterned, repetitive text such as code, HTML tables, LaTeX, lists, dates and data listings. Typical hits are indentation and whitespace before list bullets or numbers, newline runs, closing tags (tr, tbody), repeated identifiers and class names, brackets, and parts of dates (month, year digits, commas). These tokens tend to repeat or continue a pattern already set up earlier in the context.

Tokens that repeat an immediately preceding item in a run of identical elements, typically the third or later occurrence of a repeated number in lists, arrays, tables or sequences (e.g. "9, 9, 9", "10, 10, 10"). It also fires on repeated words, characters or HTML cells, and is strongest for repeated numbers in comma-separated lists.

Line-ending tokens that close a structural or delimiter element in code and markup, typically at the start of a file, such as the end of a comment banner or separator line (---⏎, **⏎, #⏎), the closing ">⏎" of an HTML or XML tag, header guards and blank lines after includes. The token marks the transition from boilerplate or formatting into the actual content. Activation is strongest at the ends of long dash or asterisk comment borders.

Vertical bar / pipe characters ("|", and similar box-drawing verticals like ⎢ or ║) used as separators or borders in tables, ASCII diagrams, comment boxes, matrices, and website navigation/metadata strips. Activation is strongest inside ASCII-art diagrams and grids with many aligned bars, and weaker for single inline separators.

Diffuse, weak activations on tokens in noisy, low-coherence or structured text: garbled/encoded strings, ASCII art, ID and part numbers, URL encodings, tables, list bullets, and run-together or spam text. It fires mostly on repeated or fragment tokens (numbers, single letters, symbols, bullets) where the next token is hard to predict. No clear semantic meaning.

A diffuse, low-specificity feature that fires mostly on unpredictable tokens in noisy or garbled text: OCR junk, mojibake, random alphanumeric codes and serial numbers, unit letters stuck to numbers, odd single characters or scripts, and gene or sequence strings. It also fires weakly on ordinary punctuation and line breaks in plain prose, which suggests it tracks high-surprise or out-of-distribution tokens rather than any one meaning.

Tokens inside verbatim repeated text. The feature fires on words or phrases that recur several times in close succession (repeated lines, chants, list items, code lines, table cells, boilerplate such as "Invalid Input" or "Show more"), usually from the second or third repetition onward, as the model predicts a copy of earlier text. Activation is strongest in long, highly regular loops of identical multi-token lines.

Separator tokens (commas, spaces, dots, newlines, <td> cells, 'x') placed between items in repetitive lists or sequences of numbers/values/words, firing most strongly when the same item is repeated many times (e.g. '50, 50, 50…').

Separator tokens such as commas, spaces, ampersands, and HTML <td> tags inside long, repetitive sequences like number lists, table rows, and coin-flip strings. Activation is strongest in the middle of a long run of repeated delimiters. Weaker activations fall on function words (and, with, that, the) in formulaic, promotional-style prose.

Fires at the very start of a document on leading boilerplate or list formatting: indentation spaces, bullet points (•) and numbering like "1.", plus the first word that follows. These are usually navigation menus, breadcrumbs and list items. It responds weakly to other opening structural markers such as runs of newlines, section commands, separator lines and stray header or menu words like "Stations".

Weak feature firing on boilerplate tokens near the very start of documents: the verb "are" in website navigation headers like "You are here / You are on page / You are viewing", plus code and markup preambles such as "<thead" after "<table>", "#include", and especially "DOCTYPE" (the strongest activation).

Tokens that end or complete a phrase which is a repeat of an earlier one in the context. Typical cases are repeated lines, list items, boilerplate and refrains (e.g. "Invalid Input", "Show more", "Monthly Budget", "lived a method", repeated numbers or units). The feature is predicting the final word of a copy. Activation is strongest in highly repetitive text and grows with the number of repetitions.

Punctuation, whitespace, newlines and separator tokens (commas, spaces, dashes, tags, line breaks) that act as delimiters between items, mostly in noisy, garbled, redacted, foreign-script or list-like text. Activation is strongest for commas separating repeated or masked items, such as runs of █ blocks or REDACTED.

Whitespace-only tokens, mostly runs of several newlines (often with indentation spaces or tabs), that form blank gaps between sections of code or documents. Activation grows with the length of the run, so long stretches of consecutive blank lines fire most strongly.

Delimiter and separator tokens, such as spaces, commas, pipes, ampersands, dashes, newlines, and quote-comma pairs, that sit between items in long repetitive sequences like number runs, page lists, table specs, and data arrays. Activation grows as the repeated pattern continues and becomes more predictable.

Tokens that repeat an immediately preceding token or short pattern. The feature fires on the second and later copies in runs of identical words, symbols, numbers, or cells, such as "H H H H", "+ + +", "Unlimited Unlimited", "agree agree", "7 7 7" and "NA NA". Activation tends to grow the longer the repetition goes on.

Tokens inside repetitive, predictable runs of text, such as repeated words or phrases ("Image Image Image", "very, very", "Skip to"), repeated symbols or separator lines, and boilerplate markup like HTML table tags (, ⏎, ),
and blockquote ">⏎" lines. Activation increases the longer the same pattern keeps repeating.

Fires weakly and broadly on tokens inside structured or templated text such as HTML table markup (especially '>⏎' after closing td/tr tags), code, markdown links, LaTeX, tables of contents with dot leaders, data listings, and headings. The activating tokens are mostly delimiters, separators or repeated elements whose position is predictable from the surrounding repetitive formatting, rather than tokens carrying particular meaning.

Tokens inside repetitive or patterned sequences: repeated numbers, symbols, separators and code lines (e.g., 30, 31, 30…; -*-*; ~~88~~88; repeated '; ' lines; 16x16x16). The token itself repeats an earlier element in the same run, and activation is strongest in highly regular, predictable repetition. Weak, scattered activation on ordinary words elsewhere.

A diffuse feature with no clear semantic content. It fires mostly on structural and formatting tokens, such as newlines, spaces, brackets, slashes, backslashes and punctuation. These usually sit inside markup, LaTeX, code, tables or garbled multilingual and symbol-heavy text, often at boundaries between segments. It also fires occasionally on ordinary function words like "of" or "in" in prose.

Tokens inside repetitive or patterned sequences, where the next token is predictable from earlier repetition: repeated phrases ("Loading...", "Final Four", "Sacred Valley"), number runs, list separators, whitespace or newline padding, HTML table tags, and repeated characters or symbols. Activations are generally weak and scattered, strongest on spaces and numbers in counting sequences.

under.name: Tokens that mark the start of unit-test code. The strongest is the ".junit" token in Java imports such as "import org.junit...", especially its first occurrence in a file. It also fires more weakly on "(test" in Rust's #[cfg(test)] attribute before a tests module. Scattered faint activations on ordinary prose and HTML tokens appear to be noise.

The first digit chunk of an article, page or grant ID number in citations, DOIs and funding notes, usually right after a volume number, period or dash. It fires most strongly on Physical Review / APS-style article numbers such as PhysRevB.94.245… or "Phys. Rev. Lett. 126, 045…", and fires weakly on page ranges and grant numbers.

Tokens in the middle of long random-looking alphanumeric strings, such as hex hashes, IDs, API keys, URL tokens and GUIDs, plus separators (dashes, spaces) inside codes and numbers. Activation peaks deep inside these unpredictable character sequences.

The pointer asterisk in Go method receivers, e.g. "func (s *Type)", and more weakly in pointer parameter types. Activation is strongest when the * follows a short receiver variable name. The other low activations are scattered noise: sentence-initial "However"/"Furthermore", German "vorhand(en)", and "GTA" in username lists.

Boilerplate method signatures in Java/C# code (Android onCreateView/onCreate, servlet doGet/doPost, C# event handlers). Activation falls mainly on the commas that separate parameters, the continuation parameters (ViewGroup container, Bundle), the alignment whitespace and the closing ') {' plus the first line of the body. It is strongest for the standard onCreateView(LayoutInflater inflater, ViewGroup container, Bundle savedInstanceState) pattern, with only weak, scattered hits in prose.

Mid-word subword tokens inside scientific names of pathogens and organisms, strongest on the malaria parasite genus 'Plasmodium' ('mod'/'ium'). It also fires on 'falciparum', the 'imal' in 'antimalarial' and 'alar' in 'malar', and other Latin genus names such as Borrelia, Babesia, Cordyceps, Oryza and Flaviviridae. Occasional weak activations on unrelated punctuation and line breaks.

Middle subword tokens inside corticosteroid drug names, strongest for "nis" in prednisone, prednisolone and methylprednisolone. Weaker on "exam" in dexamethasone and "ort"/"oster"/"one" in hydrocortisone, corticosteroids and cortisone. The few weak hits outside medical text appear to be noise.

The ".security" token in Java-style package and import paths (java.security, javax.security, org.springframework.security, and project packages). It fires most strongly on standard library and Spring imports and more weakly on custom package names. Activations elsewhere are faint and scattered, such as the French "sécurité" and random punctuation.

Boilerplate notices and disclaimers about a document: version-of-record and author-manuscript statements, copyright and takedown notices, transcript-error warnings, and instructions to cite, contact, or consult the publisher. The feature fires on the function words and phrase heads of these formulaic sentences ("Please", "is available", "may differ from the", "contact the author for the final version", "refer to the", "providing") rather than on the content nouns.

The name "Carnegie", either as the whole token or the "egie" piece after "Carn", especially as the start of an institution's name (Carnegie Mellon University, Carnegie Hall, Carnegie Institution or Endowment). It also fires weakly on other "egie" word endings.

The opening brace plus newline, and the indentation that follows it, at the start of a struct or enum definition body (mostly Rust `pub struct/enum Name {`, also Go `type X struct {`), right before the first field or variant is listed. It fires weakly on other structural separators such as list indentation, colons, and table cells.
The "throws" keyword after a method signature's closing parenthesis in Java code, declaring the exceptions the method can raise (weaker on similar post-signature keywords like Solidity "returns").

The token ".Context" in code qualified names, strongest in the Java import "android.content.Context" and weaker in other packages (org.mozilla.javascript, org.apache.catalina, echo.Context, C# namespaces). Scattered prose tokens show only negligible activation.

The "mitochond"/"ochond" word-piece within mitochondria/mitochondrial, most strongly in biology contexts. It also fires more weakly on the same "ochond" piece in other words, such as hypochondriac, endochondral and costochondral.

The middle subword token "theros" (and occasionally "ther") inside "atherosclerosis"/"atheromatous", following a split-off "a"/"A". The activation is strongest in medical and vascular contexts. Weak activations also occur on mid-word or mid-number fragments, such as trailing digits of project IDs and "-arrow" in "more-arrow".

A diffuse, low-level feature that fires most strongly and broadly across low-quality, SEO-style or machine-spun web text: promotional and advice copy about dumpsters, casinos and gambling, online therapy, antivirus software and marketing tools, often with awkward synonym substitutions and garbled grammar (e.g., "meet up with their arrangement commitments", "method or significant dumpster"). In these passages it covers long runs of ordinary words, especially second-person "you/your" phrasing. Elsewhere it gives only weak, scattered activations on isolated function words and punctuation in otherwise normal text.

Sentence- or paragraph-ending punctuation (especially a period followed by a blank line) at points where the text suddenly switches to an unrelated topic, as in spammy or stitched-together web text. Activation is strongest when the next passage is incoherent with what came before.

In academic paper author lists, the token right after an author's name that starts the affiliation marker: LaTeX superscript openers ("cript{", "(^{", "^"), opening parentheses, spaces, asterisks, or commas just before affiliation numbers/letters. Plain Unicode superscript digits and symbols (¹, †, ‡) get little or no activation.

Boilerplate and metadata in academic repository or web pages: newline breaks (often double) after URLs, IDs, dates and citation fields, separating sections such as "Submitted on", rights, permissions and citation info. The strongest activation is "contact" in the repository phrase "For more information, please contact ...", along with the email's ".edu".

Weak, diffuse activation across the text of plot summaries and story synopses (films, TV, books, fan fiction), describing what characters do and what happens to them: actions, relationships, settings and turns of events. It is strongest in dense stretches that narrate a sequence of events. Non-narrative text, such as instructions or business prose, gets only sporadic weak hits.

Scientific and taxonomic descriptive prose, mainly species and taxon descriptions in biology and paleontology (Latin genus and species names, family suffixes like -idae, author/year citations, statements of distribution, habitat and morphology). Activation lands on the function words, punctuation and name fragments inside these passages and is strongest in dense species-description text. Weak, scattered activation also appears on general academic and technical writing.

Names of news outlets, wire services and publishers given as source attributions, especially in datelines like "CITY (AP) —", after "told" (told Reuters), or in bylines and credits. It also fires on the labels "Press Release" and "News Release". Activation is strongest on agency names inside dateline parentheses such as AP, Reuters, IANS and Xinhua.

Paragraph-break tokens: sentence-final punctuation (period, closing quote, question mark, parenthesis) fused with a double newline, which ends a paragraph and moves to a new one. These are mostly in news-style prose and often come right after a quote attribution like "he said" or a quoted statement. Activation is strongest when the break follows a quoted remark in reporting.

The ".view" package segment in Java import statements, strongest right after "android" (android.view.View, LayoutInflater, Menu, etc.). It is weaker in other package paths like android.support.v4.view or custom com.*.view packages. Scattered unrelated prose tokens show only faint activation.

The "import" keyword at the start of Java import statements, mainly in the later lines of an existing import block, where it follows earlier imports, often ones that share the same package prefix. One weak exception is "to" in English prose.

Boilerplate legal and licensing text, such as copyright notices, Creative Commons license statements, permission and reproduction terms, disclaimers, and repository archive descriptions. It is strongest on the 'distributed under the terms of the Creative Commons Attribution License, which permits unrestricted use...' formula.
The token immediately following an author's surname in citations or bylines, overwhelmingly "et" in "et al.", but also commas, initials, superscript backslashes, brackets, or "on" after a username.

Numbers in game scores, win–loss records and vote tallies, especially the second number of a hyphenated pair (e.g., the 72 in "77-72"). Activation is strongest on the losing or lower score in reported sports results. It is weaker on first numbers, percentages and units like "points" or "runs".

The access modifier "protected" at the start of a method declaration in object-oriented code (Java, C#, PHP), along with the words right after it ("void", "override", "function"). It is strongest right after an @Override annotation in Android code such as "protected void onCreate(Bundle savedInstanceState)". Other method modifiers like "public" or "private void" fire weakly, and the few prose examples are only trace activations.

Narrative or report descriptions of how a storm or other natural or physical event behaves and changes over time. The strongest cases are news-style tropical cyclone reports about a named storm's intensity, strength, sustained winds, movement and forecast track (e.g. "has weakened to", "maintained its strength", "forecast to move"). Weaker activation falls on verbs, auxiliaries and connectives describing the progression of fires, earthquakes, eruptions and similar events.

Fires on word-piece tokens inside the term "microtubule", most strongly on the "ub" right after "microt", with weaker activation on related cytoskeleton words (tubulin, cytoskeleton, filaments) and on microtubule-targeting drugs (paclitaxel, docetaxel, colchicine, taxol). There is faint spillover onto other "t-ub" pieces such as "tuberculosis".

The last digit of a year inside citation keys (author name + year + title word, e.g. \cite{liu2017smart}, @article{Howell2016...}), firing on the digit that completes the year right before the title word. It is strongest in LaTeX \cite{} keys. A weak secondary response shows up on boilerplate web phrases like "Related questions" and "save at Amazon".

Person names in scholarly contexts, mainly author bylines and citations in scientific papers. It fires on first names, surname fragments, initials and the separators between authors (commas, semicolons, "and", "et al.", affiliation superscripts, years). It is strongest at the start of author lists that follow a paper title.

The ".beans" token in Java package paths, overwhelmingly in Spring imports like "org.springframework.beans.factory.annotation.Autowired". It fires much more weakly on the singular ".bean" in other package names, and only sporadically elsewhere.

The subword "is" right after "an" in the word "anisotropy"/"anisotropic" (and its plurals), across physics, magnetism, MRI and geology contexts. Related directional-property word pieces such as the "x" in uniaxial/biaxial and "isot" in isotropic activate weakly.

Fires weakly and diffusely on ordinary words inside direct quotations and reported speech, such as interview remarks ending in “,” he said. Activation tends to grow over longer spans of quoted spoken language, especially conversational or opinion-giving phrasing. Some activations appear outside quotes but are weak and scattered.

Fires on the ".ComponentModel" namespace token in C# using directives ("using System.ComponentModel", including .DataAnnotations and .Composition sub-namespaces). The similar ".ObjectModel" token in "System.Collections.ObjectModel" triggers it only weakly, and other activations elsewhere are negligible noise.

Exception/error type names in code signatures, especially Java "throws" clauses. The strongest is IOException right after "throws" or "ServletException,". Weaker on other exception classes and "Exception" suffixes (SQLException, ConfigException), Rust Result error types, and a few unrelated tokens.

Package‑name segments in code import paths, especially Java imports: strongest on Spring's ".stereotype" (preceding Service/Component/Controller/Repository), with weaker activation on other library namespaces such as lombok, butterknife, github.com/stretchr, ".RestController", and ".Spring". Rare, faint activations appear in unrelated prose.

The LaTeX citation command name "cite" (including variants like \citep, \citealt, \newcite, \textcite) right after the backslash, which marks references to literature in academic text. Activation is highest for repeated citations in a list. There are weak activations on other LaTeX reference commands like \secref and on scattered unrelated tokens.

Separators between consecutive entries in academic citation lists, chiefly the semicolon after a year in author–year in-text citations (e.g. "Smith et al., 2005; Jones, 2007"), where activation is strongest. Weaker activation falls on commas, "and" or "&" between cited works or authors, and occasionally on words leading into a cited author name.

The final digit of a publication year in an academic citation (e.g. the "6" completing "201" in "Smith et al. 2016"), occasionally with the closing punctuation. The feature also fires weakly on other closing citation markers, such as reference numbers and closing brackets.

Subword tokens inside gene and protein names in biomedical text, mostly the middle or final fragments of symbols like Pitx3, KLF5, OLIG2 and Sox9. It fires most strongly on transcription factors, and also on related words such as "factor" in "transcription factor". Weaker activations appear on other name fragments and newlines.

Second-level segments of dotted namespace/package paths in code, mostly ".Runtime" after "System" in C# using directives, ".gms" after "com.google.android" and ".minecraftforge" after "net" in Java imports. Activation is strongest in import/using statements and weaker in inline references or documentation.

The comma that separates a city name from its following state, region or country in a location or address (e.g. "St. Louis, MO", "Copenhagen, Denmark"). It is most common in academic affiliations, supplier credits and citations, and is strongest in manufacturer parentheticals such as "(Sigma-Aldrich, St. Louis, MO)". It occasionally fires weakly on similar connectors like "in" after an institution name.

Stock, formulaic web/document boilerplate: open-access license statements ("article distributed under the terms of the Creative Commons Attribution License"), copyright notices ("All rights reserved"), forum/blog UI text (Reply/Replies, bullets, post dates/times), calls to action ("Click here to", "Sign Up Now", "Please..."), and templated freelancer bid phrases ("I have X years of experience", "your project description"). Activation is strongest on the core words of the license phrase.

Package-name tokens in Java import statements, strongest by far for ".junit" right after "org" (import org.junit...). It fires more weakly on other test frameworks (testng, plain junit) and on "lombok" after "import". Activations on ordinary prose are near zero.
The final digit token(s) of long numeric identifiers (IDs, ISBNs, PMC/HAL/handle numbers, blog IDs, URL parameters) that end a code string. Activation is strongest on blogger.com blog IDs.

Separators between parts of postal or affiliation addresses (commas, newlines, the spaces after them, and country-code prefixes like "N-" or "CZ-"). Activation is strongest at the separator that comes right after a street address or PO box, just before the postal code.

over.name: Weak, diffuse activation on structural or layout tokens in formatted or non-prose text, such as whitespace runs, pipes, dashes, ampersands and digits in tables, matrices and series, and code formatting. It fires most strongly on ASCII-art characters (slashes, parentheses, backslashes and spaces) inside print strings.
Backslash characters (\\ tokens), especially in code strings, regex escapes, Windows file paths (C:\\), and LaTeX line breaks or comments. Activation is strongest in code and path contexts.

Tokens in the middle of long runs of repeated identical tokens or symbols, such as dash or asterisk separators, big blocks of whitespace, daggers, quote marks, dots, zeros, repeated table cells or matrix entries. Activation peaks deep inside decorative or filler repetition, especially symbol-based separators.

Separators and delimiters between items in long repetitive enumerations, such as commas or "and" in author and name lists, pipes in tables or menus, spaces in number sequences, newlines and tabs in lists or code, and brackets in citation runs. Activation tends to rise deeper into the sequence, and the next list item sometimes also activates.

Long runs of the same token repeated over and over, such as dashes, spaced dots, ";amp", ";\", repeated letters, or empty table cells. Activation rises the deeper it is into the repetitive run. Ordinary prose tokens get only weak activation.

Separator tokens (commas, spaces, ampersands, pipes, slashes) between items in repetitive lists, arrays, matrices, tables and other sequences of numbers or symbols, strongest in long uniform patterns like LaTeX matrix '&' cells.

Whitespace separator tokens, mostly tab characters and odd/extra spaces, that sit between fields or words rather than serving as normal word-leading spaces. Typical spots are tab-delimited columns, code indentation, headers and odd spacing in scraped web text. The strongest activations are tabs between fields in tabular data and code. There is weak firing on fragments in run-together boilerplate text (e.g., "PETITION", "Holidays").

Tokens in the last columns of grid-like, tabular, or repetitive structured text (matrices, ASCII art, tables, number grids, LaTeX arrays, repeated symbol rows), especially the last cells right before a line break or row terminator such as \\, |, or ]. It also fires weakly on the last item of repeated patterns in prose.

Highly predictable tokens inside repeated or templated text: words that copy an earlier pattern in the context, such as "Lorem ipsum", "TEXT TO BE EDITED", item_five, test3, ncis~, "Life! death!" or 제목/내용 table cells, and stock web boilerplate like "Your email address will not be published", "Tu dirección de correo" or "forgot password". Placeholder and dummy text activates most strongly.

Weak, diffuse activation on tokens inside repetitive, list-like or unstructured text that isn't ordinary prose: number and symbol sequences, code and URL fragments, keyword-stuffed tags, garbled spaced-out letters, line breaks in lists or verse, and math notation. It is strongest on repeated or sequential patterns such as "b b b 1 2 3", strings of underscores and dots, and runs of numbers.

Fires weakly on tokens that repeat or continue a pattern already in context, an induction-like copying signal. Typical cases are repeated words or strings (Image Image…, true true…, Why? Why? Why, abcabc, Omnomnom, eewwwwwww, JcakJcak), continuations of ordered sequences (alphabet letters, CDEFGABC, 12345678) and pieces of random or ID-like character strings.

Fires weakly and diffusely on tokens inside repetitive, formulaic, or low-information text. The strongest cases are HTML table cell tags (td/th and their closing brackets and newlines) and suffixes in spam-like gibberish prose (-ized, -ability, -atively). It also responds to repeated song-lyric phrases, dot leaders, LaTeX spacing runs, and lists of numbers or prices. In ordinary prose it picks up sentence-final periods and paragraph breaks where one section or topic ends and another begins.

A diffuse, low-specificity feature that fires on scattered tokens (function words, digits, operators, identifier suffixes, separators) in technical, mathematical, scientific, code and structured web text. It is strongest mid-exposition, just before a specific variable, value or quantity is introduced, as in "the number…", "is calculated as" or "v01 for this… close to v1".

A diffuse, low-specificity feature that fires mostly in structured, repetitive or technical text such as code, numeric tables, timestamps, dates, lists and file names. It favours separator and boundary tokens: commas between list items, plus signs between odds, colons in times, periods after list numbers, spaces and units in data rows, and closing braces. It also catches partial-word or number fragments inside such patterns. It rarely responds to semantic content in ordinary prose.

Tokens partway through long repetitive, highly predictable sequences, such as runs of dots, dashes, symbols or separators (table-of-contents leaders, ASCII rules), table cells (LaTeX &, HTML <td>), numeric lists and grids, and IP-address segments. The latent fires on later repeats in the pattern, where the next token can be predicted from what came before. It fires weakly on occasional ordinary words in spammy or garbled text.

Literal escaped line-break markup within text, chiefly the "\n" escape sequence (or the "n" after a backslash) inside code string literals, printf/print statements, and serialized text. It also fires more weakly on other break or separator markers, such as "<br" tags, "\t", "<td", and trailing double spaces before newlines.

A diffuse, weakly firing feature with no clear single concept. It activates sporadically on many token types: numbers and items in comma-separated lists, math operators and LaTeX symbols, punctuation, and citation brackets. It fires most strongly on hard-to-predict or surprising content, such as citation markers like "[6", nonsensical word salad, and incongruous lists of unrelated nouns.

Line breaks, closing brackets/tags and separators that end an item in a repeated, list-like or tabular structure, such as code lines, table cells, list entries or repeated phrases. Activation is strongest where the same pattern is about to repeat.

A weak, diffuse feature with no clear single-token pattern. It fires mostly on generic, low-information filler in noisy web text such as SEO spam, scrambled or nonsensical sentences, code and number snippets, and templated boilerplate. It is strongest on corporate-buzzword placeholder text (e.g., 'Organically grow the holistic world view…') and on generic website promo copy ('If you are ready, you can play some other games').

Separators inside long repetitive sequences, mostly the commas between numbers in number lists and arrays, plus spaces between numbers in columns or rows and repeated filler patterns like " -", "-*" and ";\". Activation is strongest midway through a long run of items, rather than at its start or end.

Separator tokens (spaces, newlines, double newlines, ">\n" in HTML tables, pipes, dashes) placed between items of a repetitive, predictable sequence, such as numbered pagination (1 2 3 4), number or year runs, alphabet indexes, figure labels, answer options, list entries, and table rows/cells. Activation is strongest deep inside long runs of structured, enumerated content.

Tokens inside runs of repeated characters or symbols, such as strings of the same letter or digit ("000", "111", "CCDD", "WWLLW"), elongated interjections ("yeeeah", "ooooh"), placeholder X's, repeated stars, daggers or block glyphs, and doubled backticks. The feature fires partway through the run, where a character or chunk repeats what came just before it.

Fragments inside unpredictable, high-entropy character strings: random alphanumeric IDs, hashes, URL and filename codes, passwords, MAC addresses, mojibake or garbled text, and invented or foreign names split into odd subword pieces. Activation is strongest deep inside random codes and garbled Chinese. It is weak on occasional ordinary words.

Tokens of repeated characters within elongated or repetitive strings, such as stretched words and exclamations ("yeeeeah", "Aaaaah", "maaaaybe"), repeated punctuation, laughter, block glyphs, and placeholder runs like "xxxxxxxx" or "AAAAAAAA". Activation is mostly on the middle/later chunks of the run and grows as the repetition continues.

Whitespace-only tokens (indentation spaces/tabs combined with newlines) forming blank or trailing-whitespace lines, especially between blocks of code (methods, statements) and occasionally in prose. Weak, sporadic activation on boilerplate tokens such as HTML closing tags and repeated page-template words.

Standalone punctuation or symbol tokens, often combined with newlines (e.g. "---", "…", ":", "/", ".", "{"), that act as separators or filler at section and document boundaries. They typically appear where one text segment ends and an unrelated one (a new heading, a scraped fragment, a code block) begins.

Tokens inside long runs of the same repeated character or token (dot leaders, dashes, spaces, nbsp, -*, ;\, repeated letters or symbols). Activation is strongest deep in the run, and a few sequence positions stand out as peaks. There are weak, sporadic activations on ordinary tokens, mostly prepositions like "in".

A weak, diffuse feature that fires on tokens in hard-to-predict, high-entropy text rather than on a particular word. Typical contexts are random alphanumeric strings, hashes, IDs, URLs, IP addresses and numeric lists or codes. It also fires on rare non-Latin scripts, garbled LaTeX, and incoherent spam or machine-generated prose.

Fires on structural or formatting tokens in highly patterned, repetitive text such as code, HTML tables, LaTeX, lists, dates and data listings. Typical hits are indentation and whitespace before list bullets or numbers, newline runs, closing tags (tr, tbody), repeated identifiers and class names, brackets, and parts of dates (month, year digits, commas). These tokens tend to repeat or continue a pattern already set up earlier in the context.

Tokens that repeat an immediately preceding item in a run of identical elements, typically the third or later occurrence of a repeated number in lists, arrays, tables or sequences (e.g. "9, 9, 9", "10, 10, 10"). It also fires on repeated words, characters or HTML cells, and is strongest for repeated numbers in comma-separated lists.

Line-ending tokens that close a structural or delimiter element in code and markup, typically at the start of a file, such as the end of a comment banner or separator line (---⏎, **⏎, #⏎), the closing ">⏎" of an HTML or XML tag, header guards and blank lines after includes. The token marks the transition from boilerplate or formatting into the actual content. Activation is strongest at the ends of long dash or asterisk comment borders.

Vertical bar / pipe characters ("|", and similar box-drawing verticals like ⎢ or ║) used as separators or borders in tables, ASCII diagrams, comment boxes, matrices, and website navigation/metadata strips. Activation is strongest inside ASCII-art diagrams and grids with many aligned bars, and weaker for single inline separators.

Diffuse, weak activations on tokens in noisy, low-coherence or structured text: garbled/encoded strings, ASCII art, ID and part numbers, URL encodings, tables, list bullets, and run-together or spam text. It fires mostly on repeated or fragment tokens (numbers, single letters, symbols, bullets) where the next token is hard to predict. No clear semantic meaning.

A diffuse, low-specificity feature that fires mostly on unpredictable tokens in noisy or garbled text: OCR junk, mojibake, random alphanumeric codes and serial numbers, unit letters stuck to numbers, odd single characters or scripts, and gene or sequence strings. It also fires weakly on ordinary punctuation and line breaks in plain prose, which suggests it tracks high-surprise or out-of-distribution tokens rather than any one meaning.

Tokens inside verbatim repeated text. The feature fires on words or phrases that recur several times in close succession (repeated lines, chants, list items, code lines, table cells, boilerplate such as "Invalid Input" or "Show more"), usually from the second or third repetition onward, as the model predicts a copy of earlier text. Activation is strongest in long, highly regular loops of identical multi-token lines.

Separator tokens (commas, spaces, dots, newlines, <td> cells, 'x') placed between items in repetitive lists or sequences of numbers/values/words, firing most strongly when the same item is repeated many times (e.g. '50, 50, 50…').

Separator tokens such as commas, spaces, ampersands, and HTML <td> tags inside long, repetitive sequences like number lists, table rows, and coin-flip strings. Activation is strongest in the middle of a long run of repeated delimiters. Weaker activations fall on function words (and, with, that, the) in formulaic, promotional-style prose.

Fires at the very start of a document on leading boilerplate or list formatting: indentation spaces, bullet points (•) and numbering like "1.", plus the first word that follows. These are usually navigation menus, breadcrumbs and list items. It responds weakly to other opening structural markers such as runs of newlines, section commands, separator lines and stray header or menu words like "Stations".

Weak feature firing on boilerplate tokens near the very start of documents: the verb "are" in website navigation headers like "You are here / You are on page / You are viewing", plus code and markup preambles such as "<thead" after "<table>", "#include", and especially "DOCTYPE" (the strongest activation).

Tokens that end or complete a phrase which is a repeat of an earlier one in the context. Typical cases are repeated lines, list items, boilerplate and refrains (e.g. "Invalid Input", "Show more", "Monthly Budget", "lived a method", repeated numbers or units). The feature is predicting the final word of a copy. Activation is strongest in highly repetitive text and grows with the number of repetitions.

Punctuation, whitespace, newlines and separator tokens (commas, spaces, dashes, tags, line breaks) that act as delimiters between items, mostly in noisy, garbled, redacted, foreign-script or list-like text. Activation is strongest for commas separating repeated or masked items, such as runs of █ blocks or REDACTED.

Whitespace-only tokens, mostly runs of several newlines (often with indentation spaces or tabs), that form blank gaps between sections of code or documents. Activation grows with the length of the run, so long stretches of consecutive blank lines fire most strongly.

Delimiter and separator tokens, such as spaces, commas, pipes, ampersands, dashes, newlines, and quote-comma pairs, that sit between items in long repetitive sequences like number runs, page lists, table specs, and data arrays. Activation grows as the repeated pattern continues and becomes more predictable.

Tokens that repeat an immediately preceding token or short pattern. The feature fires on the second and later copies in runs of identical words, symbols, numbers, or cells, such as "H H H H", "+ + +", "Unlimited Unlimited", "agree agree", "7 7 7" and "NA NA". Activation tends to grow the longer the repetition goes on.

Tokens inside repetitive, predictable runs of text, such as repeated words or phrases ("Image Image Image", "very, very", "Skip to"), repeated symbols or separator lines, and boilerplate markup like HTML table tags (, ⏎, ),
and blockquote ">⏎" lines. Activation increases the longer the same pattern keeps repeating.

Fires weakly and broadly on tokens inside structured or templated text such as HTML table markup (especially '>⏎' after closing td/tr tags), code, markdown links, LaTeX, tables of contents with dot leaders, data listings, and headings. The activating tokens are mostly delimiters, separators or repeated elements whose position is predictable from the surrounding repetitive formatting, rather than tokens carrying particular meaning.

Tokens inside repetitive or patterned sequences: repeated numbers, symbols, separators and code lines (e.g., 30, 31, 30…; -*-*; ~~88~~88; repeated '; ' lines; 16x16x16). The token itself repeats an earlier element in the same run, and activation is strongest in highly regular, predictable repetition. Weak, scattered activation on ordinary words elsewhere.

A diffuse feature with no clear semantic content. It fires mostly on structural and formatting tokens, such as newlines, spaces, brackets, slashes, backslashes and punctuation. These usually sit inside markup, LaTeX, code, tables or garbled multilingual and symbol-heavy text, often at boundaries between segments. It also fires occasionally on ordinary function words like "of" or "in" in prose.

Tokens inside repetitive or patterned sequences, where the next token is predictable from earlier repetition: repeated phrases ("Loading...", "Final Four", "Sacred Valley"), number runs, list separators, whitespace or newline padding, HTML table tags, and repeated characters or symbols. Activations are generally weak and scattered, strongest on spaces and numbers in counting sequences.

under.name: Tokens in the opening clause of a direct quotation, mostly a speaker's statement in news-style reporting. Activation starts just after the quote's first word ("We", "It", "The") and runs through the first phrase, typically the subject, verb and complement. It is strongest on the main assertion or verb phrase early in the quote and fades as the sentence goes on.

A weak, diffuse feature that fires on mid-sentence continuation tokens in formal, expository prose (scientific, legal, technical, business writing). It mostly hits function words that extend a phrase, such as of, the, that, as, in, for, or, and including, especially right after a noun ("types of", "range of", "factors that are"). Less often it hits modifiers or content words inside an ongoing clause ("bulk", "heavy", "defective", "substances"). It tracks the elaboration of a noun phrase or clause rather than any specific meaning.

Appositive or descriptive phrases that come right after a person's name and give their title, role, affiliation or other identifying detail (e.g. ", an analyst at", ", CEO of", "who is the adviser to", ", 66, of"). The comma right after the name and the role words are the strongest parts, typically in news-style quote attributions.

Final tokens of proper names and named entities, especially institutions, organizations, publications and place names (e.g. 'Institute in Boulder, Colo', 'University College London', 'Vanity Fair', 'Protection Agency'). Activation is strongest on the closing word of multi-word names and on location tags after affiliations, and also fires on name-completing subword pieces and unit or technical terms.

Speaker attribution in news-style prose: the closing quote punctuation, speech verbs (said/says/explained), and especially the speaker's name plus the appositive title or role that follows it (e.g., ", director of…", ", lead author, who…"). The strongest activations come right after a quotation ends.

The subject of a new sentence or paragraph, usually just after a line break, and above all the main verb that follows it (is/are/has/had/would be/was established). Activation peaks at the transition from the subject noun phrase (often the final subword of a name or the head noun) to its verb or auxiliary.

Diffuse, weak activation on scientific/academic abstract prose, strongest at sentence boundaries (periods and the following sentence starters like "The", "We show that", "Our data show") and on the causal or relational verb phrases stating findings ("is associated with", "increases", "produces", "leads to", "correlated with", "caused").

Sentence-ending punctuation, mostly a period fused with paragraph-break newlines (".⏎⏎"), marking the end of a paragraph or sentence before new content begins. It is strongest at paragraph breaks in news/expository prose and weaker on plain mid-paragraph periods or bracketed citation endings.

Diffuse, low-level activation across formal scientific and technical prose such as abstracts, papers, reports and specifications. It fires most on structural and functional tokens: sentence-ending periods, paragraph breaks, citations and reference numbers, and section headers like Introduction. It also picks up methodological phrasing in the body text, such as "we developed an analysis method", "newly developed", "these tools are developed within" and "basic design".

Fires densely across runs of generic expository or descriptive prose, strongest in SEO-style, marketing or article-spinner text with awkward synonym swaps (e.g. "video clip poker", "good mobile discussion", tire product blurbs) and in encyclopedic summary sentences. Activation spans whole clauses of content words and function words rather than single tokens. Elsewhere it fires only weakly on scattered words.

Weak, diffuse activation on boilerplate web text such as site descriptions, cookie and browser notices, newsletter or subscription prompts, repository and access notices, and product blurbs. It fires on function words and generic service phrases like "to ensure you have", "for the latest updates", "with your name and password", "uses ... that" and "for further information".

A diffuse, low-level feature for low-quality web text: SEO spam, casino and pharmacy spam, spun or machine-generated prose, and repository/metadata boilerplate. It fires most strongly inside incoherent, word-salad or mixed-language spam passages, such as pharma spam with stray Portuguese words or nonsensical essay-mill text. It fires weakly on scattered tokens in ordinary boilerplate like page view counts and archive notices.

Clause and sentence boundaries in fluent, generic expository or SEO-style web prose. Activation peaks on sentence-ending periods, especially those followed by paragraph breaks, and is somewhat lower on bare newlines before headings. Weaker activation falls on commas, conjunctions like "and" and "or", and the words that begin the next sentence (It, In, She, If you, The). When the feature is strong, it spreads across many function words and pronouns (your, her, the, to), tracking the flow of formulaic text from one phrase to the next.

A diffuse, weakly activating feature that fires on ordinary mid-sentence tokens in factual, expository or narrative prose, mainly function words, verbs and nouns that carry a statement forward. It is strongest on reporting and predicate phrases that relay facts or claims, such as "says that", "claims that", "was included in", "has risen to" and "until". It is not tied to any specific word or topic.

Punctuation that closes a direct quotation (mostly a comma fused with a closing quote mark, e.g. ,” or ,") at the end of a quoted statement, just before the speaker attribution such as "he said" or "says [name]". It is strongest on the comma+quote token in news-style quotes, weaker for periods, question marks or exclamation marks ending quotes.

Sentence- and segment-ending punctuation (mostly periods, also ?, commas, newlines) at clause/sentence boundaries, especially where web boilerplate, disclaimers, or promotional text finishes a statement and a new sentence or section begins.

Tokens that come right after a person's name, mostly a surname, especially in citations and author bylines. Typical cases are "et" in "et al.", the commas and initials in author lists, and the year digits or reference brackets that follow. It also fires on whatever follows a name in prose or headers, such as appositive commas, titles (Jr., PhD, professor), separators (|, -, —), and verbs like "said" or "explains".

Sentence boundaries in scientific or technical abstract-style prose. Activation peaks on the period closing a sentence, especially the opening background or aim sentence. It continues onto the first words of the next sentence when that sentence moves into methods, data, or findings ("The study involved", "Data were from", "Methods: This was a", "We compared"). Weaker activation falls on method and reporting phrases and on parenthetical acronyms.

Journalistic news-story prose, strongest on attribution and narrative-reporting phrases (e.g., ',” said X while attending…', 'he concluded, as reported by', 'shared:', 'Reportedly,') and clauses describing what a public figure did or is doing in celebrity, sports and news reports. Activation is weak and diffuse on other tokens.

Institutional affiliation text, typically in author bylines of academic papers. It fires on words like University, Department of, Institute, School and College, on the commas and parentheses that separate parts of the affiliation, and on the address details that follow (city, state, postal code, P.O. Box). This holds across English, Spanish, Portuguese and French forms (Universidad/Université, Instituto, Laboratoire).

Weak, diffuse feature on announcement and product or news-release prose, peaking on phrases about upcoming releases, updates, publication, availability or scheduled dates (e.g. 'to issue an update in the near future', 'later this week', 'release date', 'slated', 'forthcoming'). It also fires faintly on descriptive 'X is a/designed to' statements and on sentence ends that close an article.

The last digit of a year inside an academic in-text citation (e.g. "Smith et al., 198[8]"), firing most strongly in author–year parenthetical references. It fires weakly on numbered citation brackets, the digits in them and their commas, and on dates or other reference-like numbers.

Weak activation on attribution and credit text naming people or organizations: author bylines, affiliations, contact details, signature lines, credits like "produced by" or "photo credit", and spokesperson or title attributions. It fires mostly on parts of personal names (often the final subword), titles, affiliation markers (commas, numbers, asterisks) and the line breaks between them.

Names of academic and research institutional units in author affiliations and bios, especially subunits like "Department of", "School of", "Laboratory", "Institute" or "Center" (including non-English forms), plus the field names and "University" that follow. Activation is highest on the unit word itself, such as "Department" or "School", and on the following "of", particularly in paper headers listing affiliations.

Surnames of people, especially authors in academic citations and bylines (e.g., "X et al.", "(Name, year)", author lists). The feature fires on the surname itself or its final subword piece, often extending to the comma or initial that follows it.

A diffuse feature that fires weakly across ordinary expository and explanatory prose. It lands mostly on clause-continuing words such as verbs, abstract nouns and function words. It peaks on discourse transitions and connectives that link or extend ideas, like "for example", "In addition", "Ultimately", "but", "as ... famously put it" and "result from".

Discourse connectives and sentence openers in formal, academic-style prose. The strongest are words starting a new sentence after a citation or period, especially contrastive "However", plus "Furthermore", "Moreover", "Additionally" and existential "There is/are". Weaker hits are fixed phrase parts of scholarly boilerplate ("et al", "would like to thank", "take into account").

Spans of news-report prose, most strongly local incident and disaster reporting (accidents, fires, shootings, storm damage, attacks), where officials or investigators describe what happened and what was affected. Activation peaks on the narrative clause right after a paragraph break, such as "Investigators say the accident involved a truck and two cars". Elsewhere it gives weak, diffuse activation on ordinary factual reporting.

Diffuse, weak activation on framing language in journalistic and feature-style prose. It fires on verb and predicate phrases and evaluative transitions that set up a story's stakes, tension or significance, for example "leaves consumers in a quandary", "growing anger at the", "remains one of the most controversial topics", "researchers are again looking back" and "has yet to be carried out". These are typically clause-linking or main-predicate words in mid-sentence, pointing toward the article's key point.
Sentence-ending punctuation (mainly periods, occasionally semicolons, closing quotes/parentheses or newlines) that ends a complete clause mid-passage, marking a boundary where a new sentence follows.

Technical and scientific descriptions of physical experimental setups and methods, such as samples, apparatus, materials, dimensions, placement or mounting of objects, and measurement procedures. Activation spreads across whole clauses describing how something is prepared, positioned or configured (e.g. 'placing 10 μL on copper grids', 'glued to a 10mm-thick board', 'suspended in water'). Function words and prepositions in these descriptions fire along with the nouns, and spatial-relation words like 'near', 'under', 'through' and 'at' also activate weakly in other contexts.

Expository news-style prose. Activation peaks on the core clause of a sentence that introduces who did what, most often at the start of a new sentence or paragraph. Typical spans are the subject (a named person, organization or "The former couple"), the main verb, and the source-attribution phrasing that follows. Examples include "The attorney for … says in court papers", "According to a report produced by", "announced the split with" and "trimmed its … ownership in". Function words linking these elements (to, the, in, of, commas) are also marked, while scattered weak activations appear elsewhere.

Diffuse, low-strength activation on the content of embedded verb-phrase complements that spell out an intended action, purpose or effect. These tokens typically follow a setup word such as "to", "of", "through", "efforts", "willingness" or "help". Examples include "to provide users with", "efforts to develop a field-based test", "to figure out how to make" and "how climate change will affect sea level". The strongest activations fall on the verbs and objects in the middle of these purpose or goal clauses.

Names and descriptions of specific physical locations or venues where something happens or is situated (buildings, arenas, parks, plazas, centers, landmarks). It fires mostly on the head noun of the place name (Center, Arena, Plaza, Palace, Zone, garden), often after prepositions like 'at' or 'in', and sometimes carries through to a following 'in [City]'.

Fires on awkward, unidiomatic or incorrect word choices, typical of synonym-spun SEO text, machine paraphrasing or non-native grammar. Most often these are swapped prepositions or connectives ("within" for "in", "from"/"into" for "of"/"to", "plus" for "and", "along with", "which" for "that"). It also catches odd synonym substitutions ("returning" for "back", "fringe" for "edge", "prosperity" for "well-being", "likelihood" for "odds"). It marks the token where the phrasing deviates from what a fluent writer would say.

Lists of person names, mostly author or inventor bylines in academic papers, patents and citations. The strongest activations fall on the separators and boundaries between names: commas, the final "and", affiliation superscripts or footnote marks, bullets and line breaks. Activations are also moderate on surname endings and on the initials or first names that begin the next entry.

Language describing sports teams' competitive performance and form (e.g., playing well, scoring goals, winning, being evenly matched, outclassing opponents, best records). It fires most strongly on these team-performance phrases and only weakly and diffusely on unrelated text.

Names of and references to scientific instruments, observatories, space missions, and large data-collecting facilities or campaigns (telescopes like EELT and Herschel, radar networks like SuperDARN, satellites, the ATLAS experiment, SRTM, field campaigns). Activation is strongest on the distinctive part of an instrument or mission name and weaker on generic data-source and measurement terms such as 'missions', 'data', 'satellite' and 'resolution'.

Mentions of scheduled or time-bounded events (conferences, festivals, tournaments, ceremonies, elections, seasons, trips) and the words giving their timing, duration, or venue, such as dates, weekdays, 'two-day', 'held at', 'ends', 'last day of', 'opening'. It is strongest where an event's occurrence or ending is stated, e.g. 'The conference ends Thursday'.

Continuation tokens inside institutional names and postal addresses, especially in academic affiliation lines. The strongest cases are German or other European compound words and street names, such as -straße, -universität and -medizin. It also fires on nouns ending institution names (Center, Institute, University, Technology), on postal codes and phone digits, and on the word "version" in "Citation for published version".

A diffuse, low-level feature that fires across ordinary expository or narrative prose. It peaks mainly at clause boundaries such as commas and periods and on the connective words that continue a sentence ('and then', 'which means', 'when they', 'even if'), with weaker activation on content nouns inside these running clauses. It seems to track mid-sentence continuation and discourse flow rather than any particular topic.

Tokens inside personal names, chiefly in author lists and bylines of academic papers and reports, along with the separators between names: commas, initials, affiliation markers, superscripts and parenthetical native-script names. It fires most strongly in dense, multi-author lists. It also fires weakly on names and roles of researchers quoted in science news (e.g. 'postdoctoral research fellow') and on email domains near author blocks.

Tokens in passages about scheduled or upcoming events. It fires on the words that describe what will happen and when, such as a game, session, meeting, trial, election or launch, plus their surrounding predicate words ("will take on", "when it convenes", "next stage", "starts in January"). Activation is strongest on forward-looking descriptions of a planned occurrence, like sports matchups and legislative or calendar events.

Speech attribution in journalistic or quoted text. It fires on speaker names, pronouns (he, she) and verbs like said, says, adds, told or noting that sit next to quotes. It also fires on the punctuation and sentence or paragraph boundaries around attributed statements, with the strongest response to the speaker name and the attribution verb.

Structural and attribution tokens in news or journalistic prose: sentence and paragraph boundaries (period plus double newline, headline-ending newlines), the first word of a new paragraph, and reporting or attribution words such as "said", "according to", "announced", "stresses" and "found". It also fires on the punctuation around quotes, source names, datelines and photo credits. Activation is strongest on "said" after a quote and on paragraph breaks.

Speech-attribution phrases for quoted or reported statements: verbs of saying or thinking (said, says, explained, claims, admits, added, continues) and the speaker reference attached to them (pronoun, name ending, 'according to X', interview speaker labels). Activation is strongest right after a closing quote, as in “...,” she says.

Low-level, diffuse activation on the words of evaluative commentary about an organization's (mostly tech companies like Nintendo, Microsoft, Google, IBM, Amazon) actions, strategy, fortunes or competitive standing. Examples include whether it does enough, gets rich, taunts rivals, changes direction, lags behind or keeps impressing. Activation is strongest on the predicate describing the entity's behavior or rivalry.

Definite article "The"/"the" (occasionally other determiners like "These"/"A") at the start of a new sentence, paragraph, or clause, opening a fresh noun phrase that introduces the next topic. Activation is strongest right after a period or paragraph break.

Structural boundary tokens in web-scraped text, mainly sentence-final punctuation fused with newlines (".⏎⏎", "⏎⏎"). These mark where one section or block ends and a new, often unrelated one begins, such as a heading, byline, review, list item or boilerplate. Weaker activations fall on delimiters inside metadata like author lists, dates, prices, IDs and usernames (commas, parentheses, colons, bullets, quote marks). The strongest cases close a quoted testimonial before a new date or entry.

over.name: Separators within lists, enumerations and sequences of parallel items: commas, "and", periods, newlines, bullet dashes and pipes that sit between consecutive list elements, clauses or entries. Activation is strongest in long repetitive enumerations such as number lists, bulleted instructions and constructor initializer lists.

Short single-letter (or very short) symbols used as variable, function, or label names, especially math variables (f, g, b, t, D, rho, Delta), loop indices (i, j), type parameters, and list/section labels (D), IV, (e)). Strongest when a new variable or function is being introduced or defined.

A diffuse, weakly activating pattern centered on the final content token of a short phrase, title, question, or argument, typically just before a boundary such as a question mark, closing quote or parenthesis, comma, or line break. It is strongest in templated, SEO-style query headings, for example "Convert Decimal 0.01 to Percent", "rooms in the Bellagio?" and "on a computer?". Weaker activations land on phrase-ending nouns, date and number fields, and function-call arguments.

A diffuse, weakly activating feature. It fires mostly on structural and formatting tokens at line or section boundaries: newlines after headers, HTML/LaTeX markup (e.g. '<table>' followed by a newline, '\begin{align*}'), separators, ellipses and code braces. It also fires on highly predictable words inside boilerplate or formulaic phrases, such as 'stay tuned', 'be sure', 'every reasonable effort to ensure', 'hello there and welcome', 'Received:' and 'Subscription'.

Opening brackets, parentheses and similar delimiters ("(", "[", "{", "\(", "$", often fused with an operator like "/(", "*(", "^{", "_{", "%(") that begin a grouped sub-expression in math, code, or chemical notation. Activation is strongest when the bracket directly follows a division, multiplication, or function sign, as in "/(", "*(", or "log_b (".

Word-internal and word-final subword fragments (suffixes, inflectional endings, continuation pieces) of words split across multiple tokens, mostly in non-English or uncommon words (Latin, Slavic, Icelandic, German, Portuguese, Arabic, transliterations, rare names). The strongest activations fall on inflectional endings of heavily inflected languages.

Separator tokens that sit between two paired or listed values: commas between coordinates, function arguments, or list items; hyphens in ranges; ' x' in resolutions; slashes and colons in ratios; 'and', 'to', or 'of' joining two terms. Most often numbers, especially in code and technical text. It is weak, firing a little more on commas inside coordinate or argument pairs.

A weak, diffuse pattern that fires on tokens inside repetitive or parallel structures, such as list items and their separators, array indices, numbered sequences, table cells, and repeated math or code expressions. It responds most to separators (commas, brackets, operators) and to successive elements once the pattern has been established. Prose examples are rare and weak.

Fires on the final term of a mathematical expression, most strongly on the constant term that closes a polynomial after a + or − sign (e.g. the 8 in 7n^2−10n−8). It also fires weakly on the last number in lists, tuples and code arguments, and on trailing digits of long numbers. Isolated non-math tokens show only faint, noisy activation.

Terms about how text and data are encoded or represented: character encodings and standards (UTF-8, ASCII, coding declarations), fonts, characters and alphabets, language and format codes, and numeric or binary representation. The strongest cases are explicit encoding terms such as UTF-8 and ASCII value. Activation is weak and diffuse on other technical or standard names, such as metric spaces, the Gregorian calendar, EPSG, ipv4 and HDR.

A weak, diffuse feature. It fires on words about whether something exists, is present, or can be found. Typical cases are finding, seeing, searching for or locating things, and existing or no longer existing. It also covers deleting, removing or destroying things, membership checks ('if … not in', 'exists', a count of 0), and memory or persistence ('memory', 'souvenir', 'toujours', '思念'). This holds in both prose and code.

Weak and diffuse activations, peaking on the idea of conditionality: things that vary with or depend on circumstances. Typical triggers are “conditional logic” with :if, “depend on”, “condition-dependent”, “tailored to”, “different”/“various”/“split strategies”, and content that displays differently on desktop vs. mobile or at specific times. The many low-level activations on scattered function words, code and math tokens appear to be noise.

Structural boundary tokens that end a block or begin a new one. In code these are mostly the indentation whitespace and closing braces/brackets (}, };, }), #endif) that close nested scopes, firing most strongly on deep stacks of closing braces. Weaker activations land on similar markers in other text: closing HTML tags, paragraph breaks after a sentence, list or step numbers, and transition words like 'Also' and 'On the other hand'.

Number-theory terms for common divisors and multiples, firing most strongly on GCD/gcd, LCM/lcm, GCF, 'divisor', 'common multiple' and 'common factor', with weaker activation on related math words (modular, meet, bound, divide, denominator). Very weak activations also appear on unrelated tokens such as double newlines after 'Leave a Reply'.

Fires mainly on numbers, digits and variables inside math, code or numeric contexts (fraction denominators, exponents, decimal digits, LaTeX symbols and closing delimiters). It is strongest on the final token of a numeric or mathematical expression, just before a closing bracket, '$' or punctuation. Weaker, scattered hits land on ordinary words, commas and newlines in prose.

Fires most strongly on "HTML"/"html" and the ".html"/".htm" file extension, plus related markup or format terms like "Markup", ".xml" and "SQL". It fires weakly on other document and text-format words such as "prose", "Contents", "abstract", "summary", "APA" and "paperback".

References to lists, arrays, sequences and other collections, firing most strongly in code on list-holding variables and operations on them (.split(), list(...), len(x), x[0], sys.argv[1], shape[i], .ToList()). It fires weakly on prose and math words for sequences, series and sets.

Operators and operands inside mathematical equations, formulas and code expressions: mainly '=', '+', '-', '–' signs, plus nearby numbers, terms and separators (commas, brackets) in equations, matrices and function arguments. Activation is weak and diffuse, peaking on equals signs and arithmetic operators in linear or algebraic equations.

Tokens that open a structured element: field or label names in key–value or spec-sheet layouts (e.g., 'Last Update', 'General details', 'Longitude', 'director'), section headings, and the tag, element, or identifier name right after a delimiter such as '<', '@', '[', or '.' in markup and code (e.g., <item>, <map>, <input>, @NotNull). Activation is strongest on HTML/XML tag names.

Weak, diffuse activation on tokens inside repeated or templated text. It fires where a phrase, list pattern or format seen earlier in the context recurs, so the next token can be copied from before. Examples include a duplicated headline, "Image Credit: …", "Belgrade … ME - 4918", "Examples of … include" and "end their career". Most hits are punctuation, separators, newlines, spaces or digits within these repeating structures.

Function words directly after a word that sets up a question, task, or quantity, most strongly "of" following "probability/probabilities" (and similar heads like "possibility", "complexity", "number", "example"). Weaker hits fall on the next word after imperative or question openers in exam and problem text ("Find the", "Calculate", "What is", "determine whether"), where the token anticipates the object being asked about.

Tokens inside repetitive or patterned sequences: repeated numbers, symbols, separators and code lines (e.g., 30, 31, 30…; -*-*; ~~88~~88; repeated '; ' lines; 16x16x16). The token itself repeats an earlier element in the same run, and activation is strongest in highly regular, predictable repetition. Weak, scattered activation on ordinary words elsewhere.

Tokens inside loop and conditional control flow, mostly in code: the closing parenthesis, brace, colon, or indentation right after a while/if/else/except condition, and the loop body that follows (continue, break, increments, join, print, endl). Prose matches are weaker and come from analogous conditional or repetition phrasing, such as the comma after an "if" clause or words like "twice", "retry a total of 5 times", "every single", and "keeps".

The "h" token (often fused as "<h") that opens an HTML heading tag like <h1>–<h4>, strongest inside HTML/markup code. It also fires weakly on related mentions of headings (the word "headings", H1/H2, html.H1, HBox) and on the "h" in LaTeX commands such as \hline and \hfill.

Subword tokens inside non-English words or phrases (Spanish, German, French, Danish, Bosnian, Lithuanian, transliterated Russian) that appear within English text, often as translations, titles, or parenthetical glosses. Activation is strongest on the continuation pieces of foreign words, such as German terms in philosophy or a Spanish translated abstract title, and weak on odd fragments in URLs or rare English words.

The final token that completes a clause or sentence, typically just before punctuation or a boundary.
