These are often predictable phrase-closing words: sentence-final adverbs and particles ("too", "though", "respectively", "rn", "eh"), tag-question pronouns ("shall we", "aren't you") and fixed-phrase endings ("for example", "as follows", "over time"). It also fires on clause-final verb or particle endings in other languages, such as German verb-final suffixes ("-ellt", "-legt", "haben") and Chinese/Japanese sentence-final markers (了, 吗, です). These non-English endings activate most strongly.

The start of an explanatory annotation, chiefly code comment markers (//, #, ', bullets) at the beginning of a comment, plus the first few words after them. Weaker hits fall on verbs and function words inside descriptive or explanatory prose, such as captions, documentation and technical explanations.

A diffuse feature active across source code and technical/mathematical text, peaking in machine-learning and statistics code and prose (building or returning a model, activation functions like sigmoid, loss and likelihood functions, logistic regression, fitting and predicting). It fires mostly on structural tokens: indentation whitespace, line breaks, closing parens or braces, "=" assignments, "def"/"self", and variable names. Elsewhere it shows only weak, scattered activation on ordinary words.

Separators and connectives that come right after a negative or lower-bound number and lead into the next value. These include range words such as "to" and "and", commas, semicolons, inequality signs, and LaTeX integral bound markers like "}^{". Activation is strongest for range expressions running from a negative number to a positive one, e.g. "-5° to 36°" or "-1,1".

Tokens that close an opening tag or block header and add a line break (e.g. "> ", ""> ", "{ "). They mostly follow HTML opening tags such as , ,
and

, and mark the point where nested child content is about to start.

Tokens right after a 'Returns'/'Output'/'@return'/'Value'/'Result' label in docstrings, API docs, and problem statements, i.e. the colon, newline, indentation, bullet or opening words ('the', 'A', 'Print the single number') that begin the description of what is returned or output. It also fires weakly on commas after sentence-initial words like 'Finally' or 'Eventually' and on similar section-heading punctuation.

Tokens that mark conditioning, i.e. what something is computed or evaluated relative to. This covers the conditional bar in probability notation like P(A|B), which activates most strongly, plus similar bars and separators in math or code (restriction, set-builder, random-effect bars, ~). It also covers words like "given (the)", "assuming", "subject to", "constrained", "considering", "based on" and "from".

Hyphen/minus/dash characters and tokens naming them, usually as literal symbols in code strings, math, identifiers or separators (e.g. '-', "--", -*-, minus sign). The strongest hits are words for such punctuation ("hyphens", "hyphenated", "underscores"), with weaker hits on related naming conventions like snake_case and camelCase.

The direct object (usually a noun or noun phrase) that immediately follows a transitive verb, especially gerunds and imperatives, as in UI commands and titles, e.g. 'Transfer money', 'measuring gamma rays', 'Engineering enzyme', 'cooking dinner', 'Stop leak'. The activation is on the object token(s), not on the verb.

Separator tokens (commas, spaces, newlines, '=', ';', ':', '>' of table cells) in numeric lists, sequences, tables and citations, at the point just before the next number is expected. It fires most strongly in patterned number series such as 1978, 1987, 1996…, where the next value is predictable. Activation is weak on prose lists and other non-numeric text.

The boundary that closes a conditional or temporal subordinate clause (if/when/once/in that case/by default/when not needed) and opens the main clause. Most often it is the comma at that point, but it can also be the first word of the consequent, such as "then", "so", "otherwise", "it" or "the". The same pattern appears in other languages, for example Chinese 就 and 时候，. Activation is strongest when the condition has just ended and the result is about to begin.

Whitespace and newline tokens (mostly double newlines, sometimes fused with punctuation like ",", "{", ":", "]") that close a header, metadata line, salutation or code declaration and come right before the main body text or code block. Code-fence backticks and markup tokens at the start of a block fire more weakly.

Operations that combine or split sequences around a separator. In code this covers join and aggregation calls (.join, StringJoiner, implode, sum, collect, fold, reduce, split, sep=/delimiter=/axis= arguments); the strongest activation is on "join". In prose it covers phrases like "separated by", "separated with" and "with commas" that describe how items are delimited.

Month and hour fields in date/time format strings (e.g. the "-MM" after "yyyy", "HH", "%m", "%H" in SimpleDateFormat/strftime patterns), strongest on "-MM" in "yyyy-MM-dd". Weaker activation on time-unit words like "hours" and "month".

Tokens inside structured, list-like or quantitative content, most often numbers, variables and math operators. These include equation steps, prices, dates, units, format specifiers and answer options such as Yes/True/Never. Activation peaks at the start of a new line or item that restates or continues a calculation, e.g. "4x +" or "x > -5".

Short, non-word fragments forming abbreviations, symbols, or code-like identifiers: variable names (h, diff, lr_qi), chemical symbols (Cs, Pb, Ca/Al), acronyms (MF, LAR, FDA, USDT), codon strings (atc, atg), and digit pieces of numbers or dates. They often sit in parallel lists of similar items, and the strongest activations are on single-letter or very short suffixes that complete a compact code.

Lists of alternative choices or candidate answers, strongest on multiple-choice answer options (lettered labels such as A./B., a)/b), the options themselves, True/False, "It is impossible to tell"). It also fires weakly on informal sets of alternatives, like "X or Y", questions guessing a series of options ("Germany? The United States?"), and enumerated items with their separators.

Fires mainly on the Chinese negation character 不 inside compounds and phrases (不过, 不断, 不同, 不可行, 搜不到). It responds more weakly to English negations (not, n't) and to the Korean verb stem 하. It also fires on a space that directly precedes CJK text after a colon or bullet in mixed-language code or docs.

The double-slash token "//" in any role: code comments, integer division, URL and path separators, XPath, and decorative separators in bylines or headers. Activation peaks where it joins a URL or template placeholder (e.g. "{{site.github}}//") or appears as a quoted string literal. Weak activations also land on unrelated tokens.

Tokens containing the dollar sign "$" in any role: currency amounts, LaTeX math delimiters, shell prompts, and variable sigils in code (PHP, Perl, R, Rust macros, template ${...}). Activation runs highest for code and shell uses such as R's "\$" accessor, Perl comments, terminal prompts and PHP variables, and is weaker for plain currency and math.

Tokens that begin a new component inside a compound identifier or multi-part term, typically right after an underscore, hyphen, or camelCase boundary (e.g. in snake_case function or variable names, file paths, API names), and often only a partial-word subtoken. Activation is strongest in code identifiers; in prose it fires more weakly on the next word of a multi-word compound or name.

Tokens inside long runs of repeated filler or formatting characters, such as whitespace padding, dot leaders in tables of contents, dashes, ``` code fences, HTML/LaTeX fragments, &amp chains, and rows of symbols (†, ★, ♥). Activation is highest in the middle of the repetitive sequence. There are also weak, sporadic hits on ordinary words and punctuation.

Type conversion and casting constructs in code: function-style casts like int(), str(), list(), Convert.ToInt32, C-style (int)/(float) casts, Rust 'as' casts, static_cast<int>(). It also fires on numeric rounding and math functions (round, Math.floor, np.uint8, sqrt) and on format precision digits (%.2f, {:.4f}) that coerce how values are represented.

The word "rewrite" in any form (rewrite, rewrote, rewritten, rewriting, re-write, ReWrite), including code, linguistic rewrite rules and revising history or text. Weaker on related words for reworking something (rephrase, paraphrase, reword, rebuild, remake, rewiring) and on look-alike tokens such as the name "Rew".

Separator tokens (usually newlines, spaces, or periods) at the boundary between consecutive items in a structured, enumerated sequence such as tables of contents, numbered lists, chapter and section numbers, catalog entries, and number runs. The token fires right after one item ends, often after a trailing number, and just before the next index or title begins. There are a few scattered prose activations that don't fit.

Numeric tokens used as operands in arithmetic expressions, especially the second factor in a multiplication (conversion factors, multipliers, decimal digits after "0.") just before an equals sign or result; strongest on multiplier and conversion-factor digits in worked calculations.

The word "input" (and variants like Input, _INPUT, inputs, <input) in code and prose, especially as a programming identifier or as the HTML input element. Weaker activation on related user-entry and form-control terms such as field, textbox, checkbox, radio buttons, LineEdit, edit/insert mode and Button.

Names of software libraries, modules, packages, and their types or classes, mostly inside import/use/crate statements in code (e.g. pandas, pd, PIL, pathlib, serde_json, regex). It often fires on the later sub-token of a compound library name (bitarray, pybedtools, openpyxl) and sometimes on product or tool names mentioned in prose.

Punctuation and tokens that sit inside academic citations and references, typically right after an author name and before the year or title. Common cases are the opening parenthesis before a year ("et al (2010)", "Smith (1998)"), the comma after an author's name, "et al.", "pp"/"page" markers, and bracketed reference numbers. Weaker activations come from similar delimiters in math/LaTeX notation and other reference-like structures.

The closing bracket plus newline right after the opening tag of a structured block, usually the ">\n" ending <table> or <thead> just before <tr>. Similar tokens fire after <ul> and after LaTeX \begin{itemize}/{table}/{tabular}. Weaker activations land on the whitespace before list items. The feature marks the start of a table or list body, where row or item content is expected next.

Tokens inside dense, low-predictability symbolic or non-prose sequences: numbers in lists/tables/arrays, code arguments, math subscripts, hex/byte strings, random hashes, URL encodings, mojibake and emoji/unusual-character runs. It responds most strongly to individual elements of repetitive structured data (digits, commas, separators) and to garbled or rare-script characters. It is only weakly active on ordinary prose.

Tokens in code and math notation that begin an argument or operand: the first variable, operator or literal right after a keyword, function call, operator or delimiter (e.g. after print, if, while, return, =, +, a comma). It is strongest right after print statements.

Key-value/associative data structures in code: type names like HashMap, Map, Dict, Dictionary, BTreeMap, defaultdict, HashSet, and empty or opening dict literals ({}, = {, {$). These fire most strongly on map type annotations, with weaker activation on tuple/collection openers and on prose words like "mapping" or "from" that describe a mapping.

Keywords that open a function or method definition in code, such as def, fn, func, function, sub, and return types or modifiers like void, public, private, and static. They fire right before the function name, typically at the start of a new declaration line. Activation is strongest on return types like 'void' after an access modifier. Weak activations appear on other declaration openers (class, const, let) and occasionally on unrelated prose.

A variable or subject that is repeated from earlier in the same expression, typically the left operand of a second comparison joined by &&, ||, and, or (e.g. "c >= 'a' && c <= 'z'", "ans == 'n' or ans == 'N'"). The strongest activations are on code and math conditions. It fires weakly on repeated subjects or words in prose ("no man living and no man dead", "it never rains but it pours").

Whitespace-only tokens (indentation spaces/tabs combined with newlines) forming blank or trailing-whitespace lines, especially between blocks of code (methods, statements) and occasionally in prose. Weak, sporadic activation on boilerplate tokens such as HTML closing tags and repeated page-template words.

Weak, diffuse activation on word-internal subword fragments, mostly in non-English or non-Latin scripts (Cyrillic, Hebrew, Arabic, Bengali, Japanese, Korean, Turkish, Polish, diacritic-heavy transliterations) and in rare or nonsense English words. It also fires on long runs of dot leaders in tables of contents. The common thread is low-frequency, mid-word tokenization in unfamiliar or noisy text.

A weak, diffuse pattern. It fires most strongly in repetitive, structured text such as matrices, HTML tables, coordinate lists, subscripts, author-affiliation numbers and phone numbers. The marked token usually repeats or continues an element seen earlier in the sequence (e.g. repeated matrix entries, "1a", ">C", "blow", "(1,0)"). Elsewhere, scattered ordinary content words get low activations.

Separators and positions inside enumerations: commas, "and", newlines, bullets, pipes and table tags that sit between items of a list or sequence (names, numbers, regions, table cells). Count words that announce how many items follow (three, four) also fire. The feature tracks position within a multi-item series.

Structural boundaries where a heading, title, closing tag, string, or statement has just ended and new content is about to begin. The active tokens are mostly newline-bearing ones such as '}⏎', '>⏎', '")⏎' and '⏎⏎', plus the indentation or opening token that follows ('\', ' <', spaces). This shows up across LaTeX section headers, HTML tags, code print statements and markdown titles. The strongest cases are HTML closing tags followed by indentation and a new opening tag.

Tokens in code and command-line text that end an argument, string or path, mostly closing quotation marks (often fused with ')', ',' or ';'), closing brackets, file extensions like .zip/.yaml/.diff, and line-continuation whitespace. They fire where a literal or argument finishes and the next argument or code resumes.

A weak, diffuse feature that fires on tokens where the text becomes unexpected or incoherent. Typical triggers are spliced or spam-inserted phrases, duplicated words ('the the', 'like like'), typos ('firewords'), OCR and formatting artifacts (ligatures, broken citations, stray numbers or spaces) and abrupt topic shifts. It often lands on the noun or term right at the point of disruption.

The first item in a pair or short list of symbols, mostly single-letter variables or arguments in math and code, that is about to be followed by a comma, 'and', or hyphen and a matching second item (x, y; a, b; k, v; S, T; P and Q). It also fires on paired names like east-west, Mars and Jupiter, and Clinton-Trump.

Tokens inside repetitive, structured, list-like or tabular text (numbers, units, dimensions, dates, times, bullets, separators, repeated labels such as "Street", "dislike", "true", "logo", "button"). The feature fires on an element that repeats or continues a predictable pattern set up earlier in the sequence, such as the next item in a series, a repeated field or a boilerplate UI or metadata string, rather than on ordinary prose.

Mostly the word "inside" used as a locative preposition or adverb (contained within something, physically or abstractly, including code contexts like "inside functions"). It also fires on related spatial prepositions in other languages, such as Russian "у", Vietnamese "tại", and occasionally "beside".

Leading whitespace indentation tokens at the start of a line, appearing just before a list bullet or number (•, 2., -) or before code that dedents from a deeper block, such as closing braces/tags, else, or catch. The strongest cases are dedents in code and numbered list items.

Separator or connector tokens at the boundary between two parallel segments, marking where a second item, alias, gloss or field begins. Typical cases are opening parentheses before an explanation or alternate name, pipes, slashes, dashes, '#', ':', '; also' and 'or the'. Some hits also fall at the start of the next element in code, IDs, URLs or lists.

Separators between columns or fields in tabular and aligned text: HTML table cell tags ("<td", especially the opening tag of a second or later cell in a row), runs of spaces used to pad columns, and leader dots in tables of contents or forms that join an entry to its page number or value.

Tokens inside a condition being stated, mostly the subject or left-hand operand of a comparison or test right after 'if', 'while', 'whenever', 'when' or 'case' (e.g. "if (n > 10)", "if nums[mid] ==", "when the simulated value exceeds"). It fires most strongly on variables and operators in code conditionals, and weakly on the subject or verb of conditional and qualifying clauses in prose and math.

Tokens that link an expression or subject to its result, value, or explanation: equals signs and arrows in calculations, inline comment markers (#, //, <!--) after code, 'Output' headers, and predicate verbs like 'is/are', 'will', 'should be', 'that is' introducing what something equals or produces.

Weak, diffuse activation centered on mathematical, code and formula syntax: assignment/equals signs, operators (+, ^, \in, \Rightarrow), function names and brackets (ln(, cos(, range(, gcd), variable names being defined, plus chemical formula fragments and unit abbreviations. It fires mainly on symbolic/technical notation, with scattered low activations on ordinary prose tokens.

Negations and exclusions inside a condition, mostly in code. The strongest cases are operators and words like !, not, != and "not in" right after if, along with the thing being tested. Prose phrases of the same kind (unless, not yet, except, absence of, other than) activate weakly.

The standalone digit "0" used as a numeric value, most often in code and math (return values, function arguments, comparisons, assignments, binary 0/1 outcomes). Activation is strongest where 0 is a result or output value, as in "returns 0" or "print(0)".

under.name: Words for touring or itinerant series of appearances or performances, peaking on "tour" (book tour, speaking tour, 19-city sold-out European tour) and related terms like circuit, campaign trail, concert, live set, stint and rollout. Activation is weak and diffuse on other tokens.

Fires on the position just before or at the start of a year number in bibliographic/metadata contexts (citations, publication dates, DOIs, conference dates). It is strongest on the first three digits of a year ("199", "200", "201") or on the space or " (" right before it, and weakly on other separators in dates, page numbers and identifiers.

References to the people or agents responsible for something: names of creators, founders, authors and speakers, along with the agentive phrases attached to them ("by the same authors", "co-founder", "producer of", "he established", "I"). Activation is strongest on personal names and creator or founder roles, especially after "by" or in appositives that introduce a person.

A weak, diffuse feature found mostly in health, medical and scientific prose. It peaks in passages about obesity, chronic disease and risk, especially causal or prevalence phrasing such as 'can contribute to', 'reduced risk of chronic diseases', 'puts you at the same significant risk' and 'has increased substantially'. Elsewhere in academic or abstract-like text it fires weakly on function words, punctuation and DOI/citation markers.

Phrases in news-style sports recaps describing athletes’ or teams’ performance and results. The strongest cases are box-score statistics and outcomes such as “led a balanced attack with a game-high 14 points,” “scored nine runs in the fifth inning” and “winless in two matches.” Much weaker activation appears on similar report-style quantity or condition words in weather and nutrition text, such as clouds, rains and carbs.
Final token of a proper name (usually a person's surname or last subword piece of a name, also ships, Pokémon, products), marking completion of a multi-token named entity.

Main predicates in news-style lead sentences announcing a new event or development, especially the verb phrase right after the subject (e.g. 'has begun production in', 'has launched', 'filed a lawsuit', 'have identified a', 'announced that'). Weaker activation falls on surrounding prepositions, dates and objects in these factual report or headline sentences.

Weak, diffuse activation on biology and biochemistry vocabulary, mainly words and word pieces about organisms producing or secreting chemical compounds and their biological roles (metabolites, pheromones, antibiotics, signaling, pigments, acids, hydrocarbons). The strongest activations fall on 'secondary metabolites', pheromones and microbial production. Scattered activations on name and word fragments in scientific text are low.

Tokens in passages describing the past or history, such as historical eras, events, dates and past figures (World War One, the Nixon administration, 1984, Sept. 11, Truman/Eisenhower), childhood memories, and origins or first occurrences. The strongest activations fall on named historical periods and events that anchor a 'back then' timeframe.

The comma that separates a city name from its following state, region or country in a location or address (e.g. "St. Louis, MO", "Copenhagen, Denmark"). It is most common in academic affiliations, supplier credits and citations, and is strongest in manufacturer parentheticals such as "(Sigma-Aldrich, St. Louis, MO)". It occasionally fires weakly on similar connectors like "in" after an institution name.

Punctuation or spacing immediately following a weekday name in date headers/timestamps (the comma after "Monday", "Friday", etc., or the space after "Tuesday,"), typically right before the day/month in blog or article dateline metadata; weakly also "Posted on"/"Updated:" lead-ins to dates.

Tokens describing or attaching to institutions and organizations (especially universities). The strongest activations fall on clauses, parentheticals and prepositional phrases that add affiliation, location or descriptive detail about an institution, such as "which has affiliation with", "(formerly", "located in", acronyms in parentheses, campus suffixes, and URL or email domain parts. Activation is weak on generic function words elsewhere.

Statistical labels inside parenthetical results in scientific writing, mainly 'n =', 'P/p =' or 'p <', 'r =', 'OR', 'CI', 'AUC', plus the following '=' or '<' and sometimes the leading '0' of the value. The label letter is the strongest part; weaker hits fall on other labels placed right before a number (level, Km, Rs., table <td> cells).

The subword "toc" (or "oc" after T), strongest as the middle of "oxytocin" and in "toc" as a table-of-contents marker (e.g. {:toc}, toc = false, @[toc]); weaker for tocopherol, Tocqueville, Tocantins, and TOC.

Strongest on the "(name" token, and to a lesser degree the following "=", in ORM column annotations in code (@Column(name=…), @JoinColumn(name =…)). Otherwise it gives only faint, diffuse activation. The most frequent weak cases are the indentation space before bullet (•) or numbered list items and line breaks inside lists. It also fires faintly on scattered words such as "Casinos" and "DirectX".

Tokens that follow verbs such as "make/made" in fixed phrases about a first appearance, arrival, or milestone ("made his debut", "make their way", "made landfall", "his first", "maiden"). The possessive pronoun after "make" activates most strongly, especially when the phrase is about a debut or breakthrough.

The subject-specific middle word in the names of government or regulatory agencies, above all "Drug" in "Food and/& Drug Administration" (FDA). "Disease" in "Centers for Disease Control" activates moderately, and similar words in other agency names (Safety, Wildlife, Criminal) only weakly. Generic lowercase "drug" also activates weakly.

The word "array", especially in "microarray", used for high-throughput molecular biology assay platforms (gene expression, CGH, protein arrays). It fires more weakly on related lab and profiling technologies such as blots, RNA-seq, Affymetrix, ELISA, plates, panels, and flow cells.

Month tokens within specific dates (full names, abbreviations, or numeric month fields), usually followed by a day number. Activation is strongest for a month that begins a standalone date line, such as a timestamp or byline at the start of a line.

The separator between a date and the time that follows it in a timestamp, usually a single space but also an ISO 'T' or an '@'. It fires right before the hour digits in post dates, email headers and log metadata.

Phrases giving the location of a residence or other setting, usually right after verbs like lived, home, moved or rented. It fires mostly on locative prepositions (in, on, near, outside, next to, on the outskirts of) and on the place names or place nouns that follow (home, street, town, state names).

The last token of a multi-token proper name or technical term, mostly organization, institution and company names (suffixes like Inc, Ltd, LLC, University, Hospital, Committee), but also places, people and chemical names. It fires where the full name ends, which is often right before a comma, parenthetical acronym or the following clause.

Inner subword pieces of technical chemical, drug, toxin and biochemical names (e.g. colchicine, trichothecene, puromycin, digitalis), with the strongest activation on fragments of compounds, antibiotics and toxins in scientific contexts. A few weak hits land on related whole words like "antibiotics".

Whitespace separator tokens preceding a number in structured metadata: mainly the space before the year in dates (e.g., "Submitted on 10 Feb 2015", "June 16, 2006"), and the leading space before "1." at the start of a numbered list. Year-prefix digits like "197"/"198" also fire weakly.

The last token of a person's name, most often the surname after a first name or title, strongest for well-known political leaders (President Obama/Trump/Biden, Roosevelt). When the surname is split into pieces, the final subword fires (e.g. Gorbache-v, Hickenlo-oper), usually where the name is the subject about to say or do something.

A diffuse, low-intensity feature in scientific and technical prose. It fires on the key terms of technical noun phrases and method descriptions, such as model parameters, processes and components. It is strongest where items are paired, coordinated or contrasted, as in "X and Y", "both … as well as", "horizontal/vertical" and "possibility/impossibility".

The final digit of a year marking the end of a lifespan or period, usually a death year in a birth–death range like "(1921–1981)" or after "died in/on". It also fires weakly on other death-related words such as "died", "passed away", "d." and "dies at".

The word "City" as the final part of a multi-word place or team name (e.g., Kansas City, Salt Lake City, Manchester City, Vatican City). It fires most strongly for Kansas City, and occasionally on the abbreviation "KC".

Fires right after a C# "using System;" import line. It is strongest on the ";⏎" that ends "using System" and on the next token, usually the following "using" (or "namespace"). It responds weakly to other import/line boundaries in Python code.

Words for a first public appearance, launch or introduction, most strongly "debut" (especially debut novel, album or film), along with premiere/premiered, breakout, inaugural and opener. More weakly, related words for a leading or notable start such as flagship, career and opening.

Tokens inside long random-looking alphanumeric strings such as hex hashes, UUIDs, session IDs, URL query tokens, DOIs, and other identifier codes. Activation is strongest in the middle of high-entropy character sequences, especially mixed letter-digit runs.

Mentions of saints and other revered religious figures: "Saint", "Blessed", "holy Elder", guru and canonization, feast days and devotion/commemoration. Activation is strongest on the title words themselves ("Saint", "canonization", "Feast Day"). Weaker activation spreads to the honorific and hagiographic context around such figures, including piety, mystics, honoring legacies and the names of revered people.

Inner subword pieces of pharmaceutical drug names, mainly antibiotics and chemotherapy agents. The strongest response is to "xor" in doxorubicin; weaker responses fall on "acy" in tetracycline-family names and "yc" in doxycycline. Weak firing also occurs on similar-looking fragments outside drug names (e.g., the bitwise term "xor", "sync").

Weak, diffuse activations on words that express evidence, attestation or documentation, i.e. how something is known, recorded or dated. These include source and attribution phrases ("records say that", "data from", "tells us", "as evidenced", "reported", "report of", "observations", "known", "extant written texts"). They also include earliest-occurrence and dating phrases such as "as early as", "since at least 2017", "circa", "oldest form" and "first mentions". Activation often falls on the preposition, "as", or the date or citation token linking a claim to its supporting evidence or time point.

Words for hard or solid lumps and masses, especially ones that form inside the body or have to be removed: stones (kidney stones, hailstones), blood clots and thrombi, cataracts, polyps, crystals, microliths, floaters, ice. Strongest on 'stones' in a medical context. Weaker, scattered firings land on unrelated tokens such as paragraph breaks and 'Presentation'.

Terms for dimensionality and low-dimensional or layered geometry, mainly in physics and materials science: "-dimensional" after one, two or three, "2D" and "0D", layered, thin film, platelets, laminates, surfaces, planes and van der Waals materials. Activation is strongest for "two-dimensional crystals", "one dimensional" and "layered".

The final segment of alphanumeric classification codes, mainly in academic and patent front matter (PACS, MSC/AMS, JEL, Int. Cl., OCIS). It marks the trailing digits or letters after the code's prefix, such as the 'b' in 85.60.Jb or the '10' in 47H10. Activation is strongest on PACS letter suffixes and MSC digit endings. It is weak on stray text tokens.

The ".impl" segment in Java package and import paths (e.g. com.x.service.impl, org.apache.http.impl.client), marking implementation subpackages. Activation is strongest in import statements and package declarations. The few weak hits elsewhere are scattered ordinary prose words or commas.

Tokens inside the titles of academic papers, articles and reports, especially in citations and reference lists. Activation is strongest in the body of the title right after the citation year '(2005).' and on connecting words like 'of', 'in', 'and', subtitle colons and descriptive nouns ('Comparison of', 'Systematic Review', ': a randomised double-blind').

The number right after a hyphen or dash that closes a numeric range, and it is often abbreviated. Typical cases are the end page of a citation (e.g. 531-9, 208-14) and the end year of a span (1954-55, 1918-19). Activation is strongest for shortened end page numbers in journal references.

Structural boundary tokens in scraped web pages, mostly newlines and punctuation-plus-newline, that separate boilerplate or header metadata (titles, bylines, dates, source tags, site descriptions) from the main body text. The strongest cases are Slashdot-style headers such as story titles, 'by user (id) on' bylines and 'writes "'.

Fires on the word "serum" in lab and biology writing, most strongly in cell-culture supplement phrases like "fetal bovine/calf serum" and its abbreviation FBS. It also responds weakly to other reagent and medium components such as BSA/albumin, glycerol, methanol, NaCl, sulfate, glucose and yeast extract.

The ".security" token in Java-style package and import paths (java.security, javax.security, org.springframework.security, and project packages). It fires most strongly on standard library and Spring imports and more weakly on custom package names. Activations elsewhere are faint and scattered, such as the French "sécurité" and random punctuation.

Section headings in documents, especially academic papers, patents and reports, usually written in all caps (INTRODUCTION, ABSTRACT, MATERIALS AND METHODS, METHODOLOGY, ACKNOWLEDGMENTS, REFERENCES). The feature fires on the first token or word-piece of the heading, typically right after a line break or a section number such as "1." or "I.". It is strongest for "INT" in INTRODUCTION and "ATERIAL" in MATERIALS.

Numeric locants within names of phosphoinositide-signaling molecules, most strongly the "3" in PI3K / phosphoinositide 3-kinase. It also fires on related numbers and fragments such as the "3" in IP3, the "1" and "4" in inositol 1,4,5-trisphosphate, and "osphate". Weaker hits occur on numbers in other gene or protein names (PAR6, G6PD, SH3).

Separators and connectors (mostly commas, plus words like "in", "at the", "of", and venue words such as "Center" or "Base") inside formal location or venue strings in addresses, affiliations, event listings and citations. Typical spots are the comma between a city and its state or country, and the links between a venue and its city.

The word "injury" and its variants (injuries, injured, split forms like "In|juries"), meaning physical harm or tissue damage. Activation is strongest in medical and biological contexts such as nerve, liver, or spinal cord injury, and weaker for generic mentions in news or accident reports. Related harm terms like "infection" activate only faintly.

Word-piece suffixes (most often "ella") that complete Latin-style scientific genus/species names, especially bacterial pathogens (Salmonella, Legionella, Brucella, Campylobacter, Vibrio). Activation is strongest for well-known pathogenic bacteria and weaker for the same suffix in personal names, fungi, or unrelated words.

Separator tokens (mostly colons, also commas, 'by', dashes, newlines) that come right before an organization or publisher name in citation/metadata contexts. The strongest cases are the colon in bibliographic references between the place of publication and the publisher (e.g. 'New York: Kodansha', 'Albuquerque: University Press'). Weaker cases include field labels like 'Manufacturer:' or 'Publisher:' and taxonomic order separators.

Noun phrases naming the object or subject area of study or understanding, mostly in scientific and academic prose. They typically follow verbs or nouns like investigate, understand, insight into, shed light on, probe of, or knowledge of (e.g. 'the functions of phytohormones in…', 'an early stage of primate evolution'). Activation spans the whole object phrase, often including its internal 'of'/'in' links.

Diffuse, weak activations spread across scientific/technical prose (physics, plasma, astrophysics abstracts and reports). The highlighted tokens are mostly function words and generic noun-phrase pieces such as "the", "of", "amount of", "effect", "nature" and "confinement", often inside descriptive phrases about physical quantities and processes. There is no single specific word; the common thread is academic scientific register.

Biographical or profile-style text: fires at the points where a description of a person (or organization) moves on to the next fact about them, especially on the subject pronoun, name, or verb that opens a new clause or sentence ("He was", "She is", "who served as", "has been a", "I publish") and on articles introducing a role ("the author/director of").

Nouns naming a property or attribute category in descriptive or spec-style text, often as section headers (Personality, Screen, Voice, Inhalation, Spore Print). Activation is strongest for sensory terms, especially taste and smell (flavor, notes, inhale/exhale, odor, aroma, bite).

Website and document boilerplate addressed to the reader: calls to action, contact and feedback prompts, and instructions such as "let us know", "click the button below", "subscribe", "visit us on", "should be sent to", and "please check". Activation is strongest on the action verbs and the phrases that direct the reader to a contact point or action.

Numeric values that state a statistic, chiefly percentages and proportions. The strongest cases are numbers in parentheses right after a count, e.g. "4,104 (14.6%)" or "39 (95.1%)", where the decimal digits often score highest. Weaker activations appear on other quantities and unit conversions, such as "(525-foot)", and occasionally on words like "percent" or "cent".

Weak, diffuse feature tied to comics, cartoons, and humor writing: tokens in or near names of comic strips, cartoon characters, cartoonists, and humor columns (e.g., XKCD, Peanuts, Dennis the Menace, Gumball Watterson, Tezuka manga, Wacky Packages, Garbage Pail Kids, Topps) and descriptions of funny/surreal content, often firing on name endings or function words next to these references.

Calls to action that point the reader to more information or a resource, such as 'for more information, visit/see/call', 'you can find more details at', 'check out', 'click/buy/sign up via the link'. Activation peaks on words like 'more', 'information', 'details', 'find', 'visit', 'please' and the comma before the action verb, usually just before a URL, contact or reference.

Leading digit tokens of numbers, mainly percentages, decimals or comma-separated figures, that sit in lists of statistics or tables. The strongest activations come after earlier numbers in the same sequence, e.g. the second or third percentage in a breakdown.

Inner subword pieces of Latin-style scientific names, chiefly the species epithet of binomial nomenclature (e.g. falc-ip-arum, offic-in-ale, leg-uminos-arum). The middle fragments after the first piece of the word fire most strongly. Weaker hits come from other rare Latinate or foreign words split into odd subwords, such as medical terms and non-English names.

Tokens in attribution contexts that link a person or claim to a source: prepositions and connectors like "of", "at", "by", "with" and "from" between a person's name and their organization or outlet, plus bylines ("By", "writes", "Review by"), appositive commas after names, and source or publication names. These appear in news, reviews and citations, signaling who said or published something and where.

The word "date"/"Date" used as a metadata field label or key (YAML front matter, JSON/TOML keys, bibliographic and repository records such as "Date Published"), usually right before a timestamp value. It fires most strongly at line-initial "date:" in blog-post headers.

The ">" + newline token that closes an opening tag at a line end. It fires most strongly after "<summary" in C# XML doc comments ("/// <summary>") and weakly after HTML "<thead"/"<tbody" tags in tables.

Names of emerging/vector-borne infectious diseases, above all Zika and Lyme, plus chikungunya (the name or its final subword, e.g. "ika", "yme", "unya"). Activation is strongest on "Zika" in outbreak/virus contexts. "Lyme" fires even as a place name, though more weakly. Other weak hits are scattered noise.

Page ranges and issue/volume numbers in bibliographic citations. The strongest activations fall on the page-range portion: "pp.", "pages", "p.", or the colon/parenthesis before the start page, the starting page number, and the dash. Volume and issue numbers and other citation punctuation are weaker.

Physical locations and spatial settings in narrative or descriptive text: place nouns (area, bushes, center, forest, tunnel, coastline), named places, and the spatial prepositions and phrases that introduce them (in the middle of, outside the, at a bus stop on, through the, east of). Activation is strongest on the location head noun or the preposition that marks where an event or object is situated.

Proverbs, scripture and other moralizing or archaic text, especially Biblical verses and wise sayings ("better than", "the Lord is close to the brokenhearted", "thy lot"). It fires most on the content words of the quoted maxim or verse, plus related religious or moral vocabulary such as evil, mercy, heaven and wickedness.

Predicate language that ranks or characterizes an entity (often a place, country, or organization) by its standing relative to others: superlatives and ranking phrases like "the highest/largest/best", "among the first", "number one", "the nation's largest", "one of the most". Strongest on the article and superlative right after the subject plus verb ("X has the...", "X is the...").

Words for giving a talk or performing in front of an audience: presentations, talks, panel discussions, lectures, speakers, sessions, and verbs like present, speak about, share insights on, address. Activation is strongest on the event nouns (panel, presentation, speaker, talk) and the following 'on/about'.

Nouns naming formal institutional bodies, official documents, and expert proceedings, such as commissions, academies, consortia, summits, workshops, reports, resolutions, conventions, strategies, inquiries and recommendations. They usually appear as the head word of an organization or publication title (e.g. "National Academies", "Broadband Commission for"). Activation is strongest on the core institutional noun.

Text about problems and preventing them, such as harm, disease, damage or deterioration, often in warning or advisory language. It fires most on conditional and consequence clauses ("if... persists", "without proper treatment", "it can be", "should be considered") that state risks, the need for intervention, or recommended preventive actions.

The word completing an abbreviated author/party list after one or more names, chiefly "al" in "et al." in citations, plus "others"/"Ors" in legal case names ("X and others v Y"). Activation is strongest in reference lists that name several authors.

Metadata labels in file headers and document info, chiefly "Created" (as in "Created by"/"Created on"/"Created:") at the top of source-code comments, which fires most strongly. Similar provenance labels such as "Started", "DOI"/"doi" in citations, and "Commenced" fire weakly.

Women's first names (and full-name pieces) in family or relationship contexts, e.g. a wife, mother, sister, girlfriend or the second parent in "X and Y". Activation is strongest on the mother's or wife's name after "and" in parent or couple listings. Words like "wife" and "lady" fire weakly, as do a few unrelated name-like word pieces.

Weak, diffuse activations on the start of a sentence's main predicate after its subject in formal or expository writing. They fall mostly on auxiliaries, modals and infinitive markers ('has', 'have', 'can be', 'is', 'to') and the verbs that follow them. The clearest cases are present-perfect or passive statements about progress, development or capability, such as 'have enabled', 'has become', 'have been created' and 'can help'. Nearby quantifiers and determiners ('many', 'most', 'the') are also lightly picked up.

The word "magnetic" and its variants (magnet-, -agnetic as in geomagnetic, magnetosphere, magnetized, magnetically), especially when followed by "field(s)" in physics and astrophysics contexts. "Magnetic" activates most strongly, and "field" activates moderately. Related physics terms such as electric, polarization and turbulent activate only weakly.

Weak, diffuse activation on text about physical work done to objects, sites or environments (removal, repair, restoration, expansion, installation, clearing, land or habitat management). It peaks on the action verbs and their objects, plus nearby function words such as 'to', 'and' and 'the', e.g. 'to remove dead and decaying limbs and to prevent'.

Separators (commas, semicolons, slashes, newlines) between items in lists of classification codes or identifiers. Activation is strongest for commas and semicolons separating subject codes in academic paper front matter (PACS, MSC, AMS, JEL), and weaker for separators in patent class lists, product model numbers, emails and similar code lists.

Long runs of dot leaders (and similar filler like underscores or ellipses) that sit between an entry title and its page number, as in tables of contents or form fields. Activation is strongest on the first leader chunk after the title and drops on later chunks. Weaker activation appears on other separators between a label and its value, such as a <td> cell before a page number or a blank line after "Leave a Reply".

The trailing numeral or letter suffix (e.g., 1, 3, 21, A, E, R) that completes an alphanumeric identifier, most often a gene/protein name (Cas1, Stat3, katG, MnmE), and also cell lines, wells, and model codes. Letter suffixes on gene names activate most strongly.

middle.name: Tokens that begin with or contain the letter sequence "ab"/"AB" (e.g. abstract, abuse, ability, above, abounds, Abraham, Abass, sabre), strongest when "ab" starts the word. It also fires weakly on nearby a-initial words such as about, available, adoption and Africa.

Sentence-ending boundaries: the period fused with following newline(s) (".⏎", ".⏎⏎") marking the end of a sentence/paragraph before a new section, list item, or paragraph; also other post-sentence break tokens like extra spaces, an opening parenthesis, or a dash after a sentence ends.

Language about purpose, goals and future benefit: phrases expressing aims, importance, or enabling outcomes ("important to understand", "to improve the", "mission to develop", "paves the way to", "opens up new possibilities for", "can help", "critical to advancing"). Activation is strongest on the purpose 'to' and the following verb in promotional, scientific or mission-statement prose.

Words about safety, security, protection and risk: secure, safe, security, protect/protective, ensure/sure, threat, danger, risk, insecure, stability, integrity. The strongest activations are on "security", "secure" and "safe".

Pieces of identifiers and names, strongest in code. It fires on the later sub-tokens of compound identifiers (CamelCase or snake_case function, class and method names), especially names about to be called or defined, i.e. just before an opening parenthesis or argument list. Weaker activations land on word fragments inside URLs, email addresses, domain names and technical terms.

Marks plural noun phrases that refer to sets of several items (representatives, witnesses, presentations, books, museums, disorders, games, models), along with the words tied to them: quantifiers and counts (all, both, five, three, "of these"), plural pronouns (they, them, their, these) and plural verbs (are). Activation often extends to the following comma or period, or to list-ending brackets in code.

Relational/classifying adjectives (often ending in -al, -ic, -ical, -ological) placed before a noun to specify its domain or type (e.g., financial, legal, optical, emotional, medicinal, political), including word-piece suffixes that complete such adjectives.

Quantifiers and scope words that set how much of a group is covered, chiefly universal ones such as "all", "every", "any" and "no one". It also fires, more weakly, on other totality or extremity words like "complete", "completely", superlatives and "main"/"primary", and on the nouns they modify. Activation is strongest on "all" and "every" before a noun phrase.

Opening markup tag names and commands, mostly HTML table cell tags (<td, <th) plus <p, <strong, <br, <sub and LaTeX commands like \frac, \caption and \textsuperscript, marking the start of a formatted element just before its content.

A diffuse, weakly firing feature with no clear semantic theme. It fires on scattered tokens in ordinary prose, code and lists. The strongest hits tend to be the word or subword piece that completes a term, name or list item, where the continuation is highly predictable. Examples include "he-ifer", "mesol-imbic", "Inequal-ities", "missile attack" and "blackjack". It also fires weakly on function words and list separators.

Words expressing being outside, exterior to, or beyond some boundary or scope, chiefly "outside (of)" and "beyond". Weaker activations appear on related exclusion or separation terms such as "other than", "except", "external", "outdoor", "unrelated", "independent", "escape" and "away from".

Names of LaTeX text- and font-formatting commands written right after a backslash, such as \text, \mathrm, \operatorname, \mathbf, \textbf, \rm and \textit, usually in math mode just before a braced argument. Activation is strongest on \mathrm, the "name" part of \operatorname, and \text used in subscripts, units or labels. Other LaTeX command names (\url, \bibitem, \emph, \,) and HTML entities like ' activate only weakly.

Focusing, limiting and hedging adverbs and discourse modifiers (only, even, just, not, mainly, solely, often, almost, at least) that come right after a verb, noun or clause and come before the phrase they modify. The strongest cases are "only" and "not" restricting a following prepositional phrase or complement (e.g. "valid only if", "applied only to"). Parenthetical commas and hedge phrases ("kind of", "more or less", "I think") also activate weakly.

A diffuse, weakly activating feature with no clear semantic focus. It fires sporadically on assorted tokens in ordinary prose (news, informational, and narrative text), mostly mid-sentence content words and function words, plus sentence- or paragraph-ending punctuation and line breaks. Activation is slightly stronger in short headline-like or descriptive passages, such as a snake breaking into a shop or a question about table manners.

Tokens tied to Scandinavian/Nordic and broader Germanic (German, Dutch) origin, most strongly explicit Nordic references such as 'Scandinavian', the Norwegian domain '.no', Stockholm and Sweden. Weaker activations fall on pieces of surnames and words with that origin, e.g. Steensland, Anfinsen, Heisenberg, Vermeer, Arvid and Yuletide, plus German-language text.

Words describing violent or physical events, motion, destruction and natural disasters: crashes, explosions, floods, plummeting, firing, attacks, collapse, ruins, projectiles. It is strongest on dramatic falling or impact sequences (e.g. a plane plummeting onto a house, crash landings). It also fires weakly on surrounding action verbs, connectives and some unrelated nouns.

Concepts of supply and delivery of resources or utilities to something, especially electrical power (voltage figures, power sockets and supplies, charging, cutting off power), plus related inputs such as water, steam feeds, nutrients, internet access and network services. Strongest on "power" and voltage terms.

Diffuse, weak activation on words that start or carry a contrasting, concessive, or qualifying clause, i.e. a caveat or limitation on what came before. Typical carriers are "but", "even though", "although", "however" and "while". Hedges and negations also fire, such as "can be a challenge", "not going to", "possibly", "mainly" and "I would never say that". Peaks fall on the connective and the following few words, as in "but will not be", "but please keep in mind that" and "even though we remain".

Weak, diffuse feature centered on words about naming, expressing, and representing things: language, terms, names, notation, word, syntax, metaphor, verse, symbolism, labeling, citing, "name for", "referred to", "state that in a creative way". It responds mainly to nouns and verbs about the way something is called, phrased, or symbolically conveyed, often in meta-linguistic or definitional contexts.

Tokens naming one side of a binary contrast or choice between alternatives, such as male/female, true/false, 1/0, North/South, object/background, heat instead of ice, or one species dominating another. Activation is strongest on the chosen or winning option, e.g. “adopts $1$” and “dominance of M. domesticus”.

Tokens containing the letter sequence "cal"/"kal"/"alc" (or close variants such as "Call", "Kal", "alo", "alm"). The strongest hits are word-initial fragments like "cal" in caliber/calibre, calculus and calibration. Weaker hits include California, calendar, calculation/calculating and name fragments (Kalak, Kalousi, Falciani, chalcogenides).

Sentence- and clause-ending punctuation, mostly periods (often with following newlines), placed right after a long descriptive clause or noun phrase finishes a statement. Similar boundary tokens such as commas, closing parentheses, list bullets, and line breaks also fire.

Tokens tied to time, duration and waiting, such as timers, timeouts, delays, sleep calls, refresh/retry intervals, freezes and pauses, patience, "long enough", and units like minutes or seconds. Activation is strongest for technical timing parameters like timeouts, timers, thread sleep and TTL values.

Structural markers in log or machine-generated text, strongest on log-level prefixes and their delimiters (e.g. "DEBUG (MainThread) [", "INFO|", "[INFO]") right after timestamps. Weak activations land on formatting and separator tokens in code, markup, lists and metadata, such as pipes, brackets, @, list bullets, chat-nick prefixes and newlines before headers.

Words referring to family and domestic life, mainly offspring and dependents (children, kids, sons, daughters, baby boy, family, offspring), often after possessives like "my" or "their". It also fires more weakly on related ideas such as home, marriage, loved ones, relationships and upbringing.

Comparative and superlative constructions: comparative adjectives/adverbs ("-er" forms, "more", "less", "better", "larger", "easier") and intensifiers like "much" or "even" preceding them, plus words expressing a degree of change or improvement (e.g., "improve", "enough", "as ... as"). Activation peaks on the comparative word itself and sometimes spreads to the word it modifies.
Relative pronouns (mostly "that", also "which", "what", French "qui") that start a relative clause right after the noun they modify.

Fires most strongly on the Dutch surname particle "van"/"Van" (as in Van Halen, van de Flierdt). Weaker activations appear on look-alike name or subword fragments that contain "v" or "an"/"am" sounds, such as ivan, Evan, anders, Camp, wander, Vill, VW, visc and vagr. These are often parts of proper names.

The opening words of a subordinate or adverbial clause, mostly right after conjunctions like "when", "if", "after", "since" and "while": the subject plus verb ("they start", "we have") or a participle or gerund ("camping with", "being heated at"). Activation peaks on the main verb, the start of the clause describing the condition or time of an event.

A diffuse, weakly activating feature that fires on content-bearing noun-phrase tokens (often the start or subword pieces of rare, technical, or proper-noun terms) such as place and organization names, product codes, scientific and technical vocabulary, and the head nouns of the topic being discussed, typically right after a determiner, preposition, or verb.

A weak, diffuse signal in lofty, idealistic or inspirational passages about purpose, virtue, God, country, humanity, democracy, the earth or the world. It fires on function words and nouns within these grand statements rather than on any single token type. The strongest activations are on phrases expressing a higher calling or universal scope, such as "God. What would the world", "put on this earth to be", "Country, we advocate" and "activist on the planet".

A diffuse, weak feature tied to document structure in encyclopedic or wiki-style text. It fires most strongly on wiki boilerplate and lead-sentence phrasing ("From The … Wiki⏎⏎The", "Not to be confused with", "also known as", "Jump to navigation / search"). More commonly it fires weakly on transitions between sections: sentence-final periods followed by paragraph breaks, header and title boundaries, and the first token after a heading.

Words for soft, moldable, kneadable substances, chiefly "dough" (including "dough" within doughnut, sourdough, and the name Dougherty), along with batter, crust, clay, slurry, pulp, papier-mâché and paste. The "kne" token of knead/kneel also activates. Activation is strongest on "dough" in baking contexts.

Object pronouns (him, them, me, us, you, it, herself), and occasionally nouns that refer back to one, placed right after a verb or preposition. They point to a previously mentioned person or entity, usually one receiving the action (e.g., "given to us", "betray him").

Units of measurement and quantity labels that come right after numbers, especially scientific or technical units (mol, mL, A, J, GB, g, oz, rpm). Activation is strongest on the unit token and often carries onto the slash or "per" of a compound rate unit (mol/m², mL/min, flops/MB). Weaker activations fall on counted nouns after numbers and on parts of ratio or fraction expressions in math and code.

Nouns naming the features, functions or capabilities something offers, most often a product, software, app or system (e.g. "features", "functionality", "functions", "capabilities", "properties"). Activation peaks on "features"/"functionality" and sometimes carries onto a following "that", "of" or "are".

Expressions of quantitative comparison or relative magnitude, especially in technical and scientific text. Typical forms are "comparable to", "larger than", "much greater than", "of the same order of magnitude" and "≫". The words "than" and "to" in these comparisons are usually the strongest tokens. Weaker activations fall on nearby size, scale and quantity terms such as widths, intensities and velocities.

Technical terms for operations, transformations or mappings applied to something (function, operation, unitary transformation, map, gate, transition probabilities, update, applying), strongest in math notation defining a function "f: X \to Y"; weak elsewhere in technical/code text.

A diffuse, weak feature with no clear semantic theme. It fires on mid-phrase continuation tokens such as prepositions, verbs after a subject, the second word of a compound noun, word-suffix pieces, and code or LaTeX syntax fragments. These appear mostly in technical, code, math or documentation text. The strongest activation is on the second word of a short label inside code ("Front End" in a print call).

Words that refer back to a set of several items named earlier, often quantifiers or demonstratives such as "these/those", "both/all of which", "respectively", "the two", "each" and "the latter". The activating words are anaphoric or distributive and point to multiple entities already introduced in the text.

Word-piece tokens beginning with a consonant cluster plus "re/ren" and ending in "nt" or similar, mostly in proper names and name fragments (Trent, Brent, Brett, Laurent, Trev, Bren, -rent), along with "torrent". Activation is strongest for "Trent" and "Brent".

Formatting/structural tokens that open a new labeled item in structured documents: markdown bold "**" before Proof/Example/Definition/Figure headings, HTML "<td" opening table cells (esp. in tables of contents or figure lists), list numbering punctuation before "Theorem" entries, and separators like newlines, citation brackets, or "and" right before a theorem/figure/section reference or title.

The head noun of a clause's grammatical subject, right before its verb (e.g. 'officials talk', 'Google will add', 'the FBI has been'). Activation is strongest for named organizations, institutions, governments and companies acting as agents (Supreme Court, Google, Sony, MTV, Fed, Congress). It also fires on generic subject nouns such as customers, consumers, God, money and teeth.

The word "Microsoft" (including the lowercase "icrosoft" fragment in URLs and package names). It fires most strongly in C# using directives (e.g. "using Microsoft.AspNetCore"), assembly names and file or registry paths. Activation is weaker in ordinary prose about Microsoft products.

Weak and diffuse activations on words tied to continuation over time toward an eventual end point or outcome, such as processes going on until something stops or disappears ('went on until', 'sooner or later', 'will soon', 'end of the month', 'died out', 'ad infinitum', 'continue', 'wait much longer', 'still owe'). The strongest hit is 'until' in the gradual-erosion example. Many other activations are low-level noise on function words and punctuation.

Fires on "thereby" (strongest) and related consequence/means connectives that introduce a resulting action or the mechanism of a preceding clause: "whereby", "hereby", "thus", "thereupon", and the Chinese "从而". Activation is highest when "thereby" is followed by a participle describing the result ("thereby increasing…").

The first word of a new sentence or line, mostly after a period or line break, that opens a new section or instruction. It is strongest for "For" (especially "For more information" and "For other purposes") in boilerplate such as repository notices, copyright statements, and contact or reference lines. Other openers like "To", "See", "Other", "On" and "In" activate more weakly.

A diffuse, weak feature centered on normative or value-laden phrasing about what is best, right or beneficial for someone, such as "do what's best for your story", "the best fit for their team", "seek their greatest happiness" and "what is right". It also fires faintly on surrounding advisory or concessive language ("but", "take your time", "there is no").

Practical travel‑guide and consumer‑advice prose: tips about transport, journey times, fares, prices and costs, and conditional advice ("depending on", "unless", "check", "buy a SIM card", "use local bus/taxi"). Activation peaks on concrete logistics details such as durations and prices.

The second term in a slash-joined pair or alternative (X/Y), marked on the word or word-completion right after the slash. These are usually closely related alternatives or co-equal options such as left/right, arrival/departure, iPhone/iPad and elements/words. Weaker activations appear for similar pairings joined by hyphens, 'and', or commas in a list.

A weak, diffuse feature found mostly in personal, profile-style or promotional text such as bios, dating or classified ads, and self-descriptions. It fires on list connectors (commas, "and", "or") and on first-person words ("I", "am", "your") in enumerations of hobbies, traits or interests, e.g. "hiking, adventuring, and cuddling" or "hardworking, motivated and determined".

Technical and scientific terminology, mostly mathematical, physical, or computational, in academic writing. The feature fires on the head noun or final word-piece that completes a specialized term (e.g., "spaces", "function", "coefficient", "derivative", "matrices", "-ential"), especially in math-heavy contexts.

Words and phrases about safety, risk, and protective or regulatory considerations, such as safety concerns, hazards, danger, security, tamper-evidence, verification, legal or ethical considerations, health risks and adverse reactions. Weaker activations land on loosely related abstract nouns like trust, care, ethics, purity and regulation. Activation peaks on explicit safety, concern or hazard terms.

Words for damaging someone's reputation with false or hostile statements. Activation is strongest on defamation, libel, slander and defamatory, and weaker on smear, malign, insult, disparagement, character assassination and reputation. It also fires weakly on related legal-offense terms such as battery, trespass, treason and maliciously.

Tokens at the start of a contrasting or alternative clause, typically its connective (but, while, yet, if, and), its subject (the unhappy ones, small companies, others, some, the Italian population), or the negation it introduces (does not, didn't). The activated tokens set up a counterpoint or second case opposed to the preceding statement. Activation peaks on a subject followed by a negated verb (e.g., "nominal variables do not").

Leading keyword (modifier or type) that begins a declaration in source code with no access modifier in front of it, e.g. static, const, void, class, mod, internal. Activation is strongest for 'static' in static constructors and static nested classes or Main methods, as in C# and Java.

Verbs of directed movement, mainly "head" in the sense of going toward a destination ("headed for/to/out", "heading over"), which activate most strongly. Weaker activations come from other senses of "head" (heading as a title, headed by), from "handed/handing" (transfer to someone), and from "make their way".

A diffuse, weakly activating feature with no clear semantic theme. It fires sparsely across prose, code and data, most often on the last token of a noun phrase or clause just before a comma, period or continuation, such as a head noun, a verb, or an assignment '='.

Abbreviated suffix words that close a proper name or list, typically followed by a period: corporate designators (Inc, Corp, LLC, Co, Bros), generational suffixes (Jr, III), and other abbreviations such as Rd, Vol, Univ, ft, and list-ending 'etc'. Activation is strongest for Inc, Jr, and Corp.

Words that set the scope or domain of a topic, typically temporal spans (history, period, over time, twentieth century, a hundred years), geographic or national ranges (world, global, American, British, Africa), or academic subject areas (science, programming, literature, politics). Activation is strongest on phrases spelling out wide breadth, such as 'from all over the world' or 'the whole history of the universe'.

Action verbs or gerunds/nominalizations naming the purpose or function of a method, device, approach, or system, typically right after "method for", "approach to", "a way to", "used to" in technical or scientific abstracts and patents (e.g. measuring, detecting, reducing, managing). The following "of" is sometimes marked too.

Terms for stellar types, stages and life cycles in astrophysics: dwarfs and giants (strongest on "dwar" in "white dwarfs" and "red giants"), main-sequence, stellar progenitors, core-collapse, mass-loss, evolution models, variable stars and supernovae. It fires more weakly on the same words in other settings, such as fantasy dwarves, volcanoes and eruptions, and geological periods.

The infinitive marker "to" (and sometimes the verb itself) that follows verbs of attempt or intention, chiefly "try/tried/trying" but also "attempt", "endeavour", "want", "promise" and "careful". It marks the point where a verb of effort is about to introduce the action being attempted.

Tokens inside identifier-like strings such as filenames, image paths, URLs, DOIs and captions, mostly the final numeric suffix or last path/name segment (e.g. 'image1', '-1', '004') just before the extension or line break.

Fires on clause/sentence boundaries (periods, commas, paragraph breaks, and the conjunction or pronoun starting the next clause) right after a statement about excess, avoidance or prevention. Typical preceding words are overload, overwhelmed, overboard, too much, avoid, prevent, waste and criticise. The feature marks the end of such a cautionary or limiting clause.

Words about carrying, holding or transporting goods: cargo, freight, loads, contents, packing, containers and vehicles (trains, wagons, lorries, boxes, stuffed or full). Activation is strongest on "cargo", "load" and "full of".

Fires on tokens beginning with or containing a "u"/"ur" sound, strongest on "Ur" words and names (Ur, Urmas, Urmia, Urbana, urgencies, uit). It also fires often on the word "out", both alone and as a prefix (outplayed, outwit, out-of-the-ordinary). Weaker hits come from other U-initial capitals and acronyms (UT, UF, UCS) and stray tokens like "url" or "uh".

The word "egg"/"eggs" in any sense (food, biological ova, laying, Easter eggs, place names) plus related pieces like yolk, ovum, 蛋, and stray "gg" subword fragments (veggie, Deggendorf). Strongest when eggs are food items in lists or recipes.

Separators and lead-ins inside lists of causes, conditions, diseases or factors. Fires on commas, 'and'/'or', 'such as', 'including', 'caused by' and 'signs of', and sometimes on the first word of the next item, at points where another item is about to follow. The lists are mostly medical, causal or diagnostic (e.g., 'caused by X, Y, or Z'; 'such as A, B and C').

Past participles (and similar verbs) in passive constructions, often following 'is/was/be/can be' and preceding an agent or source phrase like 'by', 'in', 'from', 'through' (e.g. 'controlled by', 'appointed by', 'decided in').

A weak, diffuse feature that fires on words in phrases describing what something does, provides or contributes: its function, role, purpose or beneficial effect. Examples include 'play a role', 'creates jobs for', 'provide shelter and… while also offering', 'distribute heat, salt', 'feast on… specialize in consuming', 'tax revenues plus economic benefits' and 'committed to supporting'. It usually lands on the verbs, connectives ('and', 'while also', 'for', 'into') and nouns that link an entity to its impact, mostly in expository text.

Boundary tokens just before the main propositional content of a sentence, most often in scientific or expository writing. These are mainly the complementizer "that" after reporting verbs (showed, suggests, indicate, conclude). They also include the comma after discourse connectives or introductory phrases (Thus, Moreover, Therefore, In contrast), plus colons and paragraph breaks after headings. Each marks the point where the new claim or finding begins.

Words and phrases that set up a problem, difficulty, or confusing situation the writer is about to solve, often in a problem-then-solution or advice framing (e.g. "can be daunting", "a bit tricky", "overwhelmed", "unsure", "wondering", "confusion", "struggling to"). It responds to descriptions of hardship, uncertainty, or inconvenience, typically just before a reassuring turn like "but", "fortunately" or "here are some tips".

The head noun (or final token of a multi-token word) that completes a noun phrase, often an abstract or general noun right after a determiner or modifier and frequently followed by a prepositional complement such as "of" or "in" (e.g., "the mass of", "the people of", "the C-terminus").

Words that mark a temporal (sometimes spatial) reference point from which later events proceed, especially the anaphoric word after "since"/"from"/"until" ("since then", "from there", "from now on", "since that time", "has since"). Activation is strongest on "then" in "Since then". Weaker hits fall on time spans ("years", "decade") and on commas closing an introductory time phrase.

Tokens that come right after a person's (or entity's) name and open supplementary identifying information about it, such as an alternate, maiden, or former name, a nickname, birth details, or a relation. Typical triggers are an opening parenthesis, a quotation mark, or words like 'born', 'called', 'formerly', 'name was'. Activation is strongest on 'née' and its variants ('neé', 'n’ee'), which introduce a maiden name.

Line and phrase boundaries in song lyrics, poems, and verse. The strongest activations fall on line breaks, commas, and periods that close a lyric line, and on the last words of rhythmic lines or repeated refrains, as in Examples 18 and 22. Weaker activations appear on scattered punctuation in ordinary prose.

Structural boundaries between items in a sequence: list numbers ("3.", "4."), bullets, line breaks and paragraph breaks after a sentence, indentation before a new code line, table row/cell tags, and commas separating names or list items. It marks the point where one item or section ends and the next begins, and is strongest on enumeration numbers.

The word "plain" (strongest) and its forms (plains, Plain-, plaintext, plaintive), plus the related word "bare" (barefoot, bare metal, barely). Activation peaks on "plain" meaning simple/unadorned/obvious, as in "just plain", "plain and simple" or "plain text", and is weaker for geographic plains and "bare".

Separators and connecting words (mostly colons after labels like "Date", "Published", "Created", "Filed"; also "on", "(", table-cell tags) that directly precede a date or timestamp value in metadata-style text.

over.name: A diffuse, low-intensity feature with no clear semantic focus. It fires sporadically on single mid-sentence tokens such as proper-name fragments, word-piece continuations, function words, punctuation and list separators. These tend to appear in formal, technical or noisy (OCR/spam-like) text. Slightly stronger activations occur within noun phrases naming specific entities, such as 'the 1996 American Book Award', 'Mahavir Chakra' and 'graphite'.

Non-semantic formatting and filler tokens: whitespace runs, separators, symbols, box-drawing/ASCII-art characters, table delimiters, emoticon/kaomoji pieces, mojibake, and paragraph breaks within layout-heavy or garbled text. Kaomoji and decorative symbol strings activate most strongly.

Fires on the opening token of a document or structured block, such as the very first word or symbol of a text (namespace, using, #define, #ifndef, ![, <!--, titles), and especially the <thead token that starts the header right after a <table> tag.

Formatting and structural tokens in tables, code, and other structured text: row-ending pipes plus newlines, indentation and alignment whitespace, line breaks, and separators that mark cell, line, or column boundaries ahead of the next aligned item.

Separator tokens (spaces, newlines, double newlines, ">\n" in HTML tables, pipes, dashes) placed between items of a repetitive, predictable sequence, such as numbered pagination (1 2 3 4), number or year runs, alphabet indexes, figure labels, answer options, list entries, and table rows/cells. Activation is strongest deep inside long runs of structured, enumerated content.

Long runs of the same token repeated over and over, such as dashes, spaced dots, ";amp", ";\", repeated letters, or empty table cells. Activation rises the deeper it is into the repetitive run. Ordinary prose tokens get only weak activation.

Tokens that act as separators or filler inside tabular, grid-like or column-aligned layouts. Typical cases are whitespace padding between columns, table cell tags (<td>), LaTeX alignment and spacing commands (&, \quad), dashed separator lines, and numbers or labels arranged in grids. Activation is strongest on aligned numbers and spacing in ASCII layouts and on repeated delimiter runs.

Tokens that end or complete a phrase which is a repeat of an earlier one in the context. Typical cases are repeated lines, list items, boilerplate and refrains (e.g. "Invalid Input", "Show more", "Monthly Budget", "lived a method", repeated numbers or units). The feature is predicting the final word of a copy. Activation is strongest in highly repetitive text and grows with the number of repetitions.

Fires most strongly on the Thai combining vowel mark 'ั' (mai han-akat) inside Thai words. Elsewhere activation is only weak and scattered: word fragments/suffixes, Slashdot user-ID digits and spaces before emoji. Other non-Latin scripts (Korean, Chinese, Arabic, Armenian, Kannada) get no activation.

A diffuse, weakly firing feature with no clear single concept. It activates sporadically on many token types: numbers and items in comma-separated lists, math operators and LaTeX symbols, punctuation, and citation brackets. It fires most strongly on hard-to-predict or surprising content, such as citation markers like "[6", nonsensical word salad, and incongruous lists of unrelated nouns.

Tokens partway through long repetitive, highly predictable sequences, such as runs of dots, dashes, symbols or separators (table-of-contents leaders, ASCII rules), table cells (LaTeX &, HTML <td>), numeric lists and grids, and IP-address segments. The latent fires on later repeats in the pattern, where the next token can be predicted from what came before. It fires weakly on occasional ordinary words in spammy or garbled text.

Double-backtick tokens (``), mostly the opening part of Markdown code fences (```) or inline code delimiters, and also LaTeX-style opening quotation marks (``). Activation is strongest at the start of a code block or quoted span. Weak activations appear on other opening delimiters such as „ and $$.

Fires on garbled or invisible text, mainly empty/zero-width tokens, mojibake (�) fragments and stray combining diacritics inside corrupted, mis-encoded or binary-like text. It is strongest on runs of empty tokens in Cyrillic-looking binary garbage and only weak elsewhere.

Delimiter and separator tokens, such as spaces, commas, pipes, ampersands, dashes, newlines, and quote-comma pairs, that sit between items in long repetitive sequences like number runs, page lists, table specs, and data arrays. Activation grows as the repeated pattern continues and becomes more predictable.

Weak, diffuse activation on structural or layout tokens in formatted or non-prose text, such as whitespace runs, pipes, dashes, ampersands and digits in tables, matrices and series, and code formatting. It fires most strongly on ASCII-art characters (slashes, parentheses, backslashes and spaces) inside print strings.

Separator tokens (commas, spaces, dots, newlines, <td> cells, 'x') placed between items in repetitive lists or sequences of numbers/values/words, firing most strongly when the same item is repeated many times (e.g. '50, 50, 50…').

Fires weakly on tokens that repeat or continue a pattern already in context, an induction-like copying signal. Typical cases are repeated words or strings (Image Image…, true true…, Why? Why? Why, abcabc, Omnomnom, eewwwwwww, JcakJcak), continuations of ordered sequences (alphabet letters, CDEFGABC, 12345678) and pieces of random or ID-like character strings.

A weak, diffuse feature with no clear single-token pattern. It fires mostly on generic, low-information filler in noisy web text such as SEO spam, scrambled or nonsensical sentences, code and number snippets, and templated boilerplate. It is strongest on corporate-buzzword placeholder text (e.g., 'Organically grow the holistic world view…') and on generic website promo copy ('If you are ready, you can play some other games').

Stray whitespace tokens (a lone space, or spaces plus a newline) at line or paragraph starts after line breaks, marking a section or content shift. Whitespace-only lines in Markdown and code fire most strongly.

Fires weakly on segment boundaries, mostly sentence-final punctuation fused with paragraph breaks (".⏎⏎", "⏎⏎", ":⏎⏎", "...⏎⏎") where a paragraph, heading, title or list item ends and a new section or topic begins. It also fires occasionally on tokens near the very start of a document or line.
