A sparse, weak feature that fires on structural or delimiter tokens in mixed or technical text. Its strongest hits are the period or space right after a list number ("1.", "2.", "3. "). It also fires on separators such as " /" and "<![", and on spaces between English and Chinese text. A few scattered fragments activate too, such as pieces of hex hashes, timestamp digits and occasional English words. Chinese characters themselves essentially never activate it.

Tokens inside runs of repeated characters or symbols, such as strings of the same letter or digit ("000", "111", "CCDD", "WWLLW"), elongated interjections ("yeeeah", "ooooh"), placeholder X's, repeated stars, daggers or block glyphs, and doubled backticks. The feature fires partway through the run, where a character or chunk repeats what came just before it.

Double-newline paragraph-break tokens, typically with leading whitespace or punctuation fused in, that come right after a sentence or line ends and before a new paragraph, heading or code block. Activation is strongest when a space is fused before the break (" ⏎⏎") or the break falls after a math or code line.

Trailing-space line breaks (Markdown hard-break style "  ⏎"), firing most strongly after author names, list entries and table-of-contents lines. Weaker activation on superscript/subscript characters such as affiliation markers (¹, ²) and chemical or unit subscripts, and on accented or split word fragments (faç, ô, ṣ).

Tokens inside long runs of the same repeated character or token (dot leaders, dashes, spaces, nbsp, -*, ;\, repeated letters or symbols). Activation is strongest deep in the run, and a few sequence positions stand out as peaks. There are weak, sporadic activations on ordinary tokens, mostly prepositions like "in".

A weak, diffuse feature that fires on tokens in hard-to-predict, high-entropy text rather than on a particular word. Typical contexts are random alphanumeric strings, hashes, IDs, URLs, IP addresses and numeric lists or codes. It also fires on rare non-Latin scripts, garbled LaTeX, and incoherent spam or machine-generated prose.

Tokens of repeated characters within elongated or repetitive strings, such as stretched words and exclamations ("yeeeeah", "Aaaaah", "maaaaybe"), repeated punctuation, laughter, block glyphs, and placeholder runs like "xxxxxxxx" or "AAAAAAAA". Activation is mostly on the middle/later chunks of the run and grows as the repetition continues.

Tokens in the last columns of grid-like, tabular, or repetitive structured text (matrices, ASCII art, tables, number grids, LaTeX arrays, repeated symbol rows), especially the last cells right before a line break or row terminator such as \\, |, or ]. It also fires weakly on the last item of repeated patterns in prose.

Separator tokens such as commas, spaces, ampersands, and HTML <td> tags inside long, repetitive sequences like number lists, table rows, and coin-flip strings. Activation is strongest in the middle of a long run of repeated delimiters. Weaker activations fall on function words (and, with, that, the) in formulaic, promotional-style prose.

The very first token of a document, firing most strongly when the text begins mid-stream with a bare number fragment (e.g. part of a phone number, ID, count or price like "869", "837", "051"). It fires more weakly on other opening fragments such as partial words, markdown hashes, newlines or punctuation.

Whitespace/formatting tokens marking structural breaks between sections, mostly runs of multiple newlines (often with indentation or trailing punctuation) separating code blocks or paragraphs. Longer runs of blank lines, especially at the end of a document or before a new code or section header, activate most strongly. Odd or duplicated punctuation at boundaries (stray periods, quotes, commas) activates weakly.

Tokens that repeat an immediately preceding item in a run of identical elements, typically the third or later occurrence of a repeated number in lists, arrays, tables or sequences (e.g. "9, 9, 9", "10, 10, 10"). It also fires on repeated words, characters or HTML cells, and is strongest for repeated numbers in comma-separated lists.

Fragments inside unpredictable, high-entropy character strings: random alphanumeric IDs, hashes, URL and filename codes, passwords, MAC addresses, mojibake or garbled text, and invented or foreign names split into odd subword pieces. Activation is strongest deep inside random codes and garbled Chinese. It is weak on occasional ordinary words.

A diffuse, low-specificity feature that fires mostly on unpredictable tokens in noisy or garbled text: OCR junk, mojibake, random alphanumeric codes and serial numbers, unit letters stuck to numbers, odd single characters or scripts, and gene or sequence strings. It also fires weakly on ordinary punctuation and line breaks in plain prose, which suggests it tracks high-surprise or out-of-distribution tokens rather than any one meaning.

Vertical bar / pipe characters ("|", and similar box-drawing verticals like ⎢ or ║) used as separators or borders in tables, ASCII diagrams, comment boxes, matrices, and website navigation/metadata strips. Activation is strongest inside ASCII-art diagrams and grids with many aligned bars, and weaker for single inline separators.

Diffuse, weak activations on tokens in noisy, low-coherence or structured text: garbled/encoded strings, ASCII art, ID and part numbers, URL encodings, tables, list bullets, and run-together or spam text. It fires mostly on repeated or fragment tokens (numbers, single letters, symbols, bullets) where the next token is hard to predict. No clear semantic meaning.

Weak feature firing on boilerplate tokens near the very start of documents: the verb "are" in website navigation headers like "You are here / You are on page / You are viewing", plus code and markup preambles such as "<thead" after "<table>", "#include", and especially "DOCTYPE" (the strongest activation).

Line-ending tokens that close a structural or delimiter element in code and markup, typically at the start of a file, such as the end of a comment banner or separator line (---⏎, **⏎, #⏎), the closing ">⏎" of an HTML or XML tag, header guards and blank lines after includes. The token marks the transition from boilerplate or formatting into the actual content. Activation is strongest at the ends of long dash or asterisk comment borders.

Standalone punctuation or symbol tokens, often combined with newlines (e.g. "---", "…", ":", "/", ".", "{"), that act as separators or filler at section and document boundaries. They typically appear where one text segment ends and an unrelated one (a new heading, a scraped fragment, a code block) begins.

Punctuation, whitespace, newlines and separator tokens (commas, spaces, dashes, tags, line breaks) that act as delimiters between items, mostly in noisy, garbled, redacted, foreign-script or list-like text. Activation is strongest for commas separating repeated or masked items, such as runs of █ blocks or REDACTED.

Tokens that repeat an immediately preceding token or short pattern. The feature fires on the second and later copies in runs of identical words, symbols, numbers, or cells, such as "H H H H", "+ + +", "Unlimited Unlimited", "agree agree", "7 7 7" and "NA NA". Activation tends to grow the longer the repetition goes on.

Fires at the very start of a document on leading boilerplate or list formatting: indentation spaces, bullet points (•) and numbering like "1.", plus the first word that follows. These are usually navigation menus, breadcrumbs and list items. It responds weakly to other opening structural markers such as runs of newlines, section commands, separator lines and stray header or menu words like "Stations".

Whitespace-only tokens (indentation spaces/tabs combined with newlines) forming blank or trailing-whitespace lines, especially between blocks of code (methods, statements) and occasionally in prose. Weak, sporadic activation on boilerplate tokens such as HTML closing tags and repeated page-template words.

Fires weakly and broadly on tokens inside structured or templated text such as HTML table markup (especially '>⏎' after closing td/tr tags), code, markdown links, LaTeX, tables of contents with dot leaders, data listings, and headings. The activating tokens are mostly delimiters, separators or repeated elements whose position is predictable from the surrounding repetitive formatting, rather than tokens carrying particular meaning.

A diffuse feature with no clear semantic content. It fires mostly on structural and formatting tokens, such as newlines, spaces, brackets, slashes, backslashes and punctuation. These usually sit inside markup, LaTeX, code, tables or garbled multilingual and symbol-heavy text, often at boundaries between segments. It also fires occasionally on ordinary function words like "of" or "in" in prose.

Tokens inside repetitive, predictable runs of text, such as repeated words or phrases ("Image Image Image", "very, very", "Skip to"), repeated symbols or separator lines, and boilerplate markup like HTML table tags (, ⏎, ),
and blockquote ">⏎" lines. Activation increases the longer the same pattern keeps repeating.

Tokens inside repetitive or patterned sequences: repeated numbers, symbols, separators and code lines (e.g., 30, 31, 30…; -*-*; ~~88~~88; repeated '; ' lines; 16x16x16). The token itself repeats an earlier element in the same run, and activation is strongest in highly regular, predictable repetition. Weak, scattered activation on ordinary words elsewhere.

Tokens inside repetitive or patterned sequences, where the next token is predictable from earlier repetition: repeated phrases ("Loading...", "Final Four", "Sacred Valley"), number runs, list separators, whitespace or newline padding, HTML table tags, and repeated characters or symbols. Activations are generally weak and scattered, strongest on spaces and numbers in counting sequences.

Whitespace-only tokens, mostly runs of several newlines (often with indentation spaces or tabs), that form blank gaps between sections of code or documents. Activation grows with the length of the run, so long stretches of consecutive blank lines fire most strongly.

under.name: Subdomain name pieces in URLs of academic institutional repositories, strongest on "commons" in "digitalcommons" (e.g. after "Follow this and additional works at:"). Weaker on related repository names like scholarworks, escholarship, dspace, hdl.handle, eprints and repository, plus the word "works" in that boilerplate phrase.

Patent application serial numbers and their lead-in phrases, e.g. "Ser. No.", "Appl. No.:", "Application Data" and "of application No.", along with the digits that follow. The strongest response falls on the "No" and its surrounding periods in "Ser. No.", plus the number parts like "14/612,460". There is weak, scattered activation on function words in other boilerplate or formulaic text.

Asterisk (or similar star symbols like ∗, ⁎, often fused with a comma) placed right after an author's name or affiliation number in academic paper author lists, marking the corresponding author. Weak firing on other stray asterisks or bracket and label tokens that follow names.

Separator tokens inside email addresses and URLs, chiefly the "@" between user and domain, plus "://", ".com" and ".gov". They typically appear in contact or attribution boilerplate such as repository notices and author lines. There is weak activation on similar attribution or affiliation contexts (e.g., "by", "(", a trailing country name).

Affiliation markers placed right after author names in academic paper bylines: superscript numbers, letters, or symbols (1, ¹, a, †, *), including LaTeX \textsuperscript arguments. The first affiliation marker ("1"/"¹"/"a") activates most strongly, while secondary markers (2, ‡) and separating commas activate weakly.

Affiliation markers placed right after author names in academic paper bylines: superscript numbers, letters, Roman numerals, or symbols (*, †, ⋆) that point to institutional affiliations. Activation is strongest for the first affiliation marker (especially "1"/"¹"/"a") and when the same marker repeats across several authors, and weaker for later or secondary indices.

The first token right after a source file's package or namespace declaration, which opens the file body. In Java this is usually "import" (strongest), but can be "public", "/**", or the semicolon-plus-newlines that end the package line. In C# it is the newline or "{" after the namespace name. Weak activation also appears on "text" in "Sample/Example text" headers that mark where a document body begins.

Affiliation markers placed right after author names in academic paper bylines. These are superscript numbers, letters, or symbols such as †, ‡ and §, written as Unicode superscripts, LaTeX \textsuperscript or $^ $, or plain trailing digits. Activation is strongest on markers other than the first (2, 3, b, c), i.e. those indicating a second or later affiliation.

A diffuse, low-level feature that fires most strongly and broadly across low-quality, SEO-style or machine-spun web text: promotional and advice copy about dumpsters, casinos and gambling, online therapy, antivirus software and marketing tools, often with awkward synonym substitutions and garbled grammar (e.g., "meet up with their arrangement commitments", "method or significant dumpster"). In these passages it covers long runs of ordinary words, especially second-person "you/your" phrasing. Elsewhere it gives only weak, scattered activations on isolated function words and punctuation in otherwise normal text.

Separators and markers that follow an author's name in a paper's author list, such as commas, "and", affiliation numbers, symbols like *, †, §, and the closing braces or $ of superscript markup. Activation is strongest on the comma or closing token right after the affiliation superscripts.

Tokens that close a sentence or heading and start a paragraph break, mostly a period (sometimes "?") merged with a double newline, or a bare double newline after a title. They are strongest in low-quality, SEO-style web text where the next paragraph changes topic.

Line breaks, bullets, spaces and closing punctuation that separate fields in boilerplate or structured web and document text, such as metadata, HAL IDs, radio player widgets, bid listings, HTML tables and citation footers. Activation peaks at the newline that ends one metadata item and comes right before the next item.

In academic paper author lists, the token right after an author's name that starts the affiliation marker: LaTeX superscript openers ("cript{", "(^{", "^"), opening parentheses, spaces, asterisks, or commas just before affiliation numbers/letters. Plain Unicode superscript digits and symbols (¹, †, ‡) get little or no activation.

Scientific and taxonomic descriptive prose, mainly species and taxon descriptions in biology and paleontology (Latin genus and species names, family suffixes like -idae, author/year citations, statements of distribution, habitat and morphology). Activation lands on the function words, punctuation and name fragments inside these passages and is strongest in dense species-description text. Weak, scattered activation also appears on general academic and technical writing.

The ".annotation" (or ".annotations") package segment in Java import statements. Activation is strongest in Android/androidx/javax imports of nullability annotations (NonNull, Nullable) and weakest in Spring imports (beans.factory, web.bind). Other tokens fire only sporadically and weakly.

Fires weakly and diffusely on ordinary words inside direct quotations and reported speech, such as interview remarks ending in “,” he said. Activation tends to grow over longer spans of quoted spoken language, especially conversational or opinion-giving phrasing. Some activations appear outside quotes but are weak and scattered.

The ".Linq" token in C# using directives ("using System.Linq;", also System.Linq.Expressions / System.Xml.Linq), within the import block at the top of a file. Activation is strongest for the plain System.Linq import.

The LaTeX citation command name "cite" (including variants like \citep, \citealt, \newcite, \textcite) right after the backslash, which marks references to literature in academic text. Activation is highest for repeated citations in a list. There are weak activations on other LaTeX reference commands like \secref and on scattered unrelated tokens.

The "import" keyword at the start of Java import statements, mainly in the later lines of an existing import block, where it follows earlier imports, often ones that share the same package prefix. One weak exception is "to" in English prose.

Segment boundaries (periods, question marks, newlines, colons, commas) that end a sentence, title or line just before an abrupt topic shift or disjointed continuation. Activation is strongest in incoherent, spun or spam-like text where consecutive sentences are unrelated, and weaker at ordinary sentence ends or list and heading breaks.

The three-digit number chunk immediately after "10." in a DOI prefix (the publisher registrant code, e.g. 1103 for APS, 1109 for IEEE). Activation is strongest for the token "110" and weaker for other prefixes like 101, 103, 108 or 109. It also fires weakly on "110" appearing in other numeric IDs such as ISBNs or user IDs.

Spam/SEO keyword phrases abruptly spliced into unrelated prose, e.g. product or search queries like drug names, CBD gummies, casino bonuses, forex, shoes, 'essay on…', 'near me', 'where to buy'. The strongest activations fall on the start and core words of the injected keyword string where it breaks the surrounding sentence.

Attribution context for named people (often researchers or experts) in news and science writing. It fires on the words just after or around a name that describe the person's role, title, or affiliation: appositive commas, “who…”, “lead author/co-author of”, “professor”, “said/says”, “and his colleagues”, “at/of [institution]”. Activation peaks on the comma right after a name and on role words like “author” or “who” that start a description of the person's part in a study.

Head nouns that name an academic or research unit in institutional affiliations, chiefly "Department"/"Dept", plus Institute, School, Faculty, Division, Centre, Laboratory and University, along with their non-English forms. They usually begin an affiliation line in a paper's author block, often right after a superscript number or after an author's name, and are typically followed by "of". Activation is strongest for "Department" at the start of a numbered affiliation line and weaker for mentions inside running prose.

Separators and connective words inside boilerplate web and repository text, such as headers, footers, metadata labels and attribution lines ("published by", "brought to you by", "Part of", "downloaded from", "General rights", "Server:"). Activation falls on the newline, colon or preposition right after a label or stock phrase, just before its value or the next section. It is strongest on "by" in attribution lines like "open access by".

Separator (mostly a comma, sometimes a newline or ").,") that follows a department/lab/sub-unit name in academic author affiliations, right before the parent institution (e.g. "Department of Physics, University of…"). It fires most strongly after "Department of X". Weak activations appear on similar separators in addresses, citations and other text.
The ".ArrayList" token in Java "import java.util.ArrayList;" statements. Other java.util collection classes such as HashMap and Vector activate only weakly, and stray non-code tokens barely activate.

Sentence-ending punctuation fused with a paragraph break ('.⏎⏎', '?⏎⏎', '".⏎⏎') at the end of a news article's main body, right before unrelated boilerplate such as 'Related news', 'Latest News', 'More news:', or another story's headline. A mid-paragraph period gets weaker activation, and other tokens barely register.

Institution names in author affiliation or address lines, especially the start of a new segment after a comma or line break. It fires most strongly on "University (of)" and its foreign equivalents (Universität, Université, Universidad), and also on Department, Faculty, School, College, Institute and the first token of named universities.

Boilerplate and metadata in academic repository or web pages: newline breaks (often double) after URLs, IDs, dates and citation fields, separating sections such as "Submitted on", rights, permissions and citation info. The strongest activation is "contact" in the repository phrase "For more information, please contact ...", along with the email's ".edu".

Sentence- or paragraph-ending punctuation (especially a period followed by a blank line) at points where the text suddenly switches to an unrelated topic, as in spammy or stitched-together web text. Activation is strongest when the next passage is incoherent with what came before.

Text about people being hired, cast, attached, or brought onto projects (especially films, art and entertainment), with the feature firing on the predicate and function words around who joined, was chosen for a role, or collaborated (e.g. "attached … to", "was given", "who would be best for the role", "teamed up with"). There is weaker activation on scattered punctuation and connectives in similar narrative contexts.

Narrative biographical text about a person's career, especially athletes and fighters: their records, upcoming bouts and matchups, preparation, achievements and final roles (e.g. 'coming off a 41-0-1 record that includes 30 knockouts', 'was slated to face… champion', 'after his fifth, and final, role'). Function words and clause connectors in these career-history sentences activate most; scattered weak activations appear elsewhere.

The consequence clause of boilerplate website consent notices. It fires on the main clause that follows a conditional action ("By continuing to use this site", "if you continue to browse"), most strongly on ", you accept/agree to our use of cookies" and on "you're agreeing to" or "we'll assume you're ok". It also covers the same notices in other languages (Spanish, Italian). Weaker activations appear on similar call-to-action consequences, such as "you can help", "we may receive a commission" and "to keep reading".

Names of academic and research institutional units in author affiliations and bios, especially subunits like "Department of", "School of", "Laboratory", "Institute" or "Center" (including non-English forms), plus the field names and "University" that follow. Activation is highest on the unit word itself, such as "Department" or "School", and on the following "of", particularly in paper headers listing affiliations.
Commas in postal addresses and institutional affiliations that come right after a city or locality name and come before the larger region (state, province, country) or the postal code.

Weak, diffuse activation across the text of plot summaries and story synopses (films, TV, books, fan fiction), describing what characters do and what happens to them: actions, relationships, settings and turns of events. It is strongest in dense stretches that narrate a sequence of events. Non-narrative text, such as instructions or business prose, gets only sporadic weak hits.

Person names in scholarly contexts, mainly author bylines and citations in scientific papers. It fires on first names, surname fragments, initials and the separators between authors (commas, semicolons, "and", "et al.", affiliation superscripts, years). It is strongest at the start of author lists that follow a paper title.

Acknowledgment, funding and author-affiliation boilerplate in papers and reports, such as "This work was supported by", "We are grateful to", "would like to thank", "Funding:" and "Acknowledgements". Activation is strongest on the key verbs and the prepositions after them (supported/funded/grateful/thank + by/to), just before the funder or thanked person is named.

Narrative prose summarizing fictional characters' backstories and plots, as in wiki or fandom character biographies (e.g., 'X was a lab assistant to...', 'Blaze decided to travel there'). Activation is spread across the running text, mostly function words, character names, verbs and clause boundaries, and is strongest at the start of a new biography section or sentence about a character.

The Android method name "setContentView" (or its "ContentView" piece) in Java Activity code, typically called right after super.onCreate(savedInstanceState) to set the layout via R.layout. Other weak activations are scattered and uninformative.

Separators and leading fragments inside structured identifiers and timestamps, especially dates, IDs and URL numbers that repeat or closely mirror a value seen just before. Typical hits are hyphens, slashes, spaces, month names and the first digit chunk right before the repeated part, as in updated dates, HAL IDs, NPR embed IDs and ISO datetimes.

Commas that separate items in a short list of trait or attribute names, overwhelmingly inside Rust #[derive(...)] attributes (e.g. Debug, Clone, PartialEq). The strongest activations are on earlier commas in the list. Weaker firing occurs on commas in other compact attribute or tag lists, such as "(Score:3, Informative)", product feature lists, and LaTeX options.

Tokens that end the fixed boilerplate or UI text of scraped web pages, such as "Jump to navigation, search", review/bid counts on freelance sites, "Need Help", "accept rate: %", "Google Scholar", timestamps, HAL IDs and ".com" in emails. They typically come right before a line break and the start of the page's actual content.

Fires inside formulaic, boilerplate web prose such as repository and copyright notices, privacy and data-safety text, takedown policies and corporate mission or marketing statements. It mostly activates on predictable connective points within these stock phrases, like commas, 'and', prepositions and the verb or clause continuation that comes next. Example phrases include 'documents, whether', 'recognise and abide', 'please let the Library know' and 'has long inspired our commitment to'.

Final numeric digits inside bibliographic and identifier strings: DOIs, astronomy bibcodes (e.g., 2022MNRAS.511..829H), patent dates, call numbers. Activation is strongest on the page/article number just before a closing author-initial letter in bibcode-style citations, and weak on other trailing digits within such codes.

Tokens inside personal names, chiefly in author lists and bylines of academic papers and reports, along with the separators between names: commas, initials, affiliation markers, superscripts and parenthetical native-script names. It fires most strongly in dense, multi-author lists. It also fires weakly on names and roles of researchers quoted in science news (e.g. 'postdoctoral research fellow') and on email domains near author blocks.

The ".Web" token in code namespaces and imports. It fires most strongly on C# "using System.Web" (including System.Web.Mvc, .UI, .Http). It is weaker for other packages such as Java/Android imports (webkit.WebView, WebSecurityConfigurerAdapter) or project namespaces like SpotifyAPI.Web. Scattered prose tokens get only negligible activation.

The token "(View" opening a parameter list, strongest in Android onClick(View v) click-handler signatures. It is weaker in other methods taking a View argument or in setVisibility(View.VISIBLE/GONE), and also fires on "(View our Privacy Policy)"-style web links.

Tokens inside institutional affiliation and address strings, typically from academic paper author headers. The strongest activations fall on the commas, connectors ("of", "and") and words like "University", "Department" and "Centre" that join nested units (lab, department, university, city). Weaker activation appears on similar organization-name text in prose.

over.name: A diffuse, low-intensity feature with no clear semantic focus. It fires sporadically on single mid-sentence tokens such as proper-name fragments, word-piece continuations, function words, punctuation and list separators. These tend to appear in formal, technical or noisy (OCR/spam-like) text. Slightly stronger activations occur within noun phrases naming specific entities, such as 'the 1996 American Book Award', 'Mahavir Chakra' and 'graphite'.

Non-semantic formatting and filler tokens: whitespace runs, separators, symbols, box-drawing/ASCII-art characters, table delimiters, emoticon/kaomoji pieces, mojibake, and paragraph breaks within layout-heavy or garbled text. Kaomoji and decorative symbol strings activate most strongly.

Fires on the opening token of a document or structured block, such as the very first word or symbol of a text (namespace, using, #define, #ifndef, ![, <!--, titles), and especially the <thead token that starts the header right after a <table> tag.

Formatting and structural tokens in tables, code, and other structured text: row-ending pipes plus newlines, indentation and alignment whitespace, line breaks, and separators that mark cell, line, or column boundaries ahead of the next aligned item.

Separator tokens (spaces, newlines, double newlines, ">\n" in HTML tables, pipes, dashes) placed between items of a repetitive, predictable sequence, such as numbered pagination (1 2 3 4), number or year runs, alphabet indexes, figure labels, answer options, list entries, and table rows/cells. Activation is strongest deep inside long runs of structured, enumerated content.

Long runs of the same token repeated over and over, such as dashes, spaced dots, ";amp", ";\", repeated letters, or empty table cells. Activation rises the deeper it is into the repetitive run. Ordinary prose tokens get only weak activation.

Tokens that act as separators or filler inside tabular, grid-like or column-aligned layouts. Typical cases are whitespace padding between columns, table cell tags (<td>), LaTeX alignment and spacing commands (&, \quad), dashed separator lines, and numbers or labels arranged in grids. Activation is strongest on aligned numbers and spacing in ASCII layouts and on repeated delimiter runs.

Tokens that end or complete a phrase which is a repeat of an earlier one in the context. Typical cases are repeated lines, list items, boilerplate and refrains (e.g. "Invalid Input", "Show more", "Monthly Budget", "lived a method", repeated numbers or units). The feature is predicting the final word of a copy. Activation is strongest in highly repetitive text and grows with the number of repetitions.

Fires most strongly on the Thai combining vowel mark 'ั' (mai han-akat) inside Thai words. Elsewhere activation is only weak and scattered: word fragments/suffixes, Slashdot user-ID digits and spaces before emoji. Other non-Latin scripts (Korean, Chinese, Arabic, Armenian, Kannada) get no activation.

A diffuse, weakly firing feature with no clear single concept. It activates sporadically on many token types: numbers and items in comma-separated lists, math operators and LaTeX symbols, punctuation, and citation brackets. It fires most strongly on hard-to-predict or surprising content, such as citation markers like "[6", nonsensical word salad, and incongruous lists of unrelated nouns.

Tokens partway through long repetitive, highly predictable sequences, such as runs of dots, dashes, symbols or separators (table-of-contents leaders, ASCII rules), table cells (LaTeX &, HTML <td>), numeric lists and grids, and IP-address segments. The latent fires on later repeats in the pattern, where the next token can be predicted from what came before. It fires weakly on occasional ordinary words in spammy or garbled text.

Double-backtick tokens (``), mostly the opening part of Markdown code fences (```) or inline code delimiters, and also LaTeX-style opening quotation marks (``). Activation is strongest at the start of a code block or quoted span. Weak activations appear on other opening delimiters such as „ and $$.

Fires on garbled or invisible text, mainly empty/zero-width tokens, mojibake (�) fragments and stray combining diacritics inside corrupted, mis-encoded or binary-like text. It is strongest on runs of empty tokens in Cyrillic-looking binary garbage and only weak elsewhere.

Delimiter and separator tokens, such as spaces, commas, pipes, ampersands, dashes, newlines, and quote-comma pairs, that sit between items in long repetitive sequences like number runs, page lists, table specs, and data arrays. Activation grows as the repeated pattern continues and becomes more predictable.

Weak, diffuse activation on structural or layout tokens in formatted or non-prose text, such as whitespace runs, pipes, dashes, ampersands and digits in tables, matrices and series, and code formatting. It fires most strongly on ASCII-art characters (slashes, parentheses, backslashes and spaces) inside print strings.

Separator tokens (commas, spaces, dots, newlines, <td> cells, 'x') placed between items in repetitive lists or sequences of numbers/values/words, firing most strongly when the same item is repeated many times (e.g. '50, 50, 50…').

Fires weakly on tokens that repeat or continue a pattern already in context, an induction-like copying signal. Typical cases are repeated words or strings (Image Image…, true true…, Why? Why? Why, abcabc, Omnomnom, eewwwwwww, JcakJcak), continuations of ordered sequences (alphabet letters, CDEFGABC, 12345678) and pieces of random or ID-like character strings.

A weak, diffuse feature with no clear single-token pattern. It fires mostly on generic, low-information filler in noisy web text such as SEO spam, scrambled or nonsensical sentences, code and number snippets, and templated boilerplate. It is strongest on corporate-buzzword placeholder text (e.g., 'Organically grow the holistic world view…') and on generic website promo copy ('If you are ready, you can play some other games').

Stray whitespace tokens (a lone space, or spaces plus a newline) at line or paragraph starts after line breaks, marking a section or content shift. Whitespace-only lines in Markdown and code fire most strongly.

Fires weakly on segment boundaries, mostly sentence-final punctuation fused with paragraph breaks (".⏎⏎", "⏎⏎", ":⏎⏎", "...⏎⏎") where a paragraph, heading, title or list item ends and a new section or topic begins. It also fires occasionally on tokens near the very start of a document or line.

A sparse, weak feature that fires on structural or delimiter tokens in mixed or technical text. Its strongest hits are the period or space right after a list number ("1.", "2.", "3. "). It also fires on separators such as " /" and "<![", and on spaces between English and Chinese text. A few scattered fragments activate too, such as pieces of hex hashes, timestamp digits and occasional English words. Chinese characters themselves essentially never activate it.

Tokens inside runs of repeated characters or symbols, such as strings of the same letter or digit ("000", "111", "CCDD", "WWLLW"), elongated interjections ("yeeeah", "ooooh"), placeholder X's, repeated stars, daggers or block glyphs, and doubled backticks. The feature fires partway through the run, where a character or chunk repeats what came just before it.

Double-newline paragraph-break tokens, typically with leading whitespace or punctuation fused in, that come right after a sentence or line ends and before a new paragraph, heading or code block. Activation is strongest when a space is fused before the break (" ⏎⏎") or the break falls after a math or code line.

Trailing-space line breaks (Markdown hard-break style "  ⏎"), firing most strongly after author names, list entries and table-of-contents lines. Weaker activation on superscript/subscript characters such as affiliation markers (¹, ²) and chemical or unit subscripts, and on accented or split word fragments (faç, ô, ṣ).

Tokens inside long runs of the same repeated character or token (dot leaders, dashes, spaces, nbsp, -*, ;\, repeated letters or symbols). Activation is strongest deep in the run, and a few sequence positions stand out as peaks. There are weak, sporadic activations on ordinary tokens, mostly prepositions like "in".

A weak, diffuse feature that fires on tokens in hard-to-predict, high-entropy text rather than on a particular word. Typical contexts are random alphanumeric strings, hashes, IDs, URLs, IP addresses and numeric lists or codes. It also fires on rare non-Latin scripts, garbled LaTeX, and incoherent spam or machine-generated prose.

Tokens of repeated characters within elongated or repetitive strings, such as stretched words and exclamations ("yeeeeah", "Aaaaah", "maaaaybe"), repeated punctuation, laughter, block glyphs, and placeholder runs like "xxxxxxxx" or "AAAAAAAA". Activation is mostly on the middle/later chunks of the run and grows as the repetition continues.

Tokens in the last columns of grid-like, tabular, or repetitive structured text (matrices, ASCII art, tables, number grids, LaTeX arrays, repeated symbol rows), especially the last cells right before a line break or row terminator such as \\, |, or ]. It also fires weakly on the last item of repeated patterns in prose.

Separator tokens such as commas, spaces, ampersands, and HTML <td> tags inside long, repetitive sequences like number lists, table rows, and coin-flip strings. Activation is strongest in the middle of a long run of repeated delimiters. Weaker activations fall on function words (and, with, that, the) in formulaic, promotional-style prose.

The very first token of a document, firing most strongly when the text begins mid-stream with a bare number fragment (e.g. part of a phone number, ID, count or price like "869", "837", "051"). It fires more weakly on other opening fragments such as partial words, markdown hashes, newlines or punctuation.

Whitespace/formatting tokens marking structural breaks between sections, mostly runs of multiple newlines (often with indentation or trailing punctuation) separating code blocks or paragraphs. Longer runs of blank lines, especially at the end of a document or before a new code or section header, activate most strongly. Odd or duplicated punctuation at boundaries (stray periods, quotes, commas) activates weakly.

Tokens that repeat an immediately preceding item in a run of identical elements, typically the third or later occurrence of a repeated number in lists, arrays, tables or sequences (e.g. "9, 9, 9", "10, 10, 10"). It also fires on repeated words, characters or HTML cells, and is strongest for repeated numbers in comma-separated lists.

Fragments inside unpredictable, high-entropy character strings: random alphanumeric IDs, hashes, URL and filename codes, passwords, MAC addresses, mojibake or garbled text, and invented or foreign names split into odd subword pieces. Activation is strongest deep inside random codes and garbled Chinese. It is weak on occasional ordinary words.

A diffuse, low-specificity feature that fires mostly on unpredictable tokens in noisy or garbled text: OCR junk, mojibake, random alphanumeric codes and serial numbers, unit letters stuck to numbers, odd single characters or scripts, and gene or sequence strings. It also fires weakly on ordinary punctuation and line breaks in plain prose, which suggests it tracks high-surprise or out-of-distribution tokens rather than any one meaning.

Vertical bar / pipe characters ("|", and similar box-drawing verticals like ⎢ or ║) used as separators or borders in tables, ASCII diagrams, comment boxes, matrices, and website navigation/metadata strips. Activation is strongest inside ASCII-art diagrams and grids with many aligned bars, and weaker for single inline separators.

Diffuse, weak activations on tokens in noisy, low-coherence or structured text: garbled/encoded strings, ASCII art, ID and part numbers, URL encodings, tables, list bullets, and run-together or spam text. It fires mostly on repeated or fragment tokens (numbers, single letters, symbols, bullets) where the next token is hard to predict. No clear semantic meaning.

Weak feature firing on boilerplate tokens near the very start of documents: the verb "are" in website navigation headers like "You are here / You are on page / You are viewing", plus code and markup preambles such as "<thead" after "<table>", "#include", and especially "DOCTYPE" (the strongest activation).

Line-ending tokens that close a structural or delimiter element in code and markup, typically at the start of a file, such as the end of a comment banner or separator line (---⏎, **⏎, #⏎), the closing ">⏎" of an HTML or XML tag, header guards and blank lines after includes. The token marks the transition from boilerplate or formatting into the actual content. Activation is strongest at the ends of long dash or asterisk comment borders.

Standalone punctuation or symbol tokens, often combined with newlines (e.g. "---", "…", ":", "/", ".", "{"), that act as separators or filler at section and document boundaries. They typically appear where one text segment ends and an unrelated one (a new heading, a scraped fragment, a code block) begins.

Punctuation, whitespace, newlines and separator tokens (commas, spaces, dashes, tags, line breaks) that act as delimiters between items, mostly in noisy, garbled, redacted, foreign-script or list-like text. Activation is strongest for commas separating repeated or masked items, such as runs of █ blocks or REDACTED.

Tokens that repeat an immediately preceding token or short pattern. The feature fires on the second and later copies in runs of identical words, symbols, numbers, or cells, such as "H H H H", "+ + +", "Unlimited Unlimited", "agree agree", "7 7 7" and "NA NA". Activation tends to grow the longer the repetition goes on.

Fires at the very start of a document on leading boilerplate or list formatting: indentation spaces, bullet points (•) and numbering like "1.", plus the first word that follows. These are usually navigation menus, breadcrumbs and list items. It responds weakly to other opening structural markers such as runs of newlines, section commands, separator lines and stray header or menu words like "Stations".

Whitespace-only tokens (indentation spaces/tabs combined with newlines) forming blank or trailing-whitespace lines, especially between blocks of code (methods, statements) and occasionally in prose. Weak, sporadic activation on boilerplate tokens such as HTML closing tags and repeated page-template words.

Fires weakly and broadly on tokens inside structured or templated text such as HTML table markup (especially '>⏎' after closing td/tr tags), code, markdown links, LaTeX, tables of contents with dot leaders, data listings, and headings. The activating tokens are mostly delimiters, separators or repeated elements whose position is predictable from the surrounding repetitive formatting, rather than tokens carrying particular meaning.

A diffuse feature with no clear semantic content. It fires mostly on structural and formatting tokens, such as newlines, spaces, brackets, slashes, backslashes and punctuation. These usually sit inside markup, LaTeX, code, tables or garbled multilingual and symbol-heavy text, often at boundaries between segments. It also fires occasionally on ordinary function words like "of" or "in" in prose.

Tokens inside repetitive, predictable runs of text, such as repeated words or phrases ("Image Image Image", "very, very", "Skip to"), repeated symbols or separator lines, and boilerplate markup like HTML table tags (, ⏎, ),
and blockquote ">⏎" lines. Activation increases the longer the same pattern keeps repeating.

Tokens inside repetitive or patterned sequences: repeated numbers, symbols, separators and code lines (e.g., 30, 31, 30…; -*-*; ~~88~~88; repeated '; ' lines; 16x16x16). The token itself repeats an earlier element in the same run, and activation is strongest in highly regular, predictable repetition. Weak, scattered activation on ordinary words elsewhere.

Tokens inside repetitive or patterned sequences, where the next token is predictable from earlier repetition: repeated phrases ("Loading...", "Final Four", "Sacred Valley"), number runs, list separators, whitespace or newline padding, HTML table tags, and repeated characters or symbols. Activations are generally weak and scattered, strongest on spaces and numbers in counting sequences.

Whitespace-only tokens, mostly runs of several newlines (often with indentation spaces or tabs), that form blank gaps between sections of code or documents. Activation grows with the length of the run, so long stretches of consecutive blank lines fire most strongly.

under.name: Names of academic and research institutional units in author affiliations and bios, especially subunits like "Department of", "School of", "Laboratory", "Institute" or "Center" (including non-English forms), plus the field names and "University" that follow. Activation is highest on the unit word itself, such as "Department" or "School", and on the following "of", particularly in paper headers listing affiliations.

Tokens inside personal names, chiefly in author lists and bylines of academic papers and reports, along with the separators between names: commas, initials, affiliation markers, superscripts and parenthetical native-script names. It fires most strongly in dense, multi-author lists. It also fires weakly on names and roles of researchers quoted in science news (e.g. 'postdoctoral research fellow') and on email domains near author blocks.

Content words and connecting function words (prepositions, articles, of/in/on) inside dense technical or scientific prose, especially abstract-style descriptions of mechanisms, measurements, and processes (e.g., adsorption kinetics, electrical conduction, gene regulation). Activation is diffuse and spreads over noun phrases and the prepositional links between them, not over one particular word.

Tokens within lists of person names, mostly author bylines of academic papers and citations. It fires on first names, initials, surname fragments and the separating commas or affiliation markers, and is strongest in the middle of long comma-separated author lists.

The first word(s) of a new sentence or paragraph, typically a preposition, conjunction, or transition that opens an introductory/adverbial phrase (In, On, At the, Before, Since, However, Other, In addition). It fires most strongly on "In" and "On" right after a paragraph break.

A diffuse, low-level feature for low-quality web text: SEO spam, casino and pharmacy spam, spun or machine-generated prose, and repository/metadata boilerplate. It fires most strongly inside incoherent, word-salad or mixed-language spam passages, such as pharma spam with stray Portuguese words or nonsensical essay-mill text. It fires weakly on scattered tokens in ordinary boilerplate like page view counts and archive notices.

Separators (commas, newlines, spaces, " in", " (") that come right after the name of an institution, department, organization or address component, marking the boundary to the next part of an affiliation or address line (e.g. "Department of X, University of Y, City, Country"). Activation is strongest after university and department names in academic author affiliations.

Diffuse, weak activation on journalistic/news-style narration, especially the words that report factual events and their context: past-tense reporting verbs (announced, released, disclosed, convicted, died, says), time expressions (in March, earlier this year, recently, yesterday) and the sentence boundaries or commas joining such factual statements. It tracks the flow of encyclopedic or news exposition rather than any single word.

A weak, diffuse feature firing on scattered tokens (often function words, verbs and connectors following an organization name) in formal institutional prose about organizations, associations, committees and teams and their activities, missions, members or initiatives. It is strongest in newsletter, press-release and 'about us' style passages, e.g. 'Membership Team / Welcome to issue…', 'we have been privileged to welcome…' and 'manages the … Trust's website'.

City names and the state/country parts that follow them in place references. It fires hardest in formal postal addresses and academic affiliation lines, on the city, its commas, the state or province abbreviation and the postal-code start, e.g. 'Santa Rosa, CA 954' or 'Columbia, Missouri'. It is weaker on cities mentioned inside ordinary sentences.

The head word (often the final subword of a name) of a noun phrase acting as the subject at the start of a new sentence or paragraph, usually a definite or anaphoric re-mention of an entity already introduced (e.g. 'The report', 'The currency', a surname, a team or country), right before its verb.

Affiliation markers right after author names in paper bylines, mostly superscript numbers, letters, or symbols (¹ ² ³, †, ‡, \textsuperscript{a}) that tie an author to an institution. Weaker activation falls on other byline separators (commas, newlines after names), the word "Affiliations", and occasionally on citation or footnote numbers.

Evaluative commentary on a person's or thing's qualities, especially reviews praising performers or creators (acting, performances, roles, skill), most active in praise like 'strong performances by its talented cast' or 'handled the vocal duties well', often on the verbs, appositive clauses ('who also starred') and punctuation that link a named person to the assessment.

Weak, diffuse activation on boilerplate web text such as site descriptions, cookie and browser notices, newsletter or subscription prompts, repository and access notices, and product blurbs. It fires on function words and generic service phrases like "to ensure you have", "for the latest updates", "with your name and password", "uses ... that" and "for further information".

Names of people or organizations serving as the source or speaker of a quotation, statement, or claim, especially surnames in speech attributions (e.g. "X said", "says X", "X added"). The name and the following reporting verb are both marked, with the strongest activation on the final part of the name.

Timestamps and metadata in forum, Q&A and comment posts: dates, times, "X years ago" and username/byline fragments. Activation is highest on the day, year and hour/minute digits of StackExchange-style signatures (e.g. "Jul 9 '14 at 18:27"). Weaker activation falls on other boilerplate such as post numbers, "email" in comment forms and line breaks after these markers.

Organization or institution names, often abbreviated, used as domain names in email addresses and URLs. The strongest cases are the part right after "@" in academic or research emails (kit, unipr, u-psud, tudelft, mit, inpe), with weaker activation on website domain parts and institution acronyms in credits.

Fires densely and broadly across whole clauses of machine-translated Chinese web-novel prose (xianxia/cultivation stories with sects, Qi, Immortal Kings, Great Emperors), strongest in narrative and explanatory clauses such as 'it was clear how strong…' or 'realize how difficult it was…'. It is especially strong where the passages are scraped or spam-injected with unrelated keywords like 'cbd gummies'. Elsewhere it gives only weak, scattered activations on ordinary function words and phrases in awkward or translated-sounding English.

Weak activation on attribution and credit text naming people or organizations: author bylines, affiliations, contact details, signature lines, credits like "produced by" or "photo credit", and spokesperson or title attributions. It fires mostly on parts of personal names (often the final subword), titles, affiliation markers (commas, numbers, asterisks) and the line breaks between them.

Long runs of dot leaders (and similar filler like underscores or ellipses) that sit between an entry title and its page number, as in tables of contents or form fields. Activation is strongest on the first leader chunk after the title and drops on later chunks. Weaker activation appears on other separators between a label and its value, such as a <td> cell before a page number or a blank line after "Leave a Reply".

Appositive or descriptive phrases that come right after a person's name and give their title, role, affiliation or other identifying detail (e.g. ", an analyst at", ", CEO of", "who is the adviser to", ", 66, of"). The comma right after the name and the role words are the strongest parts, typically in news-style quote attributions.

Sentence boundaries in scientific or technical abstract-style prose. Activation peaks on the period closing a sentence, especially the opening background or aim sentence. It continues onto the first words of the next sentence when that sentence moves into methods, data, or findings ("The study involved", "Data were from", "Methods: This was a", "We compared"). Weaker activation falls on method and reporting phrases and on parenthetical acronyms.

Institutional affiliation text, typically in author bylines of academic papers. It fires on words like University, Department of, Institute, School and College, on the commas and parentheses that separate parts of the affiliation, and on the address details that follow (city, state, postal code, P.O. Box). This holds across English, Spanish, Portuguese and French forms (Universidad/Université, Instituto, Laboratoire).

Structured metadata and boilerplate fields in web/document text (bylines, dates, publisher, codes, versions, member counts, citation fields). Activation falls on the field separators and values after labels like 'by', 'date:', 'published', 'codes:': colons, commas, spaces, date parts, names and bullets.

A diffuse, low-level feature that fires across ordinary expository or narrative prose. It peaks mainly at clause boundaries such as commas and periods and on the connective words that continue a sentence ('and then', 'which means', 'when they', 'even if'), with weaker activation on content nouns inside these running clauses. It seems to track mid-sentence continuation and discourse flow rather than any particular topic.

Speaker attribution in news-style prose: the closing quote punctuation, speech verbs (said/says/explained), and especially the speaker's name plus the appositive title or role that follows it (e.g., ", director of…", ", lead author, who…"). The strongest activations come right after a quotation ends.

Speech-attribution phrases for quoted or reported statements: verbs of saying or thinking (said, says, explained, claims, admits, added, continues) and the speaker reference attached to them (pronoun, name ending, 'according to X', interview speaker labels). Activation is strongest right after a closing quote, as in “...,” she says.

City names and other place names, especially the final token of a city, that appear in addresses and affiliation lines (institution, city, region, country), as in academic author affiliations, publisher locations or business addresses. Neighboring parts of a location string, such as university names, states or countries, activate more weakly.

Structural boundary tokens in web-scraped text, mainly sentence-final punctuation fused with newlines (".⏎⏎", "⏎⏎"). These mark where one section or block ends and a new, often unrelated one begins, such as a heading, byline, review, list item or boilerplate. Weaker activations fall on delimiters inside metadata like author lists, dates, prices, IDs and usernames (commas, parentheses, colons, bullets, quote marks). The strongest cases close a quoted testimonial before a new date or entry.

Sentence and section boundaries: end-of-sentence punctuation (periods, question marks), colons after labels, and newlines or paragraph breaks just before new content starts, plus a few sentence-opening discourse words (Nevertheless, Indeed). Activation is strongest at periods ending sentences in spammy, incoherent or keyword-stuffed text, where the next sentence switches abruptly to an unrelated topic.

Descriptions of how a product, app, service or system works or is used, especially features and user actions (you can click/choose/contact via email, will automatically…, play games on apps, prizes awarded). The weak activations are spread over the functional and procedural wording in these explanations of capabilities, interfaces and mechanisms.

Speech attribution in journalistic or quoted text. It fires on speaker names, pronouns (he, she) and verbs like said, says, adds, told or noting that sit next to quotes. It also fires on the punctuation and sentence or paragraph boundaries around attributed statements, with the strongest response to the speaker name and the attribution verb.

Words inside fixed, formulaic multiword expressions and discourse connectives (e.g. 'as a result of', 'with regards to', 'similar to', 'in fact', 'in addition', 'despite the fact that', 'keep track of', 'pertaining to', 'ought to', 'Nonetheless/Moreover/However'), especially where the next token is a highly predictable preposition or function word ('of', 'to', 'from', ','). Common in boilerplate or spun web prose. Weak activations also appear on predictable formatting fragments (e.g. 'superscript', table tags).

Final or later tokens of organization and publication names, especially news outlets, magazines, websites, universities and institutes (e.g. Post, Tribune, Slate, News, Journal, Institute, Stanford). They often come right after 'writer for', 'told', 'at' or 'of', in bylines, attributions and affiliations. Activation is strongest on news-outlet names.

Postal addresses, mostly institutional affiliation lines in academic papers. Activation is strongest on the final digits or characters of a postal or ZIP code (e.g. "21|5", "2TT", "980-857|9") and on the comma after it or after the city name. Separators and city names in the city–country sequence activate weakly. Other number strings such as phone numbers, ISBNs and coordinates fire only faintly.

Tokens forming a person's surname (and sometimes middle initials or particles), mostly the first subword pieces of multi-token, often foreign or uncommon surnames. These usually come right after a first name or initial, as in author bylines of academic papers and in news attributions.

The first token (often a word-initial fragment) of a place name, usually a city, district, street or institution name, inside an address or affiliation line in academic or business text. It fires most strongly on city names that come right after a comma, postal code or institution name.

Sentence-ending punctuation, mostly a period fused with paragraph-break newlines (".⏎⏎"), marking the end of a paragraph or sentence before new content begins. It is strongest at paragraph breaks in news/expository prose and weaker on plain mid-paragraph periods or bracketed citation endings.

Boundaries in author-affiliation and address blocks, mainly in academic paper headers. It fires most strongly on line breaks or punctuation right after a country or postal code, and on the affiliation markers (numbers, †, ‡, superscripts) that start the next entry. It also fires on the start of the next header element, such as Department, Email:, Received, Abstract or footnotes, and on email domain endings like .edu or .id.

Weak, diffuse activation on tokens that narrate how an event unfolds over time. It is strongest in sports match reports and play-by-play: goals, scores, minute marks, wrestling moves and counts. It is weaker in event schedules and agendas (breaks, sessions, time slots), weather forecasts (tonight, tomorrow, Saturday) and other sequential narration (then, began, after which), including sentence boundaries between steps.

First names or initials of people, mostly in author/contributor lists (academic papers, bylines), with the strongest activation on given names that come after the first entry in a list of several people and sit just before the surname.

Descriptions of performances, music and entertainment such as concerts, theatre, songs, singers, shows and the audience's experience of them. It fires most on the descriptive narration of a performance or its effect (e.g., 'she was convincingly angry', 'Both of these arias', 'musicians playing', 'want to hear'), with weak, diffuse activation elsewhere.

Tokens immediately following an author's surname in academic author lists and citations, most strongly "et" (as in "et al."), plus separating commas, "and", affiliation superscripts and markers, and the citation year. It fires especially after East Asian surnames (Chen, Wang, Li, Zhang).

Expository news-style prose. Activation peaks on the core clause of a sentence that introduces who did what, most often at the start of a new sentence or paragraph. Typical spans are the subject (a named person, organization or "The former couple"), the main verb, and the source-attribution phrasing that follows. Examples include "The attorney for … says in court papers", "According to a report produced by", "announced the split with" and "trimmed its … ownership in". Function words linking these elements (to, the, in, of, commas) are also marked, while scattered weak activations appear elsewhere.

A weak, diffuse feature of news-article structure. It fires mostly at boundaries between a headline or lede and the body: the period or line break ending an opening sentence (".⏎⏎"), the first word of the next paragraph, and dateline, byline or source punctuation such as "(", ":" and "|". Activation is strongest within lede sentences that report an event with place and time details ("at an event at… Tuesday night.").

Journalistic news-story prose, strongest on attribution and narrative-reporting phrases (e.g., ',” said X while attending…', 'he concluded, as reported by', 'shared:', 'Reportedly,') and clauses describing what a public figure did or is doing in celebrity, sports and news reports. Activation is weak and diffuse on other tokens.

Final subword pieces that complete a person's surname, usually an unusual multi-token one, in author lists, citations and bylines. Activation is strongest on the closing fragment of the name and sometimes carries onto the next punctuation, affiliation superscript or line break.

Function words and discourse markers in subjective, evaluative commentary (often review-style), where the writer gives an opinion, concession, or recommendation. Typical spots are stance phrases like "I highly recommend", "to be fair, it is actually", "I'm just not happy with that", hedges and modals (may, will likely, must), and contrastive or concessive connectives (but, so it, since), with peaks at the start of the judgment clause.

Fires diffusely on assorted tokens (often function words) within passages about meeting or connecting with people through media and online platforms, especially dating, matchmaking, lonely-hearts ads, dating sites and apps. It also responds more weakly to related web-service content such as social media, chat/help apps, websites and online gambling or promotional spam. Activation is strongest in explicit online-dating or matchmaking discussions.

Sentence- and segment-ending punctuation (mostly periods, also ?, commas, newlines) at clause/sentence boundaries, especially where web boilerplate, disclaimers, or promotional text finishes a statement and a new sentence or section begins.

over.name: A weak, diffuse feature with no single clear meaning. It fires mostly on the opening piece of multi-token names or unusual terms (e.g. the first fragment of a rare word, place name or software name) and on label-like tokens in structured or boilerplate text, such as citations ("et al.", "eds", PMCID), affiliations, photo credits, numbered list entries, and code or notebook markers.

Mostly weak, diffuse activations on words about errors, failures and problems. The strongest are on "error" and related terms (error messages, error handling, error reports, errors, crash, failed, alerts, rejection, misconduct, caution/emergency). The feature also fires faintly on error-reporting code and system-message contexts such as print statements and log-like text.

The last token of an operand or left-hand side expression immediately before a relational or equation operator (=, ==, >, \geq, \rightarrow, "is equal to") in math, LaTeX and code. Weaker activations occur on prose words ending a phrase before a verb.

Mostly the first element of a paired or structured value: the first number in coordinates, dimensions (A x B), scores, ratios, ranges, intervals, array indices and function arguments, especially just after an opening parenthesis/bracket or before a separator such as a comma, x, dash or colon. Strongest on numeric coordinate arguments like moveTo(0, …) and the (1.7, 0) point. Weak, sparse firings also appear on miscellaneous tokens in code and technical text.

Numbers and operands (or the spaces before them) appearing in arithmetic expressions, especially the second operand right after an operator like ×, /, *, ^, = or a comma in function arguments, as in calculations, equations, code, and table cells. A few weak activations fall on unrelated words.

Conditional and control-flow keywords, chiefly "if"/"If" opening a condition in code (if statements, for, match, cfg) and in prose ("If I...", "what if", "Check if"), plus related condition-like words such as "場合", "Where", "as soon as" and "after". Activation is strongest on code constructs (for loops, match, cfg, if blocks).

A weak, diffuse feature that fires mostly on function words, punctuation and delimiters at clause or list-item boundaries, such as semicolons, colons followed by line breaks, underscores in variable names, and newlines between dated entries. It is strongest in repetitive, templated text, like the repeated n_1, x_1, arr_1 assignments, cast lists, numbered sections and code. There it marks the point where the next parallel item or segment is about to begin.

Fires most on the word "Sort", both as a capitalized command or label ("Sort by:", "Sort code") and in "a sort of". It fires more weakly on synonyms like "kind" and "type". It also responds weakly to related ideas of classifying, separating and working things out ("separation", "clustering", "discern", "figure out", "solved"). Scattered low activations elsewhere, often on verbs, appear to be noise.

Tokens deep inside long random-looking alphanumeric strings such as hex hashes, UUIDs, API keys, encoded URL parameters and long digit runs. Activation is strongest partway through the unpredictable character sequence, especially in hex and mixed letter-digit chunks. Weaker activation appears on IDs, DOIs, postal codes, numeric data and garbled-encoding text.

Marks where a conditional clause ends and its consequence begins: the comma, 'then', colon or brace and indentation after an if/once/given condition in prose or code (if…:, else, ') {'), plus the closing word of the condition itself (e.g. 'so', 'True', 'achieved'). Strongest on code colons and newlines following if statements.

Boundary tokens (newlines, often fused with closing punctuation like '.', '?', '!', ')', '}', or stray spaces) that end one text segment, list item, or section right before an unrelated new segment, heading, or field begins. Strongest at abrupt topic/document shifts, e.g., before a new '###' heading or after a timestamp or "more" link.

A weak, diffuse feature. It fires on words about whether something exists, is present, or can be found. Typical cases are finding, seeing, searching for or locating things, and existing or no longer existing. It also covers deleting, removing or destroying things, membership checks ('if … not in', 'exists', a count of 0), and memory or persistence ('memory', 'souvenir', 'toujours', '思念'). This holds in both prose and code.

A weak, diffuse feature that is strongest in source code, especially statements that load, read, parse or convert data: variable assignments like `data = np.genfromtxt(...)`, `Image.FromStream`, `FromStr`, Deserialize and loop bodies. In prose it fires faintly on words about handling data or structures (parsing dates, loaders reading XML, temperature data reconstructed). Elsewhere activations are scattered and low.

A diffuse, mostly weak feature that fires on scattered structural tokens, mainly in code, markup and other formatted text (HTML/XML tags, code syntax, delimiters, whitespace and line breaks). It is strongest on the opening HTML list-item and anchor tag tokens (such as <li class=""><a) inside a navigation list. Activations on ordinary prose tokens are low and show no clear pattern.

Items in the middle of an enumerated or sequential list, typically after the first one or two. These are often successive numbers, letters, ordinals, months or coordinate components (y, z). Activation is strongest deep in predictable progressions like 1, 2, 3, 4 or A B C D…, and weaker for loose comma lists of related nouns such as countries, games or chemical classes.

The opening argument or parameter token right after a function or operator name, typically a merged token like "(x", "(n", or "<T" that starts the argument list in math notation (f(x), a(n), P(S)) or code (function parameters, generic type parameters). Subscripts and indices right after a symbol also fire, more weakly.

Mostly the equals sign (and sometimes other relational symbols like <) between the two sides of a math equation or assignment. It fires most strongly when an algebraic expression comes before it and a value or expression follows. Weak activations also land on separators or transition points just before an answer or value, such as score hyphens, periods ending a numeric statement, and colons.

Short numeric constants, especially small integers, that serve as operands, mostly divisors and moduli (e.g. after %, mod, "divided by", "multiple of", /=, *) in code and math. Weaker activations land on list items or values that complete an expression.

Weak, diffuse feature that fires on nouns and phrases denoting the outcome, product, or new or modified version of a process, such as "new act", "revised decision", "resulting signal", "obtained products", "generated systems", "proposed deals", "oxide product" and "simulated pressure", and on output variables like "out =". It is often triggered by a preceding modifier like new, resulting, generated, proposed, revised or obtained. Scattered low activations also appear on punctuation and code tokens.

Newline tokens (single or double) ending a line that has no closing punctuation, such as after list items, headings, titles, code statements, or lines broken mid-sentence, marking a structural line break rather than a sentence end.

Values assigned to layout, spacing, and dimension settings, especially the separator and number in key-value pairs such as CSS 'margin: 0; padding: 0', Tkinter 'padx=1, pady=1', 'labelsize=20' and 'width="100%"'. These fire most strongly. Weak, diffuse activations also appear on measurements and units (mm, ms, dimensions) and on scattered tokens in code, markup and technical text.

A weak, diffuse feature on technical or procedural prose that explains how a tool, function or method works. It peaks on phrases about mechanism and inputs, such as "uses", "combines information from", "references", "based on", "to specify", "by using placeholders", "constraints" and "criteria". It also fires faintly on scattered tokens in code, config and math snippets.

Separator tokens (equals signs, arrows, colons, question marks followed by newlines, line breaks, spaces) that sit right before an answer, result or value is given, e.g. a calculation result, conversion value, the answer after a question, or the next field in a list or table. They mark the point where the following content is expected to be predicted.

Fires most strongly on color specifications, especially RGBA tuples like (0,0,0,1), alpha channel/alpha value mentions, ARGB/RGB formats, and Color3f. Weaker, diffuse activation appears on delimiters and parameter tokens in technical, code and scientific notation, such as commas in argument lists, separators and units.

Primarily fires on code expressions that reference variables and data structures, especially array/dictionary indexing and subscripts (e.g. data['key'][, chart[me][, cout << array, (input), plus assignment and return statements. Weaker analogous activation appears on symbolic variables and subscripts in math. Activations on ordinary prose tokens are faint and scattered.

A diffuse, weakly activating feature. It fires on subword fragments and later pieces of multi-token names, technical terms and compounds, such as surnames, mid-word pieces, list items and equation terms. It is strongest when the span repeats or copies something already seen in the context, e.g. Edward Snowden, Erez Winner, Bletchley, Plaintiff/Defendant, 4x + 3x.

Double-backtick tokens (``), mostly the opening part of Markdown code fences (```) or inline code delimiters, and also LaTeX-style opening quotation marks (``). Activation is strongest at the start of a code block or quoted span. Weak activations appear on other opening delimiters such as „ and $$.

A weak, diffuse feature that fires in mostly technical or instructional text about storing, passing, embedding or protecting data and information (secrets, input, URLs, strings, keys, text fields). It picks out the words for the data item, the container or location, or the method of conveying it (e.g. "carry it on-board as", "save data using", "in brackets", "as input").

In code, the indentation whitespace and closing braces (or else/dedent lines) that come right after a block ends with return, break or pass, i.e. the dedent where nested scopes close. It fires most strongly on leading spaces/tabs before '}' and on following 'else'/'return' lines. There are weak, sporadic hits on line breaks and structural tokens in non-code text.

Nonlinear activation and transfer functions, especially in neural networks: ReLU, sigmoid, softmax, tanh, logistic, plus words like "activation", "nonlinearity", "link function" and "hidden" layers. ReLU and sigmoid tokens activate most strongly. Weaker activations occur on related math functions (hyperbolic, sinh, clipping, max(0, …)) and on generic "function" or "layer" terms.

Spreadsheet and Excel vocabulary, chiefly the words "cell", "cells" and "range" (strongest in VBA code such as .Range(" and .Cells). Weaker activations fall on related terms like formulas, fields, tables and other object or property names in code; scattered unrelated tokens fire only faintly.

Tokens that close off a formatting or separator element, often fused with a newline: the final dashes, hashes, quotes or comment markers of a divider, banner or header line (e.g. -----, ####, //, ''', -->), and line breaks after such lines. This fires mostly in code comments, markdown and tables. Weak, scattered activations also appear on stray tokens in prose.

The first word of a message string, most strongly when that message is an error, warning, or status report. This shows up in program output and code string literals (print, log, and raise calls), and in log or error lines just after a colon. The strongest cases are error-description words right after an error prefix, like "Specified driver could not be loaded", "Unrecognized", "No suitable", and "No issue". Weaker activations land on sentence-initial words of notices or list items.

Binary operators (+, -, =, ==, /, ·) in math formulas or code, usually right after a product term or closing parenthesis, e.g. xy + ..., ps-qr, f(z))/. A few weak activations land on other separator tokens such as bullets, periods and commas.

Error and failure messages, especially software, system, or network error output such as "failed", "connection refused", "error", "could not be loaded", or "too many arguments", along with error codes and the punctuation inside them. It fires weakly on nearby tokens about things breaking, being rejected, or not working.

Whitespace tokens (spaces, trailing spaces, newlines and paragraph breaks) that come right after sentence-ending punctuation and mark the boundary before a new sentence, paragraph, heading or list item.

Standalone punctuation or symbol tokens, often combined with newlines (e.g. "---", "…", ":", "/", ".", "{"), that act as separators or filler at section and document boundaries. They typically appear where one text segment ends and an unrelated one (a new heading, a scraped fragment, a code block) begins.

Variable or symbol references in math expressions and code, especially a variable appearing again after it was already used (e.g. the x in “x = 0.6x”, “2x”, “self”, array indices). It fires most strongly on single-letter variables that follow a coefficient or operator. Weaker activations fall on pronouns and determiners that refer back to an earlier subject.

A weak, diffuse feature firing on structural boundary tokens where one unit ends and a new one begins: sentence-final periods, paragraph and line breaks, stray spaces, list and line numbers, markdown and closing markup such as ** and , and code delimiters such as ```, $$ or (['. It peaks slightly in code and markup contexts, but overall reflects text-segmentation positions rather than specific meaning.

Tokens that specify or convert a data type in code, strongest on NumPy-style "dtype" keywords and ".astype" casts. Weaker activations come from other type-casting syntax ("as" casts in Rust/SQL, "::", np.uint8 / tf.float32 arguments) and the word "type" in technical documentation.

Fires mainly on live code lines that come directly after commented-out code, especially when the active line repeats or replaces the commented version, as in '#filepath2 = …' followed by 'filepath1 = …' or a '//QGridLayout' line followed by 'QVBoxLayout *layout = new …'. Activation peaks on the identifier, assignment and declaration tokens at the start of such lines. Elsewhere there are only weak, scattered activations on miscellaneous code and prose tokens.

A diffuse, weak feature that fires on words carrying an informal, conversational or expressive tone. These include interjections and discourse markers ("Oh", "Yes,", "I guess", "Just curious", "sorry,", "Naturally!"), and colloquial or idiomatic phrasing ("good stuff", "magic touch", "sped things up"). It also covers rhetorical questions and asides ("what is it?", "(again)", "Lies... Lies"). The common thread is a shift from neutral, technical text into a chatty, emotive voice, and this holds in code comments and Chinese text too.

A diffuse, low-level feature with no clear semantic theme. It fires weakly across very different contexts: prose, math/LaTeX, code, URLs and timestamps. The activating tokens tend to sit at structurally predictable points. These include word-completing subword pieces ("ounding", "isions", "iness", "ival", "ators", "oman") and formatting or connective symbols ("://", ":", " =", "-", ")", commas).

Fires on the separator or boundary token right after a person's name, in signatures, bylines, author lists and credits, where the name gives way to a title, role, affiliation, footnote marker or handle (e.g., a newline, space, dash, parenthesis or padding before 'Chief of Police', 'Secretary', 'Blogger', a department name, or '@handle'). There are some noisy formatting and punctuation hits elsewhere.

Fires on boilerplate and setup tokens in technical or structured text. The strongest activations are on code preambles such as import/package statements and their aliases ("import numpy as np", Go import blocks, \documentclass, #include).
