Weaker activations appear on declarations, config syntax, the variable-introducing "Let ..." in math, and formulaic document structure like tables of contents, academic affiliations and forum headers.

Imperative instructions or prompts aimed at a user, as in UI/form text, input() prompts, button labels and directions (enter, select, input, submit, add, press, specify, "please …"). They appear across many languages, e.g. 'Digite', '请输入', 'зарегистрируйтесь'. The strongest signal is on the verb that starts a prompt string requesting user input.

Names of data serialization/parsing formats and libraries in code (pickle, json, csv, XML, serde_json, XmlSerializer, struct, DataStream), strongest for 'pickle' and 'json' as Python import targets; weaker for other type/parse names (Integer, int.Parse).

The word "the" coming right after a question opener or task verb ("What is", "What was", "Determine", "Calculate", "Find", "Give", "Write"). It introduces the noun phrase naming the thing to be answered or computed, as in quiz, homework and FAQ questions. Activation is strongest in math and science problem prompts.

Terms for isolated software or development environments, chiefly "virtual environment", "virtualenv"/"venv" and "Python/dev environment", with weaker activation on related concepts like chroot, sandbox, dev-container, VirtualBox and requirements files. The strongest activations fall on "environment" and "env".

A diffuse, low-level feature that fires in technical prose about web development and programming, such as HTML, CSS, JavaScript, markup and rendering. It mostly lands on function words, clause boundaries and punctuation in explanatory sentences around those mentions, not on the technical terms themselves. It is strongest where the text describes writing or needing code to make a page work, e.g. 'CSS will be needed… This is some simple CSS that will' and 'code it up and'.

Words expressing ending, leaving, exiting, or going back, such as close, quit, exit, finish, halt, terminate, return/back, done, and bye. They often appear as UI or menu commands (Close, Back, Done, OK), program control (KeyboardInterrupt, break, Disconnect) or step-by-step instructions.

Fires mainly inside code function bodies, especially on statement-boundary tokens like closing parens with newline, indentation, assignment '=', and control keywords (for/if/return), strongest in routines that manipulate or convert strings (splitting, replacing, counting, printing names). It also fires weakly and sporadically on function words in prose.

Separators (newlines, indentation, colons, pipes, closing tags, bold markers) that come right after a term, parameter name or section heading in structured documentation such as API docs, parameter lists, tables, man pages and safety data sheets, just before its description or definition text starts. Activation is strongest at the gap between a label like 'issortbool' or 'xk : ndarray' and its explanation.

Delimiter and separator tokens, such as spaces, commas, pipes, ampersands, dashes, newlines, and quote-comma pairs, that sit between items in long repetitive sequences like number runs, page lists, table specs, and data arrays. Activation grows as the repeated pattern continues and becomes more predictable.

Numeric operands that come right after an arithmetic operator (especially ×/* multiplication, also +, -, /) in equations and expressions, i.e. the second or later factor or term. It fires most strongly in chained multiplications. There are weak, sporadic activations on unrelated tokens.

Separators and items inside repetitive, enumerated sequences: page-number lists (1 2 3 4 5), table header/cell tags, column indices, and delimiters (spaces, pipes, commas, dashes, &) between successive list or table entries. It is strongest on the middle elements of consecutively numbered runs and repeated HTML th/td cells.

Highly predictable continuation tokens in repetitive code structures. It is strongest on the indentation whitespace and opening tokens of a new line that repeats a previous statement pattern, e.g. print, sb.Append, transformation.append, dataGridView1.Rows[n].Cells, or HTML tags like <li>. It also fires on line-ending punctuation such as ]);⏎ and on break statements. Activation in prose is weak and diffuse, falling on ordinary function words, paragraph breaks and predictable nouns.

Tokens that complete a highly predictable, formulaic unit, such as the final word of boilerplate phrases ("Best regards", "properly cited", "Getty Images", "In conclusion", "standard output"), measurement units after numbers (lb, MB), and closing code, LaTeX or HTML elements. These often fall right before a line break or punctuation that ends the segment.

The closing bracket plus newline right after the opening tag of a structured block, usually the ">\n" ending <table> or <thead> just before <tr>. Similar tokens fire after <ul> and after LaTeX \begin{itemize}/{table}/{tabular}. Weaker activations land on the whitespace before list items. The feature marks the start of a table or list body, where row or item content is expected next.

The "for" keyword opening a loop in code, plus its opening tokens like "(" or "(int". It fires most strongly on a nested inner loop placed directly inside another loop. Weaker hits come from other iteration constructs: foreach, SelectMany, nested LaTeX sums and integrals, and "Loop over all" in prose.

Separators that follow a parameter, field or variable name and introduce its type or description, mostly in code docstrings and API docs. Typical forms are "name : type", "param:", "x -", "# comment", "// comment" and an opening parenthesis. The strongest activations are on the colon after argument names in docstring Parameters/Args sections; the argument name and type tokens around it activate more weakly. Weak activations also appear on punctuation that starts an explanatory clause in prose.

Opening tokens of markup or code syntax at the start of a new element or line, usually after indentation: HTML/XML tag openers ("<", "><" before strong, "<tr"), LaTeX backslashes before commands like item, hline, centering or toprule, Rust "#[" attributes, and bracketed list markers. These fire mostly on structural delimiters that begin nested items in structured documents.

Literal string values or search patterns, mostly in code or technical instructions: the content inside quotes or string literals (tags, keywords, file names, path fragments, displayed messages) being matched, compared, searched for, or printed, especially just after an opening quote or as a grep/startswith/replace target.

Structural tokens inside code bodies: leading indentation whitespace, braces, closing parens with newlines, semicolons and control keywords (if/else/for/match), especially in nested conditional blocks that return or set boolean flags (return true/false, flag=false). Weak activations on punctuation and list numbering in prose.

Assignment/binding operators right after a variable or identifier name, mostly " =" in code (also R's "<-", type-annotation ":", keyword args, "from" in imports, and definitions in math or plain text). It marks the point where a name is about to be given its value, type, or definition.

Verbs (and nearby particles like 'for', 'whether', 'at') for checking, testing, detecting, monitoring, searching, or analyzing something to determine its state or a condition. Activation is strongest for 'check'/'checks', especially in code comments and procedural contexts.

Assignment and equality operators ("=", "}=", "=>", ":" in lambdas) in code and math, plus the tokens right after them where the right-hand expression or value begins, such as "$", "\frac" or "(". Activation is strongest on the "=" itself. Weaker hits fall on other expression connectors and openers like commas, opening parentheses, "return", "is"/"be" before a formula, and list bullets.

Multiplication and product concepts. It fires most strongly on "product of", on "multiply… together", and on × signs or equals signs in products such as "1 × 2 × 3 =" and "Z1 Z3 = Z2 Z4". It fires more weakly on related operations and terms like ratio, divided by, *= and Cartesian product, and faintly on unrelated tokens.

Tokens immediately preceding a multi-component value such as a coordinate pair, vector, tuple, dimensions (e.g. 640x480, 2.4m by 3.6m), grid size or array index. These are mostly opening brackets or parentheses ('[(', '((', '=[', ' (', 'vec![', 'new Point'), colons or spaces right before the first number of the group. The feature anticipates an upcoming tuple or dimension list of numbers.

A weak, diffuse feature of technical, scientific, math and code text. It fires on tokens that open or sit inside a specialized notation or reference. These include citation brackets with author abbreviations (the strongest, e.g. '[YY', '[E'), LaTeX subscripts and symbols, code operators and literals, chemical formulas and nucleotide sequences, answer labels, and spaces before numbers. It occasionally fires on ordinary verbs in expository prose.

Code tokens, chiefly indentation whitespace and closing ')', '{', ');' with newline, that come just before a control-flow exit statement such as return, break, continue, raise/throw, exit or an error print. These usually sit inside if, else, except or Err branches handling errors or edge cases. Activation is highest on the indentation directly before a return, continue or break that follows an error message.

Logical conjunction operators joining conditions, mainly "and" and "&&" (sometimes "or" or an opening parenthesis) inside if/while conditionals in code. Weaker activations come from prose "and" that joins conditional clauses ("if X and Y").

Literal symbols, characters, operators and punctuation being referred to as objects in their own right (quoted operators/delimiters in code, math symbols, words naming symbols like "question mark", "semicolon", "asterisk", "minus"), with weaker activation on mentioned words and specific item nouns (card, vase).

The determiner "the"/"The" (and occasionally other subject-starting words) opening a new noun phrase, usually at the start of a sentence or clause right after a period, newline, comma or conjunction, where it refers back to something already mentioned.

Tokens that close or finish an embedded span, such as a closing quote, bracket, brace, parenthesis, abbreviation period, or end of a code/math expression. These usually sit inside a parenthetical, argument list or citation, just before the outer context resumes (often right before a closing parenthesis or other delimiter).

Binary operators and connectors sitting between two operands, mostly arithmetic signs (+, -, /, //, %, <=, \frac's }{) in math, LaTeX, and code, especially + and - after a variable or subscript. It also fires weakly on word connectors with the same role, such as 'than', 'to' and 'by'.

Python import keywords ("import", "from", occasionally "class") at the start of a line in a file's header block, firing most strongly on the second or later import line right after an earlier import. A few weak hits land on boilerplate web text such as "Leave a Reply".

Tokens right after a statement of an action or choice that begin an explanation of its purpose, reason, or function, such as "to", "so", "because", "in order to", "make sure", "This is so", "as", "used", and opening parentheses. The strongest activations are on purpose and causal connectives in technical or instructional text.

Fires on the right-hand side of math equations: equals signs, the space after them, and the value or term just past an operator. It also fires on operators, arrows (⇒, \rightarrow) and leading whitespace in formulas and code, i.e. the point where a result or next term is about to be written. Weaker activations occur in ordinary prose, on determiners or function words (a, some, these, those) that precede the next noun phrase.

Programming/markup language names used as code labels, strongest as the language tag right after a markdown code fence (```js, ```python, ```bash, ```yaml). Weaker on other language mentions like class='java', <?php, shebang/path segments (/perl, /java), and inline names such as 'Python snippet'. There are faint hits on similar metadata labels (Pages, bib, -review).

under.name: Locations and spatial descriptions: place names (cities, regions, states, countries, landmarks), street addresses, and prepositional phrases describing where something is ("in the valley", "down the block from", "to the north of"). Activation is strongest on proper geographic names and spatial-relation words inside location phrases.

Quantitative statistics and tallies, especially numbers paired with units or counted items (yards, runs, passes, homers, calories, percent, deaths), and the connectives that chain several such figures into a list ("and", commas, "for", "in", "with"). Activation peaks on sports stat lines like "38 passes for 441 yards and three touchdowns" or "92 runs in 92 balls".

Mentions of official positions, titles, and institutional bodies. It fires most strongly on government or organizational role words (Minister, Secretary, President, director, Coordinator, Ministry, Council) and the surrounding appositive or role phrases that introduce named officials or authorities. Activation is weaker for generic group or organization nouns.

The day-of-month number in a date, plus any ordinal suffix (th, nd) or a month name that follows it. Common formats include 'May 18, 2015', '28 Feb 2024' and numeric forms like 02/26/2019 or 26.01.2018. Activation is strongest when the day follows a written month name, especially one preceded by a weekday (e.g. 'Saturday, May 11'). It is weak for purely numeric dates, timestamps and non-date numbers.

Citation and reference markers: numeric tokens inside brackets/parentheses/superscripts referring to sources (e.g., [10], (29), [1]), plus final digits of years in author-year citations. Strongest on standalone bracketed reference numbers; weaker on other trailing numbers, IDs, and page markers.

Names of news outlets and media sources, firing on the final or distinguishing token of the publication's name (Times, Post, Globe, Tribune, Weekly, Variety, Reuters, AP, AFP, Media, Eurogamer). It also responds to generic media words (newspapers, press, radio) and source attribution contexts such as photo credits and 'told X'. Weak activations occur on website domain pieces and dateline line breaks.

Segments inside hierarchical names and paths, mostly in code: package, namespace, module and import paths (calculator.ast, DataLayer.Repositories, std::chrono, django.forms.models), plus URL/domain parts and file-path components. Weaker hits fall on parts of compound names, categories and titles.

Temporal expressions, mainly the tokens that open a date or time reference: prepositions and words like "in", "since", "during", "while", "past", "last", month names and "Day", plus the space or leading digits of a year or day number (e.g. "in 201", "March 16", citation years). Activation is strongest on the space just before the day number after a month name.

A diffuse, low-level feature that fires across ordinary expository or narrative prose. It peaks mainly at clause boundaries such as commas and periods and on the connective words that continue a sentence ('and then', 'which means', 'when they', 'even if'), with weaker activation on content nouns inside these running clauses. It seems to track mid-sentence continuation and discourse flow rather than any particular topic.

Pieces of web and document metadata, especially URL parts ("://", "www", domains like ".com"/".org"/".edu", path segments), which activate most strongly. Weaker activations land on DOI numbers, file paths, citation fields (journal names, vol), site navigation, headers and names of sites or shows. Overall it tracks boilerplate reference and link text rather than ordinary prose.

Street address components, especially street-type suffixes (Road, Drive, Dr., Way, Street, Lane) and the house numbers or commas that follow the street name in postal addresses. Weaker activation appears on other structured metadata such as dates, phone numbers, emails, and separators in copyright or footer lines.

Fires most strongly across spans of biblical or scriptural verse and archaic religious prose, such as quoted passages from Daniel, Luke, Psalms and Corinthians (e.g. 'thy', 'the flesh', 'Rahab and Babylon'), building up through the quoted phrase. There are weak, scattered activations on ordinary content words (verbs, nouns, adjectives) in other texts.

Terms from developmental biology and embryology, especially organismal growth, embryos and tissue or limb or wing patterning, with the strongest response to phrases like 'limb buds', 'patterning' and 'skeletal development'. Weak, scattered activations also appear on other biomedical terms and on unrelated text.

Weak, diffuse activation on words in clauses that deliver a turn or payoff after an earlier setup. These are typically contrastive or resolving phrases following a premise, such as "but it didn't help much", "but at long last… confirmed", "Well, we can!", "Now… raises another cause for concern", "the result is" and "be in vain". Activation is strongest on "but", "now", hedges like "may" and "might have been", and the key outcome nouns and verbs.

A diffuse, weak feature that peaks in historical or war-time narratives about people fleeing, being evacuated, hiding or being mobilized. Examples include escaping Hungary as tanks rolled in, the Soviet government leaving Moscow, raising a regiment in WWI, and children hidden in a safe room. It fires across the clause describing the people and their movement or refuge, such as subject pronouns, verbs like escaped, evacuated, fleeing and tasked, and destinations. Elsewhere it shows only sparse low activation on ordinary function words.

A diffuse, weakly activating feature that fires on ordinary mid-sentence tokens in factual, expository or narrative prose, mainly function words, verbs and nouns that carry a statement forward. It is strongest on reporting and predicate phrases that relay facts or claims, such as "says that", "claims that", "was included in", "has risen to" and "until". It is not tied to any specific word or topic.

A weak, diffuse feature that fires across scientific and technical expository prose, especially biology/biomedical research writing such as abstracts and papers. It activates on scattered content words, word-piece fragments and function words, peaking on explanatory claims about mechanisms or capabilities (e.g. "can", "can be", "resulted in", "which eventually").

Tokens in citation or cross-reference markup that come just before a reference number or label: \ref, \cite{ / \citep, "Ref"/"Source", opening brackets and superscript markers, the commas or spaces separating numbers in citation lists like [2,3,5], and "image" in markdown image links such as (image2). The feature fires on the scaffolding of numbered references rather than on the numbers themselves.

Connectors placed between personal names in author lists and citations, mostly "and"/"&" (also commas) right after a surname and before the next author's name. Activation is strongest in in-text academic citations such as "(Xiong and Kupski, 1999)" or "Lavidor and Ellis".

Final word of short website navigation and boilerplate UI phrases (e.g., "Continue Reading", "Scroll to Top", "Connect with us", "Skip to content", "1 min read", "Register"). These are scraped interface labels and calls to action embedded in web text, firing most strongly on "Reading" in "Continue Reading".

Fires on the word-piece ending in "-all" that precedes a suffix, mostly "crystall" (alone or the "all" after "cryst") in crystalline/crystallize/crystallization, and more weakly "metall" in metallurgy/metallizing. It fires most on scientific and materials usage.

Line breaks and trailing punctuation (e.g. ".", "!", ")", ";" followed by newlines, and occasionally markers like "###" or "<td") at a boundary where one document, section or list item ends and an unrelated one begins, typically just before a new title, headline or heading.

The word-piece "hemorrh"/"orrh" (as in hemorrhage, hemorrhagic, haemorrhage, hemorrhoid), firing most strongly in medical bleeding contexts and also on figurative uses like "hemorrhaging staff". It fires weakly on "orrh" in mycorrhizal and on related blood terms such as "hematoma" and "bleeding".

Number chunks (usually three-digit tokens like "000", "130", "700") inside the suffix of DOI identifiers. They tend to fall in the middle of the article number after the journal or year prefix, not at the start or end.

The word "clot" (blood clot, clotting, clots, including split tokens like "cl"/"ots"/"ot"), with weaker firing on related coagulation terms such as thrombus/thrombo- and scab. It is strongest in medical contexts about blood clots blocking vessels or about the clotting process.

Tokens within formal proper names of organizations and institutions, especially academic author-affiliation lines (Department/Institute/Laboratory of …, University of …, Academy of Sciences), along with nearby author names, titles, and award or agency names, often in Chinese or East Asian contexts. Activation is strongest on the connecting words and descriptive words inside long multi-word institution names.

The top-level domain prefix (mostly "org", also "com" and "io") that begins a package path right after "import" or "import static" in Java/Scala files. "org" activates most strongly, especially for third-party libraries like Spring, JUnit and Apache, while "com" is weaker, particularly for project-local packages.

Election and electoral-geography concepts, especially the US Electoral College, electoral votes, swing/key states, and election results by state or district. It responds most strongly to "Electoral College", "electoral votes", and phrases like "key states like Pennsylvania". Weaker activation appears on related political-unit words such as states, counties, borough, electorate, voters and ballot.

Spread thinly across news-style prose, mostly on attribution and sourcing language: speech or reporting verbs (said, mentioned, suggested, reportedly), "according to", source nouns (expert, sources, studies, police, professor), and the punctuation and sentence boundaries around quotes and claims.

The final digit of a DOI's publisher prefix (the "10.xxxx" registrant code), right before the slash that starts the suffix, sometimes including the slash. Weak activation on similar URL path segments such as "/embed" or "/articles".

Words about creative authorship and composing, especially writing and composing music and songs (songwriter, composer, writing music, song-writing), plus related terms for writers, playwrights, designers, and creators. Activation is strongest for music and song writing.

The name "Roger" and similar-sounding name fragments. The first name "Roger" fires most strongly, especially before a surname or initial. The surname "Rogers"/"Rodgers" and fragments like "Rog" or "ogers" fire moderately. Weaker activations appear on phonetically similar name pieces such as Peggy/Peg, Siegel/Nigel ("-igel") and Berger.

Abstract head words in formal or literary multiword phrases, especially nouns heading an "of" construction ("the point of", "the part of", "the consequences of", "the close of the year", "the number of"). It also fires on intensifying or degree modifiers (full, utmost, total, very much, precisely) and time or quantity expressions (some time, just before, at three). Activation is broad and weak, peaking on "the point" and "the part".

Website boilerplate headers for comment, answer, review or result sections (e.g. "4 thoughts on", "8 Responses to", "Leave a Reply", "0 comentarii", "1 Answer", "Results 1-1 of"). The feature fires on the word just after the count/label, usually a preposition like "on", "to" or "for" that introduces the post title, or a plural ending. It is strongest for "N thoughts on “Title”".

Function words and nouns in website navigation and boilerplate text that invites users to search, find, browse or look up information or resources (e.g. "search for", "find something about", "list of", "reviews", "archive", "websites"). The strongest activations come on the prepositions and objects in these search-and-find calls to action.

Fires on the token "embry-" and its forms (embryo, embryos, embryonic, embryology), peaking on the "embry" piece in "embryonic". The match is by spelling, so it also fires on unrelated "Embry"/"emb" fragments. Weaker activation on related early-life and developmental terms: developmental/development, neonatal, fetal, blastocysts, trimester, seedlings, larval, intrauterine.

In dates, the separator token (a space, slash, or hyphen) that comes right before the day number. It usually follows a month name or number, or a word like 'Accepted:', 'Published:', or 'on'. It is most frequent in publication, received, and accepted dates.

Words naming one of several alternative variants or forms of the same underlying entity, mostly in scientific contexts. The strongest by far is "isoforms" (especially the "iso" token). Weaker matches include isotopes, isoenzymes, isomers, splice variants, subtypes, subsets, forms, members and paralogues.

Attribution of responsibility to a named organization or person: words like "by", "of", "from", "in" that introduce a producer, sponsor, curator, editor or affiliated institution, along with the parts of the organization names themselves (agencies, offices, departments, universities, companies). Activation is strongest on attribution phrases such as "produced by", "supported in part by", "presented by" and "a study by".

The separator token (space, end of dot leader, table cell tag, or opening parenthesis) that comes right before a page number or timestamp in tables of contents, indexes, and track or timestamp listings, i.e., the gap between an entry title and its number.

Delimiters that separate entries in a list of names or similar items: commas, semicolons, newlines, ");", "),", "],", "&" and "and". They fire at the boundary right after one item and before the next, most often in author, credit, contributor or recipient lists, and also in lists of patent classification codes.

Word-internal subword pieces of biochemical terms, chiefly the fragment just before the "-ase" suffix of enzyme names (dehydro|gen|ase, re|duct|ase, oxid|ase, ester|ase, -id|ase). The strongest activation is on "gen" in "dehydrogenase". Weaker activations fall on similar mid-word chunks of other biochemical words (heter|ot|rophic, decar|box|ylation, trans|amination).

Line breaks (often double newlines) that end a document's header or metadata line, most often a date or byline, right before the title or body text starts. Weaker activations land on other header-boundary tokens like separators, closing brackets, or 'by'.

The final word or suffix that finishes the name of a biological signaling molecule, typically "factor(s)" after a descriptor (strongest in "growth factor", "tumor necrosis factor", "Transforming Growth Factor"; weaker after "transcription"), plus head nouns and endings like "protein", "hormone", "peptide", "-ase" and "-in" in protein, hormone and cytokine names.

The separator and second number in a score, tally, or ratio comparing two opposing counts (vote splits like 7-2 or five to four, game scores, win-loss records, poll results, X-to-one margins). It fires most strongly on the hyphen or "to" and the following number, especially in court and legislative vote counts. It also fires weakly on words like "unanimously" and on the space before the second count.

Tokens right before a proper name (usually a person's surname), mostly the connector " and" between two surnames ("Simon and Doctorow", "Millican and Alexander"). Also commas, closing quotes, "says", "by", "under", and line breaks that come just before a name.

The preposition "of" (sometimes "for") right after an institutional head noun such as Department, Ministry, Bureau, Institute, School or Secretary, in the formal name of an organization or office. Activation is strongest for US federal government departments (Department of Agriculture, Defense, Energy, Transportation). It is weakest in academic affiliation lines such as university departments.

Tokens that come right after a person's name, mostly a surname, especially in citations and author bylines. Typical cases are "et" in "et al.", the commas and initials in author lists, and the year digits or reference brackets that follow. It also fires on whatever follows a name in prose or headers, such as appositive commas, titles (Jr., PhD, professor), separators (|, -, —), and verbs like "said" or "explains".

Vocabulary of the American football pass rush and defensive pressure on the quarterback: sacks (strongest), blitz, pass rush, tackles for loss, defensive end, EDGE, linebacker, and names of pass rushers. It also fires weakly on 'sacked' in the sense of a city being plundered, with faint scattered activations on unrelated function words.

Author bylines and biographical blurbs, typically at the end of an article. It fires most strongly on the words right after a person's name that introduce their role or credentials ("is a", "is the", "received his", "Senior Fellow", "contributing editor"). It also fires on the author names, contact or credit lines, and line breaks in these sections.

The predicate or evaluative word that comments on a preceding subject or topic, typically right after it or after 'is/was'. It fires most strongly on passive participles saying a situation is complicated, hampered, fuelled or obscured, often followed by 'by'. It also fires on intensifying or additive transitions such as 'Adding to the drama', 'further' and 'even gloomier'. Most other hits are weak, on ordinary copulas and adjectives like 'is', 'consistent' and 'noteworthy'.

Trailing or middle digit chunks inside long identifier strings such as IDs, URLs, hashes, DOIs and HAL/project numbers. It fires on the later sub-tokens of an ID once several digits have already appeared. Activation is strongest deep inside very long numeric IDs, like blogger IDs.

Structural boundary tokens in scraped web pages, mostly newlines and punctuation-plus-newline, that separate boilerplate or header metadata (titles, bylines, dates, source tags, site descriptions) from the main body text. The strongest cases are Slashdot-style headers such as story titles, 'by user (id) on' bylines and 'writes "'.
Line breaks and punctuation, mostly double newlines, that close a header or metadata line (title, date, byline, citation, breadcrumb, section number) right before the main body text starts.

Mostly fires on website boilerplate and user-directed calls to action, such as navigation and UI labels (Read more, Previous, Articles, Reviews), sign-up and subscription prompts, cart and stock notices, and offers of help ("we've got the right solution for you", "find answers... here"). Activation peaks on the key words or phrase endings of these promotional or instructional snippets. Weaker activations land on the final words or punctuation of list-ending or sentence-ending phrases in ordinary prose.

The definite article "the" following a preposition or verb (in, into, of, to, through, across) and preceding a noun naming a physical location, body system, anatomical structure, or environment (bloodstream, brain, soil, respiratory tract, atmosphere). Activation is strongest in scientific/biomedical contexts, especially for anatomical or biological targets reached by movement or injection.

Weak, diffuse activations on function words and continuation tokens in promotional or review-style descriptions of places and businesses, especially hotels, hostels, guest houses and other venues. The strongest firing comes right after a venue is named, as the text goes on to describe what it offers or how it is experienced (e.g., 'hotel hosts', 'specializes in', 'with easy access').

Word-initial subword fragments of long medical or scientific words that are split across tokens, most often the prefix "antim" in antimicrobial. Weaker cases include "antib" (antibacterial, antibiotic, antibody), "colore" (colorectal), and the "ib", "if", "im" fragments after "ant". The token is the incomplete start of the word, before its completion.

Words naming distant or foreign places and destinations, such as countries, cities, regions, overseas or other-world locations, usually after travel or location prepositions (to, in, from). It also often fires on the word that follows them (for, when, where, a comma). There is weaker activation on broader 'elsewhere' domains like markets, industry, territory, another dimension, or a martian base.

Tokens that complete the custom organization or project name segment early in Java-style package paths (e.g. com.<org>, org.<project>) within import statements, typically the final subword of the second or third path component just before the next dot. Weak scattered activations appear on unrelated prose.

The preposition completing a source-attribution phrase, mainly "to" in "According to" and also "per" in "As per" or Dutch "volgens". It is strongest when "According to" opens a sentence and introduces a named source such as a person, organization or publication, and weaker after a lowercase mid-sentence "according".

Words about the release format, version, or edition of a media product, such as edition, version, copy, remake, re-release, HD, Blu-ray, resolution, recording, or review. Activations are weak and diffuse. They peak in product and review listing contexts like 'Review by', price lines, Blu-ray/720p, and remake.

Language about the movement and flow of air, water and other large-scale physical systems, especially weather and oceanography: winds, currents, air masses, pressure systems, ocean circulation and weather patterns, plus the verbs and prepositions saying where they move ("blow from", "extend to", "into the weekend"). Activations are strongest on meteorological terms such as "high pressure is expected to extend", "pattern", "air" and "currents". Weaker hits fall on loosely related flow and direction words in technical or scientific text.

Continuation and final tokens that complete a multi-token named entity or fixed noun phrase, most often titles of creative works (films, TV shows, songs, books) and other proper names (brands, organizations, places, characters), plus some compound nouns. Activation is strongest in lists of an actor's credits, where it falls on the title words and closing quotes.

Text right after a statement of success, popularity, fame or some other cause, marking the start of its consequence or follow-up (e.g. "became a hit, and the Fleischers went on", "gained popularity, we have decided", "has made him a hot topic"). The marked words are mostly function words and result verbs (",", "and", "has", "became", "made", "gained", "brought") that open the resulting outcome clause.
City or town names, especially their final token(s), in addresses and affiliations (academic institutions, companies, manufacturers), typically just before a comma and a state, region, or country.

Names of specific events, especially sports competitions, tournaments and races (e.g. Grand Prix, Championship, Invitational meet, Major), along with their locations and the preceding "at the" or "win at the". The strongest activations fall on event-name words and the phrase introducing where a result happened. Weaker activations occur on venues, conferences, places and punctuation around them.

Language about ratings, reviews and aggregate scores, such as review sites (Metacritic, Goodreads), star ratings, averages, vote counts, grades and awards. It fires most strongly on review‑aggregation terms ("ritic", "Reviews", "average of", "score") and on the numbers or prepositions that introduce a rating or count.

Tokens tied to livestock and farming, chiefly cattle: cow, cattle, livestock, steer/heifer, oxen, dairy, beef, pasture, grazing, ranch, farm-raised. Cattle words activate most strongly. It also fires weakly on lookalike subwords and unrelated senses ("cow" in cowardly/cowboy, "beef up", "Beefy") and on loosely related agricultural or industry words (timber, aquaculture, animal science).

Names of terrorist, jihadist, and militant groups, strongest for ISIS / Islamic State / Daesh (including name-completing subword tokens like "esh", "ab", "aida"). It fires weakly on other extremist groups, rebels, cartels and cults, and on "Republic" after "Central African" or "Islamic". It also fires on "ISIS" even when it is an unrelated name, such as a particle accelerator.

Weak, diffuse activation on historical and proper-noun tokens, peaking around conquest and medieval European history: Norman/Normandy, conquest, conquistadors, invasion, Mongols, Anglo-Saxon, Anjou, Boniface, 'de' in noble names, battles (the Somme, Manhattan). It often fires on name fragments such as surnames, places and historical figures, and sometimes on dates.

Evaluative or critical judgments of a work, product or thing, as in reviews and critiques. It fires on the words that give a verdict on quality or merit (praise, faint praise, hedged or negative assessments such as 'just barely misses classic status', 'wasn't that great', 'was okay', 'brilliant movie') and on the framing words around them ('regard as', 'by no means a', 'but it certainly'). Activation is strongest on mixed or qualified appraisals.

Biology and genetics terms for invasive, inserted or self-copying entities, most strongly mobile genetic elements such as transposons, retrotransposons, LINEs, viral elements, prophages, plasmids and insertions. Weaker activation appears on invasive species and weeds, and on things intruding into something else, such as plutons and dikes.

Words expressing replacement or succession, where one person or thing takes the place, role, or position of another. Typical forms are "replaced (by/with/in)", "replacement for", "succeeded by", "take his place", "filled" (a role or vacancy), "successor"/"predecessor" and "stand-in". Activation is strongest on "replace"/"place"/"succeeded" forms and weaker on loosely related transition words such as "until", "after" and "new".

Structural boundary tokens in news/web articles: double newlines, periods, colons, and stray spaces that separate headlines, datelines, bylines, and paragraphs. It is strongest on broadcast-media context such as "Radio", "GMT", station call letters, "By" bylines, and "produced/broadcast" credits.

The token "Carolina" (or its fragments "olina"/"inas") referring to the U.S. states North/South Carolina, firing most strongly after "North"/"South". It fires weakly on state abbreviations like "NC"/"SC", on related names (Panthers, the name Carolina), and on a few unrelated tokens.

Personal pronouns (especially "us", "you", "them") naming a group after a partitive quantifier, as in "many of us", "those of you", "all of them", "most of us". Activation peaks in these "of"-partitive constructions and is weaker for "like me", "we all", "those people".

Phrases naming the institution, department, or person that a patient, case, or request is directed to, especially clinical case-report wording such as "was admitted/referred/presented to the [emergency department / clinic / hospital]". Activation peaks on the admission verb, the following preposition and article, and the facility noun. Weaker activation appears on general recipients of a referral, contact, or commission ("called me", "commissioned us", "hired by", "to a nearby hospital").

Weak, diffuse activations on ideologically or politically charged concepts, especially groups, movements, nations and contested social and political ideas (leftism, communism, victimhood, positive discrimination, Soros, Sharia, progressive or establishment politics). These terms typically appear in opinionated or polemical commentary. The strongest hits are victim-status and identity-politics framing.

The final digit of a year in a full date, typically a dateline or header at the top of a blog post, article or archive page (e.g. "Tuesday, May 8, 201[2]"). It fires most strongly when the date begins with a weekday name. There is weak activation on spaces after titles.

middle.name: Words tied to electricity and electromagnetism, firing hardest on "electrical" and "electro-" forms (electronegative, dielectric) and somewhat on magnetic, battery power, wire and similar physics/engineering terms. It also fires weakly and diffusely on scattered technical or scientific words and on loosely related senses such as connection, charge, voting and Magn- word pieces.

Temporal-perspective words that relate a thing's state to a different point in time than the one being narrated, usually the present or a later moment. The strongest is "now", especially in "what is now" and appositive "now a ...". Weaker ones include "today", "to this day", "later", "eventual", "will become", "still", "current", "future" and "retroactively named".

Nouns (or noun modifiers in compounds) naming the functional role, purpose, use, or domain/sector of something, often following phrases like “used as a”, “as a”, “for”, or “in the”. Examples include “tool”, “laboratory”, “food source”, “investment”, “medical applications”, “drinking water”, “training aircraft”, “entertainment world”, and “side dish”.

Code annotations, attributes and decorators that modify following declarations, such as Java @Subscribe (strongest), Rust #[derive(...)], #[allow], #[test], Blade @if and mentions of decorators. Weaker activations fall on boilerplate page and document metadata labels, e.g. 'Skip to content/navigation', 'Corresponding author', 'Open Access', 'Opinion' and 'Location', plus similar header or structural tokens in code.

Words built on the root "activ-" (active, activity, activities, activate, actively, activists, inactive), plus weaker hits on related words for being lively, busy or in operation (alive, busy, restless, vibrant, running, fire up, back to life).

Boundaries between clauses, sentences or code blocks: sentence-ending periods, closing brackets/semicolons, newlines and markdown fences, plus the first word or two of the next sentence or clause (The, This, If you, When you, For). Activation is highest where a statement or code block ends and a new one begins.

Weak, diffuse activation on the start of a noun phrase serving as the object or complement of a preceding preposition or verb. Typical governing words are 'to', 'with', 'by', 'from', 'of', 'through', 'beyond', 'around' and 'meet'. Activation covers determiners and demonstratives ('the', 'this', 'that', 'its'), pronouns and the head noun or name, as in 'to the show', 'beyond this world', 'of the Danube River' and 'by Kathleen'. It is strongest right after the governing word and fades across the rest of the phrase.

The word "New" (and equivalents like "new", "Nieuwe", "新"), strongest when capitalized as the first word of a multi-word proper name, especially places (New York, New Delhi, New Hampshire, New Zealand) or titles (New Labour, New Scientist, Newbery). It fires weakly on lowercase "new", code constructors (::new), and similar name-opening words like "Los" (Angeles), "Long" (Beach), and "Young".

Tokens that mark a first item or starting position in a sequence: the index/number "1" (or 0) after Chapter, Week, Part, No., or array brackets, plus words like "first", "start of", "opening", "begun with", "prior", "elder", "front-ended", "N-terminal", "early season", "left side", "lower end". The common thread is the beginning or front end of an ordered series.

A diffuse, weakly firing feature with no single clear meaning. It mostly lands on tokens inside multi-token names and identifiers: subword pieces, product or model names, code namespaces and methods (::multipart::Form, .assertEquals), URL path segments (/node, /ch), markup fragments and abbreviations in technical or structured text. It fires most strongly on code identifiers.

A diffuse, weakly firing latent with no clear semantic trigger. It activates sparsely on scattered mid-sentence tokens, such as content nouns, verbs, numbers, punctuation and code operators. These appear mostly in expository, technical, scientific or code text, often where a clause continues or specifies details (e.g., 'is replicated', 'execution stayed, pending', '/= d;').

Words about updating or keeping current. The strongest are forms of "update" (updated, updates, Update), especially in "Last updated"/"Updated:" metadata, and "date" in "up to date". Weaker hits include related recency and newness terms such as latest, refresh, recent, upgrade, modern and advances.

Weak activations on tokens inside predictable, boilerplate web and code text: navigation links and site chrome ("Skip to main content", "Login | Register", "Connect with us", "Leave a Reply"), metadata and licensing phrases ("Open Access", "Copyright", "Last Updated", "Issue"), and code file headers ("-*- coding", "Created on", package/import lines). The marked token is typically the word that completes the stock phrase.

Places just before a name, label or identifier is given, mostly in code and technical text. It fires on words like "name", "title", "id", "class", "called", "Identifier:" and "username". It also fires on syntax that introduces a named value, such as function-call openings, string concatenations in paths, URL and DOI segments, and phone-number endings before an email address.

Section headings at the start of a document's body, mostly the first numbered heading ("1. Introduction", "I. INTRODUCTION", \section{Introduction}). The heading word and its numeral activate most strongly. Weaker activations fall on other numbered list or section starts and on page-header words such as "How", "Post" and "updated".

Separators and items inside enumerations and lists. The strongest activations are on the commas, semicolons and 'or'/'and' between items in a series (colors, elements, metals, keywords). It also fires on numbered list markers and bullets, and on sentence or paragraph breaks that lead into the next item.

Tokens that start a new structural unit in code or documents: keywords and annotations opening a definition (especially test markers like #[test], [Test], def test_, Scenario/Given/When, plus main, pub, fn, decorators), and section headings, step/item numbers, and bibliography entry fields. The strongest activations are on test attributes.

Head nouns (occasionally pronouns or word fragments) that end a noun phrase, typically preceded by a determiner or possessive (the, that, my, his, her) and referring back to an entity already established in context, e.g. "the casino", "the drug", "the former", "my advisor", "his organization". Activations are generally weak and fire on the head word that completes the phrase.

Names and nouns for political or geopolitical entities, such as empires, dynasties, republics, territories, provinces, colonies, regions and countries. These are often adjectives like "Imperial" or "colonial" or nouns like "territory", "province" or "republic" in historical or governmental contexts. The strongest activation is on colonial/territorial concepts. Activation is weak and noisy on other proper-noun fragments.

The second item in a paired or binary construction, usually the token right after "and"/"or" in phrases like "between X and Y" or "both X and Y" (e.g., young and old, transmitting and reflecting, crop and animal). Activation is strongest on the final word of that second conjunct, especially when it completes a contrast or relationship between two entities.

Language about self-perception, ego and status: people regarding themselves as superior, in charge or entitled, plus related notions of power, dominance, hierarchy, arrogance and ambition. The strongest cases are explicit attitude phrases such as "a superior attitude towards" and "see themselves as in charge." Weaker hits are scattered words about self-regard, confidence or how one thinks of oneself.

A weak, diffuse feature that fires mostly in code, HTML tables and structured text. It peaks on the token that finishes a name, identifier or field value right before a delimiter or closing element. Typical hits are closing tags such as and , the ends of variable or ID names (_USER, ATIONS, relay, Cause), and closing quotes or commas around string keys. In prose it fires on scattered nouns or punctuation that end a term or clause.

Head nouns, or the final subword of a noun, naming a technical device, instrument, component or functional unit, often an agent noun ending in -er/-or/-ator/-iter. Examples include modulator, saturator, mixer, switch, amplifier, limiter, controller, telescope and balancer. Activation is strongest on the suffix that marks the word as a device.

Abbreviated honorifics and titles placed before a person's name, such as Dr, Prof, Mr, Mrs, Ms, Sen, Rep, Gov, Gen and Lt, usually followed by a period. 'Dr' fires most strongly, especially when it introduces a named expert after verbs like 'said', 'by' or 'contact'. Weak activations also appear on other short abbreviations, such as 'St' for saint and 'Re'.

The word "artist" and its variants (artists, artiste, artistic, artistry), meaning creative practitioners such as painters, musicians or performers. Activation is strongest on the noun "artist(s)" and weaker on the adjective forms and on related creator words like author, comedian or creative.

The token "fed"/"Fed" (also "edor"/"ed" after F), whatever it means: the Federal Reserve, "fed up", Fedora, the Fed Cup, and name fragments such as Fedorov, Federico, Feddic and Fedele. Activation is highest for capitalized "Fed" as an abbreviation or the start of a name, and weaker for the verb "fed".

Legal entity suffixes that end company names, chiefly "LLC" (strongest, especially after a comma or in copyright, applicant and manufacturer lines). "GmbH" and other forms such as L.L.C., PLLC and PLLP activate more weakly.

Words or symbols that link two quantities in a rate or ratio, mostly "per" (miles per hour, cost per click). It also fires on "/", "to" (debt to EBITDA), "vs", "in", "on" (return on investment) and "Per" in identifiers like samplesPer. Activation is strongest for "per" following a measured quantity.

Line-break and line-continuation tokens that fall mid-sentence: newlines (and following comment markers like ///, *, //, or indentation) that hard-wrap a sentence before it is finished, often right after a word that needs a continuation (articles, prepositions, adjectives, 'and', 'the'). Strongest when the newline splits a grammatical phrase.

Fires at the end of a sentence's subject noun phrase (often a proper name or organization, especially in headlines and opening sentences) and on the verb or auxiliary that immediately follows it (has, is, are, warns, gives, appears to), i.e. the subject–predicate boundary.

Historical and biographical narration about scientists, inventors and notable figures, with the strongest activations on scientist names and roles, dates and attribution phrases ("discovered", "invented in 1947 by", "developed by", "was first known as") that credit a person with a discovery or achievement. Weak activations are scattered over function words in nearby scholarly or historical text.

A diffuse, weak feature with no clear topic. It fires mid-sentence on tokens that complete a predictable collocation, fixed term or multi-token word, such as "threat status", "goals of care", "anticholinergic burden", "Care Programme", "down-grade", "Ghibellines" and "emeritus". These tokens are often the head noun of a phrase or a word-final subword piece. It also fires on some function words in formulaic phrasing like "so that it is" and "want to".

Words about cost, price and money: "cost", "costs", "-cost", "cost-effective", "price", "cheaper", "inexpensive", "budget", "cash", "profit", "investment". Activation is strongest on "cost" itself, especially in "cost-effective", "reduce the cost of" and "Cost:" labels. Weaker activations come from economic or affordability language and spending idioms such as "break the bank", "bottom line" and "spend on gas".

Leading indentation whitespace (spaces/tabs) at the start of a code line that continues a block of sequential statements at the same nesting level, typically before a new statement; weaker on paragraph/line breaks between items in prose or lists.

Prepositions, articles and partitive phrases that place an item within a larger sequence, collection or whole, e.g. after ordinals or position words like first, latest, last, part, chapter, beginning or end. The strongest cases are "in a series of", "of a", "of the" and "in the".

The final token(s) of a key, parameter, attribute or field name that comes right before its assigned value. This shows up in key=value pairs (function keyword arguments, URL query parameters, XML/HTML attributes, config entries) and in 'Label: value' metadata or measurement names (e.g., 'Email Address:', 'heart rate 133'). Activation is strongest on the closing subword of compound identifiers.

Fires weakly and diffusely at points where the main text is interrupted by inserted annotation or markup, usually right after a noun or phrase. Examples include bracketed tags and footnote markers ([VIDEO], [2], [NA], [citation needed]), citations (\cite, n.), and markup or link syntax (](, <sup>, http, ][). Trademark marks ((TM), (R)), stray artifacts (IMG, \e, Email) and odd spacing also trigger it. The strongest activations are on opening brackets of such bracketed insertions.

The main verb (often a copula or auxiliary like is/are/was/has/would/can) that comes right after a long, complex subject noun phrase, especially one containing prepositional modifiers ("the X of the Y"). It marks where the subject ends and the predicate begins. It sometimes fires on a comma or "to" sitting at the same subject–predicate boundary.

Adjectives and participles describing something left in an unfinished, unresolved, unaddressed or not-yet-acted-upon state, most often un- words (unanswered, unchecked, untreated, untapped, unexplored, unborn, unknown), plus related ideas like outstanding, open problems, loose ends, missed, pent-up and undercooked.

The integer part of a decimal number, i.e. the digits just before a decimal point (prices, measurements, percentages, coordinates), especially when a similar number appeared earlier in the context. It occasionally fires on plain integers.

Anaphoric determiners that point back to something already mentioned, chiefly "said" used in the formal/legal sense of "the aforementioned" (e.g. "the said drawings", "aforesaid"), along with Chinese 该/該 ("this/the said") and "aforementioned". Activation is strongest in legal or archaic "the said X" constructions. Weaker hits come from other uses of "said/Said" (speech verb, the surname).

Words that come just before a noun for a person or group of people (trainer, team, professionals, staff, specialists, artists, users). These are mostly prepositions and determiners such as "by", "with", "of", "our", "a" and "the", plus descriptive adjectives such as "skilled", "experienced", "talented", "licensed" and "medical". The phrases often name the people doing, helping with or collaborating on an action, e.g. "guided by a local", "consultation with a licensed", "team of skilled".

Function words and verbs in descriptions of how something was made, assembled, decorated, or equipped: materials, added components, and methods (e.g., "made out of", "with a", "and added", "attached to"). Activation is strongest on crafting narratives that list added elements ("added a piece of ribbon and lace to").

The first token of a new noun phrase, usually an entity or proper name (often only the first subword fragment of a multi-token name like Qu|attara, Bay|rd, Fat|ih). It appears right after a preposition, verb, clause boundary or line break, where the entity is introduced as subject or possessor. It is frequently followed by a possessive 's or the rest of the name.

Function words and punctuation (prepositions, conjunctions, articles, commas, relative pronouns) that come right after a complete noun phrase or clause and introduce a continuation such as a modifier, appositive, prepositional phrase or list item. The activation marks the boundary where the sentence is extended beyond a finished constituent.

Concepts of legitimacy and formal recognition of status or authority: words in contexts where something or someone is acknowledged, declared, installed, elected or proclaimed (a leader, government, spouse, heir, independence), or where legitimacy is questioned (illegitimate, illegally occupied, annexation). The strongest activations are on 'legitimacy', 'acknowledge … independence' and 'installed … government'.

Tokens inside structured or list-like text such as code, config files, URLs/query strings, metadata fields, and numbered or bulleted lists. They usually begin a value or list item, coming right after a separator like ':', '=', '|', '-', or a comma. The strongest example is host/domain values in a config element (local.net|some.host.com).

Words expressing control, power, authority, or dominance over something (e.g., "control over/of", "power", "authority", "ownership", "influence over", "governed", "ruled", "reins", "King/Queen"), often including the following preposition linking to what is controlled.

Infinitive "to" (or another verb-phrase starter like auxiliary "have"/"can", or a preposition) opening a second, parallel clause after a coordinator such as "and", "or", "but" or a comma, as in "to X and to Y". The strongest cases repeat "to" after "and".

The token right before a number or identifier code begins, usually a standalone space (also "-", "{", "(", "/", "§" or a letter prefix) that separates a label, model name, section or equation reference, or "=" from the digits that follow, as in "section 2", "Apex 90", "Eq. (1)" or "\cite{7}".

Weak, diffuse activation on content in scientific and technical text, mostly molecular biology and genetics (gene regulation, transcription, DNA, binding, cells). It fires mainly on the object or verb that completes a statement about a biological process or mechanism. The strongest response is on gene-regulation terms such as "post-transcriptional gene regulation".

The subword piece "applic"/"aplic"/"lic", the stem of words like applicability, applicator, application/aplicación. It fires most strongly on " applic" when it is split from a following suffix, especially "-ability" in phrases like "wider/practical applicability of", and weakly on related forms in other languages.

Words marking something as optional or not required, peaking on "optional"/"Optional"/"Option<T>" and especially "nullable"/"@Nullable" (strongest in JPA column definitions and schema tables). Appears in code type annotations, API docs, config/schema fields, RFC 2119 boilerplate ("OPTIONAL") and prose (optional protocol, optional dependencies); occasionally fires weakly on related notions such as "None" in type unions and "non-required".

Words and phrases about naming, labeling, or terminology, i.e. how something is called, termed, described, or referred to (name, call, term, known as, named after, refer to, describe, so-called), plus the nearby words that introduce the label.

The words right after "even" (or a similar concessive or inclusive word like "though" or "including") that introduce the surprising or extreme case being emphasized. These are mostly prepositions, determiners and noun-phrase starts such as "even in the", "even amongst those" and "even the". Sometimes "even" itself is marked.

The subword token "Dul"/"dul" (and "ul" after D) beginning words like Dulbecco, Duluth, Dulles, dulcet, dulled, and Dulce. Activation is strongest on "Dulbecco" (including its "cco" piece) in cell-culture medium names. Scattered unrelated tokens fire only weakly.

Words about periodic or cyclical timing, strongest for biological clocks and circadian rhythms (e.g. 'circadian', 'body clock', 'sleep-wake cycle'). Weaker activations cover oscillations, seasonal and annual cycles, diurnal or pulsatile variation, migration and chronobiology, often on word fragments such as 'adian', 'al' or 'oscill'.

The "tom" token beginning "tomography", firing hardest after "computed" in medical imaging contexts (CT, PET, OCT). It fires more weakly on quantum tomography, on the abbreviation "CT", and on "tom" in "tombs".

Mostly scientific and technical text. The marked words name an external input, source or stimulus that acts on a system: an applied field, voltage or current, an incident or pump laser beam, light, pressure, an input signal. They tend to follow phrases such as "presence of", "applying", "subjected to" or "external". The strongest cases are applied external fields and currents.

The token that completes a proper name or multi-token named entity, mostly the final piece of an author surname, institution, publisher or place (e.g. 'University', 'Press', 'Technology', 'iedo'), often in citations, affiliations or bylines. It also fires on the closing digit of years, phone numbers and reference indices. Weaker activations land on other phrase-final nouns.

Backslashes and math delimiters ($$, \[, \() that open a LaTeX math expression. The strongest activation is on the first backslash of a command (\frac, \sum, \mathcal, \varepsilon) that follows directly after an opening delimiter, most often in display math after $$.

Mathematical and physical terms for singular or pathological behavior, where a quantity blows up, breaks down or becomes ill-defined. The strongest cases are singularity, divergence/divergent, pole, and infinity/∞. Weaker cases include discontinuity, boundary layers, convergence issues, unboundedness, shocks, jumps, zero denominators, outliers, and whether something exists.

Words expressing localized, restricted, or subset scope, i.e. something confined to a small region, part, or specific domain. The strongest cases are "local" and "focal" with their nouns (local anomaly, local color inconsistency, focal impairment). Weaker cases include "patch of", the prefixes "sub-" and "micro", "-specific", "personal", "custom" and "intracellular". Activations are generally weak and diffuse.

Words inside parenthetical, non-restrictive modifiers that interrupt a main clause: tokens just after a noun followed by a comma (appositives, 'which/who' relative clauses, participial phrases like 'used in', 'based in', 'inspired by'). Activation peaks at the start of the inserted descriptive clause (verbs, prepositions, adjectives) before the sentence returns to its main predicate.

A diffuse feature that fires on the opening words of an expository sentence that comes right after a heading, bullet label, colon or title. It mostly lands on the subject and main verb or connective that introduces the description ("is believed to", "emphasizes that", "Go to", "is assigned to", "A one deck version"). In other words, it tracks the start of the body text that explains or defines the labelled item.

Prime and apostrophe-like marks (′ ″ ’ ' ´) that follow a number, used as notation for things like nucleic-acid ends (3′/5′, often as 3′- or 5′-), inches, decades (1970′s), and arc-minutes. Activation is strongest for the 3′/5′ end notation in molecular biology and weaker for inch and minute marks.

Numbers or letters that label a document element, such as figures, tables, chapters, sections, appendices, theorems and examples. They usually follow words like "Figure", "Fig.", "Table" or "Chapter" at the start of a caption or heading. Activation is strongest for figure and table numbers that begin captions. Weaker activation appears on section numerals and on the final digit of years in citations.

Portable consumer electronic devices, most strongly mobile/cell phones, smartphones, handhelds and related wireless gadgets (iPod, PSP, DS, cameras, Bluetooth, Nokia/Blackberry). Weaker hits land on other carried or personal items and on fragments inside such terms.

Tokens within proper titles and names: words of capitalized title-like phrases for articles, books, pages, sections, products, laws or file names. They usually follow a cue such as 'see', 'read also:', 'in', 'our', or an opening quote, and the activations are weak overall.

The word "latent" (including the "ent" piece of a split "Lat-ent"), meaning hidden or dormant, in technical uses like latent variables/spaces, latent heat, and latent viral infections, plus figurative uses. The related words "latency" and "unobserved" fire only weakly.

Words marking that a statement applies jointly to several previously mentioned entities, or to what they share or how they compare. Typical cues are collective quantifiers and plural subjects with their verbs ("both", "all of these", "each with the same", "two models are", "alike", "also", "everyone else", "interchangeably"), as in "both have to do with" or "all three options would result".

Descriptions of what someone perceives, usually seen, heard, felt or smelled, in narrative scenes. It fires on the object or phenomenon perceived (a figure, a voice, a flash of light, faint streaks, tiny dots, a smell) and on the perception verbs that introduce it (spotted, saw, hear, felt). It is strongest on sudden or vague sensory encounters, like hearing a familiar voice or a figure appearing.

Head nouns that complete a modifier+noun phrase specifying a tier, scale, or domain of operation — overwhelmingly "level"/"levels" (state level, local level, species-level), also "scale", "layer", "grade", "basis", "side", "domain", "temperature", often in "at the X level/scale" constructions.

Word-initial tokens spelling "gal"/"Gal" (Gal, Gala, Gall, gallons, gal), mostly fragments that begin a longer word or proper name (Galway, Galton, Galois, Galilee, Galatasaray, galactic, gallop, gallbladder). Strongest on the bare "Gal" start of names; weaker on whole words like "gallons" and on similar G-onset fragments (Gol, Gand, aller).

Diffuse, low-strength activation on tokens within passages about investigating, searching, or solving a problem: puzzle and riddle setups, mysteries, game mechanics, and suspenseful step-by-step narrative where a character tries to find out what happens. It falls mostly on action verbs, function words, and clause-ending punctuation in these sequences.

Tokens for the word stem "numer"/"num" (number-related words such as numerical, numerous, numeracy, numerics, numerator, numerology), firing strongest on the bare "numer"/"Numer" subword piece. There are weak activations on similar-looking stems (nomin-, humer-, iteration) and on foreign equivalents (NUM, 数).

Words about founding or creating an organization, institution, place, or group: "found/founded/founding/founder(s)/co-founder/foundation". Weaker activations go to near-synonyms like "established", "opened", "formed", "institution of", and "origins". The verb uses "founded" and "found" (as in "to found") are strongest.

Words for dead bodies and the lifeless leftovers of former life or activity: corpses, bodies, human remains, skulls, bones, fossils, mummies, ruins, debris, artifacts. Related words also activate, such as dead, lying prone, asleep, ghostly figures and silhouettes, and statues. Activation is strongest on 'remains', 'body', 'corpse(s)' and 'skull(s)'.

Words within names of organizations and institutions (universities, institutes, societies, councils, companies, clubs, associations, parties, groups), mostly the head nouns such as Institute, Society, Council, Company, Club and the 'of the…' parts of multi-word institutional names. It also fires weakly on generic collective nouns like group, industry and organizations, and often appears in membership or affiliation contexts.

Discourse connectives and conjunctive adverbs that link clauses and signal contrast, consequence or addition. "however" dominates, firing most strongly when it falls mid-sentence after a comma or semicolon rather than starting a sentence. Weaker activations come from "therefore", "hence", "otherwise", "moreover" and "nonetheless", and from the final word of multiword connectives such as "in fact", "on the other hand", "of course" and "at the same time".

over.name: A weak, diffuse feature that fires on tokens in hard-to-predict, high-entropy text rather than on a particular word. Typical contexts are random alphanumeric strings, hashes, IDs, URLs, IP addresses and numeric lists or codes. It also fires on rare non-Latin scripts, garbled LaTeX, and incoherent spam or machine-generated prose.

A weak, diffuse feature that fires on structural boundary and delimiter tokens in semi-structured text: line breaks after headers, labels or metadata fields, punctuation closing a sentence or citation, colons after field names, URL pieces (".org", "://", "/io"), HTML tag closings, and code or shell prompts ("In [", "$"). These are points where one segment or field ends and the next begins.

Tokens made of several consecutive newlines (usually four or more), often fused with the preceding punctuation such as '.', ')', ';', '}' or '。'. They mark a large blank-line gap that ends one section and starts a new one, e.g. between code functions, after imports, or between paragraphs and headings. Weaker activation appears on wiki boilerplate ('this wiki') and other block boundaries.

Diffuse, weak activations on tokens in noisy, low-coherence or structured text: garbled/encoded strings, ASCII art, ID and part numbers, URL encodings, tables, list bullets, and run-together or spam text. It fires mostly on repeated or fragment tokens (numbers, single letters, symbols, bullets) where the next token is hard to predict. No clear semantic meaning.

Long runs of the same token repeated over and over, such as dashes, spaced dots, ";amp", ";\", repeated letters, or empty table cells. Activation rises the deeper it is into the repetitive run. Ordinary prose tokens get only weak activation.

Enumeration labels for list items, sub-questions, or multiple-choice options, such as letters (a, b, c, D, E), roman numerals, and numbers, along with their parentheses, periods, and preceding newlines. Activation is highest on later labels in a sequence (b, c, d) rather than the first one. Weaker activation appears on other structural formatting tokens, such as \text in \textsuperscript author affiliations, colons, and punctuation.

Non-semantic formatting and filler tokens: whitespace runs, separators, symbols, box-drawing/ASCII-art characters, table delimiters, emoticon/kaomoji pieces, mojibake, and paragraph breaks within layout-heavy or garbled text. Kaomoji and decorative symbol strings activate most strongly.

Whitespace runs and filler/separator tokens in structured or tabular text (column padding, alignment spaces, empty HTML table cells like , LaTeX & separators, underscores/dots), plus boilerplate web text such as "Sponsored" and "Jump to"; strongest for long space runs that pad columns.

Separators inside long repetitive sequences, mostly the commas between numbers in number lists and arrays, plus spaces between numbers in columns or rows and repeated filler patterns like " -", "-*" and ";\". Activation is strongest midway through a long run of items, rather than at its start or end.

A weak, diffuse feature on structural and formatting tokens. It fires most strongly on decorative comment banners and boxed headers in code: runs of # or *, "//" and "|" borders at line ends, and "<!--" openers. It also fires weakly on markup scaffolding such as HTML table tags (td, tbody, br, p), LaTeX commands, markdown fences and dividers, and line breaks between list or table items.

The first word of an instruction or question in a problem or exercise, usually an imperative verb (Find, Calculate, Determine, Write, Show) or a question word (What, How, Which). It typically comes right after the setup or given information, often in math or science homework text. Weaker activations occur on similar sentence-initial directive words in other contexts (Share, See, Assume, Consider).

Formatting and structural tokens in tables, code, and other structured text: row-ending pipes plus newlines, indentation and alignment whitespace, line breaks, and separators that mark cell, line, or column boundaries ahead of the next aligned item.

Tokens inside verbatim repeated text. The feature fires on words or phrases that recur several times in close succession (repeated lines, chants, list items, code lines, table cells, boilerplate such as "Invalid Input" or "Show more"), usually from the second or third repetition onward, as the model predicts a copy of earlier text. Activation is strongest in long, highly regular loops of identical multi-token lines.

Tokens partway through long repetitive, highly predictable sequences, such as runs of dots, dashes, symbols or separators (table-of-contents leaders, ASCII rules), table cells (LaTeX &, HTML <td>), numeric lists and grids, and IP-address segments. The latent fires on later repeats in the pattern, where the next token can be predicted from what came before. It fires weakly on occasional ordinary words in spammy or garbled text.

Structural and formatting tokens inside tabular or grid-like layouts, such as cell separators (|, &, <td>), row starts after newlines, alignment whitespace runs, and dotted or dashed filler in markdown, HTML and LaTeX tables or matrices and ASCII-art blocks. Activation is strongest at the start of a new row or line within these structures.

Punctuation, whitespace, newlines and separator tokens (commas, spaces, dashes, tags, line breaks) that act as delimiters between items, mostly in noisy, garbled, redacted, foreign-script or list-like text. Activation is strongest for commas separating repeated or masked items, such as runs of █ blocks or REDACTED.

The very first token of a document, firing most strongly when the text begins mid-stream with a bare number fragment (e.g. part of a phone number, ID, count or price like "869", "837", "051"). It fires more weakly on other opening fragments such as partial words, markdown hashes, newlines or punctuation.

Double-backtick tokens (``), mostly the opening part of Markdown code fences (```) or inline code delimiters, and also LaTeX-style opening quotation marks (``). Activation is strongest at the start of a code block or quoted span. Weak activations appear on other opening delimiters such as „ and $$.

Fires on structural or formatting tokens in highly patterned, repetitive text such as code, HTML tables, LaTeX, lists, dates and data listings. Typical hits are indentation and whitespace before list bullets or numbers, newline runs, closing tags (tr, tbody), repeated identifiers and class names, brackets, and parts of dates (month, year digits, commas). These tokens tend to repeat or continue a pattern already set up earlier in the context.

Tokens that act as separators or filler inside tabular, grid-like or column-aligned layouts. Typical cases are whitespace padding between columns, table cell tags (<td>), LaTeX alignment and spacing commands (&, \quad), dashed separator lines, and numbers or labels arranged in grids. Activation is strongest on aligned numbers and spacing in ASCII layouts and on repeated delimiter runs.

Backslash characters (\, \\, '\\') across contexts: LaTeX commands (\textsubscript, \begin, \cite), escape sequences (\n, \t), file paths, stray escaped text, and the word "slash" in "backslash"; occasionally other odd separator/escape-like tokens.

Whitespace, newlines, and structural delimiters (pipes, ampersands, backslashes, comment slashes, table cells) within spatially laid-out text such as ASCII diagrams, tables, LaTeX arrays/matrices, and figure labels. Activation is strongest on padding spaces and line breaks that align columns or box borders in multi-line 2D layouts.

Tokens that repeat an immediately preceding item in a run of identical elements, typically the third or later occurrence of a repeated number in lists, arrays, tables or sequences (e.g. "9, 9, 9", "10, 10, 10"). It also fires on repeated words, characters or HTML cells, and is strongest for repeated numbers in comma-separated lists.

Weak feature firing on boilerplate tokens near the very start of documents: the verb "are" in website navigation headers like "You are here / You are on page / You are viewing", plus code and markup preambles such as "<thead" after "<table>", "#include", and especially "DOCTYPE" (the strongest activation).

Stray whitespace tokens (a lone space, or spaces plus a newline) at line or paragraph starts after line breaks, marking a section or content shift. Whitespace-only lines in Markdown and code fire most strongly.

Trailing-space line breaks (Markdown hard-break style "  ⏎"), firing most strongly after author names, list entries and table-of-contents lines. Weaker activation on superscript/subscript characters such as affiliation markers (¹, ²) and chemical or unit subscripts, and on accented or split word fragments (faç, ô, ṣ).

Double-newline paragraph-break tokens, typically with leading whitespace or punctuation fused in, that come right after a sentence or line ends and before a new paragraph, heading or code block. Activation is strongest when a space is fused before the break (" ⏎⏎") or the break falls after a math or code line.

Weak, diffuse activation on structural or layout tokens in formatted or non-prose text, such as whitespace runs, pipes, dashes, ampersands and digits in tables, matrices and series, and code formatting. It fires most strongly on ASCII-art characters (slashes, parentheses, backslashes and spaces) inside print strings.

A sparse, weak feature that fires on structural or delimiter tokens in mixed or technical text. Its strongest hits are the period or space right after a list number ("1.", "2.", "3. "). It also fires on separators such as " /" and "<![", and on spaces between English and Chinese text. A few scattered fragments activate too, such as pieces of hex hashes, timestamp digits and occasional English words. Chinese characters themselves essentially never activate it.

Separator tokens (spaces, newlines, double newlines, ">\n" in HTML tables, pipes, dashes) placed between items of a repetitive, predictable sequence, such as numbered pagination (1 2 3 4), number or year runs, alphabet indexes, figure labels, answer options, list entries, and table rows/cells. Activation is strongest deep inside long runs of structured, enumerated content.

Tokens that end or complete a phrase which is a repeat of an earlier one in the context. Typical cases are repeated lines, list items, boilerplate and refrains (e.g. "Invalid Input", "Show more", "Monthly Budget", "lived a method", repeated numbers or units). The feature is predicting the final word of a copy. Activation is strongest in highly repetitive text and grows with the number of repetitions.

Tokens inside long runs of the same repeated character or token (dot leaders, dashes, spaces, nbsp, -*, ;\, repeated letters or symbols). Activation is strongest deep in the run, and a few sequence positions stand out as peaks. There are weak, sporadic activations on ordinary tokens, mostly prepositions like "in".

Fires weakly on segment boundaries, mostly sentence-final punctuation fused with paragraph breaks (".⏎⏎", "⏎⏎", ":⏎⏎", "...⏎⏎") where a paragraph, heading, title or list item ends and a new section or topic begins. It also fires occasionally on tokens near the very start of a document or line.
