Separator tokens such as commas, spaces, ampersands, and HTML <td> tags inside long, repetitive sequences like number lists, table rows, and coin-flip strings. Activation is strongest in the middle of a long run of repeated delimiters. Weaker activations fall on function words (and, with, that, the) in formulaic, promotional-style prose.

Separator tokens (commas, spaces, dots, newlines, <td> cells, 'x') placed between items in repetitive lists or sequences of numbers/values/words, firing most strongly when the same item is repeated many times (e.g. '50, 50, 50…').

Tokens in the last columns of grid-like, tabular, or repetitive structured text (matrices, ASCII art, tables, number grids, LaTeX arrays, repeated symbol rows), especially the last cells right before a line break or row terminator such as \\, |, or ]. It also fires weakly on the last item of repeated patterns in prose.

Whitespace/formatting tokens marking structural breaks between sections, mostly runs of multiple newlines (often with indentation or trailing punctuation) separating code blocks or paragraphs. Longer runs of blank lines, especially at the end of a document or before a new code or section header, activate most strongly. Odd or duplicated punctuation at boundaries (stray periods, quotes, commas) activates weakly.

Line-ending tokens that close a structural or delimiter element in code and markup, typically at the start of a file, such as the end of a comment banner or separator line (---⏎, **⏎, #⏎), the closing ">⏎" of an HTML or XML tag, header guards and blank lines after includes. The token marks the transition from boilerplate or formatting into the actual content. Activation is strongest at the ends of long dash or asterisk comment borders.

Delimiter and separator tokens, such as spaces, commas, pipes, ampersands, dashes, newlines, and quote-comma pairs, that sit between items in long repetitive sequences like number runs, page lists, table specs, and data arrays. Activation grows as the repeated pattern continues and becomes more predictable.

Vertical bar / pipe characters ("|", and similar box-drawing verticals like ⎢ or ║) used as separators or borders in tables, ASCII diagrams, comment boxes, matrices, and website navigation/metadata strips. Activation is strongest inside ASCII-art diagrams and grids with many aligned bars, and weaker for single inline separators.

Standalone punctuation or symbol tokens, often combined with newlines (e.g. "---", "…", ":", "/", ".", "{"), that act as separators or filler at section and document boundaries. They typically appear where one text segment ends and an unrelated one (a new heading, a scraped fragment, a code block) begins.

Tokens that repeat an immediately preceding token or short pattern. The feature fires on the second and later copies in runs of identical words, symbols, numbers, or cells, such as "H H H H", "+ + +", "Unlimited Unlimited", "agree agree", "7 7 7" and "NA NA". Activation tends to grow the longer the repetition goes on.

Fires at the very start of a document on leading boilerplate or list formatting: indentation spaces, bullet points (•) and numbering like "1.", plus the first word that follows. These are usually navigation menus, breadcrumbs and list items. It responds weakly to other opening structural markers such as runs of newlines, section commands, separator lines and stray header or menu words like "Stations".

Whitespace-only tokens (indentation spaces/tabs combined with newlines) forming blank or trailing-whitespace lines, especially between blocks of code (methods, statements) and occasionally in prose. Weak, sporadic activation on boilerplate tokens such as HTML closing tags and repeated page-template words.

A diffuse feature with no clear semantic content. It fires mostly on structural and formatting tokens, such as newlines, spaces, brackets, slashes, backslashes and punctuation. These usually sit inside markup, LaTeX, code, tables or garbled multilingual and symbol-heavy text, often at boundaries between segments. It also fires occasionally on ordinary function words like "of" or "in" in prose.

Fires weakly and broadly on tokens inside structured or templated text such as HTML table markup (especially '>⏎' after closing td/tr tags), code, markdown links, LaTeX, tables of contents with dot leaders, data listings, and headings. The activating tokens are mostly delimiters, separators or repeated elements whose position is predictable from the surrounding repetitive formatting, rather than tokens carrying particular meaning.

Tokens inside repetitive or patterned sequences: repeated numbers, symbols, separators and code lines (e.g., 30, 31, 30…; -*-*; ~~88~~88; repeated '; ' lines; 16x16x16). The token itself repeats an earlier element in the same run, and activation is strongest in highly regular, predictable repetition. Weak, scattered activation on ordinary words elsewhere.

Tokens inside repetitive, predictable runs of text, such as repeated words or phrases ("Image Image Image", "very, very", "Skip to"), repeated symbols or separator lines, and boilerplate markup like HTML table tags (, ⏎, ),
and blockquote ">⏎" lines. Activation increases the longer the same pattern keeps repeating.

Tokens inside repetitive or patterned sequences, where the next token is predictable from earlier repetition: repeated phrases ("Loading...", "Final Four", "Sacred Valley"), number runs, list separators, whitespace or newline padding, HTML table tags, and repeated characters or symbols. Activations are generally weak and scattered, strongest on spaces and numbers in counting sequences.

Whitespace-only tokens, mostly runs of several newlines (often with indentation spaces or tabs), that form blank gaps between sections of code or documents. Activation grows with the length of the run, so long stretches of consecutive blank lines fire most strongly.

under.name: Segment-boundary tokens, mostly sentence-final periods and also commas, colons and newlines, that end a clause or list item just before an abrupt shift. It fires most strongly on periods in incoherent, spun or SEO-style filler text (e.g., essay-writing spam), where the next sentence is an unrelated non-sequitur. It fires weakly on separators in lists, metadata and boilerplate.

The final digit chunk(s) of long numeric identifiers such as article, document, product, ISBN/SKU, paper, case and cable numbers, usually in metadata headers or URLs. The completing tokens of the ID string are the ones marked.

The word introducing a reference to a numbered figure in scientific/technical writing ("Fig", "Figure", "figure", "Figures"), typically after phrases like "as shown in", "see", or at sentence start before a figure number. It fires more weakly on similar references to tables or equations ("Table", the "(" in "Eq. (1)").

Pieces of math notation used as prefixes or modifiers in named mathematical objects, chiefly the "C*-" / "C^k" / "σ-" / "K-theory" type: the letter, the superscript (^, *, ast, ∞), and the trailing "$-" hyphen that joins the symbol to a noun such as algebra or diffeomorphism. Activation is strongest on the "*$-" / "ast$-" in "C*-algebra". Weak scattered hits fall on other symbol fragments, numbers in compounds ("1-form", "NG9-1-1") and punctuation.

The word "Astronomy" (or "astronomy"), firing most strongly in academic department names such as "Department of Physics and Astronomy" in author affiliations. It also fires on other uses like "National Radio Astronomy Observatory" and the journal "Astronomy and Astrophysics." Weak activations occur on the second discipline in other compound department names (e.g., "Biochemistry," "Statistics," "Aerospace").

Trailing or middle digit chunks inside long identifier strings such as IDs, URLs, hashes, DOIs and HAL/project numbers. It fires on the later sub-tokens of an ID once several digits have already appeared. Activation is strongest deep inside very long numeric IDs, like blogger IDs.

The ".slf" token in Java logging package paths (org.slf4j, lombok.extern.slf4j), especially in import statements. Related logging-package tokens like ".log" in org.apache.log4j get weak activation. Other tokens only fire faintly.

The word "histone", with activation peaking on the "one"/"ones" piece that completes it ("hist" weaker). Histone names such as H3, H4, H2B and H2AX, and nucleosomes, also activate moderately in chromatin and epigenetics contexts. Other protein words fire only weakly.

The first token right after a source file's package or namespace declaration, which opens the file body. In Java this is usually "import" (strongest), but can be "public", "/**", or the semicolon-plus-newlines that end the package line. In C# it is the newline or "{" after the namespace name. Weak activation also appears on "text" in "Sample/Example text" headers that mark where a document body begins.

In academic paper author lists, the token right after an author's name that starts the affiliation marker: LaTeX superscript openers ("cript{", "(^{", "^"), opening parentheses, spaces, asterisks, or commas just before affiliation numbers/letters. Plain Unicode superscript digits and symbols (¹, †, ‡) get little or no activation.

Boilerplate and metadata in scraped web pages, such as forum, Q&A, freelance and research-database pages. The strongest tokens are counts that come right before or after labels like "freelancers are bidding", "comments", "views", "Citations" or "results". Other hits are UI and template fragments, such as "peer-review", "improve this question", "Reply to" and "further replies". Some are line breaks or spaces in these templates, and the highest are pieces of blogger.com email or ID strings.

A diffuse, low-level feature that fires most strongly and broadly across low-quality, SEO-style or machine-spun web text: promotional and advice copy about dumpsters, casinos and gambling, online therapy, antivirus software and marketing tools, often with awkward synonym substitutions and garbled grammar (e.g., "meet up with their arrangement commitments", "method or significant dumpster"). In these passages it covers long runs of ordinary words, especially second-person "you/your" phrasing. Elsewhere it gives only weak, scattered activations on isolated function words and punctuation in otherwise normal text.

Line breaks, bullets, spaces and closing punctuation that separate fields in boilerplate or structured web and document text, such as metadata, HAL IDs, radio player widgets, bid listings, HTML tables and citation footers. Activation peaks at the newline that ends one metadata item and comes right before the next item.

Scientific and taxonomic descriptive prose, mainly species and taxon descriptions in biology and paleontology (Latin genus and species names, family suffixes like -idae, author/year citations, statements of distribution, habitat and morphology). Activation lands on the function words, punctuation and name fragments inside these passages and is strongest in dense species-description text. Weak, scattered activation also appears on general academic and technical writing.

The ".beans" token in Java package paths, overwhelmingly in Spring imports like "org.springframework.beans.factory.annotation.Autowired". It fires much more weakly on the singular ".bean" in other package names, and only sporadically elsewhere.

Spam/SEO keyword phrases abruptly spliced into unrelated prose, e.g. product or search queries like drug names, CBD gummies, casino bonuses, forex, shoes, 'essay on…', 'near me', 'where to buy'. The strongest activations fall on the start and core words of the injected keyword string where it breaks the surrounding sentence.

The token "McC" opening a Scottish/Irish surname (McCarthy, McCain, McCloy, McCullough), activating most when it follows a first name or initial in a person's name. All-caps "MCC", lowercase "mcc", and longer pieces like "McCorm" activate weakly.

Later sub-segments of dotted package or namespace names in code declarations (Java package, C# namespace/using, Python import, include paths), especially the final descriptive module name such as .models, .service, .adapters or .view. Activation grows toward the end of the qualified name and fades after it. Only weak, scattered activation appears outside code.

Separators between parts of postal or affiliation addresses (commas, newlines, the spaces after them, and country-code prefixes like "N-" or "CZ-"). Activation is strongest at the separator that comes right after a street address or PO box, just before the postal code.

Boilerplate and metadata in academic repository or web pages: newline breaks (often double) after URLs, IDs, dates and citation fields, separating sections such as "Submitted on", rights, permissions and citation info. The strongest activation is "contact" in the repository phrase "For more information, please contact ...", along with the email's ".edu".

The words "citation" and "cite" (sometimes split as C+itation) in repository and publication front-matter boilerplate, such as "Citation for published version" and "To cite this version". Activation is strongest for "Recommended Citation", the standard header on institutional repository pages. Related boilerplate words (version, APA, Posts, Content, bib) activate weakly.

Affiliation markers placed right after author names in academic paper bylines: superscript numbers, letters, Roman numerals, or symbols (*, †, ⋆) that point to institutional affiliations. Activation is strongest for the first affiliation marker (especially "1"/"¹"/"a") and when the same marker repeats across several authors, and weaker for later or secondary indices.
The parameter name "savedInstanceState" following "Bundle" in Android Java lifecycle method signatures (onCreate, onCreateView, onCreateDialog). Other weak activations are incidental.

Separators and connective words inside boilerplate web and repository text, such as headers, footers, metadata labels and attribution lines ("published by", "brought to you by", "Part of", "downloaded from", "General rights", "Server:"). Activation falls on the newline, colon or preposition right after a label or stock phrase, just before its value or the next section. It is strongest on "by" in attribution lines like "open access by".

Boundaries in SEO spam and keyword-stuffed web text (gambling, pills, essay-writing, downloads, link farms). It fires on punctuation, line breaks, commas between keyword phrases, and tokens like " https", " online", " download", " visit", and " link", right where a junk keyword string or inserted URL begins or ends.

The "import" keyword at the start of Java import statements, mainly in the later lines of an existing import block, where it follows earlier imports, often ones that share the same package prefix. One weak exception is "to" in English prose.

The ".annotation" (or ".annotations") package segment in Java import statements. Activation is strongest in Android/androidx/javax imports of nullability annotations (NonNull, Nullable) and weakest in Spring imports (beans.factory, web.bind). Other tokens fire only sporadically and weakly.

Spam/SEO keyword phrases dropped into otherwise unrelated or machine-spun text, such as product or search-query strings (gummies, male enhancement, drug prices, loans, court records, thesis titles) that break the sentence's flow. Activation is highest on the inserted commercial keywords, especially pharmaceutical, cannabis and enhancement terms.

Subdomain name pieces in URLs of academic institutional repositories, strongest on "commons" in "digitalcommons" (e.g. after "Follow this and additional works at:"). Weaker on related repository names like scholarworks, escholarship, dspace, hdl.handle, eprints and repository, plus the word "works" in that boilerplate phrase.

Fires weakly and diffusely on ordinary words inside direct quotations and reported speech, such as interview remarks ending in “,” he said. Activation tends to grow over longer spans of quoted spoken language, especially conversational or opinion-giving phrasing. Some activations appear outside quotes but are weak and scattered.

Affiliation markers placed right after author names in academic paper bylines: superscript numbers, letters, or symbols (1, ¹, a, †, *), including LaTeX \textsuperscript arguments. The first affiliation marker ("1"/"¹"/"a") activates most strongly, while secondary markers (2, ‡) and separating commas activate weakly.

Page numbers in tables of contents, together with the dot leaders, spaces, or HTML table-cell tags (<td>, </tr>) just before them that separate section titles from their page references. The numbers themselves activate most strongly, especially when the same number repeats on consecutive entries. Line breaks after TOC entries activate weakly.
The name "Wilson" in any context: surnames of people, citations, places, institutions, and named concepts. Similar names such as "Watson" and the "son" ending of names activate only weakly.

Tokens that close a sentence or heading and start a paragraph break, mostly a period (sometimes "?") merged with a double newline, or a bare double newline after a title. They are strongest in low-quality, SEO-style web text where the next paragraph changes topic.

Long runs of dot leaders (and similar filler like underscores or ellipses) that sit between an entry title and its page number, as in tables of contents or form fields. Activation is strongest on the first leader chunk after the title and drops on later chunks. Weaker activation appears on other separators between a label and its value, such as a <td> cell before a page number or a blank line after "Leave a Reply".

Website metadata and labeling boilerplate, mainly the tagging of posts. It fires most strongly on "ged" in "Tagged", especially in "Posts Tagged" archive headers. It fires weakly on "Tags:", "tagged", "Tagged as/with", "Filed Under", "Posts by" and "archive for", which introduce the category, tag or author labels of a blog or forum page.

The Java unbounded wildcard generic token "<?>" (and " ?>"), as in Class<?>, AdapterView<?>, List<?>. It fires most strongly on AdapterView<?> in onItemClick callbacks. Other activations on ordinary prose tokens are negligible.

Separators and numeric parts inside bibliographic and citation identifiers (DOIs, journal volume/issue/page fields, URL paths, ISBN/ORCID/phone numbers). It fires on the punctuation and digits that delimit volume and issue numbers, firing hardest on the hyphen-number-hyphen segment within BMC-style DOIs (e.g. 1471-2350-11-77) and on issue-number labels.

Final token of a username or person's name in forum, comment and email bylines (e.g., 'Jeff Newmiller wrote', 'posted by'), usually a word-piece completing a surname or handle just before post metadata. It also fires weakly on the leading space of bulleted list items after a colon and on line breaks following a byline.

The Android method name "findViewById" in Java code, usually after a cast like (Button) or after a view object with a dot, e.g. "= (TextView) findViewById(R.id...)". Weak, scattered activations show up on spacing and boilerplate tokens in templated web text.

Fires on function words and verbs inside stock, formulaic phrasing typical of news writing, especially sports journalism. Examples include "held on to the one-goal lead to seal", "has been hard hit by a", "rules out knee-jerk", "coming into this fixture with some happy memories of" and "continue to dominate". These are predictable collocations and connective words (prepositions, articles, auxiliaries) within clichéd narrative expressions, rather than any specific content word.

Sentence-ending punctuation (mostly periods, sometimes with newlines, colons, ?/!) at abrupt boundaries in incoherent, spammy or machine-generated text, where the next sentence is unrelated to the previous one. Activation is strongest after citation-like fragments (years, page numbers, journal references) that are followed by an unrelated topic.

Tokens that begin a metadata or key–value field line in structured or boilerplate text, typically right after a line break. It fires most strongly on "ms" in Microsoft-docs front-matter keys (ms.date, ms.topic, ms.author). Weaker activations come from other field labels and prefixes such as "Document Version", "Molecular Weight" and "Job Type", page boilerplate, and the "ms" unit.

The ".support" package segment in code import paths, strongest in Java "import android.support..." (AppCompat, annotation, v4/v7 libraries) and weaker in other libraries (Spring, Selenium, Elasticsearch). Other package segments after a dot (.validation, .context, .Security) fire only faintly.

Tokens inside institutional affiliation and address strings, typically from academic paper author headers. The strongest activations fall on the commas, connectors ("of", "and") and words like "University", "Department" and "Centre" that join nested units (lab, department, university, city). Weaker activation appears on similar organization-name text in prose.

An opening parenthesis placed right after a Latin scientific (binomial/genus) name. It typically introduces the naming authority (e.g. "(L.)", "(Greene)", "(Linnaeus, 1758)") or a higher taxon such as order or family (e.g. "(Coleoptera: ...)"). Activation is strongest when an author citation follows, including after "Species Authority:".

Highly predictable tokens inside fixed, boilerplate sequences, mostly in code: "ServletException" after "throws" in Java servlet methods, ".openapi" in package paths like com.intellij.openapi, and ".protocol" in location.protocol or web3j.protocol. It also fires on "eiusmod" in Lorem ipsum placeholder text. Activation is strongest where the token is nearly certain from context.

The "/wp" path segment (WordPress) in URLs and file paths, usually right after a domain or directory and before "-content", "-includes" or "-json". Weaker on standalone "wp"/"WP" tokens (e.g., "wpb-js-composer" CSS classes) and other URL path segments like "/media", "/node" and "/product".

Final numeric digits inside bibliographic and identifier strings: DOIs, astronomy bibcodes (e.g., 2022MNRAS.511..829H), patent dates, call numbers. Activation is strongest on the page/article number just before a closing author-initial letter in bibcode-style citations, and weak on other trailing digits within such codes.

The first digit chunk of an article, page or grant ID number in citations, DOIs and funding notes, usually right after a volume number, period or dash. It fires most strongly on Physical Review / APS-style article numbers such as PhysRevB.94.245… or "Phys. Rev. Lett. 126, 045…", and fires weakly on page ranges and grant numbers.

over.name: A weak, diffuse feature that fires on tokens in hard-to-predict, high-entropy text rather than on a particular word. Typical contexts are random alphanumeric strings, hashes, IDs, URLs, IP addresses and numeric lists or codes. It also fires on rare non-Latin scripts, garbled LaTeX, and incoherent spam or machine-generated prose.

A weak, diffuse feature that fires on structural boundary and delimiter tokens in semi-structured text: line breaks after headers, labels or metadata fields, punctuation closing a sentence or citation, colons after field names, URL pieces (".org", "://", "/io"), HTML tag closings, and code or shell prompts ("In [", "$"). These are points where one segment or field ends and the next begins.

Tokens made of several consecutive newlines (usually four or more), often fused with the preceding punctuation such as '.', ')', ';', '}' or '。'. They mark a large blank-line gap that ends one section and starts a new one, e.g. between code functions, after imports, or between paragraphs and headings. Weaker activation appears on wiki boilerplate ('this wiki') and other block boundaries.

Diffuse, weak activations on tokens in noisy, low-coherence or structured text: garbled/encoded strings, ASCII art, ID and part numbers, URL encodings, tables, list bullets, and run-together or spam text. It fires mostly on repeated or fragment tokens (numbers, single letters, symbols, bullets) where the next token is hard to predict. No clear semantic meaning.

Long runs of the same token repeated over and over, such as dashes, spaced dots, ";amp", ";\", repeated letters, or empty table cells. Activation rises the deeper it is into the repetitive run. Ordinary prose tokens get only weak activation.

Enumeration labels for list items, sub-questions, or multiple-choice options, such as letters (a, b, c, D, E), roman numerals, and numbers, along with their parentheses, periods, and preceding newlines. Activation is highest on later labels in a sequence (b, c, d) rather than the first one. Weaker activation appears on other structural formatting tokens, such as \text in \textsuperscript author affiliations, colons, and punctuation.

Non-semantic formatting and filler tokens: whitespace runs, separators, symbols, box-drawing/ASCII-art characters, table delimiters, emoticon/kaomoji pieces, mojibake, and paragraph breaks within layout-heavy or garbled text. Kaomoji and decorative symbol strings activate most strongly.

Whitespace runs and filler/separator tokens in structured or tabular text (column padding, alignment spaces, empty HTML table cells like , LaTeX & separators, underscores/dots), plus boilerplate web text such as "Sponsored" and "Jump to"; strongest for long space runs that pad columns.

Separators inside long repetitive sequences, mostly the commas between numbers in number lists and arrays, plus spaces between numbers in columns or rows and repeated filler patterns like " -", "-*" and ";\". Activation is strongest midway through a long run of items, rather than at its start or end.

A weak, diffuse feature on structural and formatting tokens. It fires most strongly on decorative comment banners and boxed headers in code: runs of # or *, "//" and "|" borders at line ends, and "<!--" openers. It also fires weakly on markup scaffolding such as HTML table tags (td, tbody, br, p), LaTeX commands, markdown fences and dividers, and line breaks between list or table items.

The first word of an instruction or question in a problem or exercise, usually an imperative verb (Find, Calculate, Determine, Write, Show) or a question word (What, How, Which). It typically comes right after the setup or given information, often in math or science homework text. Weaker activations occur on similar sentence-initial directive words in other contexts (Share, See, Assume, Consider).

Formatting and structural tokens in tables, code, and other structured text: row-ending pipes plus newlines, indentation and alignment whitespace, line breaks, and separators that mark cell, line, or column boundaries ahead of the next aligned item.

Tokens inside verbatim repeated text. The feature fires on words or phrases that recur several times in close succession (repeated lines, chants, list items, code lines, table cells, boilerplate such as "Invalid Input" or "Show more"), usually from the second or third repetition onward, as the model predicts a copy of earlier text. Activation is strongest in long, highly regular loops of identical multi-token lines.

Tokens partway through long repetitive, highly predictable sequences, such as runs of dots, dashes, symbols or separators (table-of-contents leaders, ASCII rules), table cells (LaTeX &, HTML <td>), numeric lists and grids, and IP-address segments. The latent fires on later repeats in the pattern, where the next token can be predicted from what came before. It fires weakly on occasional ordinary words in spammy or garbled text.

Structural and formatting tokens inside tabular or grid-like layouts, such as cell separators (|, &, <td>), row starts after newlines, alignment whitespace runs, and dotted or dashed filler in markdown, HTML and LaTeX tables or matrices and ASCII-art blocks. Activation is strongest at the start of a new row or line within these structures.

Punctuation, whitespace, newlines and separator tokens (commas, spaces, dashes, tags, line breaks) that act as delimiters between items, mostly in noisy, garbled, redacted, foreign-script or list-like text. Activation is strongest for commas separating repeated or masked items, such as runs of █ blocks or REDACTED.

The very first token of a document, firing most strongly when the text begins mid-stream with a bare number fragment (e.g. part of a phone number, ID, count or price like "869", "837", "051"). It fires more weakly on other opening fragments such as partial words, markdown hashes, newlines or punctuation.

Double-backtick tokens (``), mostly the opening part of Markdown code fences (```) or inline code delimiters, and also LaTeX-style opening quotation marks (``). Activation is strongest at the start of a code block or quoted span. Weak activations appear on other opening delimiters such as „ and $$.

Fires on structural or formatting tokens in highly patterned, repetitive text such as code, HTML tables, LaTeX, lists, dates and data listings. Typical hits are indentation and whitespace before list bullets or numbers, newline runs, closing tags (tr, tbody), repeated identifiers and class names, brackets, and parts of dates (month, year digits, commas). These tokens tend to repeat or continue a pattern already set up earlier in the context.

Tokens that act as separators or filler inside tabular, grid-like or column-aligned layouts. Typical cases are whitespace padding between columns, table cell tags (<td>), LaTeX alignment and spacing commands (&, \quad), dashed separator lines, and numbers or labels arranged in grids. Activation is strongest on aligned numbers and spacing in ASCII layouts and on repeated delimiter runs.

Backslash characters (\, \\, '\\') across contexts: LaTeX commands (\textsubscript, \begin, \cite), escape sequences (\n, \t), file paths, stray escaped text, and the word "slash" in "backslash"; occasionally other odd separator/escape-like tokens.

Whitespace, newlines, and structural delimiters (pipes, ampersands, backslashes, comment slashes, table cells) within spatially laid-out text such as ASCII diagrams, tables, LaTeX arrays/matrices, and figure labels. Activation is strongest on padding spaces and line breaks that align columns or box borders in multi-line 2D layouts.

Tokens that repeat an immediately preceding item in a run of identical elements, typically the third or later occurrence of a repeated number in lists, arrays, tables or sequences (e.g. "9, 9, 9", "10, 10, 10"). It also fires on repeated words, characters or HTML cells, and is strongest for repeated numbers in comma-separated lists.

Weak feature firing on boilerplate tokens near the very start of documents: the verb "are" in website navigation headers like "You are here / You are on page / You are viewing", plus code and markup preambles such as "<thead" after "<table>", "#include", and especially "DOCTYPE" (the strongest activation).

Stray whitespace tokens (a lone space, or spaces plus a newline) at line or paragraph starts after line breaks, marking a section or content shift. Whitespace-only lines in Markdown and code fire most strongly.

Trailing-space line breaks (Markdown hard-break style "  ⏎"), firing most strongly after author names, list entries and table-of-contents lines. Weaker activation on superscript/subscript characters such as affiliation markers (¹, ²) and chemical or unit subscripts, and on accented or split word fragments (faç, ô, ṣ).

Double-newline paragraph-break tokens, typically with leading whitespace or punctuation fused in, that come right after a sentence or line ends and before a new paragraph, heading or code block. Activation is strongest when a space is fused before the break (" ⏎⏎") or the break falls after a math or code line.

Weak, diffuse activation on structural or layout tokens in formatted or non-prose text, such as whitespace runs, pipes, dashes, ampersands and digits in tables, matrices and series, and code formatting. It fires most strongly on ASCII-art characters (slashes, parentheses, backslashes and spaces) inside print strings.

A sparse, weak feature that fires on structural or delimiter tokens in mixed or technical text. Its strongest hits are the period or space right after a list number ("1.", "2.", "3. "). It also fires on separators such as " /" and "<![", and on spaces between English and Chinese text. A few scattered fragments activate too, such as pieces of hex hashes, timestamp digits and occasional English words. Chinese characters themselves essentially never activate it.

Separator tokens (spaces, newlines, double newlines, ">\n" in HTML tables, pipes, dashes) placed between items of a repetitive, predictable sequence, such as numbered pagination (1 2 3 4), number or year runs, alphabet indexes, figure labels, answer options, list entries, and table rows/cells. Activation is strongest deep inside long runs of structured, enumerated content.

Tokens that end or complete a phrase which is a repeat of an earlier one in the context. Typical cases are repeated lines, list items, boilerplate and refrains (e.g. "Invalid Input", "Show more", "Monthly Budget", "lived a method", repeated numbers or units). The feature is predicting the final word of a copy. Activation is strongest in highly repetitive text and grows with the number of repetitions.

Tokens inside long runs of the same repeated character or token (dot leaders, dashes, spaces, nbsp, -*, ;\, repeated letters or symbols). Activation is strongest deep in the run, and a few sequence positions stand out as peaks. There are weak, sporadic activations on ordinary tokens, mostly prepositions like "in".

Fires weakly on segment boundaries, mostly sentence-final punctuation fused with paragraph breaks (".⏎⏎", "⏎⏎", ":⏎⏎", "...⏎⏎") where a paragraph, heading, title or list item ends and a new section or topic begins. It also fires occasionally on tokens near the very start of a document or line.

Separator tokens such as commas, spaces, ampersands, and HTML <td> tags inside long, repetitive sequences like number lists, table rows, and coin-flip strings. Activation is strongest in the middle of a long run of repeated delimiters. Weaker activations fall on function words (and, with, that, the) in formulaic, promotional-style prose.

Separator tokens (commas, spaces, dots, newlines, <td> cells, 'x') placed between items in repetitive lists or sequences of numbers/values/words, firing most strongly when the same item is repeated many times (e.g. '50, 50, 50…').

Tokens in the last columns of grid-like, tabular, or repetitive structured text (matrices, ASCII art, tables, number grids, LaTeX arrays, repeated symbol rows), especially the last cells right before a line break or row terminator such as \\, |, or ]. It also fires weakly on the last item of repeated patterns in prose.

Whitespace/formatting tokens marking structural breaks between sections, mostly runs of multiple newlines (often with indentation or trailing punctuation) separating code blocks or paragraphs. Longer runs of blank lines, especially at the end of a document or before a new code or section header, activate most strongly. Odd or duplicated punctuation at boundaries (stray periods, quotes, commas) activates weakly.

Line-ending tokens that close a structural or delimiter element in code and markup, typically at the start of a file, such as the end of a comment banner or separator line (---⏎, **⏎, #⏎), the closing ">⏎" of an HTML or XML tag, header guards and blank lines after includes. The token marks the transition from boilerplate or formatting into the actual content. Activation is strongest at the ends of long dash or asterisk comment borders.

Delimiter and separator tokens, such as spaces, commas, pipes, ampersands, dashes, newlines, and quote-comma pairs, that sit between items in long repetitive sequences like number runs, page lists, table specs, and data arrays. Activation grows as the repeated pattern continues and becomes more predictable.

Vertical bar / pipe characters ("|", and similar box-drawing verticals like ⎢ or ║) used as separators or borders in tables, ASCII diagrams, comment boxes, matrices, and website navigation/metadata strips. Activation is strongest inside ASCII-art diagrams and grids with many aligned bars, and weaker for single inline separators.

Standalone punctuation or symbol tokens, often combined with newlines (e.g. "---", "…", ":", "/", ".", "{"), that act as separators or filler at section and document boundaries. They typically appear where one text segment ends and an unrelated one (a new heading, a scraped fragment, a code block) begins.

Tokens that repeat an immediately preceding token or short pattern. The feature fires on the second and later copies in runs of identical words, symbols, numbers, or cells, such as "H H H H", "+ + +", "Unlimited Unlimited", "agree agree", "7 7 7" and "NA NA". Activation tends to grow the longer the repetition goes on.

Fires at the very start of a document on leading boilerplate or list formatting: indentation spaces, bullet points (•) and numbering like "1.", plus the first word that follows. These are usually navigation menus, breadcrumbs and list items. It responds weakly to other opening structural markers such as runs of newlines, section commands, separator lines and stray header or menu words like "Stations".

Whitespace-only tokens (indentation spaces/tabs combined with newlines) forming blank or trailing-whitespace lines, especially between blocks of code (methods, statements) and occasionally in prose. Weak, sporadic activation on boilerplate tokens such as HTML closing tags and repeated page-template words.

A diffuse feature with no clear semantic content. It fires mostly on structural and formatting tokens, such as newlines, spaces, brackets, slashes, backslashes and punctuation. These usually sit inside markup, LaTeX, code, tables or garbled multilingual and symbol-heavy text, often at boundaries between segments. It also fires occasionally on ordinary function words like "of" or "in" in prose.

Fires weakly and broadly on tokens inside structured or templated text such as HTML table markup (especially '>⏎' after closing td/tr tags), code, markdown links, LaTeX, tables of contents with dot leaders, data listings, and headings. The activating tokens are mostly delimiters, separators or repeated elements whose position is predictable from the surrounding repetitive formatting, rather than tokens carrying particular meaning.

Tokens inside repetitive or patterned sequences: repeated numbers, symbols, separators and code lines (e.g., 30, 31, 30…; -*-*; ~~88~~88; repeated '; ' lines; 16x16x16). The token itself repeats an earlier element in the same run, and activation is strongest in highly regular, predictable repetition. Weak, scattered activation on ordinary words elsewhere.

Tokens inside repetitive, predictable runs of text, such as repeated words or phrases ("Image Image Image", "very, very", "Skip to"), repeated symbols or separator lines, and boilerplate markup like HTML table tags (, ⏎, ),
and blockquote ">⏎" lines. Activation increases the longer the same pattern keeps repeating.

Tokens inside repetitive or patterned sequences, where the next token is predictable from earlier repetition: repeated phrases ("Loading...", "Final Four", "Sacred Valley"), number runs, list separators, whitespace or newline padding, HTML table tags, and repeated characters or symbols. Activations are generally weak and scattered, strongest on spaces and numbers in counting sequences.

Whitespace-only tokens, mostly runs of several newlines (often with indentation spaces or tabs), that form blank gaps between sections of code or documents. Activation grows with the length of the run, so long stretches of consecutive blank lines fire most strongly.

under.name: Names of academic and research institutional units in author affiliations and bios, especially subunits like "Department of", "School of", "Laboratory", "Institute" or "Center" (including non-English forms), plus the field names and "University" that follow. Activation is highest on the unit word itself, such as "Department" or "School", and on the following "of", particularly in paper headers listing affiliations.

Diffuse, low-level activation across formal scientific and technical prose such as abstracts, papers, reports and specifications. It fires most on structural and functional tokens: sentence-ending periods, paragraph breaks, citations and reference numbers, and section headers like Introduction. It also picks up methodological phrasing in the body text, such as "we developed an analysis method", "newly developed", "these tools are developed within" and "basic design".

Institutional affiliation markers following a person's name: the tokens linking an author or researcher to their organization ("of", "at the", "from the", commas, newlines, footnote numbers, "Professor of", "Department of", "University of"), as seen in paper author lists, bylines, and descriptions of where someone works.

Tokens inside personal names, chiefly in author lists and bylines of academic papers and reports, along with the separators between names: commas, initials, affiliation markers, superscripts and parenthetical native-script names. It fires most strongly in dense, multi-author lists. It also fires weakly on names and roles of researchers quoted in science news (e.g. 'postdoctoral research fellow') and on email domains near author blocks.

Weak activation on attribution and credit text naming people or organizations: author bylines, affiliations, contact details, signature lines, credits like "produced by" or "photo credit", and spokesperson or title attributions. It fires mostly on parts of personal names (often the final subword), titles, affiliation markers (commas, numbers, asterisks) and the line breaks between them.

Journalistic news-story prose, strongest on attribution and narrative-reporting phrases (e.g., ',” said X while attending…', 'he concluded, as reported by', 'shared:', 'Reportedly,') and clauses describing what a public figure did or is doing in celebrity, sports and news reports. Activation is weak and diffuse on other tokens.

The first word(s) of a new sentence or paragraph, typically a preposition, conjunction, or transition that opens an introductory/adverbial phrase (In, On, At the, Before, Since, However, Other, In addition). It fires most strongly on "In" and "On" right after a paragraph break.

Diffuse, weak activation on journalistic/news-style narration, especially the words that report factual events and their context: past-tense reporting verbs (announced, released, disclosed, convicted, died, says), time expressions (in March, earlier this year, recently, yesterday) and the sentence boundaries or commas joining such factual statements. It tracks the flow of encyclopedic or news exposition rather than any single word.

Content words and connecting function words (prepositions, articles, of/in/on) inside dense technical or scientific prose, especially abstract-style descriptions of mechanisms, measurements, and processes (e.g., adsorption kinetics, electrical conduction, gene regulation). Activation is diffuse and spreads over noun phrases and the prepositional links between them, not over one particular word.

Appositive or descriptive phrases that come right after a person's name and give their title, role, affiliation or other identifying detail (e.g. ", an analyst at", ", CEO of", "who is the adviser to", ", 66, of"). The comma right after the name and the role words are the strongest parts, typically in news-style quote attributions.

A diffuse, low-level feature for low-quality web text: SEO spam, casino and pharmacy spam, spun or machine-generated prose, and repository/metadata boilerplate. It fires most strongly inside incoherent, word-salad or mixed-language spam passages, such as pharma spam with stray Portuguese words or nonsensical essay-mill text. It fires weakly on scattered tokens in ordinary boilerplate like page view counts and archive notices.

Content tokens in technical, scientific or research writing (methods, materials, research aims, specs, job/tech requirements). It fires on domain terms such as instruments, compounds, organisms, software and techniques, and on whole phrases describing research goals or findings. Activation is broad and moderate rather than tied to one word.

Language reporting quantitative changes and statistics, especially in financial or news reports: words and phrases describing increases, decreases, or levels ("dropped by 3.4 per cent on last year", "increased to", "stood at", "down almost 5%"), together with the attached numbers, percentages, currency amounts and reporting-period dates. Weaker activation appears on scattered numeric or technical tokens such as years and spec figures.

Lists of person names, mostly author or inventor bylines in academic papers, patents and citations. The strongest activations fall on the separators and boundaries between names: commas, the final "and", affiliation superscripts or footnote marks, bullets and line breaks. Activations are also moderate on surname endings and on the initials or first names that begin the next entry.

Sentence boundaries in scientific or technical abstract-style prose. Activation peaks on the period closing a sentence, especially the opening background or aim sentence. It continues onto the first words of the next sentence when that sentence moves into methods, data, or findings ("The study involved", "Data were from", "Methods: This was a", "We compared"). Weaker activation falls on method and reporting phrases and on parenthetical acronyms.

Speech and attribution verbs (mostly "said", also says/told/wrote/added/reports), plus the pronoun or speaker right before them, that credit a quote or reported statement to its source. Activation is strongest for "said" right after a closing quotation and a speaker's name or pronoun in news-style quotes, and weaker in narrative fiction or for other reporting verbs.

Separators (commas, newlines, spaces, " in", " (") that come right after the name of an institution, department, organization or address component, marking the boundary to the next part of an affiliation or address line (e.g. "Department of X, University of Y, City, Country"). Activation is strongest after university and department names in academic author affiliations.

Boundaries in author-affiliation and address blocks, mainly in academic paper headers. It fires most strongly on line breaks or punctuation right after a country or postal code, and on the affiliation markers (numbers, †, ‡, superscripts) that start the next entry. It also fires on the start of the next header element, such as Department, Email:, Received, Abstract or footnotes, and on email domain endings like .edu or .id.

Citation and reference numbers in academic or technical text, mainly numeric reference markers in brackets, parentheses, or superscripts (e.g. [1], (3–5), ^1,2) that follow a claim. Weaker activations appear on other citation-like digits: the last digit of years in author–year citations, author affiliation numbers, figure/section numbers, and LaTeX \cite.

Speaker attribution in news-style prose: the closing quote punctuation, speech verbs (said/says/explained), and especially the speaker's name plus the appositive title or role that follows it (e.g., ", director of…", ", lead author, who…"). The strongest activations come right after a quotation ends.

Sentence and section boundaries: end-of-sentence punctuation (periods, question marks), colons after labels, and newlines or paragraph breaks just before new content starts, plus a few sentence-opening discourse words (Nevertheless, Indeed). Activation is strongest at periods ending sentences in spammy, incoherent or keyword-stuffed text, where the next sentence switches abruptly to an unrelated topic.

Narrative news-report prose describing events, scenes and reactions in the past tense (who did what, where, and how people responded). The strongest activations fall on main-clause verbs, auxiliaries ("were", "was", "had"), collective subjects such as people, groups or communities, and scene-setting phrases about circumstances or aftermath. Sentence boundaries followed by paragraph breaks also activate.

Names of people or organizations serving as the source or speaker of a quotation, statement, or claim, especially surnames in speech attributions (e.g. "X said", "says X", "X added"). The name and the following reporting verb are both marked, with the strongest activation on the final part of the name.

A diffuse, low-level feature that fires across ordinary expository or narrative prose. It peaks mainly at clause boundaries such as commas and periods and on the connective words that continue a sentence ('and then', 'which means', 'when they', 'even if'), with weaker activation on content nouns inside these running clauses. It seems to track mid-sentence continuation and discourse flow rather than any particular topic.

Generic, formulaic phrasing in promotional, SEO-style or marketing web copy. It fires mostly at sentence boundaries (periods, commas) and on stock sentence openers and connectors such as "These", "This", "With", "We are", "You can", "It helps to" and "make sure that". Activation is strongest on boilerplate self-promotional claims like "We are a technical team having immense years of experience".

Diffuse, weak activation on scientific/academic abstract prose, strongest at sentence boundaries (periods and the following sentence starters like "The", "We show that", "Our data show") and on the causal or relational verb phrases stating findings ("is associated with", "increases", "produces", "leads to", "correlated with", "caused").

Tokens at structural breaks in web text, usually right after a paragraph break, where the main prose stops and boilerplate or navigation takes over. Typical cases are section headers, labels with colons, calls to action and link text. Examples include "Click here to…", "Related Stories", "READ:", "Note:", "Contact Us", "Spoiler alert" and "Continued on page". Activation is strongest on promotional or cross-reference phrases that redirect the reader.

Business and financial news context, especially funding, investment, contracts, deals and monetary amounts. Activation is weak and diffuse across function words, numbers and punctuation in such passages. It peaks on the key phrases describing money changing hands, such as "awarded a contract", "raised £270k in funding" and "amount invested was not disclosed".

Final tokens of proper names and named entities, especially institutions, organizations, publications and place names (e.g. 'Institute in Boulder, Colo', 'University College London', 'Vanity Fair', 'Protection Agency'). Activation is strongest on the closing word of multi-word names and on location tags after affiliations, and also fires on name-completing subword pieces and unit or technical terms.

Fires on verbs, prepositions and connectives in expository, technical or academic prose. It is strongest where the English is awkward or non-native: agreement and tense errors ('it has also ensure', 'has lead to', 'the excitation system perform', 'the appearance help for'), odd verb or preposition choices ('quantify significant', 'require to count', 'consists in'), and run-on clause linking ('which involves', 'can precisely capture').

Institutional affiliation text, typically in author bylines of academic papers. It fires on words like University, Department of, Institute, School and College, on the commas and parentheses that separate parts of the affiliation, and on the address details that follow (city, state, postal code, P.O. Box). This holds across English, Spanish, Portuguese and French forms (Universidad/Université, Instituto, Laboratoire).

Website and document boilerplate around the main content, such as navigation links ("Skip to main content", "Jump to: navigation"), repository and download notices, citation prompts ("To cite this version:", "Cite this article as"), copyright, license and publisher terms, metadata fields and dates, and share or sign-up text. Activation is strongest on repository and citation phrases.

Dot leaders (runs of periods/ellipses, sometimes spaces or table cell tags) that fill the gap between an entry title and its page number in tables of contents, indexes and similar listings. Activation is strongest on the final dot tokens just before the page number.

Speech and attribution markers in reported speech or news style: verbs of saying (said, added, reported, wrote, explained), the speaker or source named near a quote (he, she, Moscow, the report), and source nouns such as statement, release, interview, survey or papers. They mostly appear just after a quotation or claim, or in 'according to' constructions. The strongest activations are on 'said' and on source nouns like 'report', 'statement' and 'release'.

Words in biographical or descriptive phrases that state a person's (or thing's) role, affiliation, background or credentials, especially the prepositions and verbs linking someone to a position, organization or place (e.g. 'served on', 'used to work for', 'worked in', 'senior', 'formerly', 'one of').

Fires on function words that link phrases mid-sentence, mostly prepositions ('of', 'in', 'to', 'on') directly after a noun or verb, plus commas, 'and'/'or' and articles. It is strongest in stilted, formal or translated-sounding prose, often by Spanish or Portuguese writers, where runs of connective phrasing light up together.

A weak, diffuse feature of news-article structure. It fires mostly at boundaries between a headline or lede and the body: the period or line break ending an opening sentence (".⏎⏎"), the first word of the next paragraph, and dateline, byline or source punctuation such as "(", ":" and "|". Activation is strongest within lede sentences that report an event with place and time details ("at an event at… Tuesday night.").

Surnames of people, especially authors in academic citations and bylines (e.g., "X et al.", "(Name, year)", author lists). The feature fires on the surname itself or its final subword piece, often extending to the comma or initial that follows it.

Structural boundary tokens in news/web articles: double newlines, periods, colons, and stray spaces that separate headlines, datelines, bylines, and paragraphs. It is strongest on broadcast-media context such as "Radio", "GMT", station call letters, "By" bylines, and "produced/broadcast" credits.

Sentence-ending punctuation, mostly a period fused with paragraph-break newlines (".⏎⏎"), marking the end of a paragraph or sentence before new content begins. It is strongest at paragraph breaks in news/expository prose and weaker on plain mid-paragraph periods or bracketed citation endings.

Street-level postal address components, mostly in academic affiliation or contact blocks. The strongest signal is on "PO Box"/"P.O. Box" and its number; street numbers, street-type words (Boulevard, place de, Drive, Bank) and nearby postcode digits, commas and hyphens also fire. Weak activations appear on fragments of place names and other non-address text.

Expository news-style prose. Activation peaks on the core clause of a sentence that introduces who did what, most often at the start of a new sentence or paragraph. Typical spans are the subject (a named person, organization or "The former couple"), the main verb, and the source-attribution phrasing that follows. Examples include "The attorney for … says in court papers", "According to a report produced by", "announced the split with" and "trimmed its … ownership in". Function words linking these elements (to, the, in, of, commas) are also marked, while scattered weak activations appear elsewhere.

Location and institutional affiliation context: tokens in phrases giving where someone or something is based, such as prepositions (in, at, of, from) and names of places, universities, institutes, departments, or organizations, especially right after a person's name or role (e.g., 'professor at UC Davis', 'in Toms River', 'in the city').

Weak, diffuse activation on boilerplate web text such as site descriptions, cookie and browser notices, newsletter or subscription prompts, repository and access notices, and product blurbs. It fires on function words and generic service phrases like "to ensure you have", "for the latest updates", "with your name and password", "uses ... that" and "for further information".

Organization or institution names, often abbreviated, used as domain names in email addresses and URLs. The strongest cases are the part right after "@" in academic or research emails (kit, unipr, u-psud, tudelft, mit, inpe), with weaker activation on website domain parts and institution acronyms in credits.

Tokens that complete or continue the names of institutions and organizations, mostly research bodies, universities, academies, labs and government agencies (e.g. 'Academy of Sciences', 'CNRS', 'NASA', 'Fraunhofer Institute'). They typically appear in author affiliations, addresses and URLs. Activation is strongest on the later parts of these multi-token names and their acronyms.

Final or later tokens of organization and publication names, especially news outlets, magazines, websites, universities and institutes (e.g. Post, Tribune, Slate, News, Journal, Institute, Stanford). They often come right after 'writer for', 'told', 'at' or 'of', in bylines, attributions and affiliations. Activation is strongest on news-outlet names.

City names and other place names, especially the final token of a city, that appear in addresses and affiliation lines (institution, city, region, country), as in academic author affiliations, publisher locations or business addresses. Neighboring parts of a location string, such as university names, states or countries, activate more weakly.

Geology, earth-science and paleontology writing. The feature is strongest on phrases that place a rock unit, fossil bed or formation in space and time. Typical triggers are words like "beds", "dike swarms", "Basin" and "Island", and the prepositions and relative clauses around them ("from the late Rupelian of the Mainz Basin", "dating from the Cretaceous, which runs", "in these beds"). Elsewhere it fires weakly on scattered tokens across scientific and technical text.

Source attribution in news-style text: marks the cited person or organization behind a claim, firing most strongly on phrases like "according to [the police / the Ministry of Defence / a spokesman]" and "\", she said". It also activates more weakly on related cues such as agency and institution names (UN agency, ICE, National Ocean Service), job titles (secretary-general, spokesman), reporting verbs (say, said), and citation brackets or parentheses.
